Part 7: Production Usage

Collections in Production Systems

Choosing the Right Collection — Production Decision Tree

Need key-value lookup?
  YES → Need sorted keys?
          YES → TreeMap (or DB index)
          NO  → Need thread safety?
                  YES → ConcurrentHashMap
                  NO  → HashMap
  NO ↓

Need uniqueness?
  YES → Need sorted?
          YES → TreeSet
          NO  → Need insertion order?
                  YES → LinkedHashSet
                  NO  → HashSet
  NO ↓

Need indexed access?
  YES → ArrayList (almost always)
  NO ↓

Need FIFO/LIFO/priority?
  YES → ArrayDeque / PriorityQueue
  NO  → ArrayList

Never Return Mutable Internal Collections

// DANGEROUS — caller can mutate internal state
public List<Payment> getPayments() {
    return payments;  // internal list exposed
}

// SAFE
public List<Payment> getPayments() {
    return Collections.unmodifiableList(payments);
    // or List.copyOf(payments) — Java 10+
}

Null Handling — Know Your Implementation

Collection Null Key Null Value Production Note
HashMap 1 allowed Multiple allowed Ambiguous in distributed systems — avoid null keys
ConcurrentHashMap Not allowed Not allowed NPE on put
TreeMap Not allowed Allowed compareTo NPE if null key
ArrayList Allowed — OK but validate at boundary
HashSet 1 null element — Confusing in equals logic

Logging Collections

// BAD — logs entire 500K batch
log.info("Processing batch: {}", payments);

// GOOD — log size and sample
log.info("Processing batch: size={}, first={}", payments.size(),
    payments.isEmpty() ? "empty" : payments.get(0).id());

Production Checklist

Check Why
Presize ArrayList/HashMap when size known Avoid resize copies in batch jobs
equals/hashCode on all hash-based keys Silent lookup failures
No LinkedList for general use JDK recommends ArrayDeque
ConcurrentHashMap not Collections.synchronizedMap Better read concurrency
Return immutable copies from services Encapsulation breach
Avoid Vector/Hashtable Legacy, synchronized overhead
Profile before switching collection types Measure, don't guess

Part 8: Microservice Usage

Collections at Service Boundaries

Inside the Pod vs Across Services

INSIDE JVM (Collections OK)              ACROSS PODS (External store)
────────────────────────────             ─────────────────────────────

HashMap<AccountId, Account> cache        → Redis Hash / Caffeine + Redis
Set<PaymentId> dedup window              → Redis Set with TTL
List<Event> outbox buffer                → Kafka topic
TreeMap<Instant, Job> scheduler          → DB index or dedicated scheduler svc

Idempotency Store Pattern

Payment Service (Pod-1)                Payment Service (Pod-2)
        │                                      │
        ▼                                      ▼
   In-memory Set?  ✗ WRONG              Redis SET payment:processed:{id}
   (not shared)                         TTL = 24 hours
                                        Both pods see same state

@Service
public class IdempotentPaymentHandler {

    private final PaymentRepository paymentRepository;
    private final RedisTemplate<String, String> redis;

    public PaymentResult handle(PaymentRequest request) {
        String dedupKey = "payment:processed:" + request.paymentId();

        Boolean isNew = redis.opsForValue()
            .setIfAbsent(dedupKey, "1", Duration.ofHours(24));

        if (Boolean.FALSE.equals(isNew)) {
            return PaymentResult.duplicate(request.paymentId());
        }

        return processPayment(request);
    }
}

Kafka Consumer — Local Collection Batching

@KafkaListener(topics = "shipment-events")
public void consume(List<ShipmentEvent> events) {
    // Batch received — use ArrayList presized
    Map<String, List<ShipmentEvent>> byHub = new HashMap<>();

    for (ShipmentEvent event : events) {
        byHub.computeIfAbsent(event.hubCode(), k -> new ArrayList<>())
             .add(event);
    }

    byHub.forEach(this::processHubBatch);
}

DTO Collections in REST APIs

// API response — immutable lists
public record ShipmentManifest(
    String manifestId,
    List<ShipmentItemDto> items,    // Jackson deserializes to ArrayList
    Map<String, Integer> hubCounts
) {}

// Validate at boundary
public ShipmentManifest validate(ShipmentManifest manifest) {
    if (manifest.items() == null || manifest.items().isEmpty()) {
        throw new ValidationException("Manifest must have items");
    }
    return manifest;
}

Anti-Pattern: Shared Mutable Collection in Singleton Bean

@Service  // SINGLETON — one instance per JVM
public class PaymentCache {
    private final Map<String, Payment> cache = new HashMap<>();  // NOT thread-safe!

    // Multiple HTTP threads mutate cache concurrently → data corruption
}

Fix: ConcurrentHashMap or external cache (Redis) or @Scope("prototype") (rare).

3 pods × 280 MB = 840 MB just for cache

Part 12: Interview Questions

Junior Level

  1. What is the difference between List and Set?
  2. How does HashMap store key-value pairs?
  3. What is the difference between ArrayList and LinkedList?
  4. Can you add null to an ArrayList? To a ConcurrentHashMap?
  5. What is an Iterator? What is enhanced for-loop?

Senior Level

  1. Explain HashMap internal working in JDK 8+. What is treeify?
  2. What is load factor? What happens when HashMap resizes?
  3. Why must equals() and hashCode() be consistent for HashMap keys?
  4. What is ConcurrentModificationException? How do you avoid it?
  5. Difference between Comparable and Comparator?
  6. When would you use LinkedHashMap over HashMap?
  7. Why is String a good HashMap key?
  8. What is the time complexity of HashMap.get()? Worst case?
  9. Difference between HashSet and TreeSet?

Staff / Architect Level

  1. ConcurrentHashMap vs Collections.synchronizedMap — internals and when to choose?
  2. How would you implement an LRU cache? Compare LinkedHashMap vs Caffeine vs Redis.
  3. Design idempotency for a payment service — what data structure at what layer?
  4. HashMap is not thread-safe. What happens with two threads doing put concurrently?
  5. How does CopyOnWriteArrayList work? When is it appropriate?
  6. You have 50M records to deduplicate in a nightly batch — HashSet on heap or Bloom filter? Trade-offs?
  7. Why does iterating HashMap iterate over capacity, not size?
  8. How would you choose between in-memory TreeMap and a database index for schedule queries?

Model Answer — Q6 (HashMap Internals)

A: HashMap uses an array of buckets. put(key,value) computes hash(key), maps to bucket index via (n-1) & hash, and inserts a Node. On collision, nodes form a linked list. When a bucket's list exceeds 8 nodes and table capacity ≥ 64, the list treeifies to a Red-Black Tree for O(log n) lookups in that bucket. Load factor 0.75 triggers resize — capacity doubles, all entries rehashed. get follows the same hash → bucket → list/tree traversal. Performance degrades to O(n) if all keys collide (poor hashCode) or O(log n) per bucket when treeified.

Model Answer — Q20 (50M Deduplication)

A: HashSet of 50M IDs: if each ID is ~40 bytes + overhead ~40 bytes = ~80 bytes × 50M ≈ 4 GB heap minimum — feasible on a batch worker but expensive. Bloom filter (~10 bits per element = ~60 MB) gives probabilistic "definitely not seen" with false positives requiring confirmation — good first pass. Architect choice: partition file across workers each with local HashSet, or use database DISTINCT with index, or Redis SET with TTL for streaming dedup. Decision depends on batch vs streaming, memory budget, and false-positive tolerance.

Part 13: Common Mistakes

# Mistake Consequence Fix
1 Mutable object as HashMap key Key hash changes after insert — lost entry Immutable keys (AccountId record)
2 equals without hashCode Set/Map silent failures Override both
3 Modify list during enhanced for-loop ConcurrentModificationException Iterator.remove() or removeIf
4 LinkedList for random access O(n) performance cliff ArrayList
5 Unbounded static HashMap cache OOM Size limit + eviction (Caffeine)
6 Vector/Hashtable in new code Unnecessary lock contention Modern alternatives
7 Not presizing large collections Multiple resize copies, GC pressure Constructor with capacity
8 ConcurrentHashMap with null values NPE Validate before put
9 Returning internal mutable list Encapsulation breach List.copyOf()
10 Using TreeMap without understanding Comparable ClassCastException Provide Comparator
11 Assuming HashMap iteration order is stable Non-deterministic tests, bugs LinkedHashMap if order matters
12 subList() held after parent modification Undefined behavior Copy if needed long-term

Mutable Key Trap

Map<StringBuilder, String> map = new HashMap<>();
StringBuilder key = new StringBuilder("ACC-001");
map.put(key, "Account-1");

key.append("-UPDATED");  // mutated after insert!
map.get(new StringBuilder("ACC-001"));  // null — key hash changed

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Program to interface — List<T>, Map<K,V>, not ArrayList, HashMap in signatures
  2. Immutable keys — String, records, value objects for HashMap/HashSet keys
  3. Presize when size known — batch jobs, ETL, large imports
  4. Use Map.of(), List.of() for small immutable constants
  5. Use computeIfAbsent instead of get-then-put pattern
  6. Prefer ArrayDeque over LinkedList for queue/deque operations
  7. Use ConcurrentHashMap for shared mutable maps in services
  8. Externalize cross-pod state — Redis, not static HashMap
  9. Validate nulls at API boundary — don't propagate into ConcurrentHashMap
  10. Choose complexity consciously — document why TreeMap over HashMap in code comments only when non-obvious
// Idiomatic grouping
Map<String, List<Payment>> byCurrency = payments.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Payment::currency));

// Idiomatic map compute
accounts.computeIfAbsent(id, k -> loadAccount(k));

Part 16: Revision Notes

Quick Revision — Collections

HIERARCHY:
  Collection → List, Set, Queue
  Map (separate)

LIST:     ArrayList (default) — O(1) get, O(1)* add end
          LinkedList — O(n) get — AVOID for general use

SET:      HashSet — unique, O(1)*
          TreeSet — unique sorted, O(log n)

MAP:      HashMap — O(1)* default
          LinkedHashMap — insertion/access order, LRU
          TreeMap — sorted, O(log n)
          ConcurrentHashMap — thread-safe

HASHMAP INTERNALS:
  bucket = (n-1) & hash(key)
  collision → linked list → treeify at 8 nodes (cap ≥ 64)
  load factor 0.75 → resize double

CONTRACT: equals true → hashCode MUST match

ITERATOR: fail-fast — use removeIf or Iterator.remove()

COMPARABLE: natural order inside class
COMPARATOR: external, multiple orders

MICROSERVICES:
  In-JVM collections ≠ shared state
  Cross-pod: Redis / DB / Kafka
  Singleton bean + HashMap = thread disaster

Memory Mnemonic

"Array for access, Hash for lookup, Tree for order, Concurrent for sharing"

Part 1: Concept

What Is Functional Programming in Java?

Functional programming (FP) in Java means treating behavior as data — passing blocks of logic as arguments to methods, composing operations on collections without explicit loops, and favoring immutability and declarative style.

Java 8 (2014) introduced:
- Lambda expressions
- Functional interfaces
- Stream API
- Optional
- Default methods on interfaces (Lesson 2)

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              IMPERATIVE (pre-Java 8)     vs    DECLARATIVE (Java 8+)     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  List<Payment> valid = new ArrayList<>();     payments.stream()         │
│  for (Payment p : payments) {                 .filter(Payment::isValid) │
│      if (p.isValid()) {                       .collect(toList());        │
│          valid.add(p);                                                  │
│      }                                                                  │
│  }                                                                      │
│                                                                          │
│  WHAT to do (steps)                           WHAT you want (intent)   │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Core Building Blocks

Building Block What Syntax Example
Lambda Anonymous function (p) -> p.isValid()
Functional Interface Interface with one abstract method Predicate<Payment>
Method Reference Shorthand for lambda Payment::isValid
Stream Pipeline over data source payments.stream()
Optional Explicit absence of value Optional<Account>

Functional Interface Hierarchy (Key Types)

                        @FunctionalInterface
                               │
        ┌──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┐
        │                      │                      │
   Predicate<T>            Function<T,R>           Consumer<T>
   T → boolean             T → R                   T → void
        │                      │                      │
   BiPredicate<T,U>       BiFunction<T,U,R>       BiConsumer<T,U>
                               │
                          Supplier<T>
                          () → T

Master Table — Core Functional Interfaces

Interface Method Signature Purpose Banking Example Thread Safety
Predicate<T> test(T) T → boolean Filter p -> p.amount() > 10000 Stateless = safe
Function<T,R> apply(T) T → R Transform p -> p.accountId() Stateless = safe
Consumer<T> accept(T) T → void Side effect p -> audit.log(p) Depends on body
Supplier<T> get() () → T Lazy produce () -> loadRates() Depends on body
UnaryOperator<T> apply(T) T → T Identity transform amount -> amount.abs() Stateless = safe
BinaryOperator<T> apply(T,T) (T,T) → T Combine two BigDecimal::add Stateless = safe

Lambda Expression Anatomy

// Full form
(Payment payment) -> { return payment.isValid(); }

// Type inferred
payment -> payment.isValid()

// Method reference (preferred when possible)
Payment::isValid

// Multi-line lambda
payment -> {
    auditContext.record(payment);
    return payment.isValid();
}

LAMBDA SYNTAX GRAMMAR
─────────────────────

(parameters) -> expression
(parameters) -> { statements; return value; }

Parameter types:
  (Payment p)           explicit
  p                     inferred
  (p1, p2)              multiple
  ()                    zero (Supplier)

SOURCE → INTERMEDIATE* → TERMINAL

payments.stream()     .filter()  .map()  .sorted()     .collect()
     │                    │        │        │              │
   SOURCE            INTERMEDIATE (lazy)              TERMINAL (eager)

┌──────────┐    ┌─────────┐    ┌─────────┐    ┌─────────┐    ┌──────────┐
│  Source  │───►│ filter  │───►│   map   │───►│ sorted  │───►│ collect  │
│ Collection│    │ valid   │    │ to DTO  │    │ by date │    │ to List  │
│  array   │    │ only    │    │         │    │         │    │          │
│  Stream  │    └─────────┘    └─────────┘    └─────────┘    └──────────┘
│  .of()   │         lazy — nothing runs until terminal op executes
└──────────┘

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why Java Added Functional Programming in Java 8

Pressure (2010–2014) Problem with Old Java Java 8 Answer
Multicore CPUs Manual threading for parallelism parallelStream()
Competition Scala, Groovy, Kotlin more expressive Lambdas + Streams
Boilerplate Anonymous inner classes for every callback (x) -> x + 1
Collection processing Verbose loops, error-prone Declarative pipelines
Null safety Billion-dollar mistake (Tony Hoare) Optional (partial)

Why Architects Care

Functional style is not syntax sugar. It changes how systems are designed:

IMPERATIVE SERVICE                    FUNCTIONAL PIPELINE
────────────────────                  ─────────────────────

void process(List<Payment> ps) {      PaymentResult result = payments.stream()
  List<Payment> valid = ...;              .filter(validator::isValid)
  for (...) { ... }                       .map(processor::process)
  Map<String, ...> grouped = ...          .collect(groupingBy(
  for (...) { ... }                           Payment::currency,
}                                               toList()));
                                      // Each stage = testable function
                                      // Composition = pipeline architecture

In microservices, streams model event pipelines (Kafka → filter → map → sink) — the same mental model as Stream API.

Why Not Full Functional Language?

Java remains primarily OOP:
- Lambdas are objects (functional interface instances)
- Variables captured must be effectively final
- No tail-call optimization
- Primitive specialization limited (no Stream<int> — use IntStream)

Architect takeaway: Use FP where it clarifies intent; don't force pure FP where OOP domain models are clearer.

Part 3: Internal Working

How Lambdas Work Internally

Lambda ≠ Anonymous Inner Class (Usually)

// Java 7 — generates PaymentValidator$1.class (synthetic class)
payments.removeIf(new Predicate<Payment>() {
    @Override
    public boolean test(Payment p) {
        return p.isValid();
    }
});

// Java 8 — uses invokedynamic (LambdaMetafactory)
payments.removeIf(p -> p.isValid());

Lambda Compilation — invokedynamic

COMPILE TIME:
  p -> p.isValid()
       │
       ▼
  invokedynamic bootstrap: LambdaMetafactory.metafactory
       │
       ▼
  Synthetic method: lambda$process$0(Payment)  (in enclosing class)

RUNTIME (first call):
  LambdaMetafactory creates Predicate instance
  (may cache for same lambda site)

RUNTIME (subsequent calls):
  Reuses cached lambda instance

Bytecode (simplified):

  aload_1
  invokedynamic #0:test:(LPayment;)Z  Bootstrap: LambdaMetafactory
  invokeinterface Predicate.test

Capturing vs Non-Capturing Lambdas

// NON-CAPTURING — no external variables
payments.stream().filter(Payment::isValid)
// Lambda instance may be reused across invocations — efficient

// CAPTURING — references external variable
BigDecimal threshold = loadThreshold();
payments.stream().filter(p -> p.amount().compareTo(threshold) > 0)
// Must capture threshold — new lambda state per enclosing scope

NON-CAPTURING                    CAPTURING
─────────────                    ─────────

Lambda object                    Lambda object
  └── ref to metafactory method    └── ref to method
                                    └── captured: threshold (on heap)

Effectively final rule:

BigDecimal threshold = loadThreshold();
threshold = BigDecimal.ZERO;  // reassignment
payments.stream().filter(p -> p.amount().compareTo(threshold) > 0);
// COMPILE ERROR — threshold must be effectively final

Stream Internal Architecture

AbstractPipeline
    │
    ├── source stage (collection spliterator)
    ├── intermediate op (filter, map — wrap previous stage)
    └── terminal op (collect, reduce — triggers evaluation)

Evaluation:
  terminalOp.evaluate(pipeline)
    → fold operations into single pass where possible (fusion)
    → or build linked pipeline of stages

Spliterator — How Stream Traverses Source

ArrayList<Payment> payments = ...;
payments.stream()
// Uses ArrayList.spliterator():
//   - traverses backing array
//   - supports SIZED, SUBSIZED (for parallel split)
//   - tryAdvance / forEachRemaining

Spliterator<Payment> over ArrayList:

elementData: [P0][P1][P2][P3][P4]
              ▲
              index=0

tryAdvance: consume P0, index=1
tryAdvance: consume P1, index=2
...

parallelStream():
  split spliterator → [P0,P1] | [P2,P3,P4]
  process in ForkJoinPool.commonPool()

Lazy Evaluation — When Code Actually Runs

Stream<Payment> stream = payments.stream()
    .filter(p -> {
        log.info("filter: {}", p.id());  // NOT logged yet
        return p.isValid();
    });

// Nothing executed until terminal:
List<Payment> result = stream.collect(toList());  // NOW filter runs

Timeline:
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────►

stream()     filter()     map()        collect()
  │            │            │              │
  ▼            ▼            ▼              ▼
build        build        build         EXECUTE entire pipeline
pipeline     pipeline     pipeline      (pull model — terminal asks for elements)

Short-Circuiting Operations

boolean hasHighValue = payments.stream()
    .filter(p -> p.amount().compareTo(LIMIT) > 0)
    .findFirst()          // short-circuit — stops after first match
    .isPresent();

payments.stream()
    .anyMatch(Payment::isFraudulent);  // may not process entire stream
Short-Circuit Terminal Behavior
findFirst() / findAny() Stop after first match
anyMatch() Stop on first true
allMatch() Stop on first false
noneMatch() Stop on first true
limit(n) Stop after n elements (intermediate)

Optional Internals

public final class Optional<T> {
    private final T value;  // null = empty, non-null = present

    public static <T> Optional<T> of(T value) {
        return new Optional<>(Objects.requireNonNull(value));
    }
    public static <T> Optional<T> ofNullable(T value) {
        return value == null ? empty() : of(value);
    }
}

Optional is a container, not a field type — never class Account { Optional<String> name; }.

                                    └─────────────────────────┘

  (no lambda on stack)              │ Lambda$1 (Predicate)    │
                                    │  captured vars (if any)│
                                    └─────────────────────────┘
                                    ┌─────────────────────────┐
                                    │ Pipeline objects         │
                                    │ (stages, spliterator)    │
                                    └─────────────────────────┘
Pattern Allocations per Call GC Impact
Method reference Payment::isValid Often 0–1 lambda object Low
Capturing lambda 1+ objects + captured refs Moderate
stream().filter().map().collect() Pipeline stage objects Short-lived (Young Gen)
parallelStream() Split arrays + ForkJoin tasks Higher — task objects
Collectors.toList() New ArrayList + elements Expected output cost

Stream vs Loop Memory

FOR-LOOP:
  One iterator (or index variable) on stack
  No intermediate pipeline objects
  Often LOWER allocation

STREAM:
  Pipeline stage objects (FilterOp, MapOp, ...)
  Spliterator
  Often HIGHER allocation but SHORT-LIVED

Architect rule: Readability first. Optimize only when profiling shows
stream allocation in hot path (Lesson 6).

Primitive Streams — Avoid Boxing

// BOXED — allocates Integer per element
Stream<Integer> amounts = payments.stream().map(p -> p.amountInPaise());

// PRIMITIVE — no boxing
IntStream amounts = payments.stream()
    .mapToInt(Payment::amountInPaise);

int total = amounts.sum();  // specialized accumulator

Primitive Stream Types:
  IntStream    — int
  LongStream   — long
  DoubleStream — double

Use mapToInt, mapToLong, flatMapToInt to avoid Integer/Long boxing

Collector Memory

// groupingBy creates HashMap + ArrayLists
Map<String, List<Payment>> grouped = payments.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Payment::currency));

// Memory: HashMap buckets + one ArrayList per currency key
// For 5M payments, 10 currencies → 10 lists holding references

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Performance Characteristics

Stream vs Traditional Loop

Scenario Loop Stream Parallel Stream
Simple filter + collect Faster (less alloc) Slightly slower Slower (overhead)
Complex pipeline (5+ stages) Comparable Comparable Depends on data size
CPU-bound on 1M+ elements Good Good Can win on multi-core
I/O in stream (DB call) Bad Bad Disaster
Small collections (<100) Faster Overhead dominates Never parallel

Parallel Stream — ForkJoinPool.commonPool()

payments.parallelStream()
    .filter(validator::isValid)
    .collect(toList());

// Uses: ForkJoinPool.commonPool()
// Threads: Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() - 1

COMMON POOL (shared JVM-wide)
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Thread-1 │ Thread-2 │ Thread-3 │ Thread-4 │ ...           │
│                                                             │
│  Service A parallelStream()  ←── COMPETES ──►               │
│  Service B parallelStream()  ←── for same pool              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

RISK: Payment service parallel stream starves other parallel work

When parallel helps:
- Large in-memory dataset (100K+)
- CPU-bound pure computation per element
- No shared mutable state
- No I/O inside pipeline

When parallel hurts:
- Small lists
- I/O-bound operations
- Order-dependent side effects
- Already on ForkJoinPool worker thread (nested parallel)

Complexity — Stream Operations

Operation Complexity Notes
filter O(n) Single pass
map O(n) Single pass
sorted O(n log n) Materializes all elements
distinct O(n) HashSet internally
collect(toList()) O(n)
collect(groupingBy()) O(n) HashMap build
reduce O(n)
flatMap O(n × m) m = inner stream size

Scalability Impact

Pattern Single Pod 50 Pods
parallelStream() in request handler Contends for common pool 50× contention risk
Stateless lambda pipeline Scales horizontally Safe
Capturing mutable external state Race conditions Production incident
Stream over DB cursor Memory if collected Use reactive/streaming (Lesson 20)

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Banking — Payment Validation Pipeline

package com.bank.payments.pipeline;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public class PaymentBatchProcessor {

    private final PaymentValidator validator;

    public PaymentBatchProcessor(PaymentValidator validator) {
        this.validator = validator;
    }

    public Map<String, List<Payment>> processByCurrency(List<Payment> batch) {
        return batch.stream()
            .filter(validator::isValid)
            .filter(p -> p.amount().compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) > 0)
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                Payment::currency,
                Collectors.toList()
            ));
    }

    public BigDecimal totalValidAmount(List<Payment> batch) {
        return batch.stream()
            .filter(validator::isValid)
            .map(Payment::amount)
            .reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add);
    }

    public record Payment(String id, String currency, BigDecimal amount, String status) {}
    public interface PaymentValidator {
        boolean isValid(Payment payment);
    }
}

Example 2: Logistics — Shipment Filtering with Predicate Composition

package com.logistics.shipment.filter;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.Predicate;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public class ShipmentFilters {

    public static Predicate<Shipment> isDelayed(Instant now) {
        return s -> s.expectedDelivery().isBefore(now) && !s.isDelivered();
    }

    public static Predicate<Shipment> inHub(String hubCode) {
        return s -> hubCode.equals(s.currentHub());
    }

    public List<Shipment> findDelayedInHub(List<Shipment> shipments,
                                           String hubCode,
                                           Instant now) {
        Predicate<Shipment> filter = isDelayed(now).and(inHub(hubCode));

        return shipments.stream()
            .filter(filter)
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
    }

    public record Shipment(String id, String currentHub,
                           Instant expectedDelivery, boolean delivered) {
        boolean isDelivered() { return delivered; }
    }
}

Example 3: Transportation — Optional for Safe Lookup

package com.transport.booking.service;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;

public class SeatBookingService {

    private final Map<String, Booking> bookingsByPnr;

    public SeatBookingService(Map<String, Booking> bookingsByPnr) {
        this.bookingsByPnr = bookingsByPnr;
    }

    public Optional<Booking> findByPnr(String pnr) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(bookingsByPnr.get(pnr));
    }

    public String getPassengerNameOrDefault(String pnr, String defaultName) {
        return findByPnr(pnr)
            .map(Booking::passengerName)
            .orElse(defaultName);
    }

    public void cancelIfPresent(String pnr) {
        findByPnr(pnr)
            .filter(b -> !b.isCancelled())
            .ifPresent(this::cancelBooking);
    }

    private void cancelBooking(Booking booking) {
        // cancellation logic
    }

    public record Booking(String pnr, String passengerName, boolean cancelled) {
        boolean isCancelled() { return cancelled; }
    }
}

Example 4: Method References — Four Forms

package com.bank.payments.transform;

import java.util.function.Function;

public class MethodReferenceExamples {

  // 1. Static method reference: ClassName::staticMethod
  Function<String, Integer> parser = Integer::parseInt;

  // 2. Instance method on particular object: instance::method
  PaymentAuditor auditor = new PaymentAuditor();
  // auditor::log used as Consumer<Payment>

  // 3. Instance method on first param: ClassName::instanceMethod
  Function<Payment, String> idExtractor = Payment::id;

  // 4. Constructor reference: ClassName::new
  Function<String, PaymentId> idFactory = PaymentId::new;

  public record Payment(String id, java.math.BigDecimal amount) {}
  public record PaymentId(String value) {}
  static class PaymentAuditor {
    void log(Payment p) { /* ... */ }
  }
}

Example 5: flatMap — Nested Collections (Manifest Items)

package com.logistics.manifest;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public class ManifestFlattener {

    public List<ShipmentItem> allItems(List<Manifest> manifests) {
        return manifests.stream()
            .flatMap(m -> m.items().stream())  // Stream<Stream<Item>> → Stream<Item>
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
    }

    public List<String> allTrackingNumbers(List<Manifest> manifests) {
        return manifests.stream()
            .flatMap(m -> m.items().stream())
            .map(ShipmentItem::trackingNumber)
            .distinct()
            .sorted()
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
    }

    public record Manifest(String manifestId, List<ShipmentItem> items) {}
    public record ShipmentItem(String trackingNumber, double weightKg) {}
}

Example 6: Collectors — Advanced Aggregation

package com.bank.reports;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public class PaymentAnalytics {

    public Map<String, BigDecimal> totalByCurrency(List<Payment> payments) {
        return payments.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                Payment::currency,
                Collectors.mapping(
                    Payment::amount,
                    Collectors.reducing(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add)
                )
            ));
    }

    public Map<Boolean, Long> fraudCountPartition(List<Payment> payments) {
        return payments.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(
                Payment::isFraudulent,
                Collectors.counting()
            ));
    }

    public Payment highestValue(List<Payment> payments) {
        return payments.stream()
            .max(Comparator.comparing(Payment::amount))
            .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("Empty payment list"));
    }

    public record Payment(String id, String currency, BigDecimal amount, boolean fraudulent) {}
}

Example 7: Custom Functional Interface

package com.bank.fraud;

@FunctionalInterface
public interface FraudRule {
    FraudResult evaluate(TransactionContext context);

    // Java 8+ default method — compose rules
    default FraudRule andThen(FraudRule next) {
        return context -> {
            FraudResult result = this.evaluate(context);
            return result.isBlocked() ? result : next.evaluate(context);
        };
    }
}

// Usage:
FraudRule pipeline = new VelocityRule()
    .andThen(new GeoMismatchRule())
    .andThen(new AmountThresholdRule());

Part 7: Production Usage

Functional Programming in Production

Stream Anti-Patterns in Production

// ANTI-PATTERN 1: I/O inside stream
payments.stream()
    .map(p -> accountService.loadAccount(p.accountId()))  // N DB calls
    .collect(toList());

// FIX: batch load, then stream in memory
Set<String> accountIds = payments.stream().map(Payment::accountId).collect(toSet());
Map<String, Account> accounts = accountService.loadByIds(accountIds);

// ANTI-PATTERN 2: Side effects in forEach
payments.stream()
    .filter(Payment::isValid)
    .forEach(p -> paymentRepository.save(p));  // side effect in stream

// BETTER: collect then batch save, or explicit loop for clarity
List<Payment> valid = payments.stream().filter(Payment::isValid).toList();
paymentRepository.saveAll(valid);

// ANTI-PATTERN 3: parallelStream() by default
public List<PaymentDto> toDtos(List<Payment> payments) {
    return payments.parallelStream()  // overhead for 50 elements
        .map(this::toDto)
        .collect(toList());
}

// ANTI-PATTERN 4: Optional as field or parameter
public void process(Optional<Payment> payment) { }  // DON'T
public class Payment { Optional<String> ref; }     // DON'T

Optional — Production Patterns

// GOOD — return type for "may not exist"
public Optional<Account> findById(AccountId id) {
    return Optional.ofNullable(cache.get(id));
}

// GOOD — chain without null checks
return findById(id)
    .map(Account::getBalance)
    .orElse(BigDecimal.ZERO);

// BAD — get() without check
account.get();  // NoSuchElementException — use orElse/orElseThrow

// GOOD — orElseThrow with meaningful exception
return findById(id)
    .orElseThrow(() -> new AccountNotFoundException(id));

Logging in Streams

// DEBUG peek — remove before production or guard with log level
payments.stream()
    .filter(validator::isValid)
    .peek(p -> log.debug("Valid payment: {}", p.id()))  // OK for debug
    .map(processor::process)
    .collect(toList());

Production Checklist

Check Why
No I/O in map/filter N+1 query explosion
No parallelStream() in web request path without measurement Pool contention
Optional only as return type API clarity
Avoid stream().forEach() for mutations Use collect or loop
Use primitive streams for numeric aggregation Boxing GC
orElseThrow not get() Explicit failure
Method references where readable Less bytecode, clearer intent

Part 8: Microservice Usage

FP Patterns in Microservices

REST Controller — Stream to DTO

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/payments")
public class PaymentController {

    private final PaymentService paymentService;

    @GetMapping
    public List<PaymentResponse> list(@RequestParam String currency) {
        return paymentService.findByCurrency(currency).stream()
            .map(PaymentMapper::toResponse)
            .toList();  // Java 16+ unmodifiable list
    }
}

Kafka Consumer — Functional Event Processing

@Component
public class ShipmentEventHandler {

    public void handle(List<ShipmentEvent> events) {
        Map<String, List<ShipmentEvent>> byHub = events.stream()
            .filter(ShipmentEvent::isValid)
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(ShipmentEvent::hubCode));

        byHub.forEach(this::processHubBatch);
    }

    private void processHubBatch(String hub, List<ShipmentEvent> hubEvents) {
        hubEvents.stream()
            .map(this::enrich)
            .forEach(this::publish);
    }
}

Validation Pipeline — Predicate Composition

@Service
public class PaymentRequestValidator {

    private final List<Predicate<PaymentRequest>> rules = List.of(
        req -> req.amount() != null,
        req -> req.amount().compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) > 0,
        req -> req.debtorAccount() != null && !req.debtorAccount().isBlank(),
        req -> req.creditorAccount() != null && !req.creditorAccount().isBlank()
    );

    public ValidationResult validate(PaymentRequest request) {
        List<String> failures = rules.stream()
            .filter(rule -> !rule.test(request))
            .map(rule -> ruleName(rule))  // or track names explicitly
            .collect(Collectors.toList());

        return failures.isEmpty()
            ? ValidationResult.ok()
            : ValidationResult.failed(failures);
    }
}

Functional Thinking at Architecture Level

Pipelines Everywhere

The Stream model maps to enterprise integration:

Java Stream Stage Enterprise Equivalent

Supplier for Lazy Initialization

// Expensive resource — load only when needed
public class FxRateProvider {
    private final Supplier<Map<String, BigDecimal>> ratesSupplier =
        Suppliers.memoize(this::loadRatesFromExternalApi);

    public BigDecimal rate(String currency) {
        return ratesSupplier.get().get(currency);
    }
}

Architect use: defer expensive I/O until first use; cache with memoize (Guava) or Spring @Cacheable.

Model Answer — Q9 (orElse vs orElseGet)

// orElse — ALWAYS evaluates argument
Account fallback = loadExpensiveAccountFromDb();
Account account = findInCache(id).orElse(fallback);  // DB hit even if cache hit!

// orElseGet — evaluates Supplier ONLY if empty
Account account = findInCache(id)
    .orElseGet(() -> loadExpensiveAccountFromDb());  // DB hit only on cache miss

Model Answer — Q15 (Lambda Internals)

A: Java 8+ compiles lambdas using invokedynamic and LambdaMetafactory, not by generating a new class file per lambda (unlike anonymous inner classes). At runtime, the metafactory produces an object implementing the target functional interface. Non-capturing lambdas may be allocated once and reused. Capturing lambdas hold references to enclosed variables (must be effectively final) and are allocated per capture context. This reduces metaspace pressure vs pre-Java 8 anonymous classes.

Part 13: Common Mistakes

# Mistake Consequence Fix
1 Optional.get() without isPresent() NoSuchElementException orElse / orElseThrow
2 Optional as field/parameter API clutter Use nullable or validation
3 I/O in stream().map() N+1, timeout Batch load first
4 parallelStream() everywhere Slower + pool contention Measure; default sequential
5 Reuse stream after terminal IllegalStateException Create new stream
6 forEach with side effects Hidden mutations collect or explicit loop
7 sorted() before limit() on large data Sorts entire collection limit first if order allows
8 Mutating external collection in stream Race conditions Collect to new list
9 orElse(null) Defeats Optional purpose Return empty or throw
10 Boxing in map to Integer GC pressure mapToInt
11 peek for business logic Hidden side effects Use map explicitly
12 Nested parallelStream() Deadlock risk on common pool One level only

Stream Reuse Trap

Stream<Payment> stream = payments.stream().filter(Payment::isValid);
long count = stream.count();     // terminal — stream consumed
List<Payment> list = stream.collect(toList());  // IllegalStateException!

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Prefer method references when lambda only delegates: Payment::isValid
  2. Use toList() (Java 16+) for immutable unmodifiable lists
  3. Compose predicates — isValid.and(hasFunds).and(notDuplicate)
  4. orElseGet over orElse for expensive defaults
  5. Primitive streams for numeric aggregation
  6. Keep pipelines short — extract stages to named methods if > 4 operations
  7. No I/O in streams — batch external calls
  8. Test pipelines with unit tests on each Predicate/Function separately
  9. Document parallel decisions — only with benchmark evidence
  10. Use Stream for transformation, domain logic stays in objects
// Readable — named steps
public List<PaymentDto> exportValidPayments(List<Payment> payments) {
    return payments.stream()
        .filter(this::isValidForExport)
        .map(mapper::toDto)
        .toList();
}

Part 16: Revision Notes

Quick Revision — Functional Programming

LAMBDA: (params) -> expression | { statements; return x; }
  effectively final capture only
  compiled via invokedynamic + LambdaMetafactory

FUNCTIONAL INTERFACES:
  Predicate<T>  → boolean test(T)
  Function<T,R> → R apply(T)
  Consumer<T>   → void accept(T)
  Supplier<T>   → T get()

METHOD REFS: Static::method | instance::method | Type::method | Type::new

STREAM: source → intermediate*(lazy) → terminal(eager)

KEY OPS:
  filter, map, flatMap, distinct, sorted, limit
  collect, reduce, forEach, count, anyMatch, findFirst

OPTIONAL:
  ofNullable, map, flatMap, orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow
  NEVER: field, param, collection element, Optional.get()

PARALLEL: common ForkJoinPool — CPU-bound + large data only
  NO I/O, NO nested parallel, NO default in web requests

PRIMITIVE: mapToInt, IntStream — avoid Integer boxing

Memory Mnemonic

"Lazy until terminal, capture must be final, Optional for return not storage"

│ Optional: ofNullable | map | orElseGet(Supplier) | orElseThrow  │
│ NOT for fields/params | orElseGet lazy, orElse eager            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Lambda internals: invokedynamic, NOT anonymous class per lambda │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ parallelStream → ForkJoinPool.commonPool()                      │
│ Good: CPU-bound, large in-memory | Bad: I/O, small, nested      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Anti-patterns: I/O in map, Optional.get, stream reuse,          │
│                parallel by default, peek for business logic     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Part 1: Concept

What Is an Exception?

An exception is an object representing an abnormal condition that disrupts normal program flow. In Java, all exceptions are objects that extend Throwable, thrown via the throw keyword and propagated up the call stack until caught or the JVM terminates the thread.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    JAVA EXCEPTION HIERARCHY                              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│                          Throwable                                       │
│                         /        \                                       │
│                   Error          Exception                               │
│                  (unchecked)    /         \                            │
│                                  /           \                           │
│                          RuntimeException   Checked Exception            │
│                          (unchecked)        (must handle or declare)     │
│                                                                          │
│  Examples:                    Examples:              Examples:           │
│  OutOfMemoryError             NullPointerException   IOException         │
│  StackOverflowError           IllegalArgumentException SQLException      │
│  (JVM serious — don't catch)  IllegalStateException ClassNotFoundException│
│                               PaymentDeclinedException (custom)          │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Checked vs Unchecked — The Fundamental Split

Type Extends Compile-Time Check Must Declare throws? Philosophy
Checked Exception (not RuntimeException) Yes Yes (or catch) Recoverable external failures
Unchecked RuntimeException No No Programming errors, business rule violations
Error Error No No JVM/system failure — don't catch 
COMPILE TIME DECISION TREE
──────────────────────────

throw new IOException("file missing")
  → Caller MUST catch or declare throws IOException

throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad amount")
  → Caller NOT forced — unchecked

throw new OutOfMemoryError()
  → Don't catch — let JVM handle

Exception Object Anatomy

public class InsufficientFundsException extends RuntimeException {

    private final String accountId;
    private final BigDecimal requested;
    private final BigDecimal available;

    public InsufficientFundsException(String accountId,
                                      BigDecimal requested,
                                      BigDecimal available) {
        super(String.format("Account %s: requested %s, available %s",
            accountId, requested, available));
        this.accountId = accountId;
        this.requested = requested;
        this.available = available;
    }

    // getters for structured error handling upstream
}

Every Throwable carries:
- Message — human-readable description
- Cause — chained underlying exception (initCause / constructor)
- Stack trace — array of StackTraceElement (class, method, file, line)
- Suppressed exceptions — from try-with-resources (Java 7+)

Core Keywords

Keyword Purpose Example
throw Throw an exception instance throw new PaymentDeclinedException(...)
throws Declare checked exceptions method may throw void read() throws IOException
try Start guarded block try { ... }
catch Handle specific exception type catch (IOException e) { ... }
finally Always executes (almost) finally { close(); }
try-with-resources Auto-close AutoCloseable try (Connection c = ...) { }

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why Java Has Exceptions

Without Exceptions With Exceptions
Return codes (-1, 0, 1) at every call Explicit failure channel
Caller ignores error codes silently Unchecked failures propagate visibly
Error handling mixed with business logic Separation via try/catch
No stack context Full stack trace for debugging

Why Two Categories (Checked vs Unchecked)?

Historical Java design (1995): Checked exceptions force developers to handle recoverable external failures (I/O, DB, network).

Modern critique (Effective Java, Bloch):
- Checked exceptions break lambda/stream pipelines
- Libraries evolve — adding checked exceptions breaks callers
- Most enterprise code wraps checked in unchecked anyway

Architect reality in 2025:

BANKING / PAYMENTS TYPICAL APPROACH
────────────────────────────────────

Domain/business failures     → Unchecked custom exceptions
  PaymentDeclinedException, InsufficientFundsException

Infrastructure failures      → Wrap in unchecked or use Result type
  SQLException → DataAccessException (Spring)

Truly recoverable I/O        → try-with-resources at boundary only
  File import batch job

API layer                      → Map exceptions to HTTP status codes
  PaymentDeclined → 422
  AccountNotFound → 404

Why Stack Traces Matter in Production

When a payment fails at 2 AM:

com.bank.payments.PaymentDeclinedException: Limit exceeded
    at com.bank.payments.LimitValidator.validate(LimitValidator.java:47)
    at com.bank.payments.PaymentService.process(PaymentService.java:89)
    at com.bank.payments.PaymentController.charge(PaymentController.java:34)
Caused by: com.bank.risk.VelocityCheckException: 10 txns in 60s
    at com.bank.risk.VelocityRule.evaluate(VelocityRule.java:22)
    ... 15 more

Architect requirement: Correlation ID in MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) so stack traces tie to a single payment across microservices.

Why finally Exists

Resources must be released whether success or failure:

Without finally:
  Connection opened
  Exception during query
  Connection NEVER closed → connection pool exhaustion → production outage

With finally / try-with-resources:
  Connection always returned to pool

Part 3: Internal Working

Exception Throwing — JVM Mechanics

Stack Unwinding

public void charge() {
    validate();    // frame 3
}
public void validate() {
  checkLimit();    // frame 2
}
public void checkLimit() {
  throw new PaymentDeclinedException("limit");  // frame 1 — throw here
}

CALL STACK AT THROW TIME
────────────────────────

┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ checkLimit()          ← throw originates
├─────────────────────────────┤
│ validate()
├─────────────────────────────┤
│ charge()
├─────────────────────────────┤
│ main()
└─────────────────────────────┘

UNWINDING:
  1. JVM creates PaymentDeclinedException object on heap
  2. Captures stack trace (walks stack frames — EXPENSIVE)
  3. Pops frames until matching catch block found
  4. If no catch → thread terminates (or UncaughtExceptionHandler)

Stack Trace Capture Cost

throw new Exception()           → captures stack — moderate cost
new Exception().printStackTrace() → expensive I/O
fillInStackTrace()              → can be overridden to skip (advanced)

RULE: Don't use exceptions for control flow in hot paths
      (e.g., catching NPE instead of null check)

Multi-Catch and Precise Rethrow (Java 7+)

try {
    processFile(path);
} catch (IOException | SQLException e) {
    log.error("Processing failed", e);
    throw e;  // precise rethrow — compiler knows it's IOException OR SQLException
}

Try-With-Resources Internals

try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection();
     PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {
    ps.executeUpdate();
}
// Compiler transforms to:
Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection();
Throwable primary = null;
try {
    PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql);
    try {
        ps.executeUpdate();
    } finally {
        if (ps != null) ps.close();  // suppressed exceptions tracked
    }
} catch (Throwable t) {
    primary = t;
    throw t;
} finally {
    if (conn != null) {
        if (primary != null) {
            try { conn.close(); } catch (Throwable suppressed) {
                primary.addSuppressed(suppressed);
            }
        } else {
            conn.close();
        }
    }
}

SUPPRESSED EXCEPTIONS
─────────────────────

Primary:   SQLException "constraint violation"
Suppressed: IOException "failed to close stream"

Both preserved in getSuppressed() array

Exception in Inheritance — Overriding Rules

class Parent {
    void process() throws IOException, SQLException { }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    @Override
    void process() throws IOException { }
    // OK — can throw SUBSET of parent's checked exceptions
    // CANNOT add NEW checked exceptions
    // CAN add unchecked exceptions freely
}

Lambdas and Checked Exceptions

// DOES NOT COMPILE — Consumer.accept doesn't declare throws
files.forEach(file -> {
    readFile(file);  // throws IOException
});

// PATTERN 1: wrap in unchecked at boundary
files.forEach(file -> {
    try {
        readFile(file);
    } catch (IOException e) {
        throw new UncheckedIOException(e);
    }
});

// PATTERN 2: custom wrapper functional interface
@FunctionalInterface
interface ThrowingConsumer<T> {
    void accept(T t) throws Exception;
}

static <T> Consumer<T> wrap(ThrowingConsumer<T> consumer) {
    return t -> {
        try {
            consumer.accept(t);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            throw new RuntimeException(e);
        }
    };
}

Part 4: Memory View

Memory Impact of Exceptions

Exception Object on Heap

HEAP at throw time
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ PaymentDeclinedException object                             │
│   message: "Limit exceeded"                                 │
│   cause: ref → VelocityCheckException                       │
│   stackTrace: StackTraceElement[25]  ← array on heap        │
│   suppressedExceptions: []                                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

StackTraceElement[25]:
  Each element: className, methodName, fileName, lineNumber (Strings)
  25 frames × ~100 bytes ≈ 2.5 KB per exception with full stack
Aspect Memory Impact GC Impact
Creating exception (no throw) Object + stack trace array Young Gen, short-lived
Throwing and catching Same — caught refs die after catch Young Gen
Logging exception with stack String building for log line Additional allocation
Exception as control flow (millions/sec) Massive allocation + GC storm Production incident
Rethrowing same exception No new stack capture if same instance Lower
fillInStackTrace() disabled Minimal Rare optimization

Stack Frame vs Exception Object

STACK (ephemeral)                    HEAP (exception persists until GC)
─────────────────                    ─────────────────────────────────

During unwind, frames popped         Exception object holds COPY of
from thread stack                    stack trace at throw time

Frame: charge()                      StackTraceElement[] snapshot
Frame: validate()                    survives after frames gone
Frame: checkLimit() ← popped

try-with-resources Memory

Per try-with-resources block:
  - Resource object(s) on heap (Connection, Stream)
  - Primary exception reference (null or ref)
  - Suppressed exception array (if close() fails)

Connection pool (HikariCP):
  Connection returned in finally → pool reused
  NOT returned → pool depletes → threads block → timeout cascade

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Exception Performance Characteristics

Cost Breakdown

Operation Relative Cost When It Matters
Normal return 1× (baseline) Always
throw + catch (few levels) ~100–1000× Infrequent errors — OK
throw + catch (deep stack) Higher (more frames captured) Deep call stacks
Exception for control flow Catastrophic at scale Never in hot paths
printStackTrace() Very expensive (I/O sync) Never in production
Logging with stack (log.error("msg", e)) Moderate Acceptable for real errors

Exception as Control Flow — Anti-Pattern

// CATASTROPHIC in payment matching engine — 1M iterations
for (String id : paymentIds) {
    try {
        map.get(id).process();
    } catch (NullPointerException e) {
        handleMissing(id);
    }
}

// CORRECT
Payment payment = map.get(id);
if (payment == null) {
    handleMissing(id);
} else {
    payment.process();
}

Scalability Impact

Pattern Single Request High RPS Payment API
Domain exception per declined payment Fine — business event Fine — expected path
NPE for validation Fast fail but wrong semantics Log noise, no error code
Swallow exception in catch Request "succeeds" Silent money loss
Retry all exceptions Duplicate charges Idempotency required
Global handler maps to HTTP Clean API Consistent client experience

Thread Safety and Exceptions

// Exception objects are NOT shared across threads typically
// Each throw creates new instance (or rethrows existing)

// UNSAFE: mutable exception used as signal between threads
public class SharedExceptionHolder {
    private Exception lastError;  // race condition!
    public void setError(Exception e) { this.lastError = e; }
}

Rule: Exceptions are per-thread failure signals, not shared state.

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Banking — Domain Exception Hierarchy

package com.bank.payments.exception;

public abstract class PaymentException extends RuntimeException {
    private final String paymentId;
    private final String errorCode;

    protected PaymentException(String paymentId, String errorCode, String message) {
        super(message);
        this.paymentId = paymentId;
        this.errorCode = errorCode;
    }

    public String paymentId() { return paymentId; }
    public String errorCode() { return errorCode; }
}

public final class InsufficientFundsException extends PaymentException {
    public InsufficientFundsException(String paymentId, String message) {
        super(paymentId, "PAY_INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS", message);
    }
}

public final class PaymentDeclinedException extends PaymentException {
    public PaymentDeclinedException(String paymentId, String reason) {
        super(paymentId, "PAY_DECLINED", reason);
    }
}

public final class DuplicatePaymentException extends PaymentException {
    public DuplicatePaymentException(String paymentId) {
        super(paymentId, "PAY_DUPLICATE", "Payment already processed: " + paymentId);
    }
}

Example 2: Service Layer — Throw vs Return

package com.bank.payments.service;

import java.math.BigDecimal;

@Service
public class TransferService {

    private final AccountRepository accountRepository;
    private final IdempotencyStore idempotencyStore;

    public TransferResult transfer(TransferRequest request) {
        if (idempotencyStore.exists(request.idempotencyKey())) {
            throw new DuplicatePaymentException(request.paymentId());
        }

        Account debtor = accountRepository.findById(request.debtorAccountId())
            .orElseThrow(() -> new AccountNotFoundException(request.debtorAccountId()));

        if (debtor.availableBalance().compareTo(request.amount()) < 0) {
            throw new InsufficientFundsException(
                request.paymentId(),
                "Available: " + debtor.availableBalance()
            );
        }

        return executeTransfer(debtor, request);
    }
}

Example 3: Try-With-Resources — Batch File Import

package com.bank.reconciliation.imports;

import java.io.BufferedReader;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class NachaFileImporter {

    public List<PaymentRecord> importFile(Path filePath) throws ImportException {
        List<PaymentRecord> records = new ArrayList<>();

        try (BufferedReader reader = Files.newBufferedReader(filePath)) {
            String line;
            int lineNumber = 0;
            while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {
                lineNumber++;
                try {
                    records.add(parseLine(line));
                } catch (ParseException e) {
                    throw new ImportException(
                        "Parse error at line " + lineNumber, e);
                }
            }
        } catch (IOException e) {
            throw new ImportException("Failed to read file: " + filePath, e);
        }

        return records;
    }

    private PaymentRecord parseLine(String line) throws ParseException {
        // parsing logic
        throw new UnsupportedOperationException("implement");
    }

    public static class ImportException extends Exception {
        public ImportException(String message, Throwable cause) {
            super(message, cause);
        }
    }
}

Example 4: Exception Chaining — Logistics Integration

package com.logistics.integration;

public class CarrierApiClient {

    public ShipmentStatus track(String trackingNumber) {
        try {
            return callCarrierApi(trackingNumber);
        } catch (HttpTimeoutException e) {
            throw new CarrierUnavailableException(
                "Carrier API timeout for tracking: " + trackingNumber, e);
        } catch (HttpClientErrorException.NotFound e) {

        } catch (RestClientException e) {

Example 5: Result Type Alternative (Architect Pattern)

package com.bank.payments.domain;

public sealed interface PaymentResult permits PaymentSuccess, PaymentFailure {
    record PaymentSuccess(String paymentId, String transactionRef) implements PaymentResult {}
    record PaymentFailure(String paymentId, String errorCode, String message) implements PaymentResult {}

    static PaymentResult success(String paymentId, String transactionRef) {
        return new PaymentSuccess(paymentId, transactionRef);
    }
    static PaymentResult failure(String paymentId, String errorCode, String message) {
        return new PaymentFailure(paymentId, errorCode, message);
    }
}

// When NOT to throw — expected business outcomes
public PaymentResult attemptPayment(PaymentRequest request) {
    if (!validator.isValid(request)) {
        return PaymentResult.failure(request.id(), "INVALID", "Validation failed");
    }
    // ...
    return PaymentResult.success(request.id(), txnRef);
}

Example 6: Stream + Checked Exception Wrapper

package com.bank.reconciliation;

import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;

public class BatchFileProcessor {

    public List<PaymentRecord> processAll(List<Path> files) {
        return files.stream()
            .flatMap(path -> {
                try {
                    return importer.importFile(path).stream();
                } catch (NachaFileImporter.ImportException e) {
                    throw new BatchImportException(path, e);
                }
            })
            .toList();
    }

    public static class BatchImportException extends RuntimeException {
        public BatchImportException(Path path, Throwable cause) {
            super("Import failed: " + path, cause);
        }
    }
}

Example 7: Transportation — Retry with Exception Classification

package com.transport.booking.client;

public class SeatReservationClient {

    public ReservationResponse reserve(ReservationRequest request) {
        int attempts = 0;
        Exception lastException = null;

        while (attempts < 3) {
            try {
                return doReserve(request);
            } catch (TransientReservationException e) {
                lastException = e;
                attempts++;
                sleepBackoff(attempts);
            } catch (SeatAlreadyBookedException e) {
                throw e;  // non-retryable — business failure
            }
        }
        throw new ReservationFailedException("Exhausted retries", lastException);
    }

    private void sleepBackoff(int attempt) {
        try {
            Thread.sleep(attempt * 200L);
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            throw new ReservationFailedException("Interrupted during retry", e);
        }
    }
}

Part 7: Production Usage

Exception Handling in Production Systems

Layered Exception Strategy

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  API Layer (Controller)                                         │
│  @ExceptionHandler → HTTP status + ErrorResponse JSON           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Service Layer                                                  │
│  Domain exceptions (PaymentDeclined, InsufficientFunds)         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Repository / Integration Layer                                 │
│  Wrap SQLException, IOException → DataAccessException           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Infrastructure                                                 │
│  Raw checked exceptions at boundary only                        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Spring @ControllerAdvice Pattern (Preview)

@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

  @ExceptionHandler(PaymentDeclinedException.class)
  public ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse> handleDeclined(PaymentDeclinedException ex) {
    return ResponseEntity
        .status(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY)
        .body(new ErrorResponse(ex.errorCode(), ex.getMessage(), ex.paymentId()));
  }

  @ExceptionHandler(AccountNotFoundException.class)
  public ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse> handleNotFound(AccountNotFoundException ex) {
    return ResponseEntity
        .status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
        .body(new ErrorResponse("ACCOUNT_NOT_FOUND", ex.getMessage(), null));
  }

  @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
  public ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse> handleUnexpected(Exception ex) {
    log.error("Unexpected error", ex);
    return ResponseEntity
        .status(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)
        .body(new ErrorResponse("INTERNAL_ERROR", "An unexpected error occurred", null));
  }
}

HTTP Status Mapping — Payment API

Exception HTTP Status Retry? Client Action
ValidationException 400 Bad Request No Fix request
UnauthorizedException 401 No Re-authenticate
AccountNotFoundException 404 No Check account ID
DuplicatePaymentException 409 Conflict No Use idempotency key
InsufficientFundsException 422 Unprocessable No Insufficient balance
PaymentDeclinedException 422 No Declined by bank
RateLimitException 429 Yes (backoff) Slow down
CarrierUnavailableException 503 Yes Retry later
Unexpected Exception 500 Maybe Alert ops

Logging Best Practices

// BAD — loses stack trace
log.error("Payment failed: " + e.getMessage());

// BAD — stack trace as string concatenation
log.error("Payment failed: " + e);

// GOOD — SLF4J passes throwable, preserves stack
log.error("Payment failed: paymentId={}", paymentId, e);

// GOOD — structured fields for search
log.error("event=payment_failed paymentId={} errorCode={}",
    paymentId, ex.errorCode(), ex);

What NOT to Catch

// NEVER catch and ignore
try {
    ledger.post(entry);
} catch (Exception e) {
    // empty — silent financial data loss
}

// NEVER catch Throwable/Error
try {
    process();
} catch (Throwable t) {  // catches OutOfMemoryError!
    log.warn("oops");
}

// NEVER use exceptions for expected flow
try {
    account = map.get(id);
    balance = account.getBalance();
} catch (NullPointerException e) {
    balance = BigDecimal.ZERO;
}

Production Checklist

Check Why
Correlation ID in every log line Trace across microservices
Domain exceptions carry error codes Client handling + metrics
No empty catch blocks Silent failures
log.error(msg, exception) Preserve stack trace
Classify retryable vs non-retryable Prevent duplicate payments
Global handler for unhandled No raw stack traces to clients
try-with-resources for all I/O Pool exhaustion prevention
Don't expose internal messages in 500 responses Security

Part 8: Microservice Usage

Exceptions Across Service Boundaries

Problem: Exceptions Don't Cross Network

Payment Service                    Ledger Service
     │                                  │
     │  HTTP POST /ledger/debit         │
     │─────────────────────────────────►│
     │                                  │ throws InsufficientFundsException
     │  ◄── 422 { "code": "INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS" }
     │      (JSON — not Java exception object)
     ▼
Maps to PaymentDeclinedException locally

Architect rule: Exceptions are in-process constructs. Cross-service failures are HTTP status codes + structured error bodies or dead-letter Kafka messages.

Feign/RestClient Error Handling

@Component
public class LedgerClient {

    private final RestClient restClient;

    public void debit(DebitRequest request) {
        try {
            restClient.post()
                .uri("/ledger/debit")
                .body(request)
                .retrieve()
                .toBodilessEntity();
        } catch (HttpClientErrorException.UnprocessableEntity e) {
            ErrorResponse error = parseError(e.getResponseBodyAsString());
            if ("INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS".equals(error.code())) {
                throw new InsufficientFundsException(
                    request.paymentId(), error.message());
            }
            throw new LedgerIntegrationException(error.message(), e);
        }
    }
}

Kafka Consumer Exception Handling

Consumer poll loop
       │
       ▼
  process message
       │
   ┌───┴───┐
   │       │
 success  exception
   │       │
   ▼       ▼
 commit  classify:
 offset    ├── transient (timeout) → retry with backoff
           ├── poison message → DLQ topic
           └── business rejection → publish PaymentFailedEvent, commit

@KafkaListener(topics = "payment-initiated")
public void consume(PaymentInitiatedEvent event) {
    try {
        paymentProcessor.process(event);
    } catch (DuplicatePaymentException e) {
        log.info("Duplicate ignored: {}", event.paymentId());
        // commit offset — idempotent, no retry
    } catch (TransientException e) {
        throw e;  // let error handler retry
    } catch (PaymentException e) {
        failurePublisher.publish(event, e);
        // commit — business failure, don't block partition
    }
}

Transfer Saga:
  1. Debit debtor   ✓
  2. Credit creditor ✗ InsufficientFundsException at creditor validation
  3. COMPENSATE: reverse debit
     └── if compensation throws → manual intervention alert

Distributed Tracing with Exceptions

TraceId: abc-123 (in MDC + HTTP header + Kafka header)

payment-svc ERROR  abc-123  PaymentDeclinedException

fraud-svc   WARN   abc-123  VelocityCheckException (cause)

Part 9: Architect Perspective

Exception Strategy as Architecture Decision

Three Error Models

Model When Example
Exceptions Unexpected or exceptional failures InsufficientFundsException
Result/Either type Expected business outcomes PaymentResult.success/failure
Error codes in response API contracts { "code": "PAY_001", "message": "..." }

Architect decision for payments:

Synchronous API (user waiting)     → Result type or domain exception → HTTP mapping
Async pipeline (Kafka)             → Event types: PaymentCompleted | PaymentFailed
Batch ETL                          → Checked IOException at boundary, row-level error file

Fail-Fast vs Fail-Safe vs Fail-Soft

Strategy Behavior Use Case
Fail-fast Stop on first error Fund transfer — all or nothing
Fail-safe Degrade gracefully Show cached FX rate if API down
Fail-soft Log and continue Non-critical audit write failure

Idempotency and Exceptions

Client sends payment with idempotency-key: KEY-001
Server processes, crashes BEFORE response sent
Client retries with KEY-001

WITHOUT idempotency:
  Second attempt → DuplicatePaymentException OR double charge

WITH idempotency store:
  Second attempt → return original success response (200, not 409)

Checked Exceptions — Architectural Stance

Stance Advocates Enterprise Practice
Use checked Early Java, some libraries JDBC, batch I/O at edges
Avoid checked Bloch, Spring, modern Java Wrap at boundary in unchecked
Hybrid Pragmatic architects Checked in batch import; unchecked in REST services

Your banking context recommendation: Unchecked domain exceptions + checked only at true I/O boundaries (file import, SFTP) + Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy for DB.

Exception Metrics (Observability)

Micrometer / Prometheus counters:
  payments_declined_total{reason="INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS"}
  payments_failed_total{reason="INTERNAL_ERROR"}
  kafka_consumer_dlq_total{topic="payment-initiated"}

Alert on:
  INTERNAL_ERROR rate > 1% of requests
  DLQ rate spike
  Compensation failure (saga)

Junior Level

  2. What is a checked vs unchecked exception?

  4. What is try-with-resources?

Senior Level

  1. Should you catch Exception or Throwable? Why?
  2. What is exception chaining? Why use cause?
  3. What are the rules for overriding methods regarding throws?
  4. Why shouldn't exceptions be used for control flow?
  5. Difference between throw and throws?
  6. What are suppressed exceptions?
  7. How do you handle checked exceptions in lambda expressions?
  8. What is Optional.orElseThrow() and when do you use it?

Staff / Architect Level

  1. Critique checked exceptions. What is your team's policy?
  2. Design an exception hierarchy for a payment platform.
  3. How do exceptions propagate in a microservices architecture?
  4. How do you prevent duplicate payments when retries happen after timeout?
  5. Exception vs Result type — when do you choose each in API design?
  6. What should a global exception handler never expose to clients?
  7. How do you classify exceptions for circuit breaker retry policies?
  8. What metrics would you emit from exception handlers?
  9. How does InterruptedException relate to thread shutdown in K8s pods?

Model Answer — Q6 (Catch Exception?)

A: Catching broad Exception hides bugs and makes failures hard to diagnose. Acceptable only at system boundaries: global REST handler, Kafka error handler, main batch loop. Always log with full stack trace. Never swallow. Classify into retryable vs non-retryable. Catching Throwable or Error is dangerous — OutOfMemoryError should not be caught and suppressed; the JVM may be in an unrecoverable state.

Model Answer — Q17 (Retries + Duplicate Payments)

A: Client sends Idempotency-Key header. Server stores (key → response) before processing. On retry with same key: return stored response without reprocessing. On timeout where outcome unknown: client retries with same key. Server uses dedup store (Redis SET or DB unique constraint). Exceptions: DuplicatePaymentException becomes success response if original succeeded. Saga compensations handle partial completion. Never blindly retry non-idempotent POST without key.

Part 13: Common Mistakes

# Mistake Consequence Fix
1 Empty catch block Silent data loss Log + rethrow or handle
2 catch (Exception e) everywhere Masks bugs Catch specific types
3 e.printStackTrace() in production Sync I/O, no correlation ID SLF4J log.error(msg, e)
4 Exception for control flow GC storm, slow Use if/else or Optional
5 Expose stack trace to API client Security leak Generic 500 message
6 Catch Error JVM unstable state ignored Don't catch
7 Swallow InterruptedException Thread can't shut down Restore interrupt flag
8 Throw generic RuntimeException("failed") No error code, no handling Domain exception hierarchy
9 Checked exception through 5 layers throws pollution Wrap at boundary
10 Retry all exceptions Duplicate charges Classify retryable
11 No cause when wrapping Lost root cause in logs new DomainEx(msg, cause)
12 finally with return Suppresses exception Never return from finally

InterruptedException Trap

// WRONG — swallows interrupt
try {
    Thread.sleep(1000);
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    log.warn("sleep interrupted");
}

// CORRECT — restore interrupt, propagate or exit
try {
    Thread.sleep(1000);
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    throw new ProcessingAbortedException("Interrupted", e);
}

Finally Return Trap

public int getValue() {
    try {
        return 1;
    } finally {
        return 2;  // ALWAYS returns 2 — exception also suppressed!
    }
}

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Domain-specific unchecked exceptions with error codes for business failures
  2. Try-with-resources for every AutoCloseable (Connection, Stream, Response)
  3. Chain exceptions — preserve cause when wrapping
  4. One global handler per service for HTTP mapping
  5. Never expose internal details in 500 responses
  6. Classify retryable — document in exception type or error code
  7. Correlation ID in all error logs
  8. Optional.orElseThrow for required lookups — not bare get()
  9. Fail fast on invariant violations — Objects.requireNonNull, validate()
  10. Test exception paths — declined payment, timeout, duplicate are first-class test cases
// Template for wrapping at integration boundary
public Account loadAccount(AccountId id) {
    try {
        return jdbcTemplate.queryForObject(...);
    } catch (DataAccessException e) {
        throw new AccountLoadException("Failed to load account: " + id, e);
    }
}

Part 16: Revision Notes

Quick Revision — Exception Handling

HIERARCHY:
  Throwable → Error (don't catch) | Exception
  Exception → RuntimeException (unchecked) | Checked (IOException, SQLException)

CHECKED: must catch OR throws — compile time
UNCHECKED: RuntimeException — no declare required

KEYWORDS:
  throw = create/propagate
  throws = declare checked on method
  try/catch/finally
  try-with-resources (AutoCloseable)

RULES:
  catch specific > catch Exception
  never empty catch
  never catch Error/Throwable
  log.error("msg", e) — not printStackTrace
  chain: new DomainEx("msg", cause)
  override: can reduce checked throws, not add

LAMBDAS: checked not allowed — wrap UncheckedIOException

OPTIONAL: orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException(id))

MICROSERVICES:
  exceptions don't cross network → HTTP status + error JSON
  Kafka: retry transient, DLQ poison, commit on business fail
  idempotency key for payment retries

INTERRUPTED: always Thread.currentThread().interrupt()

Memory Mnemonic

"Throw is expensive — business decline is OK; control flow is not"

Part 1: Concept

What Is Stream Performance Engineering?

Stream performance engineering is the discipline of building declarative data pipelines that are simultaneously:

  • Correct — same result as imperative code
  • Readable — intent clear to the next engineer at 3 AM
  • Measurable — benchmarked with representative data, not guessed
  • Appropriate — sequential, parallel, SQL, or Spark chosen by evidence
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           STREAM PERFORMANCE DECISION STACK                              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  LAYER 4: ARCHITECTURE    SQL aggregation? Kafka? Spark? In-JVM?        │
│  LAYER 3: ALGORITHM       O(n) vs O(n log n) — sorted(), distinct()     │
│  LAYER 2: JVM             Boxing, allocation, GC, JIT, common pool        │
│  LAYER 1: API CHOICE      sequential vs parallel, collectors, primitives │
│                                                                          │
│  Rule: Optimize top-down. Don't parallelStream() a O(n²) algorithm.     │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Advanced Stream Concepts Map

Concept What Lesson 4 Intro Lesson 6 Depth

Pipeline fusion Combine stages into single pass Lazy eval How ops fold together
