JMH Microbenchmark harness — Evidence-based tuning

Stream Pipeline Anatomy (Advanced)

SOURCE                INTERMEDIATE OPS                    TERMINAL
──────                ────────────────                    ────────

spliterator()    →    filter → map → mapToInt    →    sum()
     │                    │       │        │              │
     │               Stateless  Stateless  Stateful?   Reduction
     │               OP         OP         (no)        accumulator
     │                                                    │
     └─────────────── FUSION where possible ──────────────┘
                      (single traversal of source)

Spliterator Characteristics

Spliterator<Payment> spl = payments.spliterator();

spl.characteristics() & Spliterator.SIZED      // known size
spl.characteristics() & Spliterator.SUBSIZED   // splits have known size
spl.characteristics() & Spliterator.NONNULL    // no null elements
spl.characteristics() & Spliterator.IMMUTABLE  // source won't change
spl.characteristics() & Spliterator.CONCURRENT // safely splittable concurrently
spl.characteristics() & Spliterator.ORDERED    // encounter order defined
Characteristic Meaning Parallel Impact
SIZED estimateSize() is exact Better split planning
SUBSIZED Each split is SIZED Even work distribution
NONNULL No nulls Skip null checks
IMMUTABLE Source won't mutate during stream Safe parallel
CONCURRENT Source thread-safe for concurrent traversal Parallel from shared source
ORDERED Encounter order matters Limits reorder optimizations

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why Performance Engineering for Streams Matters

The Gap Between Lesson 4 and Production Reality

Lesson 4 taught how to write streams. Production asks:

Nightly reconciliation job:
  8 million payment records
  SLA: complete in 45 minutes
  Pod: 2 vCPU, 4 GB heap
  Current: sequential stream — 92 minutes → MISSED SLA

Questions an Architect must answer:
  1. Is the bottleneck CPU, GC, or I/O?
  2. Will parallelStream() help or make it worse?
  3. Should aggregation move to Oracle/SQL?
  4. Is boxing causing 200M Integer allocations?

Why Java Streams Are Not "Free Abstraction"

Each pipeline stage may allocate:

payments.stream()          → Pipeline head object
  .filter(validator)        → FilterOp wrapper + Predicate (maybe capturing lambda)
  .map(enricher)           → MapOp + Function
  .mapToInt(p -> paise)    → IntPipeline
  .sum()                   → Terminal reduction

vs simple for-loop:
  int total = 0;
  for (Payment p : payments) { ... }   // zero pipeline objects

Why accept the cost? Maintainability for most paths. When reject it? When profiling proves allocation/GC in a hot path (this lesson).

Why Parallel Streams Exist

2005+: multicore CPUs ubiquitous
Problem: Java threads manual, error-prone
Java 7: ForkJoinPool
Java 8: parallelStream() — "free" parallelism for collections

Reality: parallelism is NEVER free
  - task scheduling overhead
  - shared ForkJoinPool.commonPool()
  - split quality depends on Spliterator
  - ordering, side effects, thread safety constraints

Why JMH Exists

Naive benchmark:
  long start = System.nanoTime();
  stream.sum();
  long end = System.nanoTime();
  // WRONG — JIT hasn't warmed up, GC noise, dead code elimination

JMH (Java Microbenchmark Harness):
  - warmup iterations (JIT compile)
  - multiple forks and measurement iterations
  - blackholes to prevent DCE
  - accounts for GC pauses

Part 3: Internal Working

How Streams Execute Internally

Sequential Pipeline Evaluation

Terminal collect() called
        │
        ▼
Wrap spliterator with intermediate ops (linked pipeline)
        │
        ▼
Sink chain built (internal interface — "downstream consumer")
        │
        ▼
For each element from spliterator:
  source → filterSink → mapSink → terminalSink
  (one element flows through entire chain — fusion)

FUSION EXAMPLE
──────────────

Without fusion (conceptual):
  filter entire collection → store temp → map entire temp → collect

With fusion (actual for stateless ops):
  for each element e:
    if filter.test(e):
      accumulator.accept(mapper.apply(e))

Single pass — O(n) not O(2n) with intermediate collection

Stateful Operations Break Fusion Assumptions

payments.stream()
  .filter(p -> p.amount() > 0)     // stateless — fused
  .sorted(comparing(Payment::date)) // STATEFUL — buffers ALL elements
  .limit(10)                        // can optimize with sorted heap sometimes
  .collect(toList());

sorted() MUST see all elements before emitting first
  → internal array allocated
  → O(n log n) + O(n) memory

Parallel Stream Execution

payments.parallelStream()
  .filter(...)
  .mapToInt(...)
  .sum();

STEP 1: Submit task to ForkJoinPool.commonPool()
STEP 2: Spliterator.trySplit() recursively until chunks small enough
STEP 3: Each worker processes chunk through pipeline
STEP 4: Combine results (sum partial sums)

ForkJoinPool.commonPool() — DEFAULT

                    Root Task
                   /         \
              Split A       Split B
              /    \         /    \
           W1     W2       W3     W4
           │      │        │      │
        chunk1  chunk2   chunk3  chunk4
           │      │        │      │
           └──┬───┘        └──┬───┘
              ▼               ▼
           partial sum    partial sum
              └───────┬───────┘
                      ▼
                  final sum

ArrayList Spliterator — Ideal for Parallel

ArrayList spliterator:
  - SIZED, SUBSIZED
  - trySplit() divides index range in half
  - Perfect load balance for parallel

LinkedList spliterator:
  - poor split — must traverse to midpoint
  - parallel often SLOWER than sequential

Collector Internal Structure

Collector<T, A, R>
  T = input element type
  A = mutable accumulation type (e.g., ArrayList, HashMap)
  R = final result type

Four functions:
  supplier()     → () -> new A()           // create accumulator
  accumulator()  → (A, T) -> void        // add element
  combiner()     → (A, A) -> A           // merge accumulators (parallel)
  finisher()     → A -> R                // optional transform

SEQUENTIAL collect:
  A acc = supplier.get()
  for each element: accumulator.accept(acc, element)
  return finisher.apply(acc)

PARALLEL collect:
  Worker1: A1 accumulates chunk1
  Worker2: A2 accumulates chunk2
  combiner.merge(A1, A2)
  return finisher.apply(A1)

Custom Collector Example — Internal Flow

Collector<Payment, ?, BigDecimal> summingAmount = Collector.of(
    () -> new BigDecimal[] { BigDecimal.ZERO },           // supplier
    (acc, p) -> acc[0] = acc[0].add(p.amount()),          // accumulator
    (acc1, acc2) -> { acc1[0] = acc1[0].add(acc2[0]); return acc1; }, // combiner
    acc -> acc[0]                                         // finisher
);

reduce vs collect

reduce collect
Purpose Combine to single value Mutable reduction to complex structure
Accumulator Immutable (usually) Mutable container
Parallel BinaryOperator must be associative combiner merges mutable containers
Example sum, max toList, groupingBy
Constraint reduce(identity, op) — identity must be true identity for op More flexible

Part 4: Memory View

Memory Impact of Advanced Stream Operations

Sequential vs Parallel Memory

SEQUENTIAL
──────────
Stack: pipeline object refs, loop variables
Heap:  source collection + output + short-lived pipeline stages (Young Gen)

PARALLEL
────────
Heap:  source + output
       + ForkJoinTask objects per split (many short-lived)
       + per-thread partial accumulators
       + work-stealing deque structures

Parallel uses MORE memory — only worth it when CPU savings exceed memory/GC cost

sorted() Memory Explosion

1M Payment objects in ArrayList
sorted() by date:
  - copies references into internal array: 1M × 8 bytes = 8 MB (refs only)
  - TimSort comparisons — object field access
  - Peak memory ≈ 2× reference array during sort

If Payment is 200 bytes of data + 8 byte ref:
  sorted() adds ~8 MB refs, not 200 MB duplicate objects
  BUT TimSort temporary arrays during merge

distinct() Memory

distinct() uses LinkedHashSet internally (maintains encounter order)
  → one HashSet entry per unique element
  → Payment with bad hashCode → large buckets → memory + CPU

1M payments, 50K unique accounts after distinct by accountId:
  ~50K set entries — manageable
1M unique — full set in memory

Boxing in Streams — Memory Math

map(p -> p.amountInPaise())  → Stream<Integer>
  8M payments = 8M Integer objects
  Integer object ≈ 16 bytes header + 4 bytes value = 20+ bytes
  ≈ 160 MB+ in Young Gen per pass → frequent minor GC

mapToInt(p -> p.amountInPaise()) → IntStream
  8M primitives in internal array during reduction
  8M × 4 bytes = 32 MB — no object headers

Parallel Stream — Per-Thread Buffers

ForkJoinPool with parallelism = 7 (8 cores - 1)

Each active task:
  - partial result accumulator
  - spliterator slice state

combine phase:
  merge partial HashMaps in groupingBy
  → combiner can be EXPENSIVE for large maps
  → consider sequential for groupingBy on large data

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Benchmarking Framework

When to Use What Tool

Tool Granularity Use Case
JMH Method/micro-op Stream vs loop, collector choice
Profiler (async-profiler, JFR) CPU, allocation, GC Find real hot spots in prod-like workload
Load test (Gatling, k6) End-to-end RPS/latency API SLA validation
Metrics (Micrometer) Production p50/p99 Prove deploy didn't regress

JMH Example — Sequential vs Parallel

@BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime)
@OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
@Warmup(iterations = 3, time = 2)
@Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 2)
@Fork(2)
public class PaymentSumBenchmark {

    private List<Payment> payments;

    @Setup
    public void setup() {
        payments = generatePayments(1_000_000);
    }

    @Benchmark
    public long sequentialLoop() {
        long sum = 0;
        for (Payment p : payments) {
            sum += p.amountInPaise();
        }
        return sum;
    }

    @Benchmark
    public long sequentialStream() {
        return payments.stream()
            .mapToInt(Payment::amountInPaise)
            .sum();
    }

    @Benchmark
    public long parallelStream() {
        return payments.parallelStream()
            .mapToInt(Payment::amountInPaise)
            .sum();
    }
}

Typical results (8-core, 1M ints, CPU-bound):

sequentialLoop:        ~2 ms   ← often fastest
sequentialStream:      ~3 ms   ← allocation overhead
parallelStream:        ~1 ms   ← wins on large CPU-bound primitive ops

On 10K elements:

sequentialLoop:        ~0.02 ms
parallelStream:        ~0.5 ms  ← LOSES — fork/join overhead dominates

Parallel Stream Decision Matrix (Quantitative)

Factor Favors Parallel Favors Sequential
Data size > 100K (rule of thumb) < 10K
Per-element work CPU-heavy (crypto, calc) Trivial (getter)
Data structure ArrayList, arrays, IntStream.range LinkedList, Stream.iterate
Operation mapToInt, pure filter/map sorted, groupingBy, I/O
Environment Batch job, dedicated thread HTTP request, shared common pool
Ordering required forEachOrdered (slower) Order doesn't matter

Operation Cost Ranking (In-Memory, n = 1M)

Operation Approx Complexity Memory Notes
filter + mapToInt + sum O(n) O(1) extra Best stream case
collect(toList()) O(n) O(n) output Expected
distinct() O(n) avg O(unique) HashSet backing
sorted() O(n log n) O(n) Materializes all
groupingBy O(n) avg O(groups × items) Combiner cost in parallel
flatMap O(n × m) O(n × m) m = inner size
parallel + groupingBy O(n) High Often slower than sequential

Common Pool Contention — Production Scenario

Payment API pod (8 threads handling HTTP)
  +
Background job in same JVM using parallelStream()
  =
Both compete for ForkJoinPool.commonPool()

Symptom: p99 latency spikes during batch window
Fix: Custom ForkJoinPool for batch:

ForkJoinPool customPool = new ForkJoinPool(4);
customPool.submit(() ->
    payments.parallelStream()
        .mapToInt(Payment::amountInPaise)
        .sum()
).get();

Scalability: In-JVM vs Push-Down

SCENARIO: Sum payments by currency for 50M rows

Option A: Load 50M rows → stream groupingBy
  Memory: O(50M) references — OOM on 4GB pod
  Time: network + GC death

Option B: SQL SELECT currency, SUM(amount) GROUP BY currency
  Memory: O(currencies) ≈ 10 rows
  Time: database index scan — minutes → seconds

ARCHITECT RULE: Stream performance is bounded by
  what you load into heap first.

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Banking — Optimized Reconciliation Sum

package com.bank.reconciliation;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.List;

public class ReconciliationAggregator {

    // AVOID — boxing + BigDecimal stream overhead
    public BigDecimal totalAmountSlow(List<Payment> payments) {
        return payments.stream()
            .filter(Payment::isSettled)
            .map(Payment::amount)
            .reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add);
    }

    // BETTER for millions — long paise + single convert
    public BigDecimal totalAmountFast(List<Payment> payments) {
        long totalPaise = payments.stream()
            .filter(Payment::isSettled)
            .mapToLong(Payment::amountInPaise)
            .sum();
        return BigDecimal.valueOf(totalPaise, 2);
    }

    // BEST for huge batch on multi-core — custom pool, primitive
    public BigDecimal totalAmountParallel(List<Payment> payments,
                                          java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool pool)
            throws InterruptedException, java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException {
        long totalPaise = pool.submit(() ->
            payments.parallelStream()
                .filter(Payment::isSettled)
                .mapToLong(Payment::amountInPaise)
                .sum()
        ).get();
        return BigDecimal.valueOf(totalPaise, 2);
    }

    public record Payment(String id, BigDecimal amount, boolean settled) {
        long amountInPaise() {
            return amount.movePointRight(2).longValueExact();
        }
        boolean isSettled() { return settled; }
    }
}

Example 2: Logistics — Efficient Grouping with Downstream Collector

package com.logistics.analytics;

import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public class HubWeightAnalytics {

    public Map<String, Double> totalWeightByHub(List<Shipment> shipments) {
        return shipments.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                Shipment::hubCode,
                Collectors.summingDouble(Shipment::weightKg)
            ));
    }

    public Map<String, Shipment> heaviestPerHub(List<Shipment> shipments) {
        return shipments.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                Shipment::hubCode,
                Collectors.collectingAndThen(
                    Collectors.maxBy(Comparator.comparingDouble(Shipment::weightKg)),
                    opt -> opt.orElseThrow()
                )
            ));
    }

    public record Shipment(String id, String hubCode, double weightKg) {}
}

Example 3: Custom Collector — Immutable Map Builder

package com.bank.fx;

import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.stream.Collector;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public class FxRateCollector {

    public static Collector<FxRate, ?, Map<String, java.math.BigDecimal>> toImmutableRateMap() {
        return Collectors.collectingAndThen(
            Collectors.toMap(
                FxRate::currency,
                FxRate::rate,
                (r1, r2) -> r2  // merge duplicate — keep latest
            ),
            Map::copyOf  // Java 10+ immutable
        );
    }

    public record FxRate(String currency, java.math.BigDecimal rate) {}
}

Example 4: Avoid sorted() — Top-K with PriorityQueue

package com.bank.payments.analytics;

import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;

public class TopLargePayments {

    // BAD for "top 10 of 5M" — sorts all 5M
    public List<Payment> top10Slow(List<Payment> payments) {
        return payments.stream()
            .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Payment::amount).reversed())
            .limit(10)
            .toList();
    }

    // GOOD — O(n log k) where k=10
    public List<Payment> top10Fast(List<Payment> payments) {
        PriorityQueue<Payment> heap = new PriorityQueue<>(
            11, Comparator.comparing(Payment::amount));  // min-heap

        for (Payment p : payments) {
            heap.offer(p);
            if (heap.size() > 10) {
                heap.poll();
            }
        }

        return heap.stream()
            .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Payment::amount).reversed())
            .toList();
    }

    public record Payment(String id, java.math.BigDecimal amount) {}
}

Example 5: Spliterator — Custom Batch Stream (Advanced)

package com.bank.batch;

import java.util.Spliterator;
import java.util.Spliterators;
import java.util.function.Consumer;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
import java.util.stream.StreamSupport;

public class BatchedPaymentSpliterator implements Spliterator<PaymentBatch> {

    private final PaymentSource source;
    private int offset;
    private final int batchSize;
    private final long estimatedTotal;

    public BatchedPaymentSpliterator(PaymentSource source, int batchSize) {
        this.source = source;
        this.batchSize = batchSize;
        this.estimatedTotal = source.totalCount();
    }

    @Override
    public boolean tryAdvance(Consumer<? super PaymentBatch> action) {
        if (offset >= estimatedTotal) return false;
        PaymentBatch batch = source.fetch(offset, batchSize);
        offset += batch.size();
        action.accept(batch);
        return true;
    }

    @Override
    public Spliterator<PaymentBatch> trySplit() {
        if (estimatedTotal - offset < batchSize * 2) return null;
        BatchedPaymentSpliterator split = new BatchedPaymentSpliterator(source, batchSize);
        split.offset = offset + (estimatedTotal - offset) / 2;
        long oldEnd = estimatedTotal;
        // simplified — production needs proper bounds
        return split;
    }

    @Override
    public long estimateSize() {
        return estimatedTotal - offset;
    }

    @Override
    public int characteristics() {
        return Spliterator.ORDERED | Spliterator.NONNULL | Spliterator.IMMUTABLE;
    }

    public static Stream<PaymentBatch> stream(PaymentSource source, int batchSize) {
        return StreamSupport.stream(
            new BatchedPaymentSpliterator(source, batchSize), false);
    }

    public interface PaymentSource {
        long totalCount();
        PaymentBatch fetch(int offset, int limit);
    }

    public record PaymentBatch(java.util.List<ReconciliationAggregator.Payment> payments) {
        int size() { return payments.size(); }
    }
}

Example 6: Parallel Stream — Safe vs Unsafe

package com.logistics.processor;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList;

public class ParallelPitfalls {

    // UNSAFE — ArrayList not thread-safe
    public List<String> unsafeParallelCollect(List<Shipment> shipments) {
        List<String> results = new ArrayList<>();
        shipments.parallelStream()
            .map(Shipment::id)
            .forEach(results::add);  // RACE CONDITION — lost updates
        return results;
    }

    // SAFE — use collect (thread-safe combiner)
    public List<String> safeParallelCollect(List<Shipment> shipments) {
        return shipments.parallelStream()
            .map(Shipment::id)
            .collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.toList());
    }

    // SAFE — concurrent collection (but slow for many writes)
    public List<String> safeButSlow(List<Shipment> shipments) {
        List<String> results = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
        shipments.parallelStream()
            .map(Shipment::id)
            .forEach(results::add);
        return results;
    }

    public record Shipment(String id) {}
}

Example 7: Exception Handling in Parallel Streams

package com.bank.imports;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public class ParallelImportProcessor {

    public record ProcessResult(String fileName, boolean success, String error) {}

    // Parallel + checked exception — wrap at element level
    public List<ProcessResult> processFiles(List<java.nio.file.Path> files) {
        return files.parallelStream()
            .map(path -> {
                try {
                    importFile(path);
                    return new ProcessResult(path.getFileName().toString(), true, null);
                } catch (Exception e) {
                    return new ProcessResult(path.getFileName().toString(), false, e.getMessage());
                }
            })
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
    }

    private void importFile(java.nio.file.Path path) throws Exception {
        // import logic
    }
}

Part 7: Production Usage

Stream Performance in Production

Profiling Workflow

1. PRODUCTION SYMPTOM
   "Nightly reconciliation exceeds SLA"

2. JFR / async-profiler ON STAGING (representative data)
   - CPU samples → hot methods
   - Allocation profiler → Integer, HashMap$Node, Pipeline classes

3. HYPOTHESIS
   "Boxing in mapToObj + parallel groupingBy on 8M rows"

4. JMH MICROBENCHMARK (confirm fix direction)
   mapToLong + sequential vs parallel groupingBy

5. FIX + REGRESSION TEST + DEPLOY
   Measure wall-clock in staging: 92 min → 38 min

6. PRODUCTION METRIC
   reconciliation_duration_seconds histogram

Production Patterns

// PATTERN 1: Presize + primitive + sequential (default for batch)
List<Payment> batch = new ArrayList<>(expectedSize);
// load batch...
long total = batch.stream().mapToLong(Payment::amountInPaise).sum();

// PATTERN 2: Custom ForkJoinPool for isolation
@Bean
public ForkJoinPool reconciliationPool() {
    return new ForkJoinPool(
        Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors(),
        ForkJoinPool.defaultForkJoinWorkerThreadFactory,
        null, true);
}

// PATTERN 3: Push aggregation to DB
@Query("SELECT p.currency, SUM(p.amount) FROM Payment p WHERE ... GROUP BY p.currency")
List<CurrencyTotal> sumByCurrency(...);

// PATTERN 4: Chunk processing — don't load 50M into one List
int offset = 0;
while (true) {
    List<Payment> chunk = repo.findChunk(offset, CHUNK_SIZE);
    if (chunk.isEmpty()) break;
    processChunk(chunk);
    offset += CHUNK_SIZE;
}

Micrometer Timing

@Service
public class ReconciliationService {

    private final MeterRegistry registry;

    public void reconcile(List<Payment> payments) {
        Timer.builder("reconciliation.duration")
            .tag("mode", "stream")
            .register(registry)
            .record(() -> doReconcile(payments));
    }
}

Check Why
Profile before optimizing Avoid premature parallelStream
Chunk large datasets Prevent OOM
Primitive streams for numeric aggregation Reduce GC
Custom pool for batch parallel Isolate from HTTP common pool
Avoid sorted() for top-K Use heap — O(n log k)
SQL for cross-table aggregation Push-down beats heap
JMH for micro-decisions Evidence not folklore
Monitor GC during batch G1 pause times correlate with stream allocs

Part 8: Microservice Usage

Streams in Microservice Architectures

Request Path vs Batch Path

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  REQUEST PATH (HTTP/Kafka single message)                        │
│  ─────────────────────────────────────────                       │
│  Sequential stream OK                                            │
│  NO parallelStream() — common pool contention                    │
│  Prefer DB query over in-memory filter of 1M rows                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  BATCH PATH (nightly job, Kafka batch listener)                  │
│  ─────────────────────────────────────────────                   │
│  Chunked load → primitive stream → optional custom parallel pool │
│  Metrics on duration + records/sec                               │
│  Idempotent — Lesson 5 exceptions on partial failure             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Kafka Batch Consumer — Stream Processing

@KafkaListener(topics = "payment-events", batch = "true")
public void consume(List<PaymentEvent> events) {
    Map<String, Long> countByType = events.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
            PaymentEvent::type,
            Collectors.counting()
        ));

    // Sequential — batch size typically 100-500, parallel overhead not worth it
    events.stream()
        .filter(PaymentEvent::requiresProcessing)
        .forEach(this::process);
}

API Pagination — Never Stream Entire Table

// ANTI-PATTERN
public List<PaymentDto> getAll() {
    return paymentRepository.findAll().stream()  // loads MILLIONS
        .map(mapper::toDto)
        .toList();
}

// CORRECT
public Page<PaymentDto> getPage(Pageable pageable) {
    return paymentRepository.findAll(pageable)
        .map(mapper::toDto);
}

Multi-Pod Batch Coordination

                    ┌─────────────────┐
                    │  Scheduler      │
                    │  (K8s CronJob)  │
                    └────────┬────────┘
                             │
           ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
           ▼                 ▼                 ▼
      Pod Job-0          Pod Job-1          Pod Job-2
      partition 0        partition 1        partition 2
      stream chunk       stream chunk       stream chunk

Each pod: sequential or parallel WITHIN chunk
Cross-pod: partition by key range or mod hash — NOT shared parallelStream

Pull (terminal drives) Push (publisher emits)

Part 9: Architect Perspective

Performance as Architecture Decision

The Stream vs SQL vs Spark Decision Tree

How much data?
  │
  ├─ < 100K rows in memory
  │     └─ Stream API — sequential default
  │
  ├─ 100K – 10M rows
  │     ├─ Fits in pod heap? → Chunked stream + primitive ops
  │     └─ Doesn't fit? → SQL aggregation or distributed processing
  │
  └─ > 10M rows
        ├─ Aggregation? → SQL / warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery)
        ├─ Transform ETL? → Spark / Flink
        └─ Real-time? → Kafka Streams / Flink

Cost Model — AWS EKS Example

OPTION A: Bigger pod (16 GB heap) + parallelStream
  1 × r6g.2xlarge = ~$0.40/hr × 2hr batch = $0.80/run

OPTION B: Push GROUP BY to RDS
  Same pod smaller (4 GB) + RDS compute
  Pod: $0.10/hr × 0.5hr = $0.05
  RDS: marginal query cost
  Often 10× cheaper + faster

ARCHITECT documents this in ADR (Architecture Decision Record)

ADR Template — Stream Processing Choice

## ADR-042: Payment Reconciliation Aggregation

### Context
8M payments/night, current in-memory groupingBy OOM on 4GB pods

### Decision
Move currency aggregation to Oracle SQL with covering index
Retain Java stream for in-chunk validation only (100K chunks)

### Consequences
+ Runtime 92min → 12min
+ Pod memory 4GB → 2GB
- More DB load — acceptable during batch window (02:00-04:00)

Performance Requirements in NFR Document

NFR Target Measurement
Reconciliation throughput ≥ 200K payments/min records_processed_total
API p99 (payment create) < 300ms No parallelStream in path
Batch GC pause < 500ms G1 Pause Young JFR
Heap utilization < 70% steady K8s metrics

When Streams Are the Wrong Abstraction

  1. Cross-service aggregation — use DB or OLAP
  2. Unbounded data — use reactive/Kafka Streams
  3. I/O per element — batch external calls first
  4. Transactional boundaries — imperative with explicit @Transactional chunks
  5. Hard real-time — not JVM streams

Sequential vs Parallel Stream

Criterion Sequential Parallel
Data size < 10K ✓ ✗
CPU-bound pure map/filter on 1M+ Maybe ✓ (custom pool)
groupingBy, sorted ✓ ✗ (usually)
HTTP request handler ✓ ✗

Goal Fast Collector Slow Alternative

Priority Action Typical Gain

Model Answer — Q13 (50M Reconciliation)

A: Never load 50M into one ArrayList. Partition by date or hash across K8s jobs or DB key ranges. Per chunk (100K–500K): load from DB with covering index, validate with sequential stream, push SUM/GROUP BY to SQL where possible. Use long paise for sums. If CPU-bound validation dominates and chunk is large, use dedicated ForkJoinPool (not common pool). Monitor heap and GC. Target metrics: records/sec, job duration, DB query time. ADR documenting SQL push-down vs in-memory trade-off.

Model Answer — Q8 (Common Pool)

A: parallelStream() uses ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), shared JVM-wide. Default parallelism = max(1, availableProcessors - 1). All libraries and application code sharing parallel streams compete for same workers. In a servlet container, batch parallelStream() can starve other parallel work and inflate request latency. Fix: custom ForkJoinPool for batch, or separate batch pods, or avoid parallel in request path.

Part 13: Common Mistakes

# Mistake Consequence Fix
1 parallelStream() by default Slower + contention Measure; sequential default
2 sorted().limit(K) on millions O(n log n) memory/time PriorityQueue top-K
3 Boxed map for sums GC storms mapToLong / mapToInt
4 forEach side effects in parallel Race conditions collect(toList())
5 Load entire table to stream OOM Pagination/chunking
6 I/O in map Thread pool exhaustion Batch fetch first
7 groupingBy parallel on huge data Slow combiner merge Sequential or SQL
8 Trust single nanoTime benchmark Wrong conclusions JMH
9 LinkedList + parallel Terrible splits ArrayList
10 Ignore DB for aggregation Heap death SQL GROUP BY
11 Common pool in API + batch p99 spikes Isolate pools
12 peek for transformation Hidden side effects Use map

sorted().limit() Trap

payments.stream()
    .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Payment::amount).reversed())
    .limit(5)
    .toList();
// Sorts ALL 5M — ~5M log 5M comparisons

// FIX — min-heap O(n log 5) ≈ O(n)

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Sequential by default — parallel only with JMH/profile evidence
  2. Primitive streams for numeric aggregation at scale
  3. Chunk large datasets — never findAll().stream()
  4. SQL for cross-row aggregation — streams for within-chunk logic
  5. Custom ForkJoinPool for batch jobs — isolate from common pool
  6. Top-K via PriorityQueue — not full sort
  7. Presize collections before collect when size known
  8. JMH for micro-decisions — profiler for system-level
  9. Metrics on batch jobs — records/sec, duration, GC
  10. Document in ADR when choosing stream vs SQL vs Spark
// Idiomatic high-performance batch sum
long totalPaise = chunk.stream()
    .filter(Payment::isSettled)
    .mapToLong(Payment::amountInPaise)
    .sum();

Part 16: Revision Notes

Quick Revision — Advanced Streams

DEFAULT: sequential stream
PARALLEL: only CPU-bound + large + splittable source (ArrayList)
          custom ForkJoinPool for batch — NOT in HTTP path

PRIMITIVE: mapToInt/Long/Double — avoid boxing
MONEY BATCH: long paise sum → BigDecimal at end

EXPENSIVE OPS:
  sorted()     → O(n log n) + O(n) mem — use PriorityQueue for top-K
  distinct()   → HashSet
  groupingBy parallel → slow combiner

FUSION: stateless ops fused single-pass; stateful buffer all

SPLITERATOR: SIZED|SUBSIZED = good parallel splits
  LinkedList = bad parallel

COLLECTOR: supplier → accumulator → combiner (parallel) → finisher

BENCHMARK: JMH not nanoTime; profiler for real hotspots

SCALE:
  chunk data → primitive stream → SQL for aggregation → Spark for billions

ANTI-PATTERNS:
  parallelStream in API, sorted().limit(K), findAll().stream(),
  forEach+mutate in parallel, I/O in map

Memory Mnemonic

"Chunk first, primitive second, SQL third, parallel last — with proof"

    │ Sequential      │  filter + mapToLong + sum (in-chunk)
    │ stream validate │
    └────────┬────────┘
             ▼
    ┌─────────────────┐
    │ DB: INSERT sum  │  or MERGE results
    │ or SQL GROUP BY │  ← architect preferred for aggregation
    └────────┬────────┘
             ▼
    ┌─────────────────┐
    │ Metrics:        │  reconciliation_records_total
    │ duration, GC    │  reconciliation_duration_seconds
    └─────────────────┘

Execution Flow — Parallel sum()

parallelStream().mapToInt().sum()

1. Submit root task to ForkJoinPool
2. Spliterator splits [0..500K] [500K..1M]
3. Worker-1: sum chunk A → partialSumA
4. Worker-2: sum chunk B → partialSumB
5. Combiner: partialSumA + partialSumB
6. Return final sum

Timeline:
Worker-1: ████████████████░░░░
Worker-2: ░░░░████████████████
          └─ work stealing if uneven ─┘

  • Thread lifecycle — NEW → RUNNABLE → BLOCKED → WAITING → TERMINATED
  • Race conditions — why forEach + ArrayList in parallel stream fails
  • Visibility — why volatile and synchronized exist (Lesson 8 JMM)

The custom ForkJoinPool you used in Lesson 6 is a thread pool. Lesson 7 explains what those threads actually do and why thread safety rules exist.

Part 1: Concept

What Is Multithreading?

A thread is the smallest unit of execution the OS scheduler can run within a process. A process is an independent program instance with its own memory space. Multiple threads within the same process share the heap and metaspace but each has its own stack and program counter.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         ONE JVM PROCESS (one pod)                        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  SHARED (all threads see same data)                                     │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ HEAP — Account objects, HashMap caches, payment lists            │   │
│  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
│  │ METASPACE — classes, static variables                          │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                          │
│  PER-THREAD (isolated)                                                  │
│  ┌─────────────┐  ┌─────────────┐  ┌─────────────┐  ┌─────────────┐   │
│  │  Thread-1   │  │  Thread-2   │  │  Thread-3   │  │  Thread-N   │   │
│  │  Stack      │  │  Stack      │  │  Stack      │  │  Stack      │   │
│  │  PC Register│  │  PC Register│  │  PC Register│  │  PC Register│   │
│  │  (HTTP req) │  │  (HTTP req) │  │  (Kafka)    │  │  (GC/JIT)   │   │
│  └─────────────┘  └─────────────┘  └─────────────┘  └─────────────┘   │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Process vs Thread

Aspect Process Thread
Memory Isolated address space Shares heap with siblings
Creation cost High (fork, new JVM) Low (~1 ms)
Communication IPC, network, files Shared memory (dangerous)
Failure isolation One crash ≠ other process Uncaught exception may kill thread; shared state corrupted
K8s mapping Usually 1 container = 1 JVM process Tomcat/Jetty thread pool per pod
Banking example payments-svc pod vs ledger-svc pod 200 Tomcat threads in one payment pod

Thread Lifecycle

                    start()
         NEW ─────────────────► RUNNABLE ◄──────────────┐
                                  │  ▲                   │
                     CPU schedule │  │ ready             │
                                  ▼  │                   │
                               RUNNING                    │
                                  │                       │
              ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐   │
              │                   │                   │   │
         synchronized         sleep/wait/         I/O   │
         block unavailable     join/park           block │
              │                   │                   │   │
              ▼                   ▼                   ▼   │
           BLOCKED             WAITING/TIMED_WAITING  ────┘
                                  │
                           run() completes or
                           uncaught exception
                                  │
                                  ▼
                             TERMINATED
State Meaning Banking Scenario
NEW Created, not started new Thread(r) before start()
RUNNABLE Eligible for CPU Waiting in Tomcat queue
RUNNING On CPU executing Calculating EMI
BLOCKED Waiting for monitor lock Two threads debiting same synchronized block
WAITING Waiting indefinitely lock.wait() for settlement notification
TIMED_WAITING Waiting with timeout Thread.sleep(200) retry backoff
TERMINATED Finished Request thread after response sent

Creating Threads — Three Ways

// 1. Extend Thread (avoid — breaks inheritance)
class PaymentWorker extends Thread {
    @Override
    public void run() {
        processPayments();
    }
}
new PaymentWorker().start();

// 2. Implement Runnable (preferred for task separation)
Runnable task = () -> processPayments();
new Thread(task).start();

// 3. ExecutorService (production — Lesson 10)
executor.submit(() -> processPayments());

Critical rule: Call start(), not run(). run() executes on the calling thread — no new thread created.

thread.start()  → JVM creates new thread → run() on new thread
thread.run()    → run() on CURRENT thread — common interview trap

Runnable vs Callable

Runnable Callable<V>
Method void run() V call()
Exceptions Cannot throw checked Can throw checked
Return value None Generic result
Use with Thread, ExecutorService.execute ExecutorService.submit
Example Fire-and-forget audit log Fetch FX rate, return BigDecimal 
Callable<BigDecimal> fxRateTask = () -> fxClient.getRate("USD", "INR");

Future<BigDecimal> future = executor.submit(fxRateTask);
BigDecimal rate = future.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);  // blocks until done or timeout

The Three Concurrency Bugs

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  1. RACE CONDITION    — outcome depends on interleaving timing   │
│  2. VISIBILITY        — thread A's write not seen by thread B    │
│  3. ATOMICITY VIOLATION — read-modify-write not indivisible     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Bug Example Symptom
Race condition Two threads credit same account without lock Lost update
Visibility boolean done = true without volatile Consumer thread loops forever
Atomicity balance = balance + 100 on shared long Partial/lost updates (64-bit on 32-bit; logical on all)

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why Multithreading Exists

Problem Single-Threaded Multithreaded
CPU idle during I/O Blocked on DB/network Other threads serve requests
Multi-core hardware Uses 1 core Uses all cores
Throughput 1 request at a time 200 concurrent HTTP requests
Responsiveness UI frozen (desktop) Background + foreground

Why Your Payment Pod Has 200 Threads

Tomcat default: maxThreads = 200

Each incoming HTTP request → 1 thread
  → validate payment
  → call ledger (I/O wait — thread BLOCKED)
  → call fraud (I/O wait)
  → respond

While thread waits on DB, CPU serves other requests
Without threads: serial processing → unacceptable latency at scale

Why Shared Memory Is Dangerous

Threads share heap → convenience + catastrophe:

Thread-1: read balance = 1000
Thread-2: read balance = 1000
Thread-1: write balance = 900  (debit 100)
Thread-2: write balance = 800  (debit 200)
Expected: 700
Actual: 800 or 900 — LOST UPDATE

Architect insight: Microservices reduce shared memory between services but inside one JVM Spring singletons + caches + parallel streams reintroduce it.

Why Java Exposes Threads Explicitly

Unlike Go (goroutines) or Erlang (processes), Java threads map closely to OS threads (pre-Virtual Threads). You must understand:
- Locking
- Visibility
- Pool sizing

Virtual Threads (Java 21) change the cost model but not the correctness rules — race conditions still exist.

Part 3: Internal Working

How the JVM Maps Java Threads to OS Threads

Java Thread object (heap)
        │
        ▼
JVM native thread (pthread on Linux)
        │
        ▼
OS scheduler (CFS on Linux)
        │
        ▼
CPU core execution

Thread Stack

Thread-1 Stack (default ~1 MB per thread on 64-bit Linux)
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│ processPayment() frame          │
│   local refs, primitives        │
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│ validate() frame                │
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│ Tomcat worker dispatch frame    │
└─────────────────────────────────┘

200 threads × 1 MB stack ≈ 200 MB just for stacks
Architect: thread count affects memory, not just CPU

synchronized — Monitor Lock

Every Java object has an intrinsic lock (monitor):

public void debit(BigDecimal amount) {
    synchronized (this) {
        if (balance.compareTo(amount) < 0) throw new InsufficientFundsException(...);
        balance = balance.subtract(amount);
    }
}

MONITOR (associated with Account instance)

Thread-1 enters synchronized(this):
  MONITOR acquired by Thread-1

Thread-2 enters synchronized(this):
  BLOCKED — waiting for monitor

Thread-1 exits block:
  MONITOR released
  Thread-2 → RUNNABLE → acquires MONITOR

Object Header — Mark Word (Lock State)

Object header Mark Word tracks lock state:
  01: unlocked
  00: lightweight lock (biased — optimization)
  10: heavyweight monitor (OS mutex)
  11: GC mark

Lock escalation: biased → thin → heavyweight under contention

wait() / notify() — Coordination

synchronized (settlementLock) {
    while (!settlementComplete) {
        settlementLock.wait();  // releases lock, enters WAITING
    }
    postToLedger();
}
// Another thread:
synchronized (settlementLock) {
    settlementComplete = true;
    settlementLock.notifyAll();
}

Must hold the lock before wait() — otherwise IllegalMonitorStateException.

Atomicity — Non-Atomic Operations

// Looks atomic — is NOT
balance = balance.subtract(amount);

// Bytecode:
// 1. getfield balance
// 2. invoke subtract
// 3. putfield balance
// Another thread can interleave between 1 and 3

Even count++ is three operations: read, increment, write.

Memory Visibility (Preview — Lesson 8 Deep Dive)

Thread-1 (CPU core 0)          Thread-2 (CPU core 1)
  balance = 500                   reads balance
  writes to CPU cache             reads STALE value from its cache
  may not flush to main memory    still sees 1000

Fixes: volatile, synchronized, java.util.concurrent atomic classes, final fields after construction.

Deadlock — Circular Wait

// Thread-1
synchronized (accountA) {
    synchronized (accountB) { transfer(); }
}

// Thread-2
synchronized (accountB) {
    synchronized (accountA) { transfer(); }
}

DEADLOCK CYCLE

Thread-1: holds A, waits for B
Thread-2: holds B, waits for A

Neither progresses — requires external kill or timeout

Banking fix: Lock ordering — always lock lower accountId first.

Account first = accountA.getId().compareTo(accountB.getId()) < 0 ? accountA : accountB;
Account second = first == accountA ? accountB : accountA;
synchronized (first) {
    synchronized (second) {
        // transfer
    }
}

Thread Memory Model (Simplified)

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         MAIN MEMORY (Heap)                               │
│  balance = ???  flag = ???  cache = HashMap                             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         ▲                    ▲                    ▲
         │ flush/load         │                    │
┌────────┴────────┐  ┌────────┴────────┐  ┌────────┴────────┐
│ Thread-1 Cache  │  │ Thread-2 Cache  │  │ Thread-3 Cache  │

└─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘

Without synchronization: no guarantee when writes become visible

volatile Memory Effect

private volatile boolean shutdown = false;

// Thread-1
shutdown = true;  // write flushed to main memory (happens-before)

// Thread-2
while (!shutdown) { /* work */ }  // reads fresh value from main memory
Construct Visibility Atomicity
Plain field No guarantee No for compound ops
volatile Yes Only single read/write
synchronized Yes Yes for guarded block
AtomicLong Yes Yes for CAS operations

Thread-Local Storage

private static final ThreadLocal<String> correlationId = new ThreadLocal<>();

// Each thread has its own copy — no sharing, no races
correlationId.set(requestId);
log.info("processing {}", correlationId.get());
correlationId.remove();  // CRITICAL in thread pools — prevent leak

Thread-1 ThreadLocal map:  correlationId → "req-001"
Thread-2 ThreadLocal map:  correlationId → "req-002"
Thread-3 ThreadLocal map:  (empty)

Used by: MDC in logging, SimpleDateFormat (not thread-safe), per-request context

Production leak: Thread pool reuses threads; ThreadLocal.remove() not called → old correlation IDs bleed into new requests.

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Threading Performance Trade-offs

Context Switch Cost

Thread A running on CPU
  → time slice expires or blocks on I/O
  → OS saves A's registers, loads B's state
  → cost: ~1–10 microseconds (can be higher)

Too many threads vs CPU cores:
  excessive context switching → "thrashing" → throughput drops

Sizing Thread Pools (Rule of Thumb — Refined in Lesson 10)

Workload Type Formula Payment API Example
CPU-bound threads ≈ cores Interest calculation batch
I/O-bound threads ≈ cores × (1 + wait/compute) HTTP → DB → Kafka
Mixed Measure under load Tomcat maxThreads tuning 
8 cores, I/O wait 90% of time:
  threads ≈ 8 × (1 + 9) = 80

Tomcat 200 threads on 4-core pod:
  may be OK for I/O-bound IF memory suffices
  monitor context switches and p99 latency

Lock Contention Impact

NO CONTENTION:
  synchronized block → biased lock → near-zero cost

HIGH CONTENTION:
  threads BLOCKED → OS mutex → microseconds to milliseconds
  p99 latency spikes

Architect: reduce shared mutable state > finer locks > lock-free structures

Scalability Impact

Approach Scales with pods? Thread safety burden
Stateless @Service Yes Low
synchronized singleton cache Poor per pod High
ConcurrentHashMap local cache Per pod OK Medium
Redis external cache Yes Low in JVM

Parallel Stream Revisited (Lesson 6)

parallelStream + shared ArrayList.add  → race (Lesson 6)
parallelStream + synchronized block per element → serializes → slower than sequential
parallelStream + thread-safe collect → correct

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Race Condition — Lost Update

package com.bank.concurrency.demo;

public class UnsafeCounter {
    private int count = 0;

    public void increment() {
        count++;  // NOT atomic
    }

    public int getCount() {
        return count;
    }
}

// 10 threads × 100_000 increments → often < 1_000_000

package com.bank.concurrency.demo;

public class SafeCounter {
    private final java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger count =
        new java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger(0);

    public void increment() {
        count.incrementAndGet();
    }

    public int getCount() {
        return count.get();
    }
}

Example 2: Banking Transfer — Lock Ordering Against Deadlock

package com.bank.ledger;

import java.math.BigDecimal;

public class TransferService {

    public void transfer(Account from, Account to, BigDecimal amount) {
        Account first = from.id().compareTo(to.id()) < 0 ? from : to;
        Account second = first == from ? to : from;

        synchronized (first) {
            synchronized (second) {
                from.debitInternal(amount);
                to.creditInternal(amount);
            }
        }
    }

    public static class Account {
        private final String id;
        private BigDecimal balance;

        Account(String id, BigDecimal balance) {
            this.id = id;
            this.balance = balance;
        }

        String id() { return id; }

        void debitInternal(BigDecimal amount) {
            balance = balance.subtract(amount);
        }

        void creditInternal(BigDecimal amount) {
            balance = balance.add(amount);
        }
    }
}

Example 3: Visibility — Shutdown Flag

package com.logistics.worker;

public class ShipmentPoller implements Runnable {

    private volatile boolean running = true;

    @Override
    public void run() {
        while (running) {
            pollCarrierApi();
        }
    }

    public void shutdown() {
        running = false;  // visible to poller thread immediately
    }

    private void pollCarrierApi() {
        // polling logic
    }
}

Example 4: Callable + Future — FX Rate Fetch

package com.bank.fx;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class FxRateService {

    private final ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);

    public BigDecimal getRateWithTimeout(String from, String to, long timeoutMs)
            throws TimeoutException, ExecutionException, InterruptedException {

        Callable<BigDecimal> task = () -> fetchFromExternalApi(from, to);

        Future<BigDecimal> future = executor.submit(task);
        try {
            return future.get(timeoutMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        } catch (TimeoutException e) {
            future.cancel(true);
            throw e;
        }
    }

    private BigDecimal fetchFromExternalApi(String from, String to) {
        // HTTP call
        return BigDecimal.ONE;
    }
}

Example 5: ThreadLocal — Correlation ID (MDC Pattern)

package com.bank.observability;

import org.slf4j.MDC;

public class CorrelationContext {

    private static final String CORRELATION_KEY = "correlationId";

    public static void set(String correlationId) {
        MDC.put(CORRELATION_KEY, correlationId);
    }

    public static String get() {
        return MDC.get(CORRELATION_KEY);
    }

    public static void clear() {
        MDC.remove(CORRELATION_KEY);  // MUST call in finally block in filters
    }
}

// Servlet filter pattern:
// try { CorrelationContext.set(id); chain.doFilter(); }
// finally { CorrelationContext.clear(); }

Example 6: Producer-Consumer (wait/notify)

package com.transport.booking.queue;

import java.util.LinkedList;
import java.util.Queue;

public class SeatWaitlist {

    private final Queue<String> queue = new LinkedList<>();
    private final int maxSize = 100;

    public synchronized void addPassenger(String passengerId) throws InterruptedException {
        while (queue.size() >= maxSize) {
            wait();
        }
        queue.offer(passengerId);
        notifyAll();
    }

    public synchronized String removePassenger() throws InterruptedException {
        while (queue.isEmpty()) {
            wait();
        }
        String passenger = queue.poll();
        notifyAll();
        return passenger;
    }
}

    java.time.Instant capturedAt
) {
    // Immutable — safe to share across threads without locks
    // Kafka consumers can pass to multiple handlers
}

Part 7: Production Usage

Multithreading in Production Java Services

Spring Boot + Tomcat Thread Model

Client HTTP Request
       │
       ▼
Tomcat Acceptor Thread (accepts connection)
       │
       ▼
Worker Thread from pool (maxThreads=200)
       │
       ▼
DispatcherServlet → @Controller → @Service (@Transactional)
       │
       ▼
Response returned — thread back to pool

Production config:

server:
  tomcat:
    threads:
      max: 200
      min-spare: 10
    accept-count: 100

Thread Safety Rules for @Service Beans

@Service  // SINGLETON — one instance, all threads share it
public class PaymentService {

    // SAFE — injected dependencies, stateless methods
    private final PaymentRepository repo;

    // UNSAFE — mutable instance field written by multiple threads
    // private int processedToday;

    // UNSAFE — mutable static
    // private static HashMap<String, Payment> cache = new HashMap<>();

    // SAFE — concurrent or external
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, Payment> idempotencyCache;
}

Detecting Deadlocks in Production

# jstack or kill -3 <pid>
jstack <payment-svc-pid> | grep -A 20 "Found one Java-level deadlock"

# JVM flag (dev/staging)
-XX:+PrintConcurrentLocks

Graceful Shutdown (K8s preStop)

@PreDestroy
public void shutdown() {
    poller.shutdown();           // volatile flag
    executor.shutdown();
    try {
        if (!executor.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
            executor.shutdownNow();
        }
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        executor.shutdownNow();
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

K8s sends SIGTERM → Spring Boot graceful shutdown → stop accepting new work → drain in-flight requests → exit.

Production Checklist

Check Why
@Service beans stateless Singleton shared across threads
No mutable static fields Race across all requests
ThreadLocal.remove() in filters Correlation ID leak
Lock ordering for multi-resource Prevent deadlock
InterruptedException → restore interrupt Clean pod shutdown
Thread pool sized and named Debugging, metrics
Avoid synchronized on hot path Contention kills p99
Use JFR for blocked threads Find lock bottlenecks

Technique Solves Does NOT Solve

Idempotency Store — Thread Safety

@Service
public class IdempotencyService {
    // Per-pod — NOT sufficient alone for multi-pod
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, PaymentResult> cache =
        new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public PaymentResult checkOrCompute(String key, Supplier<PaymentResult> supplier) {
        return cache.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> supplier.get());
    }
}

Multi-pod: Redis SETNX — cross-process thread safety equivalent.

Distributed Lock vs synchronized

IN-JVM:  synchronized(account)     — works within one pod only
CROSS-POD: Redis Redisson lock / DB row lock — Lesson 28 territory

Architect: payment debit needs DB transaction + unique constraint,
           not just synchronized block in Java

Part 9: Architect Perspective

Concurrency as Architecture Concern

Shared Mutable State — The Root Evil

Elimination hierarchy (prefer top):
  1. Immutable data (records, events)
  2. Thread-local context (MDC, request scope)
  3. Message passing (Kafka — no shared memory between services)
  4. Concurrent collections (ConcurrentHashMap)
  5. synchronized / locks
  6. Distributed locks (last resort for cross-pod)

Virtual Threads (Java 21) — Architect View

// Platform thread: ~1 MB stack, OS thread
// Virtual thread: ~few KB, mounted on carrier platform thread

Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()
    .submit(() -> callBlockingPaymentGateway());
Aspect Platform Threads Virtual Threads
Count Hundreds max practical Millions possible
Blocking I/O Ties up expensive thread Cheap — unmount during block
CPU-bound work Good Use platform threads
Correctness rules Race conditions apply Same — still shared heap

Architect decision: Virtual threads for I/O-heavy payment orchestration; still stateless services, still ConcurrentHashMap or DB for shared state.

Concurrency Models Comparison

Model Example Shared Memory?
Threads + locks Java classic Yes — heap
Actor model Akka Messages, no shared state
Event-driven Kafka consumers Partitions, offset state
Reactive WebFlux No blocking, event loop

ADR — Thread Pool Sizing

## ADR-058: Tomcat maxThreads = 100 (reduced from 200)

### Context
4-core pods, p99 latency spikes, 200 threads mostly BLOCKED on DB
Connection pool only 20 — thread count >> connections → queueing inside HikariCP

### Decision
maxThreads=100, HikariCP maxPoolSize=40, scale pods horizontally

### Rationale
Threads blocked waiting for connections don't increase throughput
More pods > more threads per pod

Synchronization Mechanism Selection

Mechanism Use When Avoid When
Immutability DTOs, events Mutable entity lifecycle
volatile Single flag, one writer Compound operations
synchronized Simple critical section, low contention Hot path high contention

Need Choice

Strategy Implementation
Lock ordering Always lock accountId lexicographically
Lock timeout lock.tryLock(5, SECONDS)
Avoid nested locks Coarse-grained or lock-free
Immutable data No locks needed
Single lock Simple but limits concurrency

  5. What is a race condition?

Senior Level

  1. What is deadlock? How do you prevent it in a transfer operation?
  2. Difference between synchronized and volatile?
  3. Why is ThreadLocal used? What is the leak risk?
  4. Is HashMap thread-safe? What do you use instead?
  5. What happens when multiple threads call increment() on a shared int?
  6. Explain wait(), notify(), and notifyAll().
  7. Why must InterruptedException restore the interrupt flag?

Staff / Architect Level

  1. How do you make a Spring @Service thread-safe?
  2. Tomcat 200 threads but HikariCP 20 connections — what happens?
  3. Virtual threads vs platform threads — when to use each?
  4. Design thread-safe idempotency for multi-pod payment service.
  5. How do you detect and resolve deadlocks in production?
  6. parallelStream + synchronized — discuss performance and correctness.
  7. Explain lock ordering for banking transfers between accounts A, B, C.
  8. Why is shared mutable state worse than more pods?

Model Answer — Q7 (synchronized vs volatile)

A: volatile ensures visibility — reads/writes go to main memory — and prohibits certain reorderings. It does not provide atomicity for compound operations like i++. synchronized provides both mutual exclusion (one thread at a time) and visibility (happens-before between release and acquire). Use volatile for independent single-writer flags. Use synchronized or Atomic* for read-modify-write sequences.

Model Answer — Q16 (Multi-Pod Idempotency)

A: In-JVM ConcurrentHashMap only protects within one pod. Multi-pod requires external store: Redis SET key NX EX 86400 before processing, or DB unique constraint on idempotency_key. On duplicate, return cached response. Java-level synchronized is irrelevant across pods. Thread safety is a distributed systems problem at this scale.

Part 13: Common Mistakes

# Mistake Consequence Fix
1 run() instead of start() No concurrency start()
2 Shared mutable @Service field Random corruption Stateless or concurrent structures
3 HashMap in multi-threaded service Infinite loop (JDK8+), data loss ConcurrentHashMap
4 No lock ordering on transfers Deadlock Order by accountId
5 volatile for count++ Still racy AtomicInteger
6 Forget ThreadLocal.remove() Wrong correlation IDs finally block
7 synchronized on String literal Unintended shared lock Private final lock object
8 Catch InterruptedException without restore Shutdown hangs Thread.currentThread().interrupt()
9 Assume parallelStream is thread-safe Races on shared collections collect()
10 Too many threads vs DB pool Connection starvation Align thread and pool sizes
11 wait() without while loop Spurious wakeup bugs while (!condition) wait()
12 Extend Thread instead of Runnable Poor OOP, single use Implement Runnable

synchronized(String) Trap

// DANGEROUS — same literal may intern to same lock
synchronized ("LOCK") { ... }

// BETTER
private final Object lock = new Object();
synchronized (lock) { ... }

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Prefer immutability — records, final fields, unmodifiable collections
  2. Stateless services — all state in DB/Redis/Kafka
  3. ExecutorService over raw Thread — managed lifecycle (Lesson 10)
  4. Consistent lock ordering — multi-resource operations
  5. ConcurrentHashMap for in-memory shared maps
  6. ThreadLocal + always remove() in pooled environments
  7. Align thread count with connection pool — threads ≠ throughput if blocked on pool
  8. Virtual threads for blocking I/O (Java 21) — not a substitute for correctness
  9. Test with stress tests — CountDownLatch + many threads (Lesson 9)
  10. Use DB constraints for financial invariants — not locks alone

Part 1: Concept

What Is the Java Memory Model?

The Java Memory Model (JMM) is a formal specification that defines:

  • When a write by one thread is visible to another thread
  • Which instruction reorderings the compiler and CPU may perform
  • What guarantees synchronized, volatile, and final provide

Without the JMM, multithreaded Java would be undefined behavior — your banking ledger could pass tests and fail in production on different hardware.

│                    JMM — WHO IS INVOLVED                                 │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  YOUR JAVA CODE                                                          │
│       │                                                                  │
│       ▼                                                                  │
│  COMPILER (javac + JIT)     — reorder, eliminate, cache in registers    │
│       │                                                                  │
│       ▼                                                                  │
│  CPU                        — store buffers, caches, speculative exec   │
│       │                                                                  │
│       ▼                                                                  │
│  MAIN MEMORY (Heap)         — shared truth (eventually)                 │
│                                                                          │
│  JMM = rules that make this stack predictable for correct programs       │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
