JMM Terminology Master Table

Term What Why It Matters
Main memory Shared heap where object fields live Source of truth — eventually
Working memory Thread's CPU cache / registers Fast but stale copies
Read Copy from main memory to working memory May read old value
Write Write to working memory, flush later Other threads may not see yet
Happens-before Ordering guarantee between actions If A hb B, B sees A's effects
Visibility When write becomes visible to other threads Core concurrency bug
Reordering Compiler/CPU changes execution order Breaks naive reasoning
Atomicity Operation appears indivisible volatile ≠ atomic for i++

Happens-Before Rules (Core)

If action A happens-before action B, then B observes everything A did.

Rule Description
Program order Within one thread, earlier statements hb later (with limits)
Monitor lock unlock on monitor M hb subsequent lock on M
volatile Write to volatile V hb subsequent read of V
Thread start thread.start() hb any action in started thread
Thread join All actions in thread T hb thread.join() returning
Transitivity If A hb B and B hb C, then A hb C
final fields Constructor end hb first read of final field (safe publication) 
TRANSITIVITY EXAMPLE
────────────────────

Thread-1: x = 1; volatileFlag = true;
Thread-2: reads volatileFlag == true → x == 1 guaranteed

volatile write hb volatile read → x=1 visible

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why the JMM Was Specified

The Problem Before JMM (Pre-Java 5)

// Double-checked locking — BROKEN without volatile (pre-JMM fix)
class Singleton {
    private static Singleton instance;

    static Singleton getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) {
            synchronized (Singleton.class) {
                if (instance == null) {
                    instance = new Singleton();  // REORDERED — partial object visible!
                }
            }
        }
        return instance;
    }
}

Without JMM guarantees: Another thread could see instance != null but fields still default values — partially constructed object.

Why CPUs Reorder Instructions

Layer Why Reorder Benefit
Compiler Dead code elimination, hoist invariant Faster single-threaded
CPU Pipeline, store buffer, cache Hide memory latency
CPU Speculative execution Branch prediction

Single-threaded: Reordering is invisible (as-if-serial semantics within thread).

Multi-threaded: Without synchronization, another thread sees the reordering — disaster.

Why Architects Must Understand JMM

SYMPTOM IN PRODUCTION:
  "Payment status shows COMPLETED but ledger entry is null"
  "Happens once per million under load"
  "Cannot reproduce locally"

ROOT CAUSE:
  Non-volatile flag OR unsafe publication of mutable object
  JIT + CPU reordering on multi-core AWS Graviton instances

FIX:
  volatile / synchronized / immutable / ConcurrentHashMap
  NOT "add more logging"

JMM vs Physical Memory

JMM is an ABSTRACT model — not literal hardware mapping
  "Working memory" = CPU cache + registers conceptually
  JVM and CPU cooperate to implement happens-before rules
  You reason in JMM terms; JVM implements with fences/barriers

Part 3: Internal Working

How Visibility and Reordering Work

The Visibility Problem — Step by Step

// Thread-1 (writer)              // Thread-2 (reader)
ready = true;                     while (!ready) { }
data = 42;                        print(data);

What you expect: Thread-2 exits loop, prints 42.

What can happen without synchronization:

REORDERING by compiler/CPU (Thread-1):
  data = 42 might be delayed
  ready = true might be visible to Thread-2 FIRST

Thread-2 sees ready=true, reads data=0 (default) → prints 0

OR: Thread-2 never sees ready=true (cached in CPU) → infinite loop

volatile Fixes Both Ordering and Visibility

private volatile boolean ready = false;
private int data = 0;

// Thread-1
data = 42;
ready = true;   // volatile write — flush prior writes, establish hb

// Thread-2
while (!ready) { }  // volatile read — sees true
// data == 42 guaranteed (hb chain)

volatile WRITE memory barrier:
  1. Flush all prior writes to main memory
  2. Invalidate other cores' cached copies on subsequent read

volatile READ memory barrier:
  1. Invalidate local cache
  2. Read fresh value from main memory
  3. Subsequent reads see writes that happened-before this volatile write

synchronized — Full Memory Semantics

synchronized (lock) {
    balance = balance.subtract(amount);
}

ON synchronized EXIT (unlock):
  All writes inside block flushed to main memory (release)

ON synchronized ENTER (lock):
  Invalidate cache, read fresh values (acquire)

Next thread acquiring same lock sees ALL prior writes

Instruction Reordering — Allowed vs Forbidden

int a = 0;
int b = 0;

// Thread-1                    // Thread-2
a = 1;                         b = 1;
print(b);                      print(a);
// Can print 0,0 without sync — both assignments reordered past prints
Without sync Possible outcomes
print(a), print(b) 0,0 or 1,0 or 0,1 or 1,1 — all possible

With proper synchronization: Outcomes constrained by happens-before.

Object Creation Reordering (Singleton)

instance = new Singleton();

// NOT atomic — conceptual steps:
// 1. allocate memory
// 2. construct object (init fields)
// 3. assign reference to instance

// CPU may reorder to: 1 → 3 → 2
// Another thread sees non-null instance with uninitialized fields

Fix:

private static volatile Singleton instance;  // volatile publish

static Singleton getInstance() {
    if (instance == null) {
        synchronized (Singleton.class) {
            if (instance == null) {
                instance = new Singleton();  // volatile write prevents reorder
            }
        }
    }
    return instance;
}

Modern alternative: static holder idiom or enum singleton — no DCL needed.

final Fields — Safe Publication

public final class PaymentSnapshot {
    private final String paymentId;
    private final BigDecimal amount;

    public PaymentSnapshot(String id, BigDecimal amount) {
        this.paymentId = id;
        this.amount = amount;
    }
    // After constructor completes, any thread sees fully initialized fields
    // without synchronization (JMM final field guarantee)
}

CONSTRUCTOR COMPLETION happens-before
  first read of PaymentSnapshot reference by another thread

Safe to publish immutable record to Kafka consumer threads without extra sync

Program Counter (PC Register)

Each thread has its own PC — points to current bytecode instruction

Thread-1 PC → PaymentService.process() line 47 bytecode index 12
Thread-2 PC → FraudService.evaluate() line 22 bytecode index 5

If Thread-2 crashes, stack trace shows PC-derived line numbers

Stack Frame — What's Thread-Private

Thread Stack — processPayment() frame
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Local Variable Table                │
│   paymentId (reference) ──► heap    │
│   amount (primitive long on stack)  │
│ Operand Stack                       │
│   [ intermediate calc values ]    │
│ Frame Data                          │
│   ref to constant pool              │
│   return address                    │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘

Another thread CANNOT see your local primitives or local refs
They CAN see objects on heap that your refs point to — shared mutation

Metaspace vs Heap

Metaspace Heap
Stores Class metadata, method bytecode, static field refs Object instances
GC Class unloading (rare) Object GC (constant)
OOM Metaspace OOM — classloader leak Heap OOM — object retention
Thread safety Class loading has locks Object fields need app-level sync
Banking example PaymentService.class metadata Payment instances 
static final Map<String, String> ERROR_CODES = Map.of(...);
// Reference in Metaspace (static) → Map object on Heap
// Map is immutable — thread-safe

Part 4: Memory View

Complete Memory Diagram — Two Threads, One Account

MAIN MEMORY (HEAP)
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Account object @ 0x7a00                                           │
│   balance: ref ──► BigDecimal "1000.00"                          │
│   status: ref ──► "ACTIVE"                                        │
│   lock: monitor (in Mark Word of object header)                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         ▲                              ▲
         │ flush on unlock              │ may be stale
         │                              │
┌────────┴────────────┐        ┌─────────┴───────────┐
│ Thread-1 (HTTP)     │        │ Thread-2 (HTTP)     │
│ Stack:              │        │ Stack:              │
│  local amount=100   │        │  local amount=200   │
│ Working memory:     │        │ Working memory:     │
│  cached balance?    │        │  cached balance?    │
│  (stale without sync)        │  (stale without sync)│
└─────────────────────┘        └─────────────────────┘

volatile Variable Memory Path

HEAP: volatile boolean shutdown = false

Thread-1 core:
  shutdown = true
    → store buffer → L1 cache → ... → eventually main memory
    → volatile semantics: IMMEDIATE visibility to other threads

Thread-2 core:
  while (!shutdown)
    → each read goes to main memory (or invalidated cache line)
    → sees true, exits loop

Object Header — Mark Word and Lock

Object layout (64-bit compressed oops, simplified):

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Mark Word (64 bits)                              │
│   hashCode | GC age | lock state | thread ID    │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Klass pointer → Metaspace (Account.class)      │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Instance fields (references, primitives)         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Lock in Mark Word:
  unbiased → biased (single thread) → thin lock → fat lock (OS mutex)

Memory Impact Summary

Construct Storage Cross-Thread Visibility
Local primitive Stack Not visible (isolated)
Local object ref Stack Ref private; object on heap shared
Instance field Heap Needs sync/volatile/final rules
static field Metaspace ref + Heap object Shared — all threads
volatile field Heap Immediate visibility guarantee
final field Heap Safe after construction complete
ThreadLocal Thread's hidden map Isolated per thread

Part 5: Performance Analysis

JMM Synchronization Cost

volatile Performance

Aspect Cost
Single read/write ~nanoseconds + memory fence
vs plain field Slightly slower — prevents cache optimization
vs synchronized Much cheaper — no lock acquisition
Hot path flag Acceptable — use for infrequent writes, frequent reads

Don't mark everything volatile — restricts compiler optimizations.

synchronized Performance

UNCONTENDED:
  Biased locking → often zero overhead (single thread owns lock)

MILD CONTENTION:
  Thin spin → CAS on Mark Word

HEAVY CONTENTION:
  Inflated monitor → OS mutex → microseconds + context switch
  p99 latency victim in payment API

False Sharing (Advanced)

CPU cache line ≈ 64 bytes

Thread-1 updates counterA (byte 0 of cache line)
Thread-2 updates counterB (byte 8 of same cache line)

Both cores invalidate same cache line → performance collapse

Fix: @Contended (JVM internal) or padding between hot fields
Architect: rare in business logic; matters in HFT / high-frequency counters

Scalability Impact

Pattern Multi-Core Scaling Memory Visibility
Immutable messages Linear Safe publication via final
volatile flag Good for 1 flag Coherent shutdown
synchronized hot method Poor — serializes Correct but bottleneck
ConcurrentHashMap Good read scaling Segment/node CAS
Lock-free CAS loops Good under low contention Atomic* classes

Reordering and Performance — Why JVM Does It

Single-threaded program:
  Compiler reorders to hide memory latency
  Result identical to program order (as-if-serial)

You only pay synchronization cost WHERE you need cross-thread guarantees
Default: no sync = maximum performance, zero cross-thread guarantees

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Broken Visibility — Ping-Pong Flag

package com.bank.concurrency.jmm;

public class BrokenVisibility {
    private boolean ready = false;  // NOT volatile
    private int data = 0;

    public void writer() {
        data = 42;
        ready = true;
    }

    public void reader() {
        while (!ready) {
            // may spin forever — ready cached in CPU register
        }
        System.out.println(data);  // may print 0 — reordering
    }
}

package com.bank.concurrency.jmm;

public class FixedVisibility {
    private volatile boolean ready = false;
    private int data = 0;

    public void writer() {
        data = 42;
        ready = true;  // hb edge to reader
    }

    public void reader() {
        while (!ready) { }
        System.out.println(data);  // always 42
    }
}

Example 2: Safe Publication — Immutable Payment Event

package com.bank.payments.events;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.Instant;

public final class PaymentCompletedEvent {
    private final String paymentId;
    private final String accountId;
    private final BigDecimal amount;
    private final Instant completedAt;

    public PaymentCompletedEvent(String paymentId, String accountId,
                                 BigDecimal amount, Instant completedAt) {
        this.paymentId = paymentId;
        this.accountId = accountId;
        this.amount = amount;
        this.completedAt = completedAt;
    }

    // getters only — publish reference to Kafka handler threads safely
    public String paymentId() { return paymentId; }
    public BigDecimal amount() { return amount; }
}

Example 3: Unsafe Publication of Mutable Object

package com.bank.concurrency.jmm;

public class UnsafePublication {
    private Holder holder;

    public void initialize() {
        holder = new Holder(42);  // another thread may see partial construction
    }

    public int read() {
        if (holder != null) {
            return holder.value;  // may see 0
        }
        return -1;
    }

    static class Holder {
        int value;
        Holder(int v) { this.value = v; }
    }
}

// FIX: make Holder final fields, or volatile Holder ref, or synchronize

Example 4: volatile vs AtomicLong

package com.bank.metrics;

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;

public class PaymentMetrics {

    // volatile does NOT make increment atomic
    private volatile long processedCount = 0;

    public void incrementUnsafe() {
        processedCount++;  // read-modify-write — still racy
    }

    private final AtomicLong safeCount = new AtomicLong(0);

    public void incrementSafe() {
        safeCount.incrementAndGet();  // CAS loop — atomic + visibility
    }

    public long getCount() {
        return safeCount.get();
    }
}

Example 5: Happens-Before via Thread Join

package com.logistics.batch;

public class BatchCoordinator {

    private int totalProcessed = 0;

    public void runBatch() throws InterruptedException {
        Thread worker = new Thread(() -> {
            totalProcessed = computeTotal();  // writes in worker
        });
        worker.start();
        worker.join();  // hb: worker actions hb join return
        report(totalProcessed);  // guaranteed to see computeTotal result
    }

    private int computeTotal() { return 10_000; }
    private void report(int total) { /* ... */ }
}

Example 6: Double-Checked Locking — Correct (Educational)

package com.bank.config;

public class FxRateCache {
    private static volatile FxRateCache instance;

    private FxRateCache() {}

    public static FxRateCache getInstance() {
        FxRateCache local = instance;
        if (local == null) {
            synchronized (FxRateCache.class) {
                local = instance;
                if (local == null) {
                    instance = local = new FxRateCache();
                }
            }
        }
        return local;
    }
}

// PREFERRED in modern Java:
public class FxRateCacheHolder {
    private static class Holder {
        static final FxRateCache INSTANCE = new FxRateCache();
    }
    public static FxRateCache getInstance() {
        return Holder.INSTANCE;  // class init is synchronized by JVM
    }
}

Example 7: volatile Shutdown Hook Pattern

package com.transport.scheduler;

public class DepartureScheduler implements Runnable {

    private volatile boolean running = true;

    @Override
    public void run() {
        while (running) {
            processDepartures();
        }
    }

    public void stop() {
        running = false;
    }

    private void processDepartures() { /* ... */ }
}

Exercise 1

Demonstrate the 0,0 print outcome with two threads writing/reading a and b without synchronization. Fix with CountDownLatch for observation and volatile/synchronized for fix.

Exercise 2

Explain why ConcurrentHashMap is safe without external sync but iterating it during concurrent put is weakly consistent.

Part 7: Production Usage

JMM in Production Systems

Spring Singleton + Field Visibility

@Service
public class RateLimiter {
    // WRONG — no visibility guarantee between @Scheduled writer and HTTP reader
    // private boolean circuitOpen = false;

    private volatile boolean circuitOpen = false;

    @Scheduled(fixedRate = 5000)
    public void healthCheck() {
        circuitOpen = !externalApi.isHealthy();
    }

    public boolean isCircuitOpen() {
        return circuitOpen;
    }
}

Kafka Consumer — Safe Handoff

// SAFE: publish immutable record after parse
PaymentEvent event = parse(record);  // all final fields
handler.process(event);  // safe across worker threads if event immutable

// UNSAFE: reuse mutable parser buffer across records without sync
// MutableParseBuffer buffer; // single instance field — race between partitions if parallel

Logging MDC and Thread Boundaries

// MDC is ThreadLocal — NOT propagated to:
//   - @Async threads (unless TaskDecorator configured)
//   - parallelStream workers
//   - CompletableFuture default pool (Lesson 11)

@Async
public void auditAsync(Payment payment) {
    // correlationId may be MISSING — visibility of context lost across threads
}

Fix: Explicitly pass correlationId as method parameter (happens-before via parameter passing in same thread, or message envelope across threads).

Production Debugging Visibility Bugs

Symptom Likely JMM Cause Investigation
Rare wrong balance Unsynchronized read/write JFR blocked threads, code review shared fields
Infinite loop on shutdown Non-volatile flag Find while(!flag) patterns
Partial config visible Unsafe publication Make config immutable or volatile ref
Works on x86, fails on ARM Weaker memory model on ARM AWS Graviton — test on same arch

Note: x86 has stronger hardware memory model than ARM — bugs hide on Intel, appear on Graviton.

Production Checklist

Check Why
Shutdown flags volatile Clean K8s termination
Immutable cross-thread messages Safe publication
No unsynchronized mutable singleton fields Visibility + races
@Async MDC propagation Observability
Test on ARM if prod is Graviton JMM bugs architecture-dependent
Avoid DCL without volatile Partial object
Use java.time immutable types Thread-safe by design

Part 8: Microservice Usage

JMM Across Service Boundaries

In-JVM vs Cross-Service Memory

WITHIN ONE JVM (JMM applies):
  Thread-1 writes to HashMap
  Thread-2 reads HashMap
  → Need ConcurrentHashMap or sync

ACROSS MICROSERVICES (JMM does NOT apply):
  payment-svc writes to its heap
  ledger-svc has separate heap
  → Communication via HTTP/Kafka/DB only
  → Consistency = distributed systems problem (Lesson 43)

Per-Pod Cache Coherence

Pod-1 JVM                          Pod-2 JVM
┌─────────────────┐                ┌─────────────────┐
│ local Caffeine  │                │ local Caffeine  │
│ cache (heap)    │   NO shared    │ cache (heap)    │
│                 │   memory       │                 │
└─────────────────┘                └─────────────────┘
         │                                  │
         └──────────── Redis ───────────────┘
              (external coherence)

JMM guarantees end at JVM boundary. Multi-pod cache invalidation is not a volatile fix — it's Redis pub/sub or TTL.

Event-Driven Safe Publication

Producer thread (Kafka producer):
  PaymentEvent event = new PaymentEvent(...);  // immutable
  serializer.serialize(event);
  send to broker

Consumer thread (different JVM, different pod):
  deserialize → new PaymentEvent on consumer heap
  process

No shared memory — each JVM has own JMM domain

Virtual Threads (Java 21) and JMM

Virtual threads share same heap as platform threads
  SAME JMM rules apply
  volatile, synchronized, ConcurrentHashMap — unchanged

Mount/unmount on carrier thread does NOT change visibility semantics

Part 9: Architect Perspective

JMM as Architecture Foundation

Safe Publication Patterns — Decision Tree

Publishing object to another thread?
  │
  ├─ Immutable (all final fields, no escape of mutable refs)?
  │     └─ YES → safe after constructor (JMM final rule)
  │
  ├─ Mutable object?
  │     ├─ Publish via volatile reference?
  │     ├─ Publish inside synchronized block?
  │     └─ Use concurrent collection built-in publication?
  │
  └─ Primitive flag?
        └─ volatile boolean / AtomicBoolean

Why Immutability Is Default Architect Choice

Mutable Shared State Immutable Message
Requires JMM reasoning JMM-safe by construction
Lock contention Lock-free handoff
Hard to test Deterministic
Breaks across refactors Kafka-friendly

Banking: PaymentCompletedEvent record across services; mutable Account entity only inside @Transactional boundary.

Happens-Before in Distributed Systems (Analogy)

JMM (Single JVM) Distributed (Lesson 43)
volatile write/read Kafka commit offset after process
synchronized Distributed lock
final safe publication Immutable event on log
No guarantee without sync Eventual consistency without coordination

ADR — Immutable Events Only on Kafka

## ADR-071: Kafka messages must be immutable records

### Context
Bugs from handler mutating shared event object reused by parser

### Decision
Parse to new record per message; handlers receive read-only view

### JMM Rationale
Safe publication via final fields; eliminates cross-handler races

Graviton / ARM Deployment

If migrating payment-svc from Intel to AWS Graviton:
  - Re-run concurrency stress tests
  - JMM bugs latent on x86 may surface
  - No code change if correctly synchronized
  - Incorrect code: "works for years" then fails

Model Answer — Q9 (DCL without volatile)

A: new Singleton() is not atomic. Steps allocate memory, initialize fields, assign reference. Compiler/CPU may reorder assignment before initialization. Thread B can read non-null instance with default field values. volatile write to instance establishes happens-before: all writes before volatile write are visible after volatile read. Modern code should use static holder or enum singleton instead.

Model Answer — Q15 (Graviton vs Intel)

A: Java JMM is the specification — correct code works on all platforms. However, incorrect code relying accidentally on strong hardware ordering on x86 may never show bugs in dev. ARM has weaker hardware memory model — reorderings more visible. Graviton migration exposes latent missing volatile/sync bugs. Fix code to JMM spec, don't rely on hardware luck.

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Immutable messages for cross-thread and cross-service handoff
  2. volatile for simple flags only — shutdown, circuit open
  3. Atomic* for counters and CAS — not volatile long++
  4. synchronized for multi-field invariants — keep blocks small
  5. Holder idiom / enum for singletons — not DCL
  6. Final fields on all immutable DTO fields
  7. ConcurrentHashMap — not Collections.synchronizedMap + iteration
  8. Pass correlation ID explicitly across async boundaries
  9. Stress test on production CPU architecture (Graviton)
  10. Reason at JMM level — then choose simplest correct tool

Part 16: Revision Notes

Quick Revision — Java Memory Model

AREAS:
  Stack — per thread, locals, frames
  Heap — shared objects
  Metaspace — class metadata, static refs
  PC — current instruction per thread

JMM: when writes visible across threads

HAPPENS-BEFORE:
  program order (intra-thread, limited)
  unlock → lock (same monitor)
  volatile write → volatile read
  thread.start() → thread actions
  thread actions → join() return
  final field ctor complete → first read of ref

REORDERING: compiler + CPU — safe single-thread, dangerous multi-thread

volatile: visibility + ordering, NOT i++
synchronized: visibility + atomicity in block
final fields: safe publication of immutable object

DCL: broken without volatile — use holder/enum

SAFE PUBLICATION:
  immutable + final fields
  volatile reference write
  inside synchronized

ARM/Graviton: weaker HW — latent bugs surface

JMM ends at JVM boundary — microservices need Kafka/DB consistency

Memory Mnemonic

"Stack is private, heap is shared, volatile publishes, final immutably declares"

Part 1: Concept

What Are Java Concurrency Utilities?

The java.util.concurrent (JUC) package provides battle-tested abstractions for thread coordination, atomic operations, and locks — all implemented on top of the Java Memory Model (Lesson 8).

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              java.util.concurrent — MAJOR COMPONENTS                     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  ATOMICS          LOCKS              COORDINATION         COLLECTIONS     │
│  ────────         ─────              ─────────────        ───────────     │
│  AtomicInteger    ReentrantLock      CountDownLatch       ConcurrentHashMap│
│  AtomicLong       ReadWriteLock      CyclicBarrier        CopyOnWriteArrayList│
│  AtomicReference  StampedLock        Semaphore            BlockingQueue   │
│  LongAdder        (vs synchronized)  Phaser               ConcurrentLinkedQueue│
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why Not Just synchronized?

synchronized JUC Utilities
Built-in, simple More features (tryLock, timeout, fairness)
Single wait set per monitor Multiple Condition objects per lock
No try/fail semantics tryLock(5, SECONDS)
Read and write serialize together ReadWriteLock — concurrent reads
Hard to coordinate N threads CountDownLatch, CyclicBarrier, Phaser

Master Table — Concurrency Utilities Overview

Utility Purpose Thread Safety Blocking? Reusable? Banking Example
AtomicInteger Lock-free counter Yes (CAS) No (spin) Yes Payment attempt counter
AtomicReference Atomic ref swap Yes (CAS) No Yes Compare-and-set config
LongAdder High-contention sum Yes No Yes Metrics under load
ReentrantLock Explicit mutex Yes Yes Yes Transfer with tryLock timeout
ReadWriteLock Many readers / one writer Yes Yes Yes FX rate cache
Semaphore Permit-based access Yes Yes Yes Limit mainframe connections
CountDownLatch Wait for N events Yes Yes No (one-shot) Wait for 5 batch files
CyclicBarrier N threads rendezvous Yes Yes Yes All hubs report before dispatch
Phaser Multi-phase coordination Yes Yes Yes Multi-stage settlement pipeline
ConcurrentHashMap Thread-safe map Yes Partial Yes Idempotency cache per pod

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why java.util.concurrent Was Added (Java 5, 2006)

Before JUC Pain JUC Solution
synchronized + wait/notify only Error-prone, coarse Explicit locks + Conditions
Vector, Hashtable Full-table lock Fine-grained concurrent collections
Roll-your-own spin locks Incorrect CAS usage Atomic* classes
Ad-hoc thread coordination Race on custom counters Latches, barriers, semaphores

Why Architects Standardize on JUC

CUSTOM CODE (dangerous):
  while (!done) { Thread.sleep(100); }  // busy/wait — wrong semantics

JUC (correct):
  CountDownLatch latch = new CountDownLatch(5);
  // workers countDown()
  latch.await();  // happens-before when count hits 0

In banking audits: "How do you coordinate settlement batches?" — answer with named JUC primitives, not home-grown flags.

Relationship to JMM (Lesson 8)

All JUC utilities establish happens-before edges:

AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()  → volatile-like visibility for operation
ReentrantLock.unlock()           → hb subsequent lock() by another thread
CountDownLatch.await() return    → hb all prior countDown() calls

You don't implement memory fences — JUC does it correctly.

Part 3: Internal Working

Atomic Classes — Compare-And-Swap (CAS)

CAS Operation

CAS(memoryLocation, expectedValue, newValue):
  atomically:
    if memoryLocation == expectedValue:
      memoryLocation = newValue
      return true
    else:
      return false  // someone else changed it — retry

Thread-1: read count=5
Thread-2: CAS(5→6) SUCCESS, count=6
Thread-1: CAS(5→6) FAIL (expected 5, actual 6)
Thread-1: read count=6, retry CAS(6→7) SUCCESS

AtomicInteger Internals (Simplified)

public final int incrementAndGet() {
    return unsafe.getAndAddInt(this, valueOffset, 1) + 1;
    // or CAS loop on value field (volatile int)
}

AtomicInteger object (heap):
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│ volatile int value              │  ← CAS target
└─────────────────────────────────┘

No monitor lock — threads spin-retry on contention
Under extreme contention: LongAdder stripes across cells (Lesson 9)

ABA Problem (AtomicReference)

Thread-1: reads ref=A
Thread-2: CAS A→B, then CAS B→A
Thread-1: CAS A→C succeeds — but object state changed in between

Fix: AtomicStampedReference (version stamp)
Rare in business apps; matters in lock-free data structures

ReentrantLock Internals

ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

lock.lock();
try {
    // critical section
} finally {
    lock.unlock();  // MUST be in finally
}

ReentrantLock (extends AbstractQueuedSynchronizer — AQS):

State: 0 = unlocked, 1 = locked (or hold count for reentrant)

lock():
  CAS state 0→1 success → acquired
  else → enqueue thread in CLH queue → park (OS)

unlock():
  state 1→0 → unpark next waiter

REENTRANT: same thread can lock again (hold count++)

ReadWriteLock

ReadWriteLock rwLock = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();

// Many readers OR one writer — not both

readLock().lock();   // shared — multiple threads OK
readLock().unlock();

writeLock().lock();  // exclusive — blocks all readers and writers
writeLock().unlock();

State encoding (AQS):
  high 16 bits = read hold count
  low 16 bits = write hold count

FX rate cache:
  50 threads read rate concurrently
  1 thread updates rate every 5 min — write lock brief

Semaphore

Semaphore permits = new Semaphore(10);  // max 10 concurrent

permits.acquire();   // decrement, block if 0
try {
    callLegacyMainframe();
} finally {
    permits.release();  // increment
}

Semaphore = shared pool of permits
NOT reentrant mutex — same thread can acquire multiple permits

Use: connection throttling, rate limiting (coarse), resource pools

CountDownLatch — One-Shot Gate

CountDownLatch latch = new CountDownLatch(3);

// Worker threads:
latch.countDown();  // 3 → 2 → 1 → 0

// Coordinator:
latch.await();  // blocks until count = 0
// ONE-SHOT — count cannot reset

Coordinator thread                    Worker threads
      │                                      │
      │ await() BLOCKED                      │ process file 1, countDown()
      │                                      │ process file 2, countDown()
      │                                      │ process file 3, countDown()
      │◄──────── count hits 0 ──────────────│
      │ proceed (hb all worker work)         │

CyclicBarrier — Reusable Rendezvous

CyclicBarrier barrier = new CyclicBarrier(3, () -> mergeResults());

// Each of 3 hub threads:
processLocalManifest();
barrier.await();  // all 3 must arrive before any proceeds
// optional barrier action runs once when 3rd arrives

Hub-A ──► await() ──┐
Hub-B ──► await() ──┼──► all arrived → barrier action → release all
Hub-C ──► await() ──┘

REUSABLE for next cycle (unlike CountDownLatch)
BrokenBarrierException if one thread fails/timeout

Phaser — Flexible Multi-Phase

Phaser phaser = new Phaser(3);  // 3 registered parties

// Phase 1: ingest
ingest();
phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance();

// Phase 2: validate
validate();
phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance();

// Phase 3: publish
publish();
phaser.arriveAndDeregister();

Phaser advantages over CyclicBarrier:
  - dynamic party count (register/deregister)
  - multiple phases without new object
  - per-phase arrival tracking

Settlement: debit phase → credit phase → notification phase

Part 4: Memory View

Memory Layout of Concurrent Structures

AtomicInteger vs synchronized Counter

synchronized counter:
  Thread blocked → park → OS scheduler → context switch
  Memory: monitor in object Mark Word

AtomicInteger:
  Threads spin on CAS in user space (no OS mutex if low contention)
  Memory: volatile int on heap — cache line bouncing under extreme contention

LongAdder — Striped Cells (High Contention)

LongAdder:
┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐
│ Cell[0]  │  │ Cell[1]  │  │ Cell[2]  │  ...
│ sum +=   │  │ sum +=   │  │ sum +=   │
└──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘
     ▲              ▲
  Thread-1       Thread-2
  (different cells → less cache line contention)

sum() = base + cell[0] + cell[1] + ...  (not atomic snapshot — OK for metrics)

ConcurrentHashMap — Segment/Node CAS (JDK 8+)

Similar to HashMap but:
  put: CAS on bucket head OR synchronized on first node
  get: usually no lock (volatile reads)
  size: LongAdder-style counter

Per-bucket locking → better than Hashtable full lock

Lock Queue Memory

ReentrantLock wait queue (AQS CLH queue):
  Node objects on heap per waiting thread
  Under heavy lock contention: many Node allocations + park/unpark

Architect: if lock queue grows — contention problem, not "add more threads"

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Utility Performance Characteristics

Utility Low Contention High Contention Best Use
AtomicInteger Excellent Good Counters, stats
LongAdder Excellent Excellent Metrics aggregation
synchronized Good (biased) Poor Simple critical sections
ReentrantLock Good Moderate tryLock, Conditions
ReadWriteLock Great for read-heavy Write blocks all Read-mostly caches
Semaphore Good Moderate Throttling
CountDownLatch One-time cost N/A Startup coordination

Atomic vs synchronized for Counter

1 thread:     Atomic ≈ synchronized (both fast)
4 threads:    Atomic often faster (no park)
32 threads incrementing same AtomicInteger:
              cache line bouncing — consider LongAdder

ReadWriteLock — When It Helps

Read:Write ratio 100:1, read hold 1μs, write hold 10μs
  ReadWriteLock: high throughput
  synchronized: every read serializes — bottleneck

Write-heavy workload:
  ReadWriteLock overhead NOT worth it — use simple lock

Scalability Impact

Pattern Scales Risk
LongAdder metrics per pod Linear with cores Approximate sum()
Semaphore(20) to mainframe Protects downstream Too low → starvation; too high → overload
CountDownLatch batch join Single coordinator await() blocks thread — OK in batch job
ConcurrentHashMap idempotency Per-pod only Multi-pod needs Redis

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Atomic Classes — Payment Metrics

package com.bank.metrics;

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder;

public class PaymentMetrics {

    private final AtomicInteger declinedCount = new AtomicInteger(0);
    private final LongAdder totalAmountPaise = new LongAdder();

    public void recordDeclined() {
        declinedCount.incrementAndGet();
    }

    public void recordAmount(long paise) {
        totalAmountPaise.add(paise);
    }

    public int getDeclinedCount() {
        return declinedCount.get();
    }

    public long getTotalAmountPaise() {
        return totalAmountPaise.sum();  // approximate under concurrent add
    }
}

Example 2: ReentrantLock with tryLock — Deadlock Avoidance

package com.bank.ledger;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

public class SafeTransferService {

    public boolean transferWithTimeout(Account from, Account to,
                                       BigDecimal amount, long timeoutMs)
            throws InterruptedException {

        if (!from.lock().tryLock(timeoutMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
            return false;
        }
        try {
            if (!to.lock().tryLock(timeoutMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
                return false;
            }
            try {
                if (from.balance().compareTo(amount) < 0) {
                    throw new InsufficientFundsException(from.id());
                }
                from.debit(amount);
                to.credit(amount);
                return true;
            } finally {
                to.lock().unlock();
            }
        } finally {
            from.lock().unlock();
        }
    }

    public static class Account {
        private final String id;
        private BigDecimal balance;
        private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

        public ReentrantLock lock() { return lock; }
        public String id() { return id; }
        public BigDecimal balance() { return balance; }
        void debit(BigDecimal amt) { balance = balance.subtract(amt); }
        void credit(BigDecimal amt) { balance = balance.add(amt); }

        Account(String id, BigDecimal balance) {
            this.id = id;
            this.balance = balance;
        }
    }
}

Example 3: ReadWriteLock — FX Rate Cache

package com.bank.fx;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReadWriteLock;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock;

public class FxRateCache {

    private final Map<String, BigDecimal> rates = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final ReadWriteLock lock = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();

    public BigDecimal getRate(String pair) {
        lock.readLock().lock();
        try {
            return rates.get(pair);
        } finally {
            lock.readLock().unlock();
        }
    }

    public void refreshAll(Map<String, BigDecimal> newRates) {
        lock.writeLock().lock();
        try {
            rates.clear();
            rates.putAll(newRates);
        } finally {
            lock.writeLock().unlock();
        }
    }
}

Example 4: Semaphore — Mainframe Connection Limiter

package com.bank.integration.legacy;

import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;

public class MainframeGateway {

    private static final int MAX_CONCURRENT = 15;
    private final Semaphore connectionPermits = new Semaphore(MAX_CONCURRENT);

    public String invoke(String transactionCode, String payload)
            throws InterruptedException {
        connectionPermits.acquire();
        try {
            return doMainframeCall(transactionCode, payload);
        } finally {
            connectionPermits.release();
        }
    }

    private String doMainframeCall(String code, String payload) {
        // CICS/IMS call simulation
        return "OK";
    }
}

Example 5: CountDownLatch — Nightly File Processing

package com.bank.reconciliation;

import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

public class ReconciliationCoordinator {

    public void runParallelImport(java.util.List<String> files)
            throws InterruptedException {
        CountDownLatch latch = new CountDownLatch(files.size());
        ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);

        for (String file : files) {
            executor.submit(() -> {
                try {
                    importFile(file);
                } finally {
                    latch.countDown();
                }
            });
        }

        latch.await();  // wait for all files
        executor.shutdown();
        generateSummaryReport();
    }

    private void importFile(String file) { /* ... */ }
    private void generateSummaryReport() { /* ... */ }
}

Example 6: CyclicBarrier — Logistics Hub Merge

package com.logistics.dispatch;

import java.util.concurrent.BrokenBarrierException;
import java.util.concurrent.CyclicBarrier;

public class HubDispatchCoordinator {

    private final CyclicBarrier barrier;

    public HubDispatchCoordinator(int hubCount) {
        this.barrier = new CyclicBarrier(hubCount, this::mergeAndReleaseTrains);
    }

    public void hubReady(String hubCode) throws InterruptedException, BrokenBarrierException {
        loadManifest(hubCode);
        barrier.await();  // wait for all hubs
        // all hubs continue after merge action
    }

    private void mergeAndReleaseTrains() {
        // runs once when last hub arrives
        System.out.println("All hubs ready — dispatching trains");
    }

    private void loadManifest(String hubCode) { /* ... */ }
}

Example 7: Phaser — Multi-Phase Settlement

package com.bank.settlement;

import java.util.concurrent.Phaser;

public class SettlementPipeline {

    public void execute(int participantCount) {
        Phaser phaser = new Phaser(participantCount);

        for (int i = 0; i < participantCount; i++) {
            int bankId = i;
            new Thread(() -> runSettlement(bankId, phaser)).start();
        }
    }

    private void runSettlement(int bankId, Phaser phaser) {
        debitPhase(bankId);
        phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance();

        creditPhase(bankId);
        phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance();

        notifyPhase(bankId);
        phaser.arriveAndDeregister();
    }

    private void debitPhase(int bankId) { /* ... */ }
    private void creditPhase(int bankId) { /* ... */ }
    private void notifyPhase(int bankId) { /* ... */ }
}

Part 7: Production Usage

JUC in Production Banking/Logistics

Micrometer + LongAdder

// Micrometer counters use LongAdder internally under the hood
Counter.builder("payments.declined")
    .tag("reason", "INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS")
    .register(registry)
    .increment();

HikariCP and Semaphore Analogy

HikariCP connection pool ≈ Semaphore(maxPoolSize) + queue
  acquire connection = permit
  release to pool = release permit

Tomcat 200 threads + HikariCP 20:
  180 threads block on connection acquire — NOT CPU work
  Fix: align threads, pool size, or use virtual threads (Lesson 10/21)

Idempotent Payment with ConcurrentHashMap

@Service
public class IdempotencyGuard {

    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, PaymentResult> processed =
        new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public PaymentResult processOnce(String idempotencyKey,
                                     java.util.function.Supplier<PaymentResult> processor) {
        return processed.computeIfAbsent(idempotencyKey, k -> processor.get());
    }
}

computeIfAbsent is atomic — only one thread runs processor for a key.

Production Checklist

Check Why
lock.unlock() in finally Prevent lock leak on exception
tryLock with timeout for transfers Avoid indefinite deadlock
LongAdder for high-contention metrics Less cache bouncing
Don't use CountDownLatch twice One-shot only — use CyclicBarrier or Phaser
Semaphore.release() in finally Permit leak exhausts pool
ConcurrentHashMap not Collections.synchronizedMap Performance + iteration
Multi-pod: external store for shared state JUC is in-JVM only

Part 9: Architect Perspective

Choosing the Right Coordination Primitive

Decision Tree:
──────────────

Need atomic counter/metric?
  └─ Low contention → AtomicInteger/Long
  └─ High contention → LongAdder

Need mutual exclusion?
  └─ Simple → synchronized
  └─ tryLock/timeout/fairness → ReentrantLock
  └─ Read-heavy → ReadWriteLock

Need limit concurrent access?
  └─ Semaphore

Need wait for N tasks to complete (one time)?
  └─ CountDownLatch

Need N threads rendezvous repeatedly?
  └─ CyclicBarrier

Need multi-phase dynamic parties?
  └─ Phaser

Need thread-safe map/queue?
  └─ ConcurrentHashMap, BlockingQueue (Lesson 10)

Anti-Pattern: Everything synchronized

SYMPTOM: p99 payment latency 2s, CPU low, many BLOCKED threads in jstack

CAUSE: single synchronized block around entire processPayment()
  including external HTTP calls

FIX:
  - shorten lock scope
  - ReadWriteLock for cache
  - remove lock from I/O path entirely
  - externalize idempotency to Redis

Distributed vs Local Locks — ADR

## ADR-089: Account debit locking

### Decision
Use Oracle SELECT FOR UPDATE in ledger-svc, NOT in-memory ReentrantLock

### Rationale
ReentrantLock only protects within one pod; 6 payment pods can still
double-debit. Database row lock is source of truth for financial state.
In-JVM locks only for local caches and metrics.

Model Answer — Q8 (LongAdder vs AtomicLong)

A: AtomicLong uses CAS on single variable — under many threads incrementing concurrently, cache line bounces between cores, throughput collapses. LongAdder stripes increments across internal cells, reducing contention; sum() aggregates cells (weakly consistent snapshot). Use LongAdder for metrics where exact moment-in-time sum isn't required. Use AtomicLong when you need compare-and-set or exact get() every time.

Model Answer — Q13 (Mainframe Throttling Multi-Pod)

A: Per-pod Semaphore(15) allows 10×15=150 connections — may exceed mainframe limit of 50. Need distributed semaphore (Redisson) or centralized connection pool service, or route all legacy calls through dedicated integration pod with single Semaphore. Architect tracks downstream contract limit as source of truth, not per-pod math.

Part 13: Common Mistakes

# Mistake Consequence Fix
1 Forget unlock() on exception path Deadlock finally { unlock() }
2 CountDownLatch reuse Broken coordination New instance or CyclicBarrier
3 await() without handling interrupt Stuck shutdown await() throws — restore interrupt
4 Semaphore.release() without acquire Permit inflation Only release after acquire
5 AtomicInteger for 32-thread hot counter Contention LongAdder
6 ReadWriteLock write-heavy Slower than mutex Simple lock
7 ConcurrentHashMap for cross-pod state Duplicate processing Redis
8 Lock during HTTP call Thread starvation Shrink critical section
9 computeIfAbsent long-running supplier Blocks other keys? Only fast idempotency check
10 Fair lock always Lower throughput Fair only when starvation matters

computeIfAbsent Long Operation Trap

// BAD — blocks map internals for this key's bin; can stall others
map.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> callSlowExternalApi());

// BETTER — check-then-act with external store for slow ops

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Prefer JUC over raw wait/notify — clearer intent
  2. finally for unlock() and release() — always
  3. LongAdder for metrics — AtomicLong for CAS semantics
  4. tryLock with timeout — banking transfers, resource acquisition
  5. ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent — atomic idempotency per pod
  6. Short critical sections — never I/O under lock
  7. DB/distributed lock for financial truth — JUC for local coordination
  8. Name thread pools and locks in logs — debug contention
  9. Choose right coordination primitive — latch vs barrier vs phaser
  10. Test under contention — CountDownLatch to start threads simultaneously

Part 16: Revision Notes

Quick Revision — Concurrency Utilities

ATOMICS: CAS loop — AtomicInteger, AtomicReference
  LongAdder for hot counters (metrics)
  NOT compound invariants alone

ReentrantLock: lock/unlock in finally, tryLock(timeout)
  reentrant, fair optional, multiple Conditions

ReadWriteLock: many readers OR one writer
  read-heavy caches only

Semaphore: permits acquire/release — throttling, NOT mutex reentrant

CountDownLatch: one-shot, countDown→0, await unblocks
CyclicBarrier: reusable, N threads await, barrier action
Phaser: dynamic parties, multi-phase

ConcurrentHashMap: computeIfAbsent atomic per key

JUC establishes happens-before — use named primitives

Multi-pod: JUC local only → Redis/DB for shared state
Financial debits: DB row lock not ReentrantLock

Memory Mnemonic

"Atomic for counts, Lock for sections, Semaphore for limits, Latch for join, Barrier for rendezvous"

Part 1: Concept

What Is the Executor Framework?

The Executor Framework (java.util.concurrent) decouples task submission from thread lifecycle management. Instead of new Thread(r).start() for every payment audit, you submit tasks to a managed thread pool that reuses threads, bounds concurrency, and provides lifecycle control.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              WITHOUT EXECUTOR              WITH EXECUTOR                 │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  new Thread(task).start()  × 1000          ExecutorService pool (20)    │
│       │                                          │                       │
│       ▼                                          ▼                       │
│  1000 threads created                    20 threads reuse tasks         │
│  1 GB stack memory                       bounded queue                  │
│  uncontrolled lifecycle                  shutdown + metrics             │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Core Interfaces Hierarchy

                    Executor
                       │
                       │ execute(Runnable)
                       ▼
                 ExecutorService
                       │
         ┌─────────────┼─────────────┬──────────────────┐
         │             │             │                  │
    submit()      shutdown()   invokeAll()     ScheduledExecutorService
    invoke()      awaitTerm()       │                  │
                                    │            scheduleAtFixedRate()
                                    ▼
                            ThreadPoolExecutor
                            ForkJoinPool

Master Table — Executor Components

Component Purpose Key Methods Production Use
Executor Execute task async execute(Runnable) Minimal abstraction
ExecutorService Lifecycle + futures submit, shutdown, invokeAll Standard pool
ThreadPoolExecutor Configurable pool ctor with core/max/queue Custom tuning
ScheduledExecutorService Delayed/periodic schedule, scheduleAtFixedRate In-app schedulers
ForkJoinPool Work-stealing divide-conquer submit, invoke parallelStream, recursive tasks
Future Async result handle get, cancel, isDone Timeout on FX fetch
Callable<V> Task with return value call() Callable batch jobs

ThreadPoolExecutor Parameters

ThreadPoolExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    4,                      // corePoolSize
    10,                     // maximumPoolSize
    60L, TimeUnit.SECONDS,  // keepAliveTime (non-core threads)
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100),  // work queue
    new ThreadFactoryBuilder().setNameFormat("payment-%d").build(),
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy()  // rejection handler
);

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 ThreadPoolExecutor INTERNAL MODEL                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                  │
│  ┌──────────────┐    ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ Core threads │    │         Work Queue (bounded)         │  │
│  │  (always     │    │  [task3][task4][task5]...           │  │
│  │   alive)     │    └─────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│  │  t1 t2 t3 t4 │              │                              │
│  └──────┬───────┘              │ poll                         │
│         │                      ▼                              │
│         │            ┌──────────────────┐                     │
│         └───────────►│  Worker threads  │                     │
│                      │  execute task    │                     │
│                      └──────────────────┘                     │
│  Extra threads (core < n ≤ max) created when queue FULL         │
│  Rejected when queue full AND threads == maxPoolSize            │
│                                                                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why Thread Pools Exist

Raw new Thread() Thread Pool
~1 MB stack per thread Fixed thread count
Creation cost ~1 ms Thread reuse
No backpressure Bounded queue → rejection policy
No graceful shutdown shutdown() + awaitTermination()
10,000 payments = 10,000 threads 10,000 tasks queued on 20 threads

Why Architects Care About Pool Sizing

payment-svc pod (4 vCPU, 4 GB heap):

Tomcat threads:        200  (HTTP workers)
@Async pool:            10
Batch executor:          4
ForkJoinPool.common:     3
HikariCP connections:   20

Misalignment:
  200 threads blocked on 20 DB connections
  → 180 threads WAITING — not throughput, just memory + scheduling overhead

Why Executors Factory Methods Are Discouraged

Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10);      // OK-ish — unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue hidden
Executors.newCachedThreadPool();       // DANGEROUS — unbounded threads
Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();   // OK for ordered serial work
Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(2);   // OK for light scheduling

Bloch / enterprise guidance: Prefer explicit ThreadPoolExecutor with named threads, bounded queue, and documented rejection policy.

ForkJoinPool — Why Separate Model

ThreadPoolExecutor:  one queue per pool — tasks wait for idle worker
ForkJoinPool:        work-stealing — idle workers steal from busy queues

Ideal for: recursive divide-and-conquer, parallel streams
NOT ideal for: blocking I/O tasks (blocks worker — Lesson 11 virtual threads alternative)

Part 3: Internal Working

ThreadPoolExecutor — Task Submission Flow

submit(task):
  1. if runningThreads < corePoolSize → create new worker, run task
  2. else try offer task to queue
  3. if queue full AND runningThreads < maxPoolSize → create new worker
  4. else → RejectedExecutionHandler

STATE TRANSITIONS (simplified):

Pool start → workers created up to corePoolSize
Load increases → tasks fill queue
Queue full → expand to maxPoolSize workers
Still saturated → rejection policy fires
shutdown() → no new tasks, finish queued
shutdownNow() → interrupt workers, return pending list

Rejection Policies

Policy Behavior Use When
AbortPolicy (default) Throw RejectedExecutionException Fail fast — alert ops
CallerRunsPolicy Caller thread runs task Backpressure — slows producer
DiscardPolicy Silently drop Rare — metrics loss only
DiscardOldestPolicy Drop oldest queued Real-time where fresh matters 
// Banking batch — prefer fail fast
new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy();

// Rate smoothing — caller slows down
new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy();

Worker Thread Lifecycle

Worker thread loop (internal):
  while (!interrupted):
    task = queue.poll() or queue.take()
    if task != null:
      task.run()  // your Runnable/Callable wrapper
    else if pool shutting down:
      break

Uncaught exception in task:
  → Future.get() throws ExecutionException
  → raw execute() — swallowed unless afterExecute hook

Future and Callable Internals

Future<BigDecimal> future = executor.submit(() -> fetchFxRate("USD"));

// FutureTask wraps Callable:
//   - state: NEW → COMPLETING → NORMAL (result) or EXCEPTIONAL
//   - get() blocks until done
//   - cancel(true) interrupts running thread

submit() returns immediately:
  Main thread ──► continues
  Pool thread ──► runs Callable ──► sets Future result

happens-before: Future.get() sees result after task completion

ScheduledExecutorService Internals

ScheduledExecutorService scheduler =
    Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(2);

scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(
    () -> refreshFxRates(),
    0, 5, TimeUnit.MINUTES
);

Internal: DelayedWorkQueue (priority by next execution time)
  - scheduleAtFixedRate: next = start + period (drift if task runs long)
  - scheduleWithFixedDelay: next = end + delay (safer for slow tasks)

Production: prefer external scheduler (K8s CronJob, Quartz cluster) for critical batch
  In-JVM scheduler OK for cache refresh, heartbeat

ForkJoinPool — Work Stealing

Worker-1 deque: [task][task][task]  ← push/pop own tasks (LIFO)
Worker-2 deque: [empty]            ← steals from Worker-1 tail (FIFO steal)

parallelStream() → shared commonPool()
  parallelism = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() - 1

COMMON POOL RISK (Lesson 6 revisited):

HTTP request thread
  → calls parallelStream()
    → common pool workers
      → also used by batch job in same JVM

Isolation: custom ForkJoinPool for batch work

Graceful Shutdown Sequence

executor.shutdown();           // stop accepting new tasks
if (!executor.awaitTermination(60, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
    executor.shutdownNow();      // interrupt workers
    if (!executor.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
        log.error("Pool did not terminate");
    }
}

K8s SIGTERM → Spring @PreDestroy → shutdown sequence
  In-flight payments must complete or timeout before pod killed

Part 4: Memory View

Memory Impact of Thread Pools

Per-Thread Memory

Platform thread stack (default -Xss1m):
  20 pool threads ≈ 20 MB stack space (reserved)
  + Thread object on heap
  + Worker object (ThreadPoolExecutor inner class)

Virtual threads (Java 21):
  ~few KB per virtual thread — millions possible
  Carrier platform threads still limited

Queue Memory

ArrayBlockingQueue(1000) with PaymentTask refs:
  1000 × 8 bytes refs = 8 KB queue structure
  + 1000 PaymentTask objects on heap

Unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue (Executors.newFixedThreadPool default):
  Tasks keep enqueueing faster than processing
  → millions of tasks queued → OutOfMemoryError
Queue Type Bounded? Risk
ArrayBlockingQueue Yes RejectedExecutionException when full
LinkedBlockingQueue (unbounded) No OOM under load spike
SynchronousQueue Zero capacity Direct handoff — CachedThreadPool
PriorityBlockingQueue Unbounded OOM + priority inversion risk

ForkJoinPool Memory

Each worker: work-stealing deque
Parallel task split: subtasks as ForkJoinTask objects on heap
Deep recursion: stack on worker + task objects

Risk: blocking inside ForkJoinPool task pins worker
  → use ManagedBlocker or separate thread pool for I/O

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Thread Pool Sizing

CPU-Bound Tasks

threads ≈ number of CPU cores (or cores + 1)

Example: interest calculation, encryption, large JSON parsing
4 vCPU pod → pool size 4
More threads → context switching, no gain

I/O-Bound Tasks

threads ≈ cores × (1 + wait_time / compute_time)

Example: payment orchestration — 50ms CPU, 450ms I/O per request
  wait/compute = 9
  4 cores × 10 = 40 threads reasonable

NOT 200 if DB pool is 20 — threads block on connections

Pool Size vs Connection Pool

GOLDEN ALIGNMENT (starting point):

Tomcat maxThreads  ≤  HikariCP maxPoolSize × acceptable_wait_factor

OR reduce Tomcat threads and scale pods horizontally

Example:
  HikariCP maxPoolSize = 40
  Tomcat maxThreads = 80  (2× — some threads doing non-DB work)
  NOT 200

Throughput vs Latency

Setting Throughput p99 Latency
Small pool + small queue Lower peak Stable
Large pool Higher until resource limit Spikes under contention
Unbounded queue Hides overload Terrible — minutes old tasks
CallerRunsPolicy Self-throttling Producer slows

ForkJoinPool vs ThreadPoolExecutor

ThreadPoolExecutor ForkJoinPool
Work model Independent tasks Divide-and-conquer
Queue Shared blocking queue Per-worker deques
Blocking I/O Acceptable Bad — pins workers
parallelStream N/A commonPool
Typical use HTTP async, batch jobs CPU parallel, streams

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Production ThreadPoolExecutor — Payment Async

package com.bank.payments.config;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;

import java.util.concurrent.*;

@Configuration
public class ExecutorConfig {

    @Bean(name = "paymentAsyncExecutor", destroyMethod = "shutdown")
    public ExecutorService paymentAsyncExecutor() {
        ThreadPoolExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
            4,
            10,
            60L, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
            new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(500),
            r -> {
                Thread t = new Thread(r, "payment-async-" + System.nanoTime());
                t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((thread, ex) ->
                    org.slf4j.LoggerFactory.getLogger(ExecutorConfig.class)
                        .error("Uncaught in {}", thread.getName(), ex));
                return t;
            },
            new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy()
        );
        executor.allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true);
        return executor;
    }
}

Example 2: Callable + Future with Timeout — FX Rate

package com.bank.fx;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class FxRateClient {

    private final ExecutorService executor;

    public FxRateClient(ExecutorService executor) {
        this.executor = executor;
    }

    public BigDecimal getRate(String pair, long timeoutMs)
            throws TimeoutException, ExecutionException, InterruptedException {

        Callable<BigDecimal> task = () -> callExternalApi(pair);
        Future<BigDecimal> future = executor.submit(task);

        try {
            return future.get(timeoutMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        } catch (TimeoutException e) {
            future.cancel(true);
            throw e;
        }
    }

    private BigDecimal callExternalApi(String pair) {
        return new BigDecimal("83.25");
    }
}

Example 3: invokeAll — Parallel Fraud Checks

package com.bank.fraud;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class FraudCheckOrchestrator {

    private final ExecutorService executor;
    private final List<FraudRule> rules;

    public FraudCheckOrchestrator(ExecutorService executor, List<FraudRule> rules) {
        this.executor = executor;
        this.rules = rules;
    }

    public FraudResult evaluate(TransactionContext ctx)
            throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException {

        List<Callable<FraudResult>> tasks = new ArrayList<>();
        for (FraudRule rule : rules) {
            tasks.add(() -> rule.evaluate(ctx));
        }

        List<Future<FraudResult>> futures = executor.invokeAll(tasks, 2, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

        for (Future<FraudResult> future : futures) {
            FraudResult result = future.get();
            if (result.isBlocked()) {
                return result;
            }
        }
        return FraudResult.pass();
    }
}

Example 4: CountDownLatch + Executor — Batch Import (Lesson 9 + 10)

package com.bank.reconciliation;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class ParallelFileImporter {

    private final ExecutorService executor;

    public ParallelFileImporter(ExecutorService executor) {
        this.executor = executor;
    }

    public void importAll(List<String> files) throws InterruptedException {
        CountDownLatch latch = new CountDownLatch(files.size());

        for (String file : files) {
            executor.submit(() -> {
                try {
                    importFile(file);
                } finally {
                    latch.countDown();
                }
            });
        }

        latch.await(30, TimeUnit.MINUTES);
    }

    private void importFile(String file) { /* ... */ }
}

Example 5: ScheduledExecutor — Cache Refresh

package com.bank.config;

import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

public class RateCacheRefresher implements AutoCloseable {

    private final ScheduledExecutorService scheduler =
        Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(1, r -> new Thread(r, "fx-refresh"));

  public void start(java.util.function.Runnable refreshTask) {
        scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(refreshTask, 0, 5, TimeUnit.MINUTES);
    }

    @Override
    public void close() {
        scheduler.shutdown();
        try {
            scheduler.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            scheduler.shutdownNow();
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }
}

Example 6: Custom ForkJoinPool — Isolated Batch (Lesson 6)

package com.bank.batch;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool;

public class IsolatedParallelProcessor {

    public long sumAmountsPaise(List<PaymentRecord> records) throws InterruptedException {
        ForkJoinPool customPool = new ForkJoinPool(4);
        try {
            return customPool.submit(() ->
                records.parallelStream()
                    .mapToLong(PaymentRecord::amountInPaise)
                    .sum()
            ).get();
        } finally {
            customPool.shutdown();
        }
    }

    public record PaymentRecord(String id, long amountInPaise) {}
}

import org.springframework.scheduling.annotation.Async;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class AuditService {

    @Async("paymentAsyncExecutor")
    public void auditAsync(String paymentId, String action) {
        // runs on paymentAsyncExecutor pool — NOT Tomcat thread
        writeToAuditStore(paymentId, action);
    }

    private void writeToAuditStore(String paymentId, String action) { /* ... */ }
}

Part 7: Production Usage

Executors in Production

Spring Boot Thread Pools

DEFAULT (often overlooked):
  Tomcat: server.tomcat.threads.max
  @Async: SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor (NEW THREAD PER TASK!) unless configured
  @Scheduled: single thread by default
  ForkJoinPool.commonPool: JVM global

EXPLICIT CONFIG required for production @Async

Monitoring Thread Pools

// Expose via Micrometer / Actuator custom metric
ThreadPoolExecutor pool = (ThreadPoolExecutor) executor;

Gauge.builder("executor.active", pool, ThreadPoolExecutor::getActiveCount)
    .tag("pool", "payment-async")
    .register(registry);

Gauge.builder("executor.queue.size", pool, e -> e.getQueue().size())
    .tag("pool", "payment-async")
    .register(registry);

Alert when:
- queue.size > 80% capacity sustained
- RejectedExecutionException in logs
- activeCount == maxPoolSize for extended period

Virtual Threads (Java 21) — Production Pattern

@Bean(destroyMethod = "shutdown")
public ExecutorService virtualThreadExecutor() {
    return Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();
}

// Each blocking I/O task gets cheap virtual thread
// NOT for CPU-bound parallel computation
Platform Pool Virtual Threads
200 × 1 MB stacks Millions of tasks
Tune pool size carefully Tune downstream limits (DB, HTTP)
CPU-bound work Blocking I/O orchestration

Production Checklist

Check Why
Bounded queue always Prevent OOM
Named threads jstack readability
Rejection policy explicit Predictable overload behavior
destroyMethod = shutdown on @Bean Clean K8s termination
Pool metrics exported Alert before failure
@Async uses configured pool Not one thread per task
Don't block inside ForkJoinPool Worker starvation
Align threads with connection pools Avoid false capacity

Part 8: Microservice Usage

Executors Across Microservice Architecture

Thread Domains in One Pod

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  payment-svc Pod                                                 │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Tomcat pool (HTTP)          ──► client-facing latency          │
│  Kafka listener container    ──► consumer concurrency           │
│  @Async paymentAsyncExecutor ──► audit, notifications           │
│  Scheduler (1 thread)        ──► cache refresh                  │
│  ForkJoinPool.commonPool     ──► parallelStream (avoid in API)  │
│  HikariCP housekeeper          ──► pool maintenance               │

Each domain needs separate tuning — NOT one global "200 threads"

Kafka Listener Concurrency

spring:
  kafka:
    listener:
      concurrency: 3  # 3 consumer threads per topic in this pod

3 threads × 3 pods = 9 consumers (if same group)
Must be ≤ partition count for full parallelism
Each thread: sequential processing per partition — thread safety simplified

Bulkhead with Dedicated Executors (Lesson 29)

@Bean("legacyExecutor")
public ExecutorService legacyExecutor() {
    return new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 5, 60L, SECONDS,
        new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(50),
        new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy());
}

@Bean("corePaymentExecutor")
public ExecutorService corePaymentExecutor() {
    return new ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 16, 60L, SECONDS,
        new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(200),
        new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
}

Legacy slowness cannot exhaust core payment pool.

Cross-Service Async

HTTP thread should NOT:
  - run 30s batch job
  - block on CompletableFuture.get() without timeout (Lesson 11)

Pattern:
  accept payment → enqueue Kafka → return 202 Accepted
  consumer pool processes asynchronously

Part 9: Architect Perspective

Executor Strategy as Architecture

Pool per Concern

Concern Pool Size Guidance
HTTP Tomcat I/O bound, align with DB
Async audit paymentAsyncExecutor Small — fire and forget
Batch import Dedicated batch pool core = CPUs, bounded queue
Scheduled refresh 1-2 threads Single-threaded refresh OK
CPU parallel Custom ForkJoinPool = CPUs, isolated from common
Blocking I/O (Java 21) Virtual thread executor Limited by downstream

ADR — Thread Pool Sizing

## ADR-102: payment-svc thread configuration

### Context
p99 1.8s, CPU 30%, HikariCP threads blocked, queue depth 0

### Decision
Tomcat maxThreads 80 → 50
HikariCP maxPoolSize 20 → 40
paymentAsyncExecutor: core 4, max 8, queue 500
HPA on RPS not CPU

### Rationale
Threads were waiting on connections, not computing.
More pods with fewer blocked threads beats one fat pod.

When NOT to Use In-JVM Executors

Scenario Better Alternative
Nightly 2-hour ETL K8s CronJob separate deployment
Critical schedule Quartz cluster / external scheduler
Massive parallel CPU Spark / distributed compute
Work across pods Kafka consumer scale-out

Executor + Resilience (Preview Lesson 29)

Thread pool full → RejectedExecutionException
  → Circuit breaker open
  → Return 503 with Retry-After
  → NOT hang forever

Model Answer — Q6 (ThreadPoolExecutor Parameters)

A: corePoolSize: threads always kept alive (unless allowCoreThreadTimeOut). New tasks create threads up to core before queueing. maximumPoolSize: when bounded queue is full, pool expands up to max. keepAliveTime: idle threads above core die after timeout. workQueue: holds tasks waiting for thread; bounded queue enables backpressure. When queue full and threads at max, RejectedExecutionHandler runs. Order: fill core → queue → expand to max → reject.

Model Answer — Q14 (Tomcat vs HikariCP)

A: 200 Tomcat threads accept work but only 20 can hold DB connections simultaneously; ~180 block in getConnection(), wasting ~180 MB stacks and scheduler overhead without increasing throughput. Fix: reduce maxThreads toward 2× maxPoolSize, increase HikariCP if DB allows, scale pods on RPS. Root issue is oversubscription of threads relative to bottleneck resource (DB), not insufficient threads.

Part 13: Common Mistakes

# Mistake Consequence Fix
1 newCachedThreadPool() under load Thousands of threads, OOM Bounded ThreadPoolExecutor
2 Unbounded queue Hidden latency, OOM ArrayBlockingQueue
3 execute() ignoring exceptions Silent task failure submit() + get() or handler
4 No shutdown on @Bean Zombie threads on redeploy destroyMethod = "shutdown"
5 @Async default executor New thread per async call Named pool bean
6 Future.get() without timeout Hang forever get(timeout, unit)
7 Blocking I/O in ForkJoinPool Steals worker capacity Separate pool or virtual threads
8 Same pool for all concerns Bulkhead failure Dedicated executors
9 Pool size >> connection pool Thread pile-up Align sizing
10 shutdownNow() as first resort Incomplete payments shutdown() + await first

CachedThreadPool Disaster

// Under spike: unbounded thread creation
ExecutorService bad = Executors.newCachedThreadPool();
for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) {
    bad.submit(() -> processPayment(i));  // OOM or system thrashing
}

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Explicit ThreadPoolExecutor — bounded queue, named threads, rejection policy
  2. submit + timeout for external calls — always
  3. Separate pools per domain — HTTP, async, batch, legacy bulkhead
  4. Shutdown gracefully — K8s preStop + awaitTermination
  5. Export pool metrics — active count, queue size, rejections
  6. Align with HikariCP — threads reflect real capacity
  7. Custom ForkJoinPool for batch parallel — not common pool in API path
  8. Virtual threads for I/O-heavy (Java 21) — not CPU parallel
  9. Don't run batch on request threads — Kafka/CronJob
  10. Document pool sizes in ADR — ops needs runbooks
