Part 1: Concept

What Is CompletableFuture?

CompletableFuture<T> is an implementation of Future<T> and CompletionStage<T> that supports non-blocking composition of asynchronous operations. You chain transformations and reactions instead of calling future.get() and blocking the calling thread.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           BLOCKING (Future)          vs    COMPOSABLE (CompletableFuture)│
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  Future<Rate> f = pool.submit(...);     supplyAsync(() -> fetchRate())  │
│  Rate r = f.get();  // BLOCKS thread         .thenApply(r -> convert(r)) │
│  convert(r);                                 .thenCompose(...);          │
│                                              // thread not blocked        │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

CompletionStage Chain Model

supplyAsync ──► thenApply ──► thenCompose ──► thenAccept
   (async           (sync            (flatMap           (terminal
    start)           map)             async)             side effect)

                    thenCombine ──► merge two async results
                    allOf       ──► wait for all
                    anyOf       ──► first to complete

Master Table — CompletableFuture API

Method Input → Output Async? Purpose Banking Example
supplyAsync(Supplier) () → T → CF<T> Yes Start async work Fetch FX rate
runAsync(Runnable) () → void → CF<Void> Yes Fire-and-forget Write audit log
thenApply(fn) T → U No (same thread as prior stage) Transform result Map to DTO
thenApplyAsync(fn) T → U Yes (default or custom pool) Transform on pool Heavy mapping
thenCompose(fn) T → CF<U> Flattens nested CF Chain async calls Rate → convert → ledger
thenCombine(other, fn) (T,U) → V When both done Parallel merge Balance + FX → amount
thenAccept(Consumer) T → void Terminal Side effect Publish event
allOf(CF...) CF<Void> All complete Join parallel Fraud + limit + FX checks
anyOf(CF...) CF<Object> First wins Race/alternative Fastest rate provider
exceptionally(fn) Throwable → T Error recovery Fallback rate Default FX on timeout
handle(fn) (T, Throwable) → U Success or fail Unified handler Log + map either way
orTimeout(ms) — Java 9+ Timeout 2s fraud check limit

Future vs CompletableFuture

Future CompletableFuture
Completion Wait with get() Callbacks + get()
Chaining Manual thenApply, thenCompose
Manual complete No complete(), completeExceptionally()
Combine multiple invokeAll (blocking) allOf, thenCombine
Exception handling ExecutionException on get exceptionally, handle
Production Legacy Preferred for orchestration

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why CompletableFuture Was Added (Java 8)

Pain with Future CompletableFuture Answer
get() blocks thread Callback composition
No way to chain async steps thenCompose (flatMap)
Combining 3 async calls = 3 blocks or manual latches allOf, thenCombine
Error handling only at get() exceptionally, handle
Callback hell in nested async (pre-Java 8) Fluent pipeline

Why Architects Use It in Payment Orchestration

SYNCHRONOUS PAYMENT (blocks Tomcat thread 800ms):
  validate → fraud → FX → ledger → notify
  Thread occupied entire time (even during I/O waits)

COMPLETABLE FUTURE ORCHESTRATION:
  Same steps chained — still uses threads from pools during I/O
  BUT: clearer composition, timeout per stage, parallel checks with allOf
  WITH VIRTUAL THREADS (Java 21): simpler blocking style often wins

Architect choice 2025:
  CompletableFuture for explicit parallel composition + timeouts
  Virtual threads for straightforward sequential I/O orchestration

Relationship to Reactive (Lesson 20)

CompletableFuture:  single-value async, thread-pool based
Mono/Flux:          reactive streams, backpressure, non-blocking I/O

CompletableFuture fits Spring MVC (blocking servlet stack)
WebFlux often uses reactive types end-to-end

Part 3: Internal Working

How CompletableFuture Executes

Internal State Machine

CompletableFuture states (simplified):
  NEW → COMPLETING → NORMAL (result set)
                   → EXCEPTIONAL (exception set)

When complete(result):
  1. Set outcome (CAS)
  2. Fire all registered dependent stages (thenApply callbacks)
  3. Dependent stages run on:
       - same thread (thenApply) — caller-runs / completing thread
       - ForkJoinPool.commonPool() (thenApplyAsync default)
       - custom Executor (thenApplyAsync(fn, executor))

thenApply vs thenApplyAsync

CompletableFuture<Payment> cf = CompletableFuture
    .supplyAsync(() -> loadPayment(), executor);  // runs on executor

cf.thenApply(p -> enrich(p));        // may run on SAME thread that completed supplyAsync
cf.thenApplyAsync(p -> enrich(p));   // runs on commonPool (or specified executor)

thenApply (non-async):
  Completing thread executes next stage — fast, no thread handoff
  Risk: heavy work blocks completion of upstream CF chain

thenApplyAsync:
  Submits to executor — extra handoff overhead
  Good for CPU work after I/O stage

thenApply vs thenCompose (Critical Distinction)

// WRONG — nested CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<LedgerResult>>
CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<LedgerResult>> nested =
    cf.thenApply(p -> postToLedgerAsync(p));

// CORRECT — flattened CompletableFuture<LedgerResult>
CompletableFuture<LedgerResult> flat =
    cf.thenCompose(p -> postToLedgerAsync(p));

thenApply:  f: T → U           result CF<U>
thenCompose: f: T → CF<U>      result CF<U>  (monadic flatMap)

allOf Internal Behavior

CompletableFuture<Void> all = CompletableFuture.allOf(fraudCf, fxCf, limitCf);
all.thenRun(() -> proceed());  // runs when ALL complete (success or exceptional)

allOf:
  - Waits for all to complete (any outcome)
  - Does NOT propagate exceptions automatically
  - Returns Void — you must inspect each CF individually:

fraudCf.exceptionally(ex -> FALLBACK).join();

Thread Pool Selection — Critical

// BAD — supplyAsync with NO executor → ForkJoinPool.commonPool()
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> callPaymentGateway());

// GOOD — explicit executor
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> callPaymentGateway(), paymentExecutor);

Same lesson as Lesson 6/10: default async CF stages use common pool unless you pass executor.

Memory and happens-before

CF completion happens-before:
  - any thenApply/thenAccept registered before completion
  - get()/join() return after completion

Result stored in volatile outcome field — visible to dependent stages (JMM)

Part 4: Memory View

Memory Impact of CompletableFuture Chains

HEAP per orchestrated payment:

CompletableFuture<PaymentResult>  (main CF object)
  ├── outcome / stack of Completion objects (linked list of stages)
  ├── dependent thenApply nodes
  └── possibly nested CF from thenCompose

Each stage: Completion object (~几十 bytes) + capturing lambda

10-stage chain × 1000 concurrent payments = thousands of short-lived objects (Young Gen)
Usually acceptable — profile if orchestration creates 50+ stages per request
Pattern Allocation GC
Short chain (3-5 stages) Low Young Gen
allOf with 10 CFs 10 CF objects + 1 aggregator Young Gen
Blocking get() in loop Thread blocked + CF objects Thread pool pressure worse than memory
join() in parallel stream Anti-pattern — blocks FJP worker Lesson 6

Thread Stack vs Async

BLOCKING get():
  Tomcat thread stack (~1 MB) held 800ms

ASYNC chain:
  Tomcat thread releases after starting CF (if not joined on request thread)
  Worker threads from paymentExecutor do I/O — stacks from pool

Virtual thread alternative:
  Tomcat virtual thread blocks on I/O cheaply — simpler code, similar throughput

Part 5: Performance Analysis

CompletableFuture Performance Considerations

When CF Helps

Scenario Benefit
Parallel independent checks (allOf) Wall-clock = max(checks), not sum
Per-stage timeout (orTimeout) Fail fast without killing thread pool
Explicit executor injection Isolation from common pool
Non-blocking HTTP thread (async servlet) Higher connection acceptance

When CF Hurts

Scenario Problem
Simple sequential I/O Verbose vs virtual thread blocking code
thenApplyAsync on every stage Thread handoff overhead
join() on request thread Still blocks — no benefit
Deep nested thenCompose Callback hell, hard to debug
CPU-bound on common pool Starves parallelStream

Parallel Fraud + FX + Limit Check

Sequential: 120ms + 80ms + 50ms = 250ms
allOf parallel (3 executors or 1 pool with 3 threads): ~120ms (max)

Payment API p99 improvement when checks are independent

Scalability

Pattern Scales
CF + bounded executor + async HTTP response Good
CF + join() on Tomcat thread Same as sync — no win
CF + common pool for all services Cross-service contention
Virtual threads + blocking JDBC Often simpler at scale (Java 21)

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Basic Chain — Payment Enrichment

package com.bank.payments.orchestration;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;

public class PaymentEnrichmentPipeline {

    private final ExecutorService executor;
    private final FxRateClient fxClient;
    private final AccountClient accountClient;

    public PaymentEnrichmentPipeline(ExecutorService executor,
                                     FxRateClient fxClient,
                                     AccountClient accountClient) {
        this.executor = executor;
        this.fxClient = fxClient;
        this.accountClient = accountClient;
    }

    public CompletableFuture<EnrichedPayment> enrich(PaymentRequest request) {
        return CompletableFuture
            .supplyAsync(() -> accountClient.loadAccount(request.debtorAccountId()), executor)
            .thenApply(account -> validateAccount(account, request))
            .thenCompose(validated ->
                fxClient.fetchRateAsync(validated.currency(), "INR")
                    .thenApply(rate -> new EnrichedPayment(validated, rate)));
    }

    private ValidatedPayment validateAccount(Account account, PaymentRequest request) {
        // validation logic
        return new ValidatedPayment(request, account);
    }

    public record PaymentRequest(String debtorAccountId, String currency, BigDecimal amount) {}
    public record Account(String id, BigDecimal balance) {}
    public record ValidatedPayment(PaymentRequest request, Account account) {}
    public record EnrichedPayment(ValidatedPayment validated, BigDecimal fxRate) {}
}

Example 2: thenCombine — Balance and Limit Check

package com.bank.payments.orchestration;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;

public class DualCheckService {

    private final ExecutorService executor;
    private final AccountClient accounts;
    private final LimitClient limits;

    public CompletableFuture<CheckResult> verify(String accountId, BigDecimal amount) {
        CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> balanceCf =
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> accounts.getBalance(accountId), executor);

        CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> limitCf =
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> limits.getDailyRemaining(accountId), executor);

        return balanceCf.thenCombine(limitCf, (balance, remaining) -> {
            if (balance.compareTo(amount) < 0) {
                return CheckResult.fail("INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS");
            }
            if (remaining.compareTo(amount) < 0) {
                return CheckResult.fail("LIMIT_EXCEEDED");
            }
            return CheckResult.ok();
        });
    }

    public record CheckResult(boolean success, String code) {
        static CheckResult ok() { return new CheckResult(true, null); }
        static CheckResult fail(String code) { return new CheckResult(false, code); }
    }
}

Example 3: allOf — Parallel Pre-Authorization

package com.bank.payments.orchestration;

import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;

public class PreAuthOrchestrator {

    private final ExecutorService executor;
    private final FraudService fraud;
    private final SanctionsService sanctions;
    private final VelocityService velocity;

    public CompletableFuture<PreAuthResult> preAuthorize(PaymentContext ctx) {
        CompletableFuture<Boolean> fraudCf =
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fraud.check(ctx), executor);
        CompletableFuture<Boolean> sanctionsCf =
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> sanctions.check(ctx), executor);
        CompletableFuture<Boolean> velocityCf =
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> velocity.check(ctx), executor);

        return CompletableFuture.allOf(fraudCf, sanctionsCf, velocityCf)
            .thenApply(v -> {
                if (!fraudCf.join()) return PreAuthResult.declined("FRAUD");
                if (!sanctionsCf.join()) return PreAuthResult.declined("SANCTIONS");
                if (!velocityCf.join()) return PreAuthResult.declined("VELOCITY");
                return PreAuthResult.approved();
            });
    }

    public record PaymentContext(String paymentId, String accountId, java.math.BigDecimal amount) {}
    public record PreAuthResult(boolean approved, String reason) {
        static PreAuthResult approved() { return new PreAuthResult(true, null); }
        static PreAuthResult declined(String r) { return new PreAuthResult(false, r); }
    }
}

Example 4: Error Handling — exceptionally, handle, orTimeout

package com.bank.fx;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

public class ResilientFxService {

    private static final BigDecimal FALLBACK_RATE = new BigDecimal("83.00");

    private final ExecutorService executor;
    private final FxRateClient primary;
    private final FxRateClient secondary;

    public CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> getRate(String pair) {
        return CompletableFuture
            .supplyAsync(() -> primary.fetch(pair), executor)
            .orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
            .exceptionally(ex -> {
                log.warn("Primary FX failed: {}", ex.getMessage());
                return null;
            })
            .thenCompose(rate -> {
                if (rate != null) {
                    return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(rate);
                }
                return CompletableFuture
                    .supplyAsync(() -> secondary.fetch(pair), executor)
                    .orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
                    .exceptionally(ex2 -> FALLBACK_RATE);
            });
    }

    private void log(String level, String msg, Object arg) {
        org.slf4j.LoggerFactory.getLogger(ResilientFxService.class).warn(msg, arg);
    }
}

Example 5: handle — Unified Success and Failure

package com.logistics.tracking;

import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;

public class TrackingAggregator {

    private final ExecutorService executor;

    public CompletableFuture<TrackingResponse> fetchTracking(String trackingId) {
        return CompletableFuture
            .supplyAsync(() -> callCarrierApi(trackingId), executor)
            .handle((result, ex) -> {
                if (ex != null) {
                    return TrackingResponse.error(trackingId, ex.getMessage());
                }
                return TrackingResponse.success(result);
            });
    }

    private TrackingData callCarrierApi(String id) { return new TrackingData(id, "IN_TRANSIT"); }

    public record TrackingData(String id, String status) {}
    public record TrackingResponse(boolean ok, String id, String status, String error) {
        static TrackingResponse success(TrackingData d) {
            return new TrackingResponse(true, d.id(), d.status(), null);
        }
        static TrackingResponse error(String id, String msg) {
            return new TrackingResponse(false, id, null, msg);
        }
    }
}

Example 6: anyOf — Fastest Rate Provider Wins

package com.bank.fx;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;

public class RacingFxProviders {

    private final ExecutorService executor;

    public CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> fastestRate(String pair) {
        CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> providerA =
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchFromA(pair), executor);
        CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> providerB =
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchFromB(pair), executor);

        return (CompletableFuture<BigDecimal>) CompletableFuture.anyOf(providerA, providerB);
    }

    private BigDecimal fetchFromA(String pair) { /* ... */ return BigDecimal.ONE; }
    private BigDecimal fetchFromB(String pair) { /* ... */ return BigDecimal.ONE; }
}

Example 7: Controller — Don't Block Without Timeout

package com.bank.payments.api;

import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/payments")
public class AsyncPaymentController {

    private final PaymentOrchestrator orchestrator;

    @PostMapping
    public CompletableFuture<PaymentResponse> create(@RequestBody PaymentRequest request) {
        return orchestrator.process(request)
            .orTimeout(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
            .exceptionally(ex -> PaymentResponse.failed(request.id(), ex.getMessage()));
    }
}

Refactor sequential fraud → FX → ledger calls into thenCompose chain with orTimeout on each external step (2s, 2s, 5s).

Exercise 2

Implement preAuthorize with allOf but replace .join() inside thenApply with thenCombine chaining for cleaner exception propagation.

Part 7: Production Usage

CompletableFuture in Production

Golden Rules

1. ALWAYS pass explicit Executor to supplyAsync/thenApplyAsync
2. NEVER join()/get() on Tomcat thread without timeout
3. Use orTimeout/completeOnTimeout on external calls
4. exceptionally/handle for fallbacks — not empty catch
5. Keep chains readable — extract methods, max ~5 stages visible
6. Log correlation ID in each async stage (MDC propagation)
7. Cancel upstream on timeout if possible (future.cancel(true))

MDC Propagation Across CF Stages

public <T> CompletableFuture<T> supplyAsyncWithMdc(
        Supplier<T> supplier, ExecutorService executor) {
    Map<String, String> context = org.slf4j.MDC.getCopyOfContextMap();
    return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
        if (context != null) org.slf4j.MDC.setContextMap(context);
        try {
            return supplier.get();
        } finally {
            org.slf4j.MDC.clear();
        }
    }, executor);
}

Async Servlet / Spring MVC

// Return CF directly — Tomcat thread released until completion (async mode)
@GetMapping("/status/{id}")
public CompletableFuture<StatusResponse> status(@PathVariable String id) {
    return statusService.fetchAsync(id);
}

Production Checklist

Check Why
Explicit executor on all async stages Avoid common pool pollution
Timeout every external CF Prevent hung requests
Exception handling in chain No broken CF hanging forever
MDC copied to async threads Traceability
Don't join() in parallelStream FJP deadlock risk
Monitor executor queue + CF timeouts Early overload detection
Integration tests for failure paths exceptionally branches

Part 8: Microservice Usage

Async Orchestration Across Services

Payment Saga with CompletableFuture (In-Pod Orchestration)

Client POST /payments
       │
       ▼
PaymentOrchestrator (CF chain in payment-svc)
       │
       ├── supplyAsync → fraud-svc (HTTP)
       ├── supplyAsync → fx-svc (HTTP)
       └── thenCompose → ledger-svc (HTTP)
       │
       ▼
CompletableFuture<PaymentResponse> → client

Cross-service failures → exceptionally map to domain error codes
NOT shared CF — each HTTP call is separate CF in one JVM

vs Kafka Choreography

Orchestration (CF in one service) Choreography (Kafka)
Synchronous feel to client Event-driven, async client
CF chains HTTP calls Events between services
Tight temporal coupling Looser coupling
Good for user-facing payment Good for settlement pipelines

CompletableFuture vs Virtual Threads (Java 21)

// Virtual thread style — often clearer for sequential I/O
try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    Future<FraudResult> fraud = executor.submit(() -> fraudClient.check(ctx));
    Future<FxRate> fx = executor.submit(() -> fxClient.getRate(pair));
    // still need get with timeout — but code reads synchronously
}

Architect 2025: Virtual threads simplify sequential orchestration; CF still wins for explicit parallel allOf and fluent timeout composition.

Bulkhead with Executors

// Separate executors — CF stages don't starve each other
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> legacyCall(), legacyExecutor);
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> corePayment(), paymentExecutor);

Part 9: Architect Perspective

When to Use CompletableFuture

USE CompletableFuture:
  ✓ Parallel independent checks (allOf)
  ✓ Async HTTP response (Spring MVC CompletableFuture return)
  ✓ Per-step timeout and fallback composition
  ✓ Combine two async results (thenCombine)

CONSIDER virtual threads instead:
  ✓ Sequential I/O chain, Java 21+, simple readability priority

USE Kafka / workflow engine:
  ✓ Long-running saga hours/days
  ✓ Cross-service compensation
  ✓ Durability required across restarts

AVOID CompletableFuture:
  ✗ CPU-bound pipeline on common pool
  ✗ join() on request thread without async servlet
  ✗ 15-level nested thenCompose (workflow engine)

Timeout Budget Architecture

Total SLA: 10s client timeout

Budget allocation:
  fraud:    2s (orTimeout)
  fx:       2s
  ledger:   5s
  buffer:   1s

orTimeout on each CF — fail fast, trigger fallback or 503

ADR — Async Payment API

## ADR-115: CompletableFuture orchestration in payment-svc

### Decision
Orchestrate fraud + FX + ledger with CF + dedicated paymentExecutor
Return CompletableFuture from controller (async Tomcat)

### Alternatives rejected
- Blocking sequential: holds platform thread 800ms avg
- @Async fire-and-forget: no composed response to client
- Full WebFlux: team skill / ecosystem migration cost

### Constraints
Java 21 — revisit virtual thread blocking style in 6 months

Senior Level

  2. How do you handle exceptions in CompletableFuture?
  3. What is wrong with CompletableFuture.supplyAsync() without executor?
  4. Does allOf fail if one CF fails?
  5. Difference between exceptionally and handle?
  6. What is join() vs get()?
  7. How do you add timeout to CompletableFuture?

Staff / Architect Level

  1. Design async payment orchestration with fraud, FX, ledger — CF vs virtual threads.
  2. How do you propagate MDC/correlation ID across CF stages?
  3. allOf then join() inside thenApply — problems and alternatives?
  4. CompletableFuture returned from Spring controller — what happens to Tomcat thread?
  5. Risk of join() inside ForkJoinPool / parallelStream?
  6. When does callback hell appear with CF? How do you refactor?
  7. anyOf for redundant providers — how to cancel losing requests?
  8. CompletableFuture vs reactive Mono for payment API?

Model Answer — Q9 (allOf failure)

A: allOf completes when all constituent CFs complete, regardless of success or failure. It does not short-circuit on exception and does not unwrap exceptions. If fraudCf fails exceptionally, allOf still completes, but fraudCf.join() throws CompletionException wrapping the cause. You must handle each CF's exception individually, or use CompletableFuture.allOf(...).thenCompose(v -> combineResults()) with explicit exception checks, or use libraries like resilience4j, or virtual threads with structured concurrency (Java 21 preview/incubator patterns).

Model Answer — Q13 (CF vs Virtual Threads)

A: For parallel fraud+FX+limits, allOf with dedicated executor gives clear timeout per stage and good wall-clock time. For sequential ledger after validation, virtual threads with blocking HTTP clients reduce callback complexity with similar I/O throughput on Java 21. CF fits Spring MVC async return and explicit parallel composition. Virtual threads fit readable sequential orchestration. Neither replaces Kafka for durable multi-hour sagas. Choose based on team readability, Java version, and parallel vs sequential dominance.

Part 13: Common Mistakes

# Mistake Consequence Fix
1 thenApply instead of thenCompose Nested CF thenCompose for async chain
2 No executor on supplyAsync Common pool contention Pass paymentExecutor
3 join() on HTTP thread Blocked thread — no async benefit Return CF to framework
4 Ignore allOf failures Silent partial failure Check each CF
5 Long chain in one method Unreadable Extract named methods
6 No timeout Hung requests orTimeout
7 exceptionally returns null without type care NPE downstream Typed fallback
8 MDC not propagated Lost correlation ID Copy MDC in supplier
9 join() in parallelStream Deadlock Never
10 Swallow exception in whenComplete Still exceptional CF Use handle/exceptionally

Nested CF Bug

// BUG
CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<PaymentResult>> bad =
    start.thenApply(id -> processAsync(id));

// FIX
CompletableFuture<PaymentResult> good =
    start.thenCompose(id -> processAsync(id));

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Explicit executor on every async factory and async stage
  2. thenCompose for async sequencing; thenApply for sync map
  3. allOf for parallel; thenCombine for two-way merge
  4. orTimeout on external dependencies
  5. handle/exceptionally with domain fallbacks
  6. Return CF from controller for true async servlet behavior
  7. Propagate MDC into async suppliers
  8. Keep chains short — refactor to named private methods
  9. Test timeout and failure paths
  10. Re-evaluate with Java 21 virtual threads for sequential I/O

Part 16: Revision Notes

Quick Revision — CompletableFuture

CF = composable Future + CompletionStage

START: supplyAsync(Supplier, executor) | runAsync(Runnable, executor)
  default executor = ForkJoinPool.commonPool() — AVOID

thenApply:     T → U (sync map)
thenApplyAsync: T → U (on pool)
thenCompose:   T → CF<U> (flatMap — chain async)
thenCombine:   merge 2 CFs when both done
allOf:         wait all (check exceptions individually!)
anyOf:         first complete

END: thenAccept | join | get(timeout)

ERRORS: exceptionally | handle | whenComplete
TIMEOUT: orTimeout | completeOnTimeout

RULES:
  explicit executor
  no join on Tomcat without async return
  thenCompose not thenApply for async next step
  MDC propagation
  orTimeout external calls

Memory Mnemonic

"Supply with your pool, compose don't nest, timeout every hop, handle every fail"

│ allOf does NOT fail-fast — check each CF for exceptions         │
│ join() unchecked | get() checked | both BLOCK if misused         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Return CF from Spring MVC → async servlet releases thread       │
│ Virtual threads (21): simpler sequential I/O alternative        │
│ Kafka/workflow: durable saga — not CF across restarts           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Part 1: Concept

What Is the JVM?

The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) is the runtime engine that executes bytecode, manages memory, performs just-in-time compilation, and runs garbage collection. Your Spring payment service is not "Java code running on Linux" — it is bytecode interpreted, then JIT-compiled, on a managed heap with concurrent GC threads.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         JVM INTERNAL ARCHITECTURE                        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  CLASS LOADER SUBSYSTEM          RUNTIME DATA AREAS (Lesson 8)          │
│  ─────────────────────           ─────────────────────────────          │
│  Bootstrap → Platform → App      Heap | Stack | Metaspace | PC | Code   │
│                                                                          │
│  EXECUTION ENGINE                GARBAGE COLLECTOR                       │
│  ─────────────────               ─────────────────                       │
│  Interpreter                     G1 (default Java 9+)                    │
│  JIT (C1/C2)                     ZGC / Shenandoah (low pause)            │
│  GC safepoints                   Parallel GC (throughput batch)          │
│                                                                          │
│  NATIVE METHOD INTERFACE (JNI)   JVM TOOL INTERFACE (JFR, jcmd)         │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

End-to-End Execution Pipeline

PaymentService.java
       │ javac
       ▼
PaymentService.class (bytecode)
       │ ClassLoader.load → Link → Init
       ▼
Metaspace: PaymentService metadata
       │
       ▼
Interpreter executes hot loops (slow)
       │
       ▼
JIT C1 → JIT C2 (native code in Code Cache)
       │
       ▼
Objects allocated on Heap → GC reclaims unreachable

JVM Performance Pillars Master Table

Pillar What Tuning Knob Payment SLA Impact
Class loading Load/link/init classes Class path, Spring fat JAR Startup / cold deploy time
Bytecode + JIT Compile hot methods Tiered compilation, Code cache p99 after warmup
Heap layout Young / Old regions -Xmx, -Xms OOM vs headroom
GC algorithm Pause vs throughput -XX:+UseG1GC, -XX:+UseZGC p99 latency spikes
Metaspace Class metadata -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize Metaspace OOM on redeploy
Off-heap Direct buffers, Netty -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize Native OOM
Safepoints Stop-the-world coordination -XX:+PrintGC, JFR Mysterious pauses

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why the JVM Architecture Looks This Way

Design Goal Mechanism Trade-Off
Portability Bytecode + JVM Startup + memory overhead vs native
Safety Verifier, GC, no raw pointers CPU + pause cost
Performance JIT optimizes hot code Warmup period
Dynamic loading Class loaders Metaspace, classloader leaks
Multithreading JMM, GC threads Complexity

Why Architects Must Own JVM Tuning (Not Only "DevOps")

INCIDENT: payment-svc p99 = 2s after deploy, settles to 400ms after 15 min

DEVOPS: "scale pods"
ARCHITECT: "JIT warmup + cold cache + G1 young GC tuning"

INCIDENT: nightly batch OOMKilled at 3.8 GB on 4 GB limit

DEVOPS: "increase memory limit"
ARCHITECT: "heap dump shows 2M String duplicates in reconciliation — fix code + G1 heap region sizing"

Why GC Exists (Lesson 1 Recap — Now Deep)

Manual free() in 24/7 payment systems caused:
- Memory leaks in long-lived services
- Fragmentation
- Security vulnerabilities

GC trades: developer safety and productivity for pause times and tuning burden — the core architect decision for latency-sensitive vs batch workloads.

Part 3: Internal Working

Class Loading — Three Phases

┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐
│   LOADING    │───►│           LINKING                │───►│    INIT     │
│              │    │  Verify → Prepare → Resolve      │    │             │
│ Find binary  │    │                                  │    │ <clinit>()  │
│ Define Class │    │  static fields default values    │    │ static {}   │
└──────────────┘    └──────────────────────────────────┘    └─────────────┘
Phase What Happens Example
Loading Read .class, create Class<?> object PaymentService.class → Metaspace
Verification Bytecode safety checks Stack won't underflow
Preparation Allocate static field slots, default values static int count = 0
Resolution Symbolic refs → direct (may defer) Account ref resolved
Initialization Execute <clinit> static blocks static { loadRules(); }

Class Loader Hierarchy (Delegation Model)

Bootstrap ClassLoader (null in Java API)
    │  java.base, java.lang.*
    ▼
Platform ClassLoader
    │  javax.*, XML, etc.
    ▼
Application ClassLoader
    │  your JARs, Spring Boot classes
    ▼
Custom ClassLoaders
    Spring Boot LaunchedURLClassLoader
    OSGi, plugin frameworks

Delegation: child asks parent first — prevents core class spoofing.

Spring Boot Fat JAR Loading

payment-service.jar
  JarLauncher → LaunchedURLClassLoader
    loads BOOT-INF/classes/
    loads BOOT-INF/lib/*.jar

Startup time = scan + load thousands of classes (Hibernate, Kafka, Spring)
  → Metaspace footprint 80–150 MB typical
  → Spring AOT / GraalVM native (Lesson architect topic) reduces this

Bytecode — What the JVM Executes

public int debit(int amount) {
    return balance - amount;
}

Bytecode (javap -c):
  iload_1          // load amount param
  aload_0          // load this
  getfield balance // read field
  isub             // subtract
  ireturn

Bytecode Verification

Verifier checks:
  - No stack overflow/underflow
  - Type safety on operand stack
  - No illegal field/method access

Prevents malicious or corrupt .class from crashing JVM native layer

JIT Compilation — Tiered Compilation

Invocation count threshold reached (default ~10,000 for C2)

Tier 0: Interpreter                    (cold)
Tier 1: C1 (client) compiler           (quick opts)
Tier 2: C1 + profiling                 (collect branch data)
Tier 3: C2 (server) compiler           (aggressive opts)

Hot method → native machine code stored in CODE CACHE

OPTIMIZATIONS C2 APPLIES:
  - Inlining (small methods)
  - Escape analysis (stack allocate / eliminate locks)
  - Loop unrolling
  - Devirtualization (monomorphic calls — Lesson 2)
  - Dead code elimination

Deoptimization

JIT speculated: PaymentGateway always = NeftGateway
  → inlined neft.charge()

New gateway RazorpayGateway deployed → megamorphic site
  → deopt → back to interpreter → re-profile → recompile

Symptom: latency spike after deploy when call sites change

Code Cache

-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize=256m  (default often 240m)

Full code cache:
  "CodeCache is full. Compiler has been disabled"
  → permanent interpreter fallback → severe perf degradation

Fix: increase code cache, reduce generated classes (dynamic proxies)

Garbage Collection — Object Lifecycle

new Payment() in processRequest()
       │
       ▼
Eden (Young Gen) — bump pointer allocation (~ nanoseconds)
       │
 Minor GC (Stop-The-World, usually short)
       │
  alive → Survivor (S0/S1) → tenured promotions
  dead  → reclaimed
       │
 After ~15 promotions (default) → Old Gen
       │
 Major / Mixed GC (G1) or Full GC

Reachability and GC Roots

GC ROOTS:
  - Stack local refs (all threads)
  - Static fields
  - JNI refs
  - JVM internal refs

Reachable from roots → retained
Unreachable → collectible (safepoint pause, mark phase)

G1 GC (Default Since Java 9)

HEAP divided into equal-sized REGIONS (1–32 MB, typically)

┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐
│ E  │ E  │ S  │ O  │ O  │ H  │ F  │ E  │  ...
└────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘
  Eden  Eden Sur  Old  Old  Hum  Free Eden

E=Eden, S=Survivor, O=Old, H=Humongous (>50% region), F=Free

G1 GOAL: meet pause time target (default MaxGCPauseMillis=200ms)
  - collects regions with most garbage first (Garbage First)
  - Mixed GC: young + selected old regions

Humongous objects: large byte[], big HashMap tables — special regions, fragmentation risk.

ZGC (Java 15+ production, Java 21 low-latency default candidate)

ZGC characteristics:
  - Sub-millisecond pauses (typically < 1ms) on large heaps
  - Colored pointers + load barriers
  - Scales to multi-TB heaps
  - Throughput slightly lower than G1 — trade pause for CPU

Use: payment API strict p99, large heap (8–32 GB), Java 17+
Flags: -XX:+UseZGC

GC Comparison Quick Reference

Collector Pause Throughput Heap Size Use Case
G1 Low–moderate (target 200ms) Good 4–64 GB Default enterprise
ZGC Very low (<1ms typ) Good Large Latency-sensitive API
Parallel GC Higher Best throughput Batch jobs Nightly reconciliation
Shenandoah Very low Similar ZGC Large Alternative to ZGC

Safepoints

JVM needs all threads at safepoint for:
  - GC mark phase
  - Deoptimization
  - Some JVMTI operations

Thread at safepoint: paused at known location
Long counted loops without safepoint poll → GC pause delay

Rare in business code; matters in tight compute loops

Part 4: Memory View

Complete Heap Map Under G1

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  HEAP (-Xmx4g)                                                         │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ G1 Regions (2048 × 2MB example)                                  │   │
│  │                                                                  │   │
│  │  Young collection set: Eden + Survivors                          │   │
│  │  Old regions: long-lived Account caches, connection pool objects   │   │
│  │  Humongous: large batch arrays                                   │   │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  METASPACE (class metadata)          -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m          │
│  PaymentService.class, Hibernate entities, Kafka serializers           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  CODE CACHE (JIT native code)        -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize=256m     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  DIRECT MEMORY (Netty, NIO)          -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=1g         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  THREAD STACKS (N × -Xss)            200 threads × 1MB = 200MB          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

CONTAINER LIMIT 4Gi must cover ALL — not just -Xmx
Rule: MaxRAMPercentage ~75% of container, leave room for native

Object Allocation Fast Path

Eden allocation (TLAB — Thread Local Allocation Buffer):

Each thread gets TLAB chunk in Eden
  bump pointer within TLAB → no synchronization
  TLAB full → new TLAB or slow path (atomic Eden alloc)

Lesson 6 stream allocations → many short-lived objects → Young GC frequency

Promotion and Premature Tenuring

Long-lived objects should reach Old Gen quickly
Short-lived (DTOs, stream pipeline) should die in Young GC

PREMATURE PROMOTION PROBLEM:
  Young GC survivor space too small
  Short-lived objects survive GC → promoted to Old
  Old Gen fills faster → Mixed GC / Full GC → longer pauses

Fix: increase heap, tune InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent, reduce allocation rate

Memory Leak vs Memory Pressure

Memory Leak Memory Pressure
Cause Strong refs to unused objects Legitimate high volume
Old Gen Grows until OOM Stable after peak
Heap dump Duplicate retained objects Expected caches
Fix Code fix (close connections, cache TTL) Bigger heap, GC tune, chunk data
Banking example Static HashMap idempotency unbounded 8M payment batch

Part 5: Performance Analysis

JVM Performance Workflow

1. DEFINE SLA
   p99 < 500ms, GC pause < 100ms, startup < 60s

2. MEASURE (production-like)
   JFR, async-profiler, Micrometer, GC logs

3. IDENTIFY dominant cost
   Allocation rate? GC? JIT? I/O? Locks?

4. FIX cheapest layer first
   Algorithm > allocation > GC tune > hardware

5. REGRESS with JMH + load test
   Gatling/k6 at 2× expected RPS

Key JVM Metrics

Metric Source Alert Threshold (example)
GC pause p99 JFR / GC log > 200ms
Allocation rate JFR TLAB Spike 2× baseline
Heap after full GC GC log Continuously rising → leak
Metaspace used jcmd VM.metaspace > 90% max
Code cache used jcmd CodeCache > 90%
JIT compile rate JFR Post-deploy spike OK

GC Logging (Java 9+ Unified)

-Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20M

Sample interpretation:
[2.345s][info][gc] GC(12) Pause Young (Normal) 512M->48M(4096M) 23.456ms

Young GC reclaimed 464MB in 23ms — healthy
If Old=3800M growing every Mixed GC → leak or undersized heap

Memory Tuning Flags — Container (K8s)

# Java 10+ container-aware (default on)
-XX:+UseContainerSupport
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0
-XX:InitialRAMPercentage=50.0

# Explicit if needed
-Xms2g -Xmx2g

# G1 tuning starting points (4–8 GB heap, API service)
-XX:+UseG1GC
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200
-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=45

# ZGC for strict latency (Java 17+)
-XX:+UseZGC
-XX:+ZGenerational   # Java 21+ generational ZGC

Docker Example — payment-svc

ENV JAVA_OPTS="\
  -XX:+UseContainerSupport \
  -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 \
  -XX:+UseG1GC \
  -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 \
  -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError \
  -XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp/heapdump.hprof \
  -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError \
  -Xlog:gc*:stdout:time,level,tags"

Performance Optimization Hierarchy (Lesson 6 + 12 Unified)

Priority Action Example Gain
1 Fix algorithm / push to SQL 10–100×
2 Reduce allocation rate 2–5× GC reduction
3 Primitive streams, avoid boxing Less Young GC
4 Right GC for workload p99 stability
5 Heap sizing Avoid OOM

7 -XX micro-tuning Last resort

Startup / Warmup Strategies

COLD START PROBLEM (Lesson 6):
  Lambda, streams, new code paths → interpreter → JIT over 2–15 min

MITIGATIONS:
  - Readiness probe delay / warmup endpoint
  - Pre-warm: synthetic traffic before receiving prod traffic
  - Spring Boot 3 AOT (native hints, faster startup)
  - GraalVM native-image (extreme — trade JIT peak perf)
  - CDS (Class Data Sharing) — faster class loading

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Class Loading — Static Initialization Order

package com.bank.config;

public class FraudRuleEngine {

    private static final java.util.Map<String, String> RULES = loadRules();

    static {
        System.out.println("FraudRuleEngine initialized");
    }

    private static java.util.Map<String, String> loadRules() {
        return java.util.Map.of("VELOCITY", "enabled");
    }

    // First reference to FraudRuleEngine triggers:
    // Loading → Linking → <clinit> (static init + static field init in source order)
}

Example 2: Allocation Hot Spot — Object Creation in Loop

package com.bank.reconciliation;

// BAD — 8M PaymentSummary objects per nightly run
public class SlowReconciliation {
    public long sumAmounts(java.util.List<Payment> payments) {
        long total = 0;
        for (Payment p : payments) {
            PaymentSummary s = new PaymentSummary(p.id(), p.amountInPaise()); // allocation
            total += s.paise();
        }
        return total;
    }
    record PaymentSummary(String id, long paise) {}
    record Payment(String id, long amountInPaise) {}
}

// GOOD — no intermediate object
public class FastReconciliation {
    public long sumAmounts(java.util.List<Payment> payments) {
        long total = 0;
        for (Payment p : payments) {
            total += p.amountInPaise();
        }
        return total;
    }
    record Payment(String id, long amountInPaise) {}
}

Example 3: JFR Event — Custom Allocation Tracking Hook

package com.bank.observability;

import jdk.jfr.Event;
import jdk.jfr.Label;
import jdk.jfr.Name;

@Name("com.bank.PaymentProcessed")
@Label("Payment Processed")
public class PaymentProcessedEvent extends Event {

    @Label("Payment Id")
    public String paymentId;

    @Label("Duration Ms")
    public long durationMs;

    public static void record(String paymentId, long durationMs) {
        PaymentProcessedEvent event = new PaymentProcessedEvent();
        event.paymentId = paymentId;
        event.durationMs = durationMs;
        event.commit();
    }
}

Example 4: try-with-resources — Prevent Connection Leak (Metaspace/Heap Pressure)

package com.bank.imports;

import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.SQLException;

public class SettlementFileLoader {

    public void load(java.nio.file.Path file) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection();
             var stmt = conn.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO staging ...")) {
            // process file
        } // conn returned to HikariCP — NOT leaked
    }

    private final javax.sql.DataSource dataSource;
    public SettlementFileLoader(javax.sql.DataSource dataSource) {
        this.dataSource = dataSource;
    }
}

Example 5: Weak References for Cache (Architect Pattern)

package com.bank.fx;

import java.lang.ref.WeakReference;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;

public class SoftFxCache {

    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, WeakReference<BigDecimal>> cache =
        new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public BigDecimal get(String pair) {
        WeakReference<BigDecimal> ref = cache.get(pair);
        return ref != null ? ref.get() : null;
    }

    public void put(String pair, BigDecimal rate) {
        cache.put(pair, new WeakReference<>(rate));
    }
    // GC can reclaim rates under memory pressure — avoid unbounded heap growth
}

JVM Operations in Production

OOM Types and Response

OOM Type Cause Immediate Action
Java heap space Object retention / undersized heap Heap dump, -Xmx, code fix
Metaspace Classloader leak, too many classes Restart, MaxMetaspaceSize, fix redeploy
Direct buffer memory Netty/Kafka direct buffers MaxDirectMemorySize, leak fix
unable to create native thread Too many threads Reduce Tomcat/ pool sizes
CodeCache is full Too much JIT/dynamic codegen Increase code cache

jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof

Check Why

Part 8: Microservice Usage

JVM Per Pod — Multiply Everything

payment-svc:  6 pods × 3 GB heap = 18 GB
ledger-svc:   4 pods × 4 GB heap = 16 GB
fraud-svc:    3 pods × 2 GB heap =  6 GB
                              Total JVM heap ≈ 40 GB cluster

Architect decisions:
  - Fewer larger JVMs vs more smaller pods
  - ZGC on API pods, Parallel GC on batch CronJob pods
  - Separate batch deployment — don't run 8M record job in API pod

Sidecar vs Embedded JVM

API pod:
  payment-svc JVM (G1/ZGC, low pause)
  + optional: OpenTelemetry agent (native memory overhead)

NOT: batch reconciliation in same JVM as HTTP during peak hours

Kafka + JVM Memory

Consumer fetch buffers → heap or direct memory
Large messages → humongous G1 regions
Serialization (Avro) → object allocation per message

Tune:
  fetch.max.bytes
  heap headroom for consumer lag spikes

JVM Mode Native Image
Startup 10–30s <1s
Peak throughput JIT optimized Lower (no C2)
Reflection/Spring Full Configuration required
Use Default enterprise Lambda, edge, instant scale

GC and Workload Matching

WORKLOAD MATRIX:

                    LATENCY SENSITIVE          THROUGHPUT SENSITIVE
                    (payment API p99)          (nightly batch)
HEAP MEDIUM (4GB)   G1 or ZGC                  Parallel GC
HEAP LARGE (32GB)   ZGC                        G1 or Parallel

ADR — ZGC for Payment API

## ADR-128: ZGC for payment-svc (Java 21)

### Context
G1 Mixed GC pauses 80–150ms causing p99 SLA breach at 500K RPS aggregate

### Decision
-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational, MaxRAMPercentage=70

### Trade-off
~5% throughput vs G1 — acceptable for 40ms p99 improvement
Batch jobs remain on Parallel GC in separate CronJob deployment

Class Loading and Startup Architecture

Problem: 60s Spring Boot startup on scale-out

Options:
  1. Spring Boot 3 AOT (process classes at build time)
  2. CDS shared archive
  3. Lazy bean init (careful with first-request latency)
  4. GraalVM native (high migration cost)
  5. Keep minimum pod baseline — HPA from warm pool

When to Escalate Beyond JVM Tuning

Signal Escalation
Allocation rate fundamental to domain Algorithm / SQL / streaming
Heap > 32 GB per pod Partition service, cache external
GC pauses still high on ZGC CPU steal, cgroup throttling, investigate safepoints
Metaspace grows unbounded Classloader leak — dev fix

Staff / Architect Level

  1. G1 vs ZGC — when do you choose each for payment API?
  2. Pod OOMKilled vs Java heap OOM — difference and diagnosis?
  3. Explain premature promotion and its symptoms.
  4. How do you diagnose a Metaspace leak on repeated deploys?
  5. Code cache full — symptoms and fix?
  6. Container memory limit 4Gi — how do you set JVM heap?
  7. Post-deploy latency spike — JIT, GC, or cache? How to prove?
  8. GraalVM native vs HotSpot JVM — trade-offs for Lambda vs EKS?
  9. How does escape analysis help performance?
  10. What JVM flags would you set for nightly 8M record batch job?

Model Answer — Q18 (Container 4Gi)

A: Enable -XX:+UseContainerSupport. Set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70–75 (~2.8–3 Gi heap), not -Xmx4g which ignores native overhead and causes OOMKilled. Reserve space for metaspace (~150–256m cap), thread stacks (200 threads × 1MB = 200MB if default), code cache (256m), direct memory (Netty/Kafka), and native libraries. Add -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError, GC logging, heap dump on OOM. Validate under load with pod memory metrics, not just heap usage.

Model Answer — Q13 (G1 vs ZGC)

A: G1: default, good balance, tunable pause target ~200ms, excellent for 4–8 GB API heaps. ZGC: sub-millisecond pauses, ideal when p99 SLA strict (e.g., <50ms) and heap large or pause spikes from G1 Mixed GC hurt. ZGC trades small throughput for pause stability. For payment API with p99 problems traced to GC in JFR, move to ZGC on Java 21 with generational ZGC. Keep batch on Parallel GC for throughput. Prove with GC logs and load tests, not theory.

Part 13: Common Mistakes

# Mistake Consequence Fix
1 -Xmx = container limit OOMKilled 137 MaxRAMPercentage
2 Ignore GC logs Blind tuning -Xlog:gc*
3 Huge heap without need Long GC pauses Right-size + ZGC
4 Batch job in API JVM p99 spikes Separate deployment
5 Classloader leak on redeploy Metaspace OOM Fix hot deploy, restart
6 Assume deploy slowness is GC Wrong fix Check JIT warmup
7 Full GC thrashing Stop world seconds Increase heap, fix leak
8 Object churn in hot path Constant Young GC Reduce allocation
9 No heap dump on OOM No root cause HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
10 Tune -XX before profiling Wasted effort JFR first

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Profile first — JFR, async-profiler, GC logs
  2. Container-aware memory — MaxRAMPercentage
  3. Match GC to workload — ZGC API, Parallel batch
  4. Reduce allocation rate — biggest GC win in app code
  5. ExitOnOutOfMemoryError — let K8s restart
  6. Heap dump on OOM — always
  7. Warmup strategy for scale-out
  8. Separate batch from API JVM processes
  9. Monitor Metaspace on frequent deploys
  10. Document JVM flags in ADR — reproducible ops

Part 16: Revision Notes

Quick Revision — JVM Internals

CLASS LOADING: Load → Link(Verify,Prepare,Resolve) → Init(<clinit>)
  Delegation: Bootstrap → Platform → Application

BYTECODE: javac → .class → interpreter
JIT: C1 → C2 hot methods → Code Cache
  Warmup: deploy latency — readiness + synthetic traffic

HEAP (G1): regions Eden/Survivor/Old/Humongous
  TLAB: per-thread bump alloc in Eden
  Promotion: survivors → Old (premature promotion = problem)

GC:
  G1 default — pause target 200ms
  ZGC — sub-ms, large heap, API p99
  Parallel — batch throughput

NON-HEAP: Metaspace, Code Cache, Direct, Thread stacks

CONTAINER:
  MaxRAMPercentage 70-75
  NOT -Xmx = limit
  ExitOnOutOfMemoryError, GC logs, heap dump on OOM

TUNE ORDER: algorithm → allocation → GC choice → heap size → -XX micro

Memory Mnemonic

"Classes in Metaspace, objects in Eden, hot code in Cache, pauses in GC logs"

Part 1: Concept

What Is Spring Core?

Spring Core is the foundation of the Spring Framework. Its central idea is Inversion of Control (IoC) — the framework creates, configures, and wires objects (beans) instead of your code calling new everywhere. Dependency Injection (DI) is how Spring delivers those dependencies.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    WITHOUT SPRING              WITH SPRING (IoC)         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  public class PaymentService {          @Service                         │
│    private LedgerClient ledger =        public PaymentService(           │
│      new LedgerClientImpl();              LedgerClient ledger) {         │
│    // tight coupling                      this.ledger = ledger;         │
│  }                                      }                                │
│                                                                          │
│  YOU control object creation            CONTAINER controls creation      │
│  hard to test, swap, configure          inject interface, mock in tests  │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Spring Container Hierarchy

                    BeanFactory (minimal)
                         │
                         ▼
              ApplicationContext (full-featured)
                         │
         ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
         │               │               │
  AnnotationConfig   ClassPathXml    WebApplicationContext
  ApplicationContext ApplicationContext  (Spring MVC/Boot)
         │
         ▼
  Spring Boot creates AnnotationConfigApplicationContext
  + auto-configuration + component scanning

Core Concepts Master Table

Concept What Why Banking Example
IoC Control of object creation inverted to container Decouple construction from use Swap NEFT vs UPI gateway via config
DI Dependencies provided externally Testability, modularity Inject AccountRepository into TransferService
Bean Object managed by Spring container Lifecycle, scope, proxying @Service PaymentService singleton
ApplicationContext IoC container + enterprise services Events, i18n, AOP integration Spring Boot application context
Component Scan Auto-detect @Component classes Convention over configuration Scan com.bank.payments.*
Configuration @Configuration + @Bean methods Third-party beans, explicit wiring DataSource bean
Dependency What a bean needs to work Explicit graph TransferService → LedgerClient

Bean Definition vs Bean Instance

BEAN DEFINITION (metadata — loaded at startup)
  - bean class: PaymentService
  - scope: singleton
  - constructor args: LedgerClient ref
  - init method: @PostConstruct
  - lazy: false

BEAN INSTANCE (object on heap — created per scope)
  - singleton: ONE instance per ApplicationContext (per JVM pod)
  - prototype: new instance each injection/getBean

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why Spring and IoC Were Created

Pre-Spring Enterprise Java (EJB 2.x) Spring (2003+)
Heavy application server required Lightweight container
JNDI lookups everywhere Constructor injection
Interface + home + remote boilerplate POJO + annotations
Hard to unit test @MockBean, @InjectMocks
Tangled object creation Centralized wiring

Why Architects Standardize on Spring in Banking

REQUIREMENTS IN BANKING:
  - 50+ services, 200+ developers
  - Replace Oracle with PostgreSQL in ledger
  - Mock fraud engine in CI
  - Configure different payment gateways per region
  - Singleton services MUST be stateless (Lesson 7)

SPRING ANSWERS:
  Interface + @Autowired → swap implementation
  @Profile("prod") / @Profile("test") → environment beans
  @Primary / @Qualifier → disambiguation
  Container-managed lifecycle → @PreDestroy cleanup

IoC Is an Architectural Pattern — Not Just a Framework Feature

DEPENDENCY INVERSION PRINCIPLE (Lesson 2):
  High-level TransferService depends on AccountPort abstraction
  Low-level JpaAccountAdapter implements AccountPort
  Spring container injects adapter at runtime

Spring is the MECHANISM for DIP at enterprise scale

Why Constructor Injection Won (Spring Team Recommendation)

Constructor Field @Autowired Setter
Immutable deps Mutable after construction Mutable
Required deps explicit Hidden Optional feel
Test-friendly Needs reflection/Spring new Service(mock)
Null-safe Can forget injection —
Recommended Discouraged Legacy

Part 3: Internal Working

ApplicationContext Startup (Spring Boot Simplified)

SpringApplication.run(PaymentApplication.class, args)

1. Create ApplicationContext
2. Prepare Environment (properties, profiles, YAML)
3. Print banner (optional)
4. Refresh Context:
   a. Load bean definitions (@Component scan, @Configuration, auto-config)
   b. BeanFactoryPostProcessor (modify definitions — @Configuration parsing)
   c. Register BeanPostProcessors (AOP wrappers — Lesson 15)
   d. Instantiate singleton beans (non-lazy)

   f. Initialize beans (@PostConstruct, InitializingBean)
   g. ContextRefreshedEvent
5. Run CommandLineRunners / ApplicationRunners
6. Start embedded Tomcat (Web)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────►
0s        5s         15s        25s        40s
│         │          │          │          │
context   bean       Hibernate  Tomcat     ready
create    scan       init       start      probe OK
          2000+ classes loaded (Lesson 12 Metaspace)

Component Scanning Internals

@SpringBootApplication
public class PaymentApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(PaymentApplication.class, args);
    }
}

// @SpringBootApplication = @Configuration + @EnableAutoConfiguration
//                        + @ComponentScan (same package and below)

@ComponentScan("com.bank.payments"):
  Classpath scanning (ASM bytecode read — no class init yet)
  Finds classes annotated @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller
  Registers BeanDefinition for each

  @Service is @Component stereotype
  @Repository is @Component + exception translation
  @Controller is @Component + MVC

Dependency Injection — Resolution Algorithm

@Autowired PaymentService needs LedgerClient

1. Find bean of type LedgerClient (or compatible)
2. If multiple candidates:
     a. @Primary bean wins
     b. @Qualifier("jpaLedgerClient") disambiguates
     c. Parameter name matching (LedgerClient jpaLedgerClient)
     d. Fail: NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
3. If none: NoSuchBeanDefinitionException (unless @Autowired(required=false))
4. Create proxy if @Transactional/@Cacheable (Lesson 15/18)
5. Inject via constructor (preferred)

DEPENDENCY GRAPH (simplified):

PaymentController
       │
       ▼
PaymentService ──────► FraudService
       │                      │
       ├──► LedgerClient      └──► FraudRule[]
       │
       └──► PaymentRepository ──► EntityManager ──► DataSource

Circular Dependency Problem

@Service
class A { A(B b) {} }

@Service
class B { B(A a) {} }  // constructor cycle → FAIL at startup

Spring CAN resolve setter/field cycle with early singleton exposure (三级缓存)
  BUT constructor injection cycle → BeanCurrentlyInCreationException

ARCHITECT FIX: refactor — extract shared logic to C, or use @Lazy on one side
NEVER rely on field injection to "fix" design smell

Bean Lifecycle — Full Sequence

1. Instantiate bean (constructor)
2. Populate properties / inject dependencies
3. BeanNameAware, BeanFactoryAware, ApplicationContextAware
4. BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization
5. @PostConstruct
6. InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()
7. Custom init-method
8. BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization  ← AOP proxy often here
9. Bean ready for use
10. @PreDestroy on shutdown
11. DisposableBean.destroy()

PaymentService bean lifecycle:

new PaymentService(ledger, fraud)  ← constructor
  → inject dependencies
  → @PostConstruct loadCache()
  → (AOP proxy wrapped if @Transactional)
  → serve HTTP requests (singleton — all threads share)
  → @PreDestroy shutdown executor

@Configuration and @Bean — Method Interception

@Configuration
public class AppConfig {

    @Bean
    public ObjectMapper objectMapper() {
        return new ObjectMapper();
    }

    @Bean
    public PaymentValidator paymentValidator(ObjectMapper mapper) {
        return new PaymentValidator(mapper);  // single ObjectMapper bean injected
    }
}

@Configuration class is CGLIB-enhanced subclass:
  @Bean methods intercepted — singleton beans returned from cache
  Calling objectMapper() twice returns SAME instance within config

@Component + @Bean methods NOT guaranteed singleton unless @Configuration

Spring Container Memory Footprint

HEAP (one pod, one ApplicationContext)

│ SINGLETON BEANS (shared by all Tomcat threads)                   │
│  PaymentService @7a001                                           │
│  TransferService @7a002                                          │

└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

METASPACE (Lesson 12)
  Spring framework classes
  CGLIB enhanced subclasses ($$EnhancerBySpringCGLIB)
  Hibernate entity metadata
  ~80–200 MB typical

Singleton Scope and Thread Safety (Lesson 7 Connection)

@Service  ← ONE instance in heap
public class PaymentService {
    private final LedgerClient ledger;  // immutable ref — SAFE
    // private int count;  // UNSAFE — all threads mutate
    // private List<X> cache;  // UNSAFE unless concurrent
}
Field Type Singleton Safe?
final injected dependency Yes
Immutable config (final String region) Yes
ConcurrentHashMap cache Yes with care
Mutable ArrayList No
static mutable No

Proxy Memory Overhead

PaymentService (concrete class)
  → CGLIB subclass proxy (if @Transactional on class methods)
  → extra Metaspace class + heap proxy instance

JDK dynamic proxy (if interface-based):
  Proxy implements PaymentService interface
  InvocationHandler delegates to target

Each proxied bean: ~2 objects (proxy + target) — Lesson 15 deep dive

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Spring Container Performance

Startup Time Breakdown

Phase Typical % Tuning
Classpath scan + bean definition 20–30% Narrow scan base, exclude unused
Auto-configuration evaluation 15–25% @SpringBootApplication(exclude=...)
Hibernate/JPA metadata 20–40% Lazy init (careful)
Bean instantiation + DI 10–20% Reduce unnecessary beans
Tomcat/Netty start 10–15% —

Runtime Overhead

DI at startup ONLY for singletons — zero injection cost per HTTP request
Runtime cost comes from:
  - AOP proxies (method interception — nanoseconds to microseconds)
  - @Transactional (connection acquisition — milliseconds)
  - Reflection (minimal after JIT inlines hot paths)

Spring is NOT slow at runtime for well-designed services
Slowness = DB, external HTTP, allocation (Lessons 6, 12)

Lazy Initialization

@Lazy
@Service
public class HeavyReportingService { ... }

// Bean created on first use, not at startup
// Trade-off: faster startup, slower first request, later failure discovery
@Lazy on bean @Lazy on injection point
Entire bean deferred Breaks circular dependency (band-aid)
Slower first access Dependency proxy injected

Scalability

Aspect Impact
One ApplicationContext per pod Horizontal scale = duplicate beans per pod
Singleton stateless services Scales linearly with pods
@Cacheable singleton Per-pod cache — use Redis for shared
Heavy @PostConstruct Slow startup × replica count on deploy

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Constructor Injection — Payment Service

package com.bank.payments.service;

import com.bank.payments.gateway.PaymentGateway;
import com.bank.payments.repository.PaymentRepository;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class PaymentService {

    private final PaymentRepository paymentRepository;
    private final PaymentGateway paymentGateway;

    public PaymentService(PaymentRepository paymentRepository,
                          PaymentGateway paymentGateway) {
        this.paymentRepository = paymentRepository;
        this.paymentGateway = paymentGateway;
    }

    public PaymentResult process(PaymentRequest request) {
        paymentRepository.savePending(request);
        return paymentGateway.charge(request);
    }
}

Example 2: Interface + Multiple Implementations — @Primary / @Qualifier

package com.bank.payments.gateway;

public interface PaymentGateway {
    PaymentResult charge(PaymentRequest request);
}

@Service
@Primary  // default when multiple beans
public class NeftGateway implements PaymentGateway {
    @Override
    public PaymentResult charge(PaymentRequest request) { /* ... */ return null; }
}

@Service
@Qualifier("upiGateway")
public class UpiGateway implements PaymentGateway {
    @Override
    public PaymentResult charge(PaymentRequest request) { /* ... */ return null; }
}

@Service
public class PaymentRouter {

    private final PaymentGateway defaultGateway;
    private final PaymentGateway upiGateway;

    public PaymentRouter(PaymentGateway defaultGateway,
                         @Qualifier("upiGateway") PaymentGateway upiGateway) {
        this.defaultGateway = defaultGateway;
        this.upiGateway = upiGateway;
    }

    public PaymentResult route(PaymentRequest request) {
        PaymentGateway gateway = "UPI".equals(request.mode())
            ? upiGateway : defaultGateway;
        return gateway.charge(request);
    }
}

Example 3: @Configuration — DataSource and Third-Party Beans

package com.bank.payments.config;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;

@Configuration
public class InfrastructureConfig {

    @Bean
    public ObjectMapper objectMapper() {

            .findAndRegisterModules();

Example 4: Bean Lifecycle — @PostConstruct / @PreDestroy

package com.bank.payments.integration;

import jakarta.annotation.PostConstruct;
import jakarta.annotation.PreDestroy;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

@Service
public class LegacyBridgeService {

    private ExecutorService executor;

    @PostConstruct
    public void init() {
        executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, r -> new Thread(r, "legacy-bridge"));
    }

    @PreDestroy
    public void shutdown() {
        executor.shutdown();
        try {
            if (!executor.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
                executor.shutdownNow();
            }
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            executor.shutdownNow();
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }
}

Example 5: @Profile — Environment-Specific Beans

package com.bank.payments.config;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Profile;

@Configuration
public class GatewayConfig {

    @Bean
    @Profile("prod")
    public PaymentGateway prodGateway() {
        return new LiveNeftGateway();
    }

    @Bean
    @Profile({"dev", "test"})
    public PaymentGateway mockGateway() {
        return new StubPaymentGateway();
    }
}

Example 6: Conditional Beans — @ConditionalOnProperty

package com.bank.fraud.config;

import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.condition.ConditionalOnProperty;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;

@Configuration
public class FraudConfig {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "fraud.engine", havingValue = "enabled", matchIfMissing = true)
    public FraudService liveFraudService() {
        return new LiveFraudService();
    }

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "fraud.engine", havingValue = "disabled")
    public FraudService noOpFraudService() {
        return request -> FraudResult.pass();
    }
}

Example 7: Port and Adapter (Hexagonal + Spring)

package com.bank.ledger.port;

import com.bank.ledger.domain.LedgerAccount;
import java.util.Optional;

public interface AccountPort {
    Optional<LedgerAccount> findById(String accountId);
    void save(LedgerAccount account);
}

@Repository
public class JpaAccountAdapter implements AccountPort {
    private final AccountJpaRepository jpaRepository;

    public JpaAccountAdapter(AccountJpaRepository jpaRepository) {
        this.jpaRepository = jpaRepository;
    }

    @Override
    public Optional<LedgerAccount> findById(String accountId) {
        return jpaRepository.findById(accountId).map(this::toDomain);
    }

    @Override
    public void save(LedgerAccount account) {
        jpaRepository.save(toEntity(account));
    }

    private LedgerAccount toDomain(AccountEntity e) { /* ... */ return null; }
    private AccountEntity toEntity(LedgerAccount a) { /* ... */ return null; }
}

Part 8: Microservice Usage

Spring Core in Microservice Architecture

One ApplicationContext Per Pod

┌──────────────── payment-svc pod ─────────────────┐
│  ApplicationContext (singleton scope default)   │
│  ┌─────────────┐  ┌─────────────┐              │
│  │ PaymentSvc  │  │ FraudSvc    │  ONE each    │
│  └──────┬──────┘  └─────────────┘              │
│         │ @Autowired IN-JVM only                │
└─────────┼───────────────────────────────────────┘
          │ HTTP / Kafka (NOT Spring DI)
          ▼
┌──────────────── ledger-svc pod ─────────────────┐
│  Separate ApplicationContext                     │
│  LedgerService — different JVM, different beans  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Critical: @Autowired LedgerClient injects local adapter that calls remote service — not remote bean.

Shared Library Anti-Pattern

WRONG: common.jar with @Service PaymentHelper shared across microservices
  → duplicate bean definitions, version coupling, distributed monolith

RIGHT: common.jar with DTOs, exceptions, API contracts ONLY
  → each service defines own @Service beans

Model Answer — Q14 (Stateless @Service)

A: Default scope is singleton — one instance per ApplicationContext per pod. All Tomcat threads share it. Mutable instance fields create race conditions (Lesson 7). Stateless means dependencies injected via final constructor refs, no mutable shared fields; all request state in method parameters or thread-local MDC. Financial correctness requires external store (DB/Redis) for shared state, not bean fields. Scale horizontally by adding pods, each with own singleton instances.

Model Answer — Q9 (Bean Lifecycle)

A: Container instantiates bean via constructor, injects dependencies, calls Aware interfaces, BeanPostProcessor before init, @PostConstruct, InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet, custom init, BeanPostProcessor after init (AOP proxy may wrap here), bean ready. On shutdown: @PreDestroy, DisposableBean.destroy, custom destroy. Singletons created eagerly at refresh unless @Lazy. Prototype beans: full lifecycle per creation, container doesn't destroy prototypes.

Part 13: Common Mistakes

# Mistake Consequence Fix
1 Field @Autowired Untestable, mutable Constructor injection
2 Mutable state in @Service Race conditions Stateless + external store
3 @ComponentScan too broad Slow startup, wrong beans Narrow base package
4 Circular dependency via constructors Startup failure Refactor design
5 @Bean on @Component without @Configuration Multiple instances Move to @Configuration
6 Business logic in @Configuration Wrong layer @Service
7 @Autowired optional everywhere Hidden failures Required constructor deps
8 Shared @Service JAR across MS Coupling API jar only
9 Heavy @PostConstruct Slow/killed startup Async or lazy
10 God @Service with 20 deps Monolith smell Split bounded context

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Constructor injection with final fields
  2. Interface-based dependencies for ports/adapters
  3. Stateless @Service singletons
  4. @ConfigurationProperties for typed config
  5. Narrow @ComponentScan
  6. @PreDestroy for resource cleanup
  7. Domain module free of Spring annotations (hexagonal)
  8. @Qualifier or strategy map for multiple implementations
  9. Fail at startup — validate beans, config in @PostConstruct early
  10. Test without full context when possible — plain unit tests + constructor
