Part 1: Concept

What Are Spring Internals?

Spring Internals is the machinery beneath @Service and @Autowired: how the container stores bean metadata, creates instances, resolves scopes, breaks or detects cycles, and wraps beans in proxies. Understanding this separates a Tech Lead who configures Spring from a Solution Architect who debugs startup failures, memory leaks, and wrong-bean bugs in production.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    SPRING CONTAINER INTERNAL LAYERS                      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  LAYER 4: YOUR CODE          @Service, @Controller, @Bean              │
│  LAYER 3: INFRASTRUCTURE     BeanPostProcessor, AOP, Event listeners     │
│  LAYER 2: CORE CONTAINER     ApplicationContext / BeanFactory          │
│  LAYER 1: METADATA           BeanDefinition, BeanDefinitionRegistry      │
│                                                                          │
│  refresh() walks top-down: metadata → create → post-process → ready      │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext

BeanFactory ApplicationContext
What Core IoC container interface Extended container
Bean creation Lazy by default Eager singletons at startup
Features getBean, containsBean, isSingleton + Events, i18n, ResourceLoader, automatic BeanPostProcessor registration
Used directly Almost never in modern apps Spring Boot default
Implementation DefaultListableBeanFactory AnnotationConfigApplicationContext, etc.
Analogy Engine Engine + transmission + dashboard 
BeanFactory = "I can give you beans if you ask"
ApplicationContext = "I prepare the whole system at startup and integrate everything"

Bean Scopes — Master Table

Scope Instances per Context Lifecycle Thread Safety Banking Use
singleton (default) 1 Context lifetime Must be stateless @Service, @Repository
prototype New per getBean/inject Container doesn't destroy Per-instance Stateful parser (rare)
request 1 per HTTP request Request start → end Isolated per request Request-scoped user context
session 1 per HTTP session Session lifetime Per user session Legacy web apps
application 1 per ServletContext App lifetime Shared in web app Servlet-level config

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why Two Container Abstractions?

Historical Need BeanFactory ApplicationContext
Minimal footprint (applet era) ✓ Lazy load Heavier
Enterprise integration (AOP, events) Insufficient alone ✓ Built-in
Fail fast at startup Lazy hides misconfig Eager exposes errors before traffic
Automatic infrastructure beans Manual registration Auto-detect BeanPostProcessors

Spring Boot uses ApplicationContext so miswired payment services fail at deploy — not on first production transaction.

Why Scopes Exist

PROBLEM:
  UserContext holds current user's permissions — cannot be singleton (all users share)
  PaymentService holds business logic — should be singleton (one instance, stateless)

SOLUTION:
  singleton PaymentService + request-scoped UserContext injected via proxy

Why Architects Need Internals Knowledge

PRODUCTION INCIDENTS REQUIRING INTERNALS:

1. "Wrong gateway used in prod" → @Primary vs @Qualifier resolution order
2. "Memory grows after redeploys" → prototype beans or classloader leak
3. "Random NPE in request scope bean from @Async" → scope propagation failure
4. "Startup fails after refactor" → circular dependency in constructor graph
5. "Two ObjectMapper beans, wrong one injected" → @Bean method proxy vs @Component

Part 3: Internal Working

DefaultListableBeanFactory — The Heart

ApplicationContext (facade)
       │
       delegates to
       ▼
DefaultListableBeanFactory
  ├── beanDefinitionMap: Map<String, BeanDefinition>
  ├── singletonObjects: Map<String, Object>           (一级缓存)
  ├── earlySingletonObjects: Map<String, Object>      (二级缓存)
  ├── singletonFactories: Map<String, ObjectFactory>  (三级缓存)
  └── singletonsCurrentlyInCreation: Set<String>

BeanDefinition — Metadata Before Instance

// Conceptual — not API you write daily
BeanDefinition bd = new RootBeanDefinition(PaymentService.class);
bd.setScope(BeanDefinition.SCOPE_SINGLETON);
bd.setLazyInit(false);
bd.getConstructorArgumentValues().addGenericArgumentValue(ledgerClientRef);

BeanDefinition contains:
  - beanClassName / factoryMethod
  - scope, lazyInit, primary, depends-on
  - constructor argument values
  - property values (legacy XML)
  - init/destroy method names
  - role (ROLE_APPLICATION, ROLE_INFRASTRUCTURE)

Context Refresh — 12 Phases (Simplified)

AbstractApplicationContext.refresh():

1.  prepareRefresh()
2.  obtainFreshBeanFactory() / prepareBeanFactory()
3.  invokeBeanFactoryPostProcessors()     ← @Configuration parsing, @Value resolution
4.  registerBeanPostProcessors()          ← AOP, @Autowired annotation processors
5.  initMessageSource()
6.  initApplicationEventMulticaster()
7.  onRefresh()                           ← Tomcat starts here (ServletWebServer)
8.  registerListeners()
9.  finishBeanFactoryInitialization()     ← CREATE ALL NON-LAZY SINGLETONS ★
10. finishRefresh()                       ← ContextRefreshedEvent
11. (listeners run)

Phase 9 is where your 300 @Service beans materialize — Lesson 12 Metaspace and startup time.

Singleton Bean Creation Pipeline

getBean("paymentService"):

1. Transform bean name (alias resolution)
2. If singleton and already in singletonObjects → return cached
3. Check singletonsCurrentlyInCreation → circular dependency detection
4. getSingleton(beanName, ObjectFactory) — create if absent
5. createBean():
     a. resolveBeanClass()
     b. apply BeanPostProcessors before instantiation (can short-circuit)
     c. instantiate: constructor autowire
     d. applyMergedBeanDefinitionPostProcessors
     e. apply BeanPostProcessors after instantiation (AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor injects fields if any)
     f. initializeBean():
          - invokeAwareMethods
          - applyBeanPostProcessorsBeforeInitialization
          - invokeInitMethods (@PostConstruct)
          - applyBeanPostProcessorsAfterInitialization (AOP proxy)
6. Put finished bean in singletonObjects (一级缓存)
7. Return bean (or proxy)

CREATION FLOW DIAGRAM:

BeanDefinition ──► instantiate ──► populate ──► initialize ──► (proxy?) ──► singleton cache
                         │              │            │
                    constructor    @Autowired    @PostConstruct
                                   injection      InitializingBean

Three-Level Cache — Circular Dependency (Setter/Field Only)

A depends on B (field/setter), B depends on A (field/setter)

Create A:
  1. Put A factory in singletonFactories (三级)
  2. Populate A → needs B → create B
  3. Create B:
       Put B factory in singletonFactories
       Populate B → needs A → getBean(A)
       A factory returns early reference (二级 earlySingletonObjects)
       B completes → singleton cache
  4. A completes with B injected

CONSTRUCTOR cycle A(B), B(A): CANNOT expose early ref before ctor completes → FAIL

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SINGLETON CACHE (conceptual)                                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  一级 singletonObjects      → complete beans               │
│  二级 earlySingletonObjects → early exposed (incomplete)   │
│  三级 singletonFactories    → factories for early exposure   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Prototype Scope Internals

getBean(prototypeBean):
  createBean() every time
  NO caching in singletonObjects
  Container does NOT call @PreDestroy on prototypes
  YOU own cleanup

Injection of prototype into singleton:
  SINGLETON gets ONE prototype instance at creation time (wrong for per-use)
  FIX: ObjectFactory<PrototypeBean> or @Scope(proxyMode=TARGET_CLASS) or Provider<T>

Request Scope + Scoped Proxy

@Component
@Scope(value = WebApplicationContext.SCOPE_REQUEST, proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)
public class RequestPaymentContext {
    private String correlationId;
    // set per HTTP request
}

INJECTION INTO SINGLETON:

PaymentService (singleton) holds proxy → RequestPaymentContext$$Enhancer

Each method call on proxy:
  → looks up current HttpServletRequest in RequestContextHolder
  → delegates to REAL request-scoped bean for THIS request

Without proxy: singleton would hold stale/wrong request bean reference

FactoryBean — Bean That Creates Beans

public class ConnectionFactoryBean implements FactoryBean<Connection> {
    @Override
    public Connection getObject() { return DriverManager.getConnection(...); }
    @Override
    public Class<?> getObjectType() { return Connection.class; }
}

// Container registers factory bean "connectionFactoryBean"
// getBean("connectionFactoryBean") → FactoryBean instance
// getBean("&connectionFactoryBean") → prefix & = factory itself
// getBean by type Connection → product from getObject()

MyBatis SqlSessionFactoryBean, JPA EntityManagerFactory — FactoryBean pattern.

Environment and PropertySource Chain

ConfigurableEnvironment
  └── MutablePropertySources (ordered chain, first match wins)

  Command line args          (highest priority in Boot)
  SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON
  ServletConfig/ServletContext
  systemProperties
  systemEnvironment
  application-{profile}.yml
  application.yml            (lowest)

@Value("${payment.limit}") resolved from highest precedence source containing key
@ConfigurationProperties binds prefix at startup (BeanPostProcessor)

Part 4: Memory View

Container Memory Layout in One Pod

HEAP
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ DefaultListableBeanFactory                                       │
│   beanDefinitionMap: ~500 entries (metadata objects, small)       │
│   singletonObjects: ~300 bean instances (THE bulk of Spring heap)  │
│     paymentService → PaymentService@7a001 (or CGLIB proxy)        │
│     transferService → TransferService@7a002                       │
│     jpaAccountAdapter → JpaAccountAdapter@7a003                   │
│     dataSource → HikariDataSource@7a004 (pool inside)           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ REQUEST SCOPE (if used)                                           │
│   requestScopeCache: Map<requestId, Map<beanName, instance>>    │
│   destroyed at request end — short-lived                          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ PROTOTYPE instances — only if repeatedly created (leak if retained)│
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

METASPACE
  CGLIB: PaymentService$$SpringCGLIB$$0, RequestContext$$Enhancer
  Spring internal: BeanPostProcessor impl classes
  Hibernate entity metadata

Scope Memory Impact

Scope Heap Pressure GC Risk
singleton Fixed at startup Long-lived Old Gen Mutable state = bugs
prototype Per creation Young Gen if discarded Retained refs = leak
request Per HTTP request Young Gen Forgotten if async escapes request
session Per user session Can accumulate Memory leak in long sessions

Proxy Duplication

@Service @Transactional
public class PaymentService { ... }

Memory:
  PaymentService target instance
  CGLIB proxy subclass instance (holds ref to target)
  Metaspace: generated proxy class

300 proxied beans → 300 extra proxy objects + Metaspace classes
Acceptable; watch Metaspace on hot redeploy without restart

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Container Performance Characteristics

Startup vs Runtime

Phase Cost Frequency
Component scan (ASM) CPU + I/O Every startup
Bean definition registration Memory Every startup
Singleton instantiation CPU + Metaspace Every startup
Dependency injection graph CPU Every startup
HTTP request getBean Cache hit — O(1) Never per request for singletons

Singleton lookup at runtime: hash map get from singletonObjects — nanoseconds. Spring DI is NOT your latency bottleneck.

Scope Performance

Scope Request Overhead
singleton None
prototype Full creation each time — expensive
request + proxy Proxy dispatch + ThreadLocal lookup per method call
session + proxy Similar + session map lookup

Avoid request scope on hot path methods called thousands of times per request unless necessary.

Lazy Initialization Impact

@Lazy
@Service
public class HeavyReportService { ... }

Startup: skip creation → faster deploy, less Metaspace immediate pressure
First getBean: pay creation cost + possible failure late
Cold first request: latency spike

Architect: @Lazy on entire context (--spring.main.lazy-initialization=true) for dev only
Production: fail fast at startup preferred for payment services

Circular Dependency @Lazy Injection Point

@Service
public class A {
    public A(@Lazy B b) { ... }  // injects B proxy, defers B creation
}

Breaks cycle at cost of proxy indirection + later failure if B fails init
Design fix > @Lazy band-aid

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Explicit Bean Scopes

package com.bank.payments.context;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Scope;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.ScopedProxyMode;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.web.context.WebApplicationContext;

@Component
@Scope(value = WebApplicationContext.SCOPE_REQUEST,
       proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)
public class PaymentRequestContext {

    private String correlationId;
    private String userId;

    public void initialize(String correlationId, String userId) {
        this.correlationId = correlationId;
        this.userId = userId;
    }

    public String correlationId() { return correlationId; }
    public String userId() { return userId; }
}

Example 2: Prototype via ObjectFactory — Correct Pattern

package com.bank.imports;

import org.springframework.beans.factory.ObjectFactory;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class FileImportOrchestrator {

    private final ObjectFactory<ImportBatchProcessor> processorFactory;

    public FileImportOrchestrator(ObjectFactory<ImportBatchProcessor> processorFactory) {
        this.processorFactory = processorFactory;
    }

    public void processFile(String path) {
        ImportBatchProcessor processor = processorFactory.getObject(); // new prototype each call
        processor.process(path);
    }
}

@Component
@Scope(ConfigurableBeanFactory.SCOPE_PROTOTYPE)
class ImportBatchProcessor {
    private final java.util.List<String> errors = new java.util.ArrayList<>();

    void process(String path) { /* state isolated per file */ }
}

Example 3: ApplicationContext Events — Decoupled Notification

package com.bank.payments.events;

import org.springframework.context.ApplicationEvent;
import org.springframework.context.ApplicationEventPublisher;
import org.springframework.context.event.EventListener;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class PaymentService {

    private final ApplicationEventPublisher publisher;

    public PaymentService(ApplicationEventPublisher publisher) {
        this.publisher = publisher;
    }

    public void completePayment(String paymentId) {
        // business logic
        publisher.publishEvent(new PaymentCompletedEvent(this, paymentId));
    }
}

public class PaymentCompletedEvent extends ApplicationEvent {
    private final String paymentId;
    public PaymentCompletedEvent(Object source, String paymentId) {
        super(source);
        this.paymentId = paymentId;
    }
    public String paymentId() { return paymentId; }
}

@Component
class PaymentAuditListener {
    @EventListener
    void onCompleted(PaymentCompletedEvent event) {
        // audit — runs synchronously on same thread by default
    }
}

Example 4: @DependsOn — Initialization Order

@Configuration
public class CacheConfig {

    @Bean
    @DependsOn("dataSource")  // dataSource fully initialized first
    public FxRateCache fxRateCache(DataSource dataSource) {
        return new FxRateCache(dataSource);
    }
}

Example 5: Programmatic Bean Registration (Advanced)

@Configuration
public class DynamicGatewayConfig {

    @Bean
    public BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor gatewayRegistrar() {
        return registry -> {
            RootBeanDefinition def = new RootBeanDefinition(RtgsGateway.class);
            def.setScope(BeanDefinition.SCOPE_SINGLETON);
            registry.registerBeanDefinition("rtgsGateway", def);
        };
    }
}

Example 6: Inspecting Container — Debug Production

@Component
public class BeanInspector implements ApplicationContextAware {

    private ApplicationContext context;

    @Override
    public void setApplicationContext(ApplicationContext ctx) {
        this.context = ctx;
    }

    public void logPaymentBeans() {
        String[] names = context.getBeanNamesForType(PaymentGateway.class);
        for (String name : names) {
            Object bean = context.getBean(name);
            System.out.println(name + " -> " + bean.getClass().getName()
                + " singleton=" + context.isSingleton(name));
        }
    }
}

Exercise 1

Explain why injecting a prototype bean directly into a singleton @Service gives one shared prototype instance. Fix with ObjectProvider<ImportBatchProcessor>.

Part 7: Production Usage

Spring Internals in Production

Fail Fast at Startup

ApplicationContext eager init:
  Missing LedgerClient bean → startup fails → K8s CrashLoopBackOff → alert
  NOT missing bean → first payment at 2 AM → NPE → financial incident

Request Scope + @Async Trap

@Service
public class PaymentService {
    @Async
    public void notifyAsync(PaymentRequestContext ctx) {
        // ctx may be WRONG or null — request scope ended when HTTP returned
        ctx.correlationId();  // disaster
    }
}

// FIX: pass correlationId as String parameter, not request-scoped bean

Multiple ApplicationContext (Rare Pitfall)

Parent/child contexts in legacy apps:
  getBean might resolve from parent — wrong bean version

Spring Boot: single context per app — standard
Avoid manual parent context unless you know why

Production Checklist

Check Why

Part 9: Architect Perspective

Scope and Lifecycle as Design Decisions

Scope Decision Tree

Does state belong to entire service?
  YES → singleton (stateless fields only)
  NO ↓

Does state belong to one HTTP request?
  YES → request scope + proxy OR pass as parameter (preferred)
  NO ↓

Does state belong to one operation/batch file?
  YES → prototype via ObjectProvider OR plain new in method
  NO ↓

Does state belong to user session?
  RARE in REST APIs → JWT stateless preferred
  Legacy web → session scope + proxy

Singleton Default Is an Architectural Constraint

Spring assumes: most beans are singleton
Architect assumes: microservice instances are stateless

These align. Fighting singleton with mutable state causes production races.
Fighting with excessive prototype creates GC pressure.

ADR — No Request Scope in Payment API

## ADR-138: Correlation ID via MDC, not request-scoped beans

### Decision
Pass correlationId explicitly; use ThreadLocal MDC in filter; no @Scope request beans in payment API

### Rationale
@Async and Kafka listeners break request scope; explicit params work everywhere
Avoids scoped proxy overhead on hot path

BeanFactoryPostProcessor vs BeanPostProcessor (Architect Awareness)

BeanFactoryPostProcessor BeanPostProcessor
Runs Before bean instantiation Per bean create
Modifies BeanDefinition Bean instance
Example @Configuration parsing @Autowired, AOP proxy
Architect impact Changes what gets created Wraps/changes instances

  4. Why does ApplicationContext startup fail fast benefit payment systems?
  5. Design: tenant-specific beans vs tenant config in singleton?

  7. BeanFactoryPostProcessor vs BeanPostProcessor — use cases?
  8. Multiple beans same type — resolution algorithm order?
  9. Programmatic bean registration — when would architect use it?

Model Answer — Q7 (Circular Dependency)

A: For setter/field injection cycles, Spring creates bean A, exposes early reference via singleton factory (三级缓存) before completing property injection, creates B, B gets early A reference, B completes, A completes. For constructor cycles, object doesn't exist until constructor returns — no early reference possible — BeanCurrentlyInCreationException. Fix by redesigning dependencies, extracting shared component, or @Lazy proxy on one constructor arg (defers creation). Constructor injection failure is desirable — forces clean graph.

Model Answer — Q9 (Scoped Proxy)

A: Singleton lives entire context lifetime; request bean lives one HTTP request. Injecting request bean directly into singleton would capture one instance forever — wrong. Scoped proxy injects CGLIB/JDK proxy into singleton. Each method call resolves current request from RequestContextHolder and delegates to correct request instance. Performance cost: proxy dispatch + lookup. Alternative: pass request data as method parameters — simpler and works with async.

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Singleton + stateless for all microservice beans
  2. Explicit parameters over request scope where possible
  3. ObjectProvider / Provider for prototype needs
  4. Constructor injection — let cycles fail loudly
  5. One ApplicationContext per application
  6. @Configuration for all @Bean method classes
  7. @Primary documented when multiple impls
  8. Avoid session scope in REST APIs
  9. Use events for decoupling over circular deps
  10. Actuator /conditions to debug auto-config in prod issues

Part 1: Concept

What Is AOP?

Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP) separates cross-cutting concerns — logging, security, transactions, metrics — from business logic. Spring AOP implements this with proxies that wrap beans and run advice before, after, or around target methods.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    WITHOUT AOP                 WITH SPRING AOP             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  public void transfer() {               @Transactional                   │
│    log.start();                         public void transfer() {       │
│    tx.begin();                            // only business logic         │
│    // business                            debit(); credit();             │
│    tx.commit();                         }                                │
│    log.end();                           // tx + logging in aspect        │
│  }                                                                       │
│                                                                          │
│  duplicated in 200 methods              centralized, consistent            │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

AOP Terminology Master Table

Term What Banking Example
Aspect Module of cross-cutting logic @Aspect audit logging
Join Point Point in execution (method call) TransferService.transfer() invocation
Pointcut Predicate selecting join points execution(* com.bank..*Service.*(..))
Advice Action at join point @Before, @Around, @AfterReturning
Target Object being advised Raw PaymentService instance
Proxy Wrapped object client calls PaymentService$$SpringCGLIB$$0
Weaving Linking aspects to targets Runtime proxy (Spring) vs compile-time (AspectJ)

Spring AOP vs Full AspectJ

Spring AOP AspectJ
Weaving Runtime proxy Compile/load-time weaving
Join points Method execution only (default) Methods, fields, constructors, etc.
Performance Proxy overhead Woven bytecode, lower overhead
Usage 99% of Spring Boot apps When field interception needed
Annotation @Aspect + @EnableAspectJAutoProxy @Aspect + AspectJ compiler

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why AOP Exists in Enterprise Java

Cross-Cutting Concern Without AOP With AOP
@Transactional Manual commit/rollback everywhere Declarative on service layer
Security @PreAuthorize duplicated checks Method security aspect
Audit logging Copy-paste in every method @Around aspect
Metrics Micrometer calls scattered @Timed / custom aspect
Exception mapping try/catch boilerplate @ControllerAdvice (related pattern)

Why Architects Care About Proxies

SYMPTOM: "@Transactional doesn't work"
CAUSE:   self-invocation this.save() bypasses proxy

SYMPTOM: "Wrong user authorized"
CAUSE:   internal method call skips @PreAuthorize proxy

SYMPTOM: "Memory grows after deploys"
CAUSE:   CGLIB proxy classes in Metaspace per advised bean

Understanding AOP = understanding HOW Spring actually runs your code

Why Runtime Proxies (Not Compile-Time)

Spring chose proxy-based AOP for:
- No special compiler required
- Works with existing POJOs
- Integrates with IoC lifecycle (Lesson 14 BeanPostProcessor)

Trade-off: Only public method calls through proxy are advised (Spring AOP limitation for class-based proxies).

Part 3: Internal Working

Proxy Creation — BeanPostProcessor Pipeline

Lesson 14: initializeBean()
       │
       ▼
AbstractAutoProxyCreator.postProcessAfterInitialization()
       │
       ├── Is bean already proxied? skip
       ├── Any advisor matches this bean? (pointcut match)
       │     NO → return raw bean
       │     YES ↓
       ├── Target has interfaces? JDK proxy OR CGLIB (config)
       └── Return PROXY (client gets proxy, not target)

CLIENT CALL:

paymentService.transfer(request)
       │
       ▼
┌──────────────────┐
│  PROXY           │
│  invoke()        │
│    → chain of    │
│      interceptors│
│        → target  │
└──────────────────┘

JDK Dynamic Proxy

public interface PaymentGateway {
    PaymentResult charge(PaymentRequest request);
}

@Service
public class NeftGateway implements PaymentGateway { ... }

JDK Proxy (requires interface):

Proxy.newProxyInstance(
  classLoader,
  [PaymentGateway.class],
  InvocationHandler
)

Client type: PaymentGateway (interface)
Cannot cast to NeftGateway concrete class
InvocationHandler invokes target NeftGateway.charge()

┌─────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────┐
│   Client    │────────►│ JDK Proxy           │────────►│ NeftGateway │
│             │         │ implements Gateway  │         │ (target)    │
└─────────────┘         └─────────────────────┘         └─────────────┘
                        InvocationHandler chain
                        (TransactionInterceptor, etc.)

CGLIB Proxy

@Service  // no interface required
public class PaymentService {
    @Transactional
    public void process(PaymentRequest req) { ... }
}

CGLIB creates SUBCLASS at runtime:

PaymentService$$SpringCGLIB$$0 extends PaymentService

Overrides non-final public methods
Callback intercepts method call → advisors → super.method()

CANNOT proxy:
  - final class
  - final methods
  - private methods (not overridden)

┌─────────────┐         ┌──────────────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────┐
│   Client    │────────►│ PaymentService$$CGLIB$$0     │────────►│ target bean │
│             │         │ extends PaymentService       │         │ (delegate)  │
└─────────────┘         └──────────────────────────────┘         └─────────────┘
                        MethodInterceptor chain

JDK vs CGLIB — Spring Boot Default

Spring Boot 2.x+: default proxyTargetClass = true (CGLIB) when no interface

Interface present:
  Can use JDK (proxyInterfaces) or CGLIB (proxyTargetClass=true)
  @Transactional on concrete class → CGLIB preferred

No interface:
  CGLIB required
JDK Dynamic Proxy CGLIB
Requires interface Yes No
Proxy type Interface Subclass
Final methods N/A Not advised
Constructor Reflective Subclass instantiation
Metaspace Minimal Extra class per proxied bean
Cast to concrete No Yes (to subclass, not original)

Advice Types and Order

@Aspect
@Component
@Order(1)
public class AuditAspect {

    @Before("execution(* com.bank.payments.service.*.*(..))")
    public void logBefore(JoinPoint jp) {
        log.info("Entering: {}", jp.getSignature().getName());
    }

    @AfterReturning(pointcut = "...", returning = "result")
    public void logAfterReturning(Object result) { ... }

    @AfterThrowing(pointcut = "...", throwing = "ex")
    public void logError(Exception ex) { ... }

    @Around("@annotation(Timed)")
    public Object timed(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable {
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        try {
            return pjp.proceed();  // call target
        } finally {
            metrics.record(System.nanoTime() - start);
        }
    }
}

ADVICE ORDER for @Around:

@Order(1) outer aspect: before
  @Order(2) inner aspect: before
    target method
  @Order(2) inner aspect: after
@Order(1) outer aspect: after

Lower @Order value = higher precedence (outer)

@Transactional Internals (Preview Lesson 18)

Client calls proxy.transfer()

TransactionInterceptor.invoke():
  1. getTransactionManager
  2. tm.getTransaction(propagation, isolation)
  3. try {
       result = joinPoint.proceed()  // actual method
       tm.commit()
     } catch (RuntimeException) {
       tm.rollback()
       throw
     }

PROXY REQUIRED — transaction bound to ThreadLocal Connection
Self-invocation this.internal() → NO proxy → NO transaction

Self-Invocation Problem

@Service
public class PaymentService {

    @Transactional
    public void process(PaymentRequest req) {
        savePayment(req);
        postToLedger(req);  // internal call
    }

    @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void postToLedger(PaymentRequest req) {
        // EXPECT new transaction — DOES NOT HAPPEN via this.postToLedger()
    }

    private void savePayment(PaymentRequest req) {
        this.postToLedger(req);  // BYPASSES PROXY — no REQUIRES_NEW
    }
}

FIX OPTIONS:
  1. Inject self @Lazy PaymentService self; self.postToLedger()
  2. Move method to another @Service bean
  3. AopContext.currentProxy() (exposeProxy=true) — rarely recommended
  4. AspectJ compile-time weaving (full AspectJ)

Pointcut Expression (AspectJ Syntax Subset)

// execution modifiers? return-type declaring-type? method-name(params) throws?

@Pointcut("execution(public * com.bank.payments.service..*(..))")
public void paymentServiceMethods() {}

@Pointcut("@annotation(org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional)")
public void transactionalMethods() {}

@Pointcut("paymentServiceMethods() && @annotation(Transactional)")
public void transactionalPaymentOps() {}

Part 4: Memory View

Proxy Memory and Metaspace

SINGLE @Service @Transactional bean:

HEAP:
  PaymentService target @7a001
  PaymentService$$CGLIB$$0 proxy @7a002 (holds ref to target)

METASPACE:
  PaymentService.class (original)
  PaymentService$$SpringCGLIB$$0.class (generated)
  FastClass / callback helper classes

Typical overhead per proxied bean: small (KB Metaspace + one proxy object)
300 proxied beans × ~10-50 KB Metaspace ≈ few MB — usually fine
Hot redeploy without restart: Metaspace leak risk (Lesson 12)

JDK Proxy Memory

JDK proxy:
  Proxy class (Metaspace — one per interface combination per classloader)
  Proxy instance (heap)
  InvocationHandler holding target ref

Fewer generated classes than CGLIB per bean IF many beans share same interface

ThreadLocal in Transaction AOP

TransactionSynchronizationManager (ThreadLocal):
  Thread-1: [Connection from HikariCP, transaction active]
  Thread-2: [different Connection]

Proxy ensures transaction interceptor runs on CALLER thread
@Async method → different thread → @Transactional needs propagation REQUIRES_NEW or separate tx setup

Part 5: Performance Analysis

AOP Performance Impact

Proxy Invocation Cost

Step Cost
Proxy method entry Nanoseconds
Interceptor chain (1-3 advisors) Nanoseconds–microseconds
@Transactional Milliseconds (DB connection, commit)
@Around with logging Microseconds + I/O if logging
CGLIB vs JDK Comparable after JIT; CGLIB slightly more Metaspace

Rule: AOP proxy overhead is negligible vs DB/network. Optimize transactions and queries first.

Too Many Aspects

20 @Around aspects on same pointcut:
  20 × proceed() chain depth
  Measurable micro overhead + log I/O explosion

Architect: consolidate aspects; use @Order; narrow pointcuts

Final Methods and Performance Illusion

@Service
public class PaymentService {
    public final void process() { ... }  // NOT proxied — @Transactional IGNORED
}

Scalability

Concern Impact
Singleton proxy shared by all threads Safe if advice is stateless
ThreadLocal transactions One transaction per thread per request
@Async + @Transactional Wrong thread — transaction doesn't propagate as expected

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Custom Audit Aspect — Banking

package com.bank.payments.audit;

import org.aspectj.lang.ProceedingJoinPoint;
import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.Around;
import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.Aspect;
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.slf4j.MDC;
import org.springframework.core.annotation.Order;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Aspect
@Component
@Order(10)
public class PaymentAuditAspect {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(PaymentAuditAspect.class);

    @Around("execution(* com.bank.payments.service.PaymentService.process(..)) && args(request)")
    public Object auditPayment(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp, PaymentRequest request) throws Throwable {
        String paymentId = request.id();
        MDC.put("paymentId", paymentId);
        long start = System.currentTimeMillis();
        try {
            Object result = pjp.proceed();
            log.info("event=payment_success paymentId={} durationMs={}",
                paymentId, System.currentTimeMillis() - start);
            return result;
        } catch (Throwable ex) {
            log.error("event=payment_failed paymentId={} durationMs={}",
                paymentId, System.currentTimeMillis() - start, ex);
            throw ex;
        } finally {
            MDC.remove("paymentId");
        }
    }

    public record PaymentRequest(String id, String accountId, java.math.BigDecimal amount) {}
}

Example 2: Fixing Self-Invocation — Extract Bean

@Service
public class PaymentService {

    private final LedgerPostingService ledgerPostingService;

    public PaymentService(LedgerPostingService ledgerPostingService) {
        this.ledgerPostingService = ledgerPostingService;
    }

    @Transactional
    public void process(PaymentRequest request) {
        savePayment(request);
        ledgerPostingService.postToLedger(request);  // goes through proxy
    }

    private void savePayment(PaymentRequest request) { /* ... */ }
}

@Service
public class LedgerPostingService {

    @Transactional(propagation = org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void postToLedger(PaymentRequest request) {
        // new transaction — proxy invoked from PaymentService
    }
}

@Configuration
@EnableAspectJAutoProxy(proxyTargetClass = true, exposeProxy = false)
public class AopConfig {
    // proxyTargetClass=true → CGLIB even if interface exists
    // exposeProxy=false → default; avoid AopContext unless necessary
}

Example 4: Pointcut Reuse

@Aspect
@Component
public class ServiceLayerMetrics {

    @Pointcut("within(com.bank..service..*)")
    public void serviceLayer() {}

    @Around("serviceLayer()")
    public Object recordTime(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable {
        String name = pjp.getSignature().toShortString();
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        try {
            return pjp.proceed();
        } finally {
            long duration = System.nanoTime() - start;
            // record to Micrometer
        }
    }
}

Example 5: Interface-Based JDK Proxy Scenario

public interface FraudRule {
    FraudResult evaluate(TransactionContext ctx);
}

@Service
public class VelocityFraudRule implements FraudRule {
    @Override
    public FraudResult evaluate(TransactionContext ctx) { /* ... */ return null; }
}

// If only JDK proxy used and injected as FraudRule — works
// If injected as VelocityFraudRule concrete and JDK proxy — ClassCastException risk
// Spring Boot CGLIB: proxy extends VelocityFraudRule — cast OK

log.info("Target class: {}", AopUtils.getTargetClass(paymentService));

Production Checklist

Check Why
@Transactional on public service methods Private = not advised
No self-invocation for tx boundaries REQUIRES_NEW breaks
Narrow pointcuts Performance + clarity
@Order on aspects Predictable advice chain
Avoid exposeProxy=true globally Complexity
Final methods not @Transactional Silently ignored
Test through Spring context Unit test raw object misses AOP

Part 8: Microservice Usage

AOP in Microservice Architecture

AOP Is Local to Pod

payment-svc:
  PaymentService proxy → @Transactional → local DataSource

ledger-svc:
  Separate JVM — NO Spring AOP across HTTP call
  @Transactional in payment-svc does NOT span ledger HTTP POST

Distributed transactions: Saga, outbox (Lesson 28) — not @Transactional alone

@Transactional Boundary = Single Service DB

CORRECT ARCHITECTURE:

PaymentService @Transactional:
  - update payment table in payment DB
  - call ledger via HTTP (outside transaction)
  - on failure → compensating call or outbox event

WRONG:
  Assume @Transactional rolls back remote ledger call

API Gateway vs Service AOP

API Gateway: auth, rate limit, routing
Service AOP: transactions, audit, method security

Don't duplicate audit in gateway AND service unless requirements differ

Micrometer + AOP in K8s

@Timed on service methods → Prometheus scrape → Grafana
Per-pod metrics — aggregate at cluster level
AOP overhead negligible vs HTTP export

Part 9: Architect Perspective

When to Use AOP vs Explicit Code

Use AOP Use Explicit Code
@Transactional on service layer Complex conditional tx logic
Uniform audit for regulatory Business-specific audit fields
Security @PreAuthorize Fine-grained dynamic auth
Metrics on all service methods Critical path only with rich context
Retry on infrastructure calls Idempotency-aware retry (Lesson 29)

ADR — Service Layer Transaction Boundary

## ADR-142: @Transactional only on @Service layer

### Decision
Controllers and repositories must not declare @Transactional
All write operations through service public methods (proxy-visible)

### Rationale
Single transaction boundary; avoids self-invocation in controller
Ensures CGLIB proxy applies consistently

Aspect Proliferation Smell

IF audit aspect + logging aspect + metrics aspect + security aspect
   ALL @Around on same methods:
     → consolidate OR use filter/interceptor at web layer for HTTP concerns
     → keep service AOP for transactions + domain audit only

Proxy Type Selection

Scenario Proxy
Interface-based bean, JDK OK JDK or CGLIB (Boot default CGLIB)
Class without interface CGLIB
@Transactional on concrete class CGLIB (proxyTargetClass=true)
Final class Cannot proxy — refactor
Full field interception AspectJ, not Spring AOP

Self-Invocation Fix Matrix

Fix Recommendation
Extract to another @Service Best
@Lazy self-injection Works, slightly hacky
AopContext.currentProxy() Last resort
AspectJ weaving Heavyweight

Advice Type Selection

Need Advice
Wrap with try/finally, control proceed @Around
Before method @Before
After success @AfterReturning
After exception @AfterThrowing
After either (like finally) @After
Transaction @Transactional (interceptor)

Spring AOP AspectJ

Part 12: Interview Questions

Junior Level

  1. What is AOP?
  2. What is a proxy in Spring?
  3. Difference between JDK proxy and CGLIB?
  4. What is @Aspect?
  5. What is @Transactional related to AOP?

Senior Level

  1. How does Spring AOP work internally?
  2. Why doesn't @Transactional work on self-invocation?
  3. Can @Transactional apply to private methods?
  4. Difference between @Before and @Around?
  5. What is a pointcut?
  6. What is ProceedingJoinPoint.proceed()?
  7. When does Spring use JDK vs CGLIB proxy?

Staff / Architect Level

  1. Explain TransactionInterceptor call chain through proxy.
  2. Fix REQUIRES_NEW not working — root cause and solutions.
  3. Spring AOP vs AspectJ — when migrate to AspectJ?
  4. @Transactional on controller — why avoid?
  5. Performance impact of 10 @Around aspects?
  6. How do you debug "transaction not rolling back"?
  7. Distributed transaction across microservices — does @Transactional help?
  8. Metaspace impact of CGLIB in large Spring apps?
  9. @Order on multiple aspects — execution order?

Model Answer — Q7 (Self-Invocation)

A: Spring applies @Transactional via proxy wrapping the bean. External calls go through proxy → TransactionInterceptor → target. Internal this.method() calls use raw target reference, bypassing proxy — no interceptor, no transaction boundary change. REQUIRES_NEW on internally called method is ignored. Fix: move method to separate @Service, inject and call through Spring bean (proxy), or use AspectJ weaving. Preferred: separate bean — clearest design.

Model Answer — Q19 (Distributed TX)

A: @Transactional is local to one DataSource in one JVM — binds JDBC connection to thread via TransactionSynchronizationManager. HTTP call to ledger-svc is outside transaction. Commit in payment DB does not roll back ledger. Use Saga choreography, outbox pattern, or 2PC (rare) for cross-service consistency. Architect never assumes declarative TX spans microservices.

Part 13: Common Mistakes

# Mistake Consequence Fix
1 Self-invocation Tx doesn't apply Separate service
2 @Transactional on private method Silently ignored Public service method
3 @Transactional on controller Wrong layer, partial proxy Move to service
4 Final class @Service Cannot CGLIB proxy Remove final
5 Unit test without Spring context Tx appears to "work" manually @SpringBootTest integration
6 Over-broad pointcut Advise everything — slow Narrow expression
7 @Around without proceed() Method never runs Always pjp.proceed()
8 Assume TX spans HTTP Inconsistent data Saga/outbox
9 Cast proxy to wrong type (JDK) ClassCastException Inject interface or use CGLIB
10 @Async + @Transactional same method Tx context wrong thread Separate concerns

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. @Transactional on @Service public methods only
  2. Extract beans instead of self-invocation
  3. proxyTargetClass = true (Boot default) for concrete services
  4. Narrow pointcuts — package-scoped
  5. @Order documented for aspect precedence
  6. Test with real proxy — integration tests for tx
  7. Don't AOP domain pure logic — keep aspects infrastructure
  8. Consolidate overlapping @Around aspects
  9. Use @ControllerAdvice for HTTP errors, AOP for service cross-cutting
  10. Understand proxy = what runs in production

Part 16: Revision Notes

Quick Revision — Spring AOP

AOP: cross-cutting via aspects (audit, tx, security)
Spring AOP: RUNTIME PROXY, method execution join points

TERMS: Aspect, Pointcut, Advice, Join Point, Target, Proxy

PROXY CREATION: BeanPostProcessor after initialization
  advisors match → JDK (interface) or CGLIB (subclass)

JDK: Proxy implements interface — needs interface
CGLIB: extends class — no final class/methods

ADVICE: @Before @After @Around @AfterReturning @AfterThrowing
@Around must call pjp.proceed()

@Transactional = TransactionInterceptor via proxy
SELF-INVOCATION this.method() → NO PROXY → tx broken

FIX: separate @Service bean, @Lazy self (hack)

Spring AOP vs AspectJ: Spring = proxy, method only
AspectJ = compile-time, all join points

Microservices: @Transactional ONE service ONE database
Cross-service: Saga/outbox, NOT @Transactional

Memory Mnemonic

"You call the proxy, not the target — this.method() is the enemy of @Transactional"

Part 1: Concept

What Is Spring Boot?

Spring Boot is an opinionated layer on Spring Framework that provides:

  • Auto-configuration — beans created from classpath conditions
  • Starters — curated dependency bundles
  • Embedded servers — Tomcat/Jetty/Netty in-process
  • Production features — Actuator, metrics, externalized config
  • Minimal boilerplate — @SpringBootApplication replaces XML

│              TRADITIONAL SPRING              SPRING BOOT                 │

│                                                                          │
│  200 lines XML + @Configuration           @SpringBootApplication        │
│  Manual DataSource bean                   auto-config if Hikari on CP    │
│  Deploy WAR to WebLogic                    java -jar payment.jar         │
│  Manual health checks                      /actuator/health              │
│  Manual metrics wiring                     Micrometer auto-export        │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Spring Boot Architecture Layers

├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why Spring Boot Was Created (2014)

Pain with Spring alone Boot solution
"Spring is heavy to configure" Sensible defaults
Dependency version hell BOM manages versions
External app server required Embedded Tomcat
No standard ops endpoints Actuator
Long time-to-first-API Spring Initializr + starters

Why Banks Adopted Spring Boot Rapidly

REGULATORY + OPERATIONAL NEEDS:
  - Repeatable deployable artifact (fat JAR)
  - Health endpoints for load balancers
  - External config (12-factor) without WebLogic console
  - Same stack across 50 microservices

Boot = organizational standardization + faster audit of dependencies (BOM)

Auto-Configuration Philosophy

"If PostgreSQL driver + HikariCP on classpath AND spring.datasource.url set
 → create DataSource bean UNLESS user defined own @Bean DataSource"

Convention over configuration — override with your @Bean or properties
Fail fast if required property missing (strict in prod)

Part 3: Internal Working

SpringApplication.run — Full Bootstrap

@SpringBootApplication
public class PaymentApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(PaymentApplication.class, args);
    }
}

Startup Sequence (Detailed)

1. Create SpringApplication instance
     - deduce application type (SERVLET, REACTIVE, NONE)
     - load ApplicationContextInitializers (Boot)
     - load ApplicationListeners

2. Run listeners: ApplicationStartingEvent, EnvironmentPreparedEvent

3. Prepare Environment
     - application.properties / yml
     - profile-specific files
     - env vars, command line args (highest precedence)

4. Print banner (optional)

5. createApplicationContext()
     - Servlet → AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext

6. prepareContext()
     - load sources (PaymentApplication class)
     - apply Initializers
     - load bean definitions from:
         a. @ComponentScan (your app)
         b. @Import (including @EnableAutoConfiguration)
         c. spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports

7. refreshContext()  ← Lesson 14 full refresh pipeline
     - create all singleton beans
     - embed Tomcat (WebServerStartStopLifecycle)

8. callRunners()
     - CommandLineRunner, ApplicationRunner

9. ApplicationReadyEvent → accept traffic (if readiness configured)

TIMELINE (payment-svc typical):
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────►
0s      5s       15s      25s       35s      40s
│       │        │        │         │        │
start   env      scan     JPA       Tomcat   Ready
        load     auto-    EMF       start    probe OK
                 config   init

@SpringBootApplication Decomposition

@SpringBootConfiguration   // @Configuration meta
@EnableAutoConfiguration   // @Import AutoConfigurationImportSelector
@ComponentScan             // scan current package downward
public @interface SpringBootApplication { ... }

Auto-Configuration Loading Mechanism

Spring Boot 3.x (your stack):

META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports

File lists fully qualified class names, one per line:
org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration
org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.orm.jpa.HibernateJpaAutoConfiguration
org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.kafka.KafkaAutoConfiguration
... ~130+ auto-config classes

Spring Boot 2.x (legacy): META-INF/spring.factories key EnableAutoConfiguration

AutoConfigurationImportSelector:
  1. Load all auto-config class names from imports files
  2. Filter with @ConditionalOn* (classpath, properties, missing bean)
  3. Sort by @AutoConfigureBefore / @AutoConfigureAfter / @AutoConfigureOrder
  4. Register surviving configs as @Configuration classes

Conditional Annotations — How Decisions Work

Annotation Condition True When
@ConditionalOnClass Class present on classpath
@ConditionalOnMissingClass Class absent
@ConditionalOnBean Bean already registered
@ConditionalOnMissingBean No bean of type
@ConditionalOnProperty Property matches
@ConditionalOnWebApplication Servlet or reactive web app
@ConditionalOnExpression SpEL evaluates true 
// Simplified from DataSourceAutoConfiguration
@Configuration
@ConditionalOnClass({ DataSource.class, HikariDataSource.class })
@ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class)
@EnableConfigurationProperties(DataSourceProperties.class)
public class DataSourceAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ConfigurationProperties("spring.datasource.hikari")
    HikariDataSource dataSource(DataSourceProperties properties) {
        return properties.initializeDataSourceBuilder()
            .type(HikariDataSource.class).build();
    }
}

DECISION FLOW:

Is HikariDataSource on classpath?  YES
Did user define @Bean DataSource?  NO
Is spring.datasource.url set?      YES
  → CREATE HikariDataSource bean

User adds @Bean DataSource → auto-config backs off (@ConditionalOnMissingBean)

Starters — What They Actually Are

<!-- pom.xml — NOT a framework, a Maven dependency bundle -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>

spring-boot-starter-web TRANSITIVELY brings:
  spring-boot-starter
  spring-boot-starter-json (Jackson)
  spring-boot-starter-tomcat
  spring-webmvc
  spring-web

spring-boot-starter-parent (or BOM import) pins VERSIONS

Starter = curated POM + auto-config classes triggered by classpath

Actuator Internals

spring-boot-starter-actuator adds:
  - Endpoint beans (@Endpoint, @WebEndpoint)
  - HealthContributor beans
  - Micrometer registry auto-config
  - Optional exposure via management.endpoints.web.exposure.include

/actuator/health → HealthEndpoint → aggregates HealthIndicators
  - db: DataSourceHealthIndicator
  - diskSpace, ping, custom KafkaHealthIndicator

/actuator/metrics → MeterRegistry (Prometheus scrape via micrometer-registry-prometheus)

K8s PROBES:

livenessProbe:  /actuator/health/liveness   (app alive)
readinessProbe: /actuator/health/readiness  (ready for traffic)

Startup probe: slow Boot apps (Lesson 12 warmup)

Embedded Tomcat Lifecycle

ServletWebServerApplicationContext.onRefresh():
  createWebServer() → TomcatServletWebServerFactory
  start Tomcat on server.port (default 8080)

Tomcat runs IN SAME JVM as payment beans
  Share heap, GC, thread pools (Lesson 10)

Graceful shutdown:
  server.shutdown=graceful
  spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=30s
  → stop accepting, drain in-flight, @PreDestroy

Configuration Properties Binding

@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "payment.gateway")
public record GatewayProperties(
    String defaultMode,
    Duration timeout,
    int maxRetries
) {}

Binding pipeline:
  @EnableConfigurationProperties or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan
  → ConfigurationPropertiesBindingPostProcessor
  → binds Environment properties to POJO/record
  → validated with @Validated + Jakarta validation

Type-safe vs scattered @Value("${payment.gateway.max-retries}")

Fat JAR Structure and Class Loading

payment-service.jar
├── BOOT-INF/
│   ├── classes/              ← your .class files
│   └── lib/                  ← all dependency JARs (100+ MB)
├── META-INF/
└── org/springframework/boot/loader/
    JarLauncher               ← custom classloader loads nested JARs

LaunchedURLClassLoader:
  loads from nested JARs without extracting
  Metaspace holds all loaded classes — large classpath = startup cost

Actuator Endpoint Memory

/actuator/beans → introspects entire context — expensive, disable in prod public exposure
/health → lightweight aggregation
/metrics → Micrometer registry (counters in heap, LongAdder-style)

Expose minimally in prod: health, prometheus, info (secured)

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Boot Startup Performance

Startup Time Contributors

Phase % Typical Mitigation
Classpath scan + auto-config eval 15-25% Narrow @ComponentScan, exclude unused auto-config
Hibernate/JPA metadata 25-40% ddl-auto=validate, reduce entities scan
Bean instantiation 15-25% @Lazy (careful in prod)
Tomcat start 5-10% —
CommandLineRunners Variable Defer heavy work 
@SpringBootApplication(exclude = {
    org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.kafka.KafkaAutoConfiguration.class
})
// Only if Kafka not used — removes unnecessary condition evaluation

Runtime Performance

Auto-configuration at runtime: ZERO cost — decisions only at startup
Runtime cost = your code + frameworks (Hibernate, Tomcat, AOP proxies)

Boot adds no per-request overhead beyond beans it created at startup

Lazy Initialization Mode

spring.main.lazy-initialization=true
Benefit Cost
Faster apparent startup First request latency
Later failure discovery Harder prod debugging
Dev/test useful Not recommended payment prod

Actuator and Security Overhead

Every /actuator/prometheus scrape: iterate meters — low cost
Health check every 5s from K8s: DB ping if db health included — tune!

spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=40
  + readiness checks DB every probe
  = connection churn if pool validation heavy

Use custom readiness: check app state, not full DB every 2s (architect tune)

package com.bank.platform.autoconfigure;

import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.condition.ConditionalOnClass;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.condition.ConditionalOnMissingBean;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.EnableConfigurationProperties;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;

@AutoConfiguration
@ConditionalOnClass(PaymentAuditPublisher.class)
@EnableConfigurationProperties(AuditProperties.class)
public class PaymentAuditAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean
    public PaymentAuditPublisher paymentAuditPublisher(AuditProperties props) {
        return new PaymentAuditPublisher(props.getKafkaTopic());
    }
}

Example 3: ApplicationRunner — Startup Validation

@Component
public class PaymentConfigValidator implements ApplicationRunner {

    private final GatewayProperties gatewayProperties;

    public PaymentConfigValidator(GatewayProperties gatewayProperties) {
        this.gatewayProperties = gatewayProperties;
    }

    @Override
    public void run(ApplicationArguments args) {
        if (gatewayProperties.maxRetries() < 0) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("payment.gateway.max-retries must be >= 0");
        }
    }
}

Example 4: Custom Health Indicator — Kafka

@Component
public class KafkaHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {

    private final KafkaAdmin kafkaAdmin;

    public KafkaHealthIndicator(KafkaAdmin kafkaAdmin) {
        this.kafkaAdmin = kafkaAdmin;
    }

    @Override
    public Health health() {
        try {
            kafkaAdmin.describeCluster().clusterId().get(3, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
            return Health.up().withDetail("cluster", "reachable").build();
        } catch (Exception e) {
            return Health.down(e).build();
        }
    }
}

  8. Spring Boot 3 Jakarta migration impact?
  9. Custom @AutoConfiguration for shared audit library — design?

Model Answer — Q6 (Auto-Configuration)

A: @EnableAutoConfiguration imports AutoConfigurationImportSelector, which loads candidate configuration classes from META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports. Each class is a @Configuration guarded by @ConditionalOn* annotations evaluating classpath, existing beans, and properties. Matching configs register bean definitions during context refresh. User-defined @Bean methods take precedence via @ConditionalOnMissingBean. Result: sensible defaults without manual wiring, overridable at any point.

Model Answer — Q19 (Graceful Shutdown)

A: K8s sends SIGTERM → Spring Boot server.shutdown=graceful stops accepting new HTTP connections on Tomcat. spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase waits for in-flight requests and @PreDestroy hooks (executor shutdown, Kafka consumer close). Readiness fails so LB stops routing new traffic. After timeout, forceful shutdown. Payment architect ensures idempotency for clients retrying during drain window. Combine with K8s terminationGracePeriodSeconds > shutdown phase timeout.

Part 1: Concept

What Are JPA and Hibernate?

JPA (Jakarta Persistence API) is the specification for ORM (Object-Relational Mapping) in Java. Hibernate is the most common implementation, integrated via Spring Data JPA in Boot applications.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    PERSISTENCE STACK (typical banking service)           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  @RestController                                                         │
│       │                                                                  │
│       ▼                                                                  │
│  @Service @Transactional                                                 │
│       │                                                                  │
│       ▼                                                                  │
│  Spring Data JPA Repository (interface)                                  │
│       │                                                                  │
│       ▼                                                                  │
│  EntityManager / Hibernate Session                                       │
│       │                                                                  │
│       ▼                                                                  │
│  JDBC / HikariCP                                                         │
│       │                                                                  │
│       ▼                                                                  │
│  Oracle / PostgreSQL / DB2                                               │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Core Concepts Master Table

Concept What Why Banking Example
Entity @Entity class mapped to table OOP + relational bridge PaymentEntity → PAYMENTS
Persistence Context Session-scoped cache of managed entities Avoid duplicate loads, track changes One Account instance per id per tx
EntityManager JPA API for persistence CRUD + queries em.find(Account.class, id)
Repository Spring abstraction over EM No boilerplate DAO PaymentRepository.findByStatus()
Mapping Object ↔ column/row Schema alignment @Column(name="ACCT_ID")
FetchType When to load associations Performance control LAZY payments on Account
Flush SQL sync to DB (not commit) Ordering of SQL statements Before native query in same tx
N+1 1 query + N lazy loads Classic perf bug 1 account list + N payment fetches

JPA vs Hibernate vs Spring Data JPA

Layer Role
JPA API specification (@Entity, EntityManager)
Hibernate Engine (SQL generation, cache, dirty checking)
Spring Data JPA Repository interfaces, @Query, paging
Spring ORM @Transactional + EntityManager integration

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why ORM Exists in Enterprise Banking

Raw JDBC JPA/Hibernate
Manual row mapping Automatic entity mapping
Verbose SQL for CRUD save(), derived queries
No change tracking Dirty checking flushes updates
Boilerplate DAO layer Spring Data repositories
Database portability (partial) Dialect abstraction

Why Architects Still Worry About ORM

ORM PROMISE: "Don't think about SQL"
ORM REALITY: "You will think about SQL at 3 AM when N+1 takes down p99"

Architect role:
  - Define entity boundaries (bounded context)
  - Enforce LAZY + fetch joins where needed
  - Separate API DTOs from entities (Lesson 13)
  - Transaction boundaries on service layer (Lesson 15)
  - Never expose entities on REST API

Why Spring Data JPA Dominates Microservices

payment-svc owns PAYMENTS table → PaymentEntity + PaymentRepository
ledger-svc owns ACCOUNTS table → AccountEntity + AccountRepository

NO shared entities across services (Lesson 13)
Each service: Boot starter-data-jpa + Oracle/PostgreSQL driver

Part 3: Internal Working

Entity Lifecycle — Four States

┌──────────────┐    persist()/merge()    ┌──────────────┐
│  TRANSIENT   │ ───────────────────────►│   MANAGED    │
│  (new object)│                         │ (in PC cache)│
└──────────────┘                         └──────┬───────┘
       ▲                                        │
       │                                        │ detach()/close EM
       │              remove()                  ▼
       │         ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐
       └─────────│   REMOVED    │◄────────│  DETACHED    │
                 │ (scheduled   │  merge()│ (no longer   │
                 │  for DELETE)  │         │  tracked)    │
                 └──────────────┘         └──────────────┘
State Meaning Dirty Checking DB Identity
Transient New, no @Id persisted No Not in DB
Managed Attached to persistence context Yes In DB
Detached Was managed, EM closed No In DB
Removed Managed + scheduled delete Delete on flush Row deleted on flush/commit

Persistence Context (First-Level Cache)

One @Transactional service method = typically one Persistence Context

Thread-1 Transaction:
  em.find(Account, "ACC-001")  → SELECT ... → Account@7a001 MANAGED
  em.find(Account, "ACC-001")  → CACHE HIT — no second SELECT
  account.setBalance(500)      → dirty — no immediate UPDATE

  tx commit → flush → UPDATE accounts SET balance=500 WHERE id=...

PERSISTENCE CONTEXT (Session)

┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Identity Map:                           │
│   "ACC-001" → Account@7a001 (managed)   │
│   "ACC-002" → Account@7a002 (managed)   │
│ Dirty Set: { Account@7a001 }            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

Flush Modes and Timing

@Transactional
public void transfer() {
    Account from = repo.findById("A").orElseThrow();
    from.debit(100);           // dirty in PC
    repo.flush();              // forces SQL UPDATE now (before commit)
    jdbcTemplate.callProc();   // native proc sees updated balance
    // commit at method end
}
FlushMode Behavior
AUTO (default) Flush before query if needed, at commit
COMMIT Flush only at commit
MANUAL Explicit flush() only

Hibernate Dirty Checking

Managed entity fields tracked (snapshot at load time)

On flush/commit:
  compare current field values vs snapshot
  if different → generate UPDATE only for changed columns (partial update if configured)

No need for em.merge() on managed entity — automatic update at commit

Spring Data JPA Repository Proxy

public interface PaymentRepository extends JpaRepository<PaymentEntity, String> {
    List<PaymentEntity> findByStatus(PaymentStatus status);
}

Spring creates JDK proxy implementing PaymentRepository
  → SimpleJpaRepository delegate
  → EntityManager operations
  → @Transactional on class methods (read-only for getters, tx for writes)

Derived query: findByStatus → parse method name → JPQL → SQL

SQL Generation Pipeline

Repository.findByStatus(PENDING)
    → JpaQueryMethod
    → JPQL: SELECT p FROM PaymentEntity p WHERE p.status = :status
    → Hibernate AST
    → SQL: SELECT p.id, p.amount, ... FROM payments p WHERE p.status = ?
    → PreparedStatement via JDBC
    → ResultSet mapping → PaymentEntity instances (managed if in tx)

Part 4: Memory View

ORM Memory Footprint

HEAP per @Transactional request:

Persistence Context (first-level cache):
  - Managed entity instances (full object graphs if EAGER fetched)
  - Snapshots for dirty checking (duplicate field copies internally)

Example: load 1000 AccountEntity with EAGER List<PaymentEntity>:
  1000 accounts + potentially 1000×avg payments objects in heap
  → Young/Old Gen pressure, long GC on large reports

LAZY (default for collections):
  Load 1000 accounts → 1000 objects
  Access each .getPayments() → N additional queries + N×payments loaded

Entity Object Layout

PaymentEntity @ heap
┌────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Object header                          │
│ id: String ref → "PAY-001"             │
│ amount: BigDecimal ref                 │
│ account: AccountEntity ref (LAZY proxy)│──► AccountEntity$HibernateProxy
│ status: enum ref                       │
└────────────────────────────────────────┘

LAZY association:
  Hibernate injects RUNTIME PROXY (subclass or bytebuddy)
  First access to account.getName() → triggers SELECT

Second-Level Cache (Optional)

┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ L1: Persistence Context (per tx)        │  always on (managed entities)
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ L2: SessionFactory cache (shared)       │  @Cacheable entity — rare in MS
│     EhCache / Infinispan region         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Query cache                             │  cached query result IDs
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

Microservices: prefer Redis for shared cache, not Hibernate L2 across pods
L2 per pod → stale data risk between payment-svc instances

Connection vs Memory

HikariCP pool: connections are native + small heap wrappers
Persistence context: heap-heavy with large graphs

OOM usually from loading too much data (missing pagination), not from EM itself

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Fetch Types — LAZY vs EAGER

@Entity
public class AccountEntity {
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "account", fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    private List<PaymentEntity> payments;
}

@Entity
public class PaymentEntity {
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)  // default for @ManyToOne in Boot 2.2+
    private AccountEntity account;
}
Fetch When Loaded Risk Use
LAZY On first access N+1 if loop Default for collections
EAGER With parent Cartesian product, memory Avoid except small static data

N+1 Problem — Anatomy

@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public List<AccountDto> listAccounts() {
    List<AccountEntity> accounts = accountRepo.findAll(); // 1 query
    return accounts.stream()
        .map(a -> new AccountDto(a.getId(), a.getPayments().size())) // N queries
        .toList();
}

SQL EXECUTION:
  Query 1: SELECT * FROM accounts                    (1 row set)
  Query 2: SELECT * FROM payments WHERE account_id=?  (account 1)
  Query 3: SELECT * FROM payments WHERE account_id=?  (account 2)
  ...
  Query 1001: ...                                     (account 1000)

1001 queries — p99 disaster

N+1 Fixes

// 1. JOIN FETCH in JPQL
@Query("SELECT DISTINCT a FROM AccountEntity a LEFT JOIN FETCH a.payments WHERE a.status = :status")
List<AccountEntity> findWithPayments(@Param("status") Status status);

// 2. @EntityGraph
@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"payments"})
List<AccountEntity> findByStatus(Status status);

// 3. Batch fetching (Hibernate)
@BatchSize(size = 25)  // on collection or class level

// 4. DTO projection — best for read APIs
@Query("SELECT new com.bank.dto.AccountSummary(a.id, COUNT(p)) FROM AccountEntity a LEFT JOIN a.payments p GROUP BY a.id")
List<AccountSummary> summarize();

JOIN FETCH:
  Single SQL with JOIN — watch duplicate root entities (use DISTINCT)

BATCH SIZE:
  1 query accounts + ceil(N/25) batch payment queries — compromise

Pagination — Mandatory for Lists

// BAD
List<PaymentEntity> all = repo.findAll();  // 5M rows → OOM

// GOOD
Page<PaymentEntity> page = repo.findByStatus(status, PageRequest.of(0, 50));
Slice<PaymentEntity> slice = repo.findByCreatedAtAfter(since, PageRequest.of(0, 50));

Read-Only Transactions

@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public AccountDto getAccount(String id) {
    // Hibernate may skip dirty checking
    // DB driver may optimize read-only connection
}

Scalability Impact

Pattern Single pod Fleet
N+1 in report job Slow batch Slow × replicas if duplicated
EAGER all graphs Heap spike OOMKill risk
L2 cache uncoordinated Stale balance Financial correctness risk
DTO projection Minimal heap Scales

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Entity Mapping — Payment

package com.bank.payments.infra.persistence;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.Instant;

@Entity
@Table(name = "PAYMENTS", indexes = {
    @Index(name = "idx_payments_account", columnList = "account_id"),
    @Index(name = "idx_payments_status", columnList = "status")
})
public class PaymentEntity {

    @Id
    @Column(name = "payment_id", length = 36)
    private String paymentId;

    @Column(name = "account_id", nullable = false, length = 20)
    private String accountId;

    @Column(name = "amount", nullable = false, precision = 19, scale = 4)
    private BigDecimal amount;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    @Column(name = "status", length = 20)
    private PaymentStatus status;

    @Column(name = "created_at", nullable = false)
    private Instant createdAt;

    @Version
    @Column(name = "version")
    private Long version;  // optimistic locking

    protected PaymentEntity() {}  // JPA required

    // getters/setters
}

public enum PaymentStatus { PENDING, COMPLETED, FAILED }

Example 2: Repository + Derived Query

package com.bank.payments.infra.persistence;

import org.springframework.data.domain.Page;
import org.springframework.data.domain.Pageable;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.EntityGraph;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.Query;
import org.springframework.data.repository.query.Param;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;

public interface PaymentRepository extends JpaRepository<PaymentEntity, String> {

    Page<PaymentEntity> findByStatus(PaymentStatus status, Pageable pageable);

    Optional<PaymentEntity> findByPaymentIdAndAccountId(String paymentId, String accountId);

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"auditEntries"})  // if association exists
    @Query("SELECT p FROM PaymentEntity p WHERE p.accountId = :accountId AND p.createdAt >= :since")
    List<PaymentEntity> findRecentWithAudit(@Param("accountId") String accountId,
                                            @Param("since") Instant since);
}

Example 3: Service Layer — Domain vs Entity

package com.bank.payments.service;

import com.bank.payments.domain.PaymentRequest;
import com.bank.payments.domain.PaymentResult;
import com.bank.payments.infra.persistence.PaymentEntity;
import com.bank.payments.infra.persistence.PaymentMapper;
import com.bank.payments.infra.persistence.PaymentRepository;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Service
public class PaymentService {

    private final PaymentRepository paymentRepository;
    private final PaymentMapper paymentMapper;

    public PaymentService(PaymentRepository paymentRepository, PaymentMapper paymentMapper) {
        this.paymentRepository = paymentRepository;
        this.paymentMapper = paymentMapper;
    }

    @Transactional
    public PaymentResult process(PaymentRequest request) {
        PaymentEntity entity = paymentMapper.toEntity(request);
        entity.setStatus(PaymentStatus.PENDING);
        paymentRepository.save(entity);  // persist → managed → flush on commit
        // business logic...
        entity.setStatus(PaymentStatus.COMPLETED);
        return paymentMapper.toResult(entity);
    }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public PaymentResult get(String paymentId) {
        return paymentRepository.findById(paymentId)
            .map(paymentMapper::toResult)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new PaymentNotFoundException(paymentId));
    }
}

    private final PaymentRepository paymentRepository;

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public List<PaymentSummaryDto> summarizeByAccount(List<String> accountIds) {
        return paymentRepository.summarizeByAccountIds(accountIds);
    }
}

public interface PaymentRepository extends JpaRepository<PaymentEntity, String> {

    @Query("""
        SELECT new com.bank.payments.api.PaymentSummaryDto(p.accountId, SUM(p.amount), COUNT(p))
        FROM PaymentEntity p
        WHERE p.accountId IN :accountIds AND p.status = 'COMPLETED'
        GROUP BY p.accountId
        """)
    List<PaymentSummaryDto> summarizeByAccountIds(@Param("accountIds") List<String> accountIds);
}

Model Answer — Q8 (N+1)

A: N+1 occurs when one query loads N parent entities, then accessing a lazy association triggers one additional query per parent (N queries), totaling N+1. Common in loops over accounts loading payments. Fix: JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph in repository query for required associations; @BatchSize to batch lazy loads; best for read APIs — DTO projection with single GROUP BY or JOIN query returning only needed columns. Detect with Hibernate statistics or datasource proxy logging query count per request.

Model Answer — Q17 (L2 Cache)

A: Hibernate second-level cache is shared across persistence contexts in one JVM. In multi-pod payment-svc, each pod has independent L2 — no coherence when pod A updates balance and pod B serves read from stale cache — unacceptable for financial data unless TTL extremely short and business accepts eventual consistency (rare for balances). Prefer database as source of truth, short @Transactional reads, Redis for explicitly designed read models with invalidation strategy, not transparent entity L2.
