Part 1: Concept

What Is a Transaction?

A transaction is a unit of work that either commits entirely or rolls back entirely (ACID). In Spring, @Transactional declares transactional boundaries; Spring Transaction Management coordinates JDBC/JPA resources through a PlatformTransactionManager.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    @Transactional EXECUTION MODEL                        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  Client → PaymentService PROXY                                           │
│              │                                                           │
│              ▼                                                           │
│       TransactionInterceptor (AOP — Lesson 15)                           │
│              │ begin transaction (bind Connection to ThreadLocal)        │
│              ▼                                                           │
│       PaymentService.process()                                           │
│              │ EntityManager uses SAME connection                        │
│              │ repo.save(), flush, ...                                   │
│              ▼                                                           │
│       commit OR rollback (unbind Connection, return to HikariCP)         │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

ACID in Banking Context

Property Meaning Payment Example
Atomicity All or nothing Debit + credit both succeed or neither
Consistency Valid state before/after Balance never negative if rule enforced
Isolation Concurrent txs don't corrupt each other Two transfers from same account
Durability Committed survives crash Completed payment survives DB restart

Spring Transaction Master Table

Concept What Default Banking Note
@Transactional Declarative boundary — On @Service public methods
Propagation Join or create new tx REQUIRED REQUIRES_NEW for audit log
Isolation Visibility of other txs DB default (usually READ_COMMITTED) Rarely changed — know phantom reads
readOnly Hint for ORM/DB false true on query services
rollbackFor Which exceptions rollback Runtime + Error Add checked business exceptions
timeout Max seconds -1 (none) Prevent hung tx holding locks
PlatformTransactionManager Coordinates commit JpaTransactionManager One per DataSource

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why Declarative Transactions Exist

Manual JDBC Spring @Transactional
setAutoCommit(false) Automatic begin
commit() / rollback() in finally AOP on success/exception
Connection leak on exception path Spring unbinds in finally
Easy to forget rollback Default rollback on RuntimeException
Cross-repository coordination hard One tx spans all repo calls in method

Why Architects Define Transaction Boundaries at Service Layer

CONTROLLER @Transactional — WRONG
  - Long tx if HTTP slow client
  - Partial rollback scope wrong
  - Security layer outside tx awkwardly

REPOSITORY @Transactional — FRAGMENTED
  - Each repo method own tx → partial commits
  - transfer debit succeeds, credit separate tx fails → money lost

SERVICE @Transactional — CORRECT
  - One business operation = one atomic unit
  - Matches bounded context use case

Why Propagation and Isolation Matter in Production

INCIDENT: Audit log missing but payment committed
CAUSE: Audit in REQUIRES_NEW swallowed exception incorrectly

INCIDENT: Phantom report totals wrong during batch
CAUSE: READ_COMMITTED + concurrent inserts — expected unless SERIALIZABLE or locking

INCIDENT: Deadlock ORA-00060 on hot account row
CAUSE: Two txs lock accounts in different order (Lesson 7 lock ordering applies to DB)

Part 3: Internal Working

TransactionInterceptor — Step by Step

@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRED, rollbackFor = PaymentDeclinedException.class)
public PaymentResult process(PaymentRequest request) {
    paymentRepository.save(pending);
    ledgerAdapter.debit(request);  // if same DB + same tx manager — same tx
    return PaymentResult.success();
}

TransactionInterceptor.invoke():

1. tm = transactionManagerRegistry.getManager(this)
2. txAttr = resolve transaction attribute (@Transactional metadata)
3. txInfo = tm.getTransaction(txAttr)     // begin or join
4. try {
     result = joinPoint.proceed()
   } catch (Throwable ex) {
     completeTransactionAfterThrowing(ex)  // rollback?
     throw ex
   }
5. commitTransactionAfterReturning(txInfo) // commit

Connection Binding — ThreadLocal

TransactionSynchronizationManager (ThreadLocal maps):

Thread-1 (Tomcat worker):
  ResourceHolder: HikariCP Connection #7
  EntityManager Session bound to Connection #7
  isActualTransactionActive: true
  isCurrentTransactionReadOnly: false

Thread-2:
  Different connection — isolated

@Async worker thread:
  NO transaction unless @Transactional on async method with proper setup
  Lesson 11/15: tx does NOT propagate to CompletableFuture thread automatically

┌─────────────── Thread-1 ───────────────┐
│ TransactionSynchronizationManager    │
│   Connection #7 (active tx)           │
│   EntityManager (Hibernate Session)  │
└──────────────────────────────────────┘
         │
         ▼
    HikariCP pool
         │
         ▼
    Oracle session (DB transaction)

Propagation Behaviors — Internal Semantics

Propagation If tx exists If no tx
REQUIRED (default) Join existing Create new
REQUIRES_NEW Suspend current, create new Create new
NESTED Nested savepoint Same as REQUIRED
SUPPORTS Join Non-transactional
NOT_SUPPORTED Suspend, run non-tx Non-transactional
MANDATORY Join Throw exception
NEVER Throw exception Non-transactional 
REQUIRES_NEW timeline:

Outer tx (PaymentService.process)     Inner tx (AuditService.log)
─────────────────────────────────     ─────────────────────────────
BEGIN outer
  debit account
  call audit.log() REQUIRES_NEW
    SUSPEND outer ───────────────────► BEGIN inner
                                       INSERT audit
                                       COMMIT inner
    RESUME outer ◄───────────────────
  credit account
COMMIT outer

Inner commit visible even if outer later rolls back (independent tx)

Isolation Levels (JDBC / SQL Standard)

Level Dirty Read Non-Repeatable Read Phantom Read
READ_UNCOMMITTED Possible Possible Possible
READ_COMMITTED No Possible Possible
REPEATABLE_READ No No Possible
SERIALIZABLE No No No 
Dirty read:        Tx A reads uncommitted write from Tx B
Non-repeatable:    Tx A reads row twice, Tx B changed it between reads
Phantom read:      Tx A runs same range query twice, Tx B inserted new rows

Oracle default: READ_COMMITTED
PostgreSQL default: READ COMMITTED
MySQL InnoDB default: REPEATABLE_READ

Spring default: use database default unless @Transactional(isolation = ...)

Rollback Rules

@Transactional(rollbackFor = { PaymentDeclinedException.class, IOException.class })
public void process() { ... }
Exception Default Rollback?
RuntimeException Yes
Error Yes
Checked Exception No (commits!)
Custom checked business exception No unless rollbackFor 
@Transactional
public void bad() throws Exception {
    paymentRepository.save(payment);
    throw new Exception("checked");  // COMMITS — catastrophic if not intended
}

Flush and Commit (Lesson 17 Connection)

@Transactional method end (success):
  1. Hibernate flush (SQL to DB, still in tx)
  2. transactionManager.commit()
  3. JDBC connection.commit()
  4. Connection returned to pool

Rollback:
  connection.rollback()
  persistence context cleared

NESTED vs REQUIRES_NEW

NESTED: uses JDBC savepoint
  Outer rollback → inner nested work rolled back too
  Inner rollback → outer can continue (if caught)

REQUIRES_NEW: independent transaction
  Inner commits → durable even if outer rolls back
  Outer rollback → inner stays committed

NESTED: not all drivers support savepoints equally — test on Oracle/PostgreSQL.

Part 4: Memory View

Transaction Scope and Memory

ONE @Transactional method — ONE persistence context (typical JPA):

HEAP during tx:
  Managed entities in PC (Lesson 17)
  Dirty checking snapshots
  Pending SQL in session

Long-running @Transactional:
  Large PC → heap growth → GC
  Holds DB connection from pool (Lesson 10 alignment)
  Holds row locks on updated rows

SHORT TRANSACTIONS = less memory + less lock contention

Connection Pool Interaction

HikariCP maxPoolSize=40
Tomcat maxThreads=80

During tx:
  Thread holds connection until method completes
  @Transactional on slow external HTTP inside method → connection held idle IN TX
  → pool exhaustion

ARCHITECT: external calls OUTSIDE tx or after commit (outbox/event)

Suspended Transaction (REQUIRES_NEW)

Outer tx suspended — connection may remain bound but tx inactive (implementation detail)
Inner REQUIRES_NEW gets new connection from pool (often second connection same thread)

Thread holds 2 connections briefly — rare pool spike if many REQUIRES_NEW nested

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Transaction Performance

Lock Duration = Transaction Duration

BAD:
@Transactional
public void process(PaymentRequest req) {
    accountRepo.lock(accountId);
    fraudClient.check(req);        // 200ms HTTP — holds DB lock
    paymentRepo.save(...);
}

GOOD:
fraudClient.check(req);            // outside tx
@Transactional
public void processAfterFraud(...) {
    accountRepo.update(...);
}

Isolation vs Performance

Isolation Locking Throughput Banking use
READ_COMMITTED Minimal Highest Default acceptable
REPEATABLE_READ More Lower Reporting consistency
SERIALIZABLE Heavy Lowest Rare; use optimistic @Version instead

Architect: Don't set SERIALIZABLE globally — deadlock and throughput collapse.

Read-Only Optimization

@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public Page<PaymentDto> search(...) { ... }

Hibernate: skip dirty checking
PostgreSQL: connection read-only flag
Oracle: hint to driver
Still uses connection from pool — not free

Timeout

@Transactional(timeout = 30)  // seconds — default rollback if exceeded

Prevents infinite lock hold on stuck operation — important for hot account rows.

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Service Boundary — Transfer

package com.bank.payments.service;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Service
public class TransferService {

    private final AccountRepository accountRepository;
    private final PaymentRepository paymentRepository;

    @Transactional(rollbackFor = InsufficientFundsException.class)
    public TransferResult transfer(TransferCommand cmd) {
        var debtor = accountRepository.findByIdForUpdate(cmd.debtorId())
            .orElseThrow(() -> new AccountNotFoundException(cmd.debtorId()));
        var creditor = accountRepository.findByIdForUpdate(cmd.creditorId())
            .orElseThrow(() -> new AccountNotFoundException(cmd.creditorId()));

        if (debtor.getAvailableBalance().compareTo(cmd.amount()) < 0) {
            throw new InsufficientFundsException(cmd.debtorId());
        }

        debtor.debit(cmd.amount());
        creditor.credit(cmd.amount());

        paymentRepository.save(buildPaymentRecord(cmd));
        return TransferResult.success(cmd.transferId());
    }
}

// Repository — pessimistic lock for financial correctness
@Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
@Query("SELECT a FROM AccountEntity a WHERE a.accountId = :id")
Optional<AccountEntity> findByIdForUpdate(@Param("id") String id);

Example 2: REQUIRES_NEW — Independent Audit Trail

@Service
public class AuditService {

    private final AuditRepository auditRepository;

    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void recordAttempt(String paymentId, String action, String detail) {
        auditRepository.save(new AuditEntity(paymentId, action, detail, Instant.now()));
        // Commits independently — survives outer rollback if called before failure
    }
}

@Service
public class PaymentService {

    @Transactional
    public void process(PaymentRequest req) {
        auditService.recordAttempt(req.id(), "START", null);  // separate tx commits
        try {
            doProcess(req);
        } catch (RuntimeException ex) {
            auditService.recordAttempt(req.id(), "FAILED", ex.getMessage());
            throw ex;
        }
    }
}

Example 3: Rollback on Checked Exception

@Transactional(rollbackFor = PaymentValidationException.class)
public void validateAndSave(PaymentRequest request) throws PaymentValidationException {
    if (!validator.isValid(request)) {
        throw new PaymentValidationException("Invalid payment");
    }
    paymentRepository.save(mapper.toEntity(request));
}

Example 4: readOnly Query Service

@Service
public class PaymentQueryService {

    private final PaymentRepository paymentRepository;
    private final PaymentMapper mapper;

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public PaymentDetailDto getDetail(String paymentId) {
        PaymentEntity entity = paymentRepository.findWithAuditByPaymentId(paymentId)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new PaymentNotFoundException(paymentId));
        return mapper.toDetailDto(entity);  // touch lazy associations inside tx
    }
}

Example 5: Programmatic Transaction (Rare)

@Service
public class BatchSettlementService {

    private final TransactionTemplate transactionTemplate;

    public BatchSettlementService(PlatformTransactionManager tm) {
        this.transactionTemplate = new TransactionTemplate(tm);
        transactionTemplate.setPropagationBehavior(TransactionDefinition.PROPAGATION_REQUIRES_NEW);
    }

    public void settleChunk(List<SettlementItem> chunk) {
        transactionTemplate.executeWithoutResult(status -> {
            for (SettlementItem item : chunk) {
                processItem(item);
            }
        });
    }
}

Example 6: Self-Invocation Fix — Separate Bean (Lesson 15)

@Service
public class PaymentOrchestrator {

    private final PaymentWriter paymentWriter;

    @Transactional
    public void orchestrate(PaymentRequest req) {
        validateExternal(req);  // no tx needed — call before or outside
        paymentWriter.writePending(req);  // through proxy — REQUIRES_NEW if configured there
    }
}

@Service
public class PaymentWriter {
    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void writePending(PaymentRequest req) { ... }
}

Part 7: Production Usage

Transactions in Production

Transaction Boundary Checklist

ONE business use case = ONE @Transactional service method (REQUIRED)

Inside tx:
  ✓ DB reads/writes via repositories
  ✓ JPA dirty checking updates
  ✓ Same DataSource operations

Outside tx (before/after):
  ✓ HTTP to other microservices
  ✓ Kafka publish (prefer outbox in same tx — Lesson 28)
  ✓ Email/notification
  ✓ Long fraud ML scoring if lock held

HikariCP + Transaction Alignment

spring:
  datasource:
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 40
      connection-timeout: 5000
      max-lifetime: 1800000

server:
  tomcat:
    threads:
      max: 50

Rule: threads waiting for connection ≈ threads blocked in @Transactional holding connections.

Monitoring

Metrics:
  hikaricp.connections.active
  hikaricp.connections.pending
  transaction.count / rollback count (custom or Micrometer)

Logs:
  Unexpected transaction rollback — correlate with paymentId

Oracle:
  v$lock, deadlock trace files

Production Checklist

Check Why
@Transactional on service only Correct boundary
rollbackFor on checked business exceptions No silent commit
Short transactions Locks + pool
readOnly=true on queries ORM optimization
timeout on contentious operations Avoid hung locks
No HTTP inside locked tx Pool + deadlock
Test rollback paths Integration tests
Idempotency outside or REQUIRES_NEW Retry safety

Part 8: Microservice Usage

Local Transactions vs Distributed

Single Microservice — Single Database

payment-svc:
  @Transactional on PaymentService
  paymentRepository + outboxRepository (same DB)
  → atomic commit: payment row + outbox row

Cross-Microservice — NOT One @Transactional

payment-svc @Transactional:
  UPDATE payments SET status=COMPLETED
  ledgerClient.debit()  → HTTP to ledger-svc

ledger-svc has OWN @Transactional on ledger_db

TWO separate commits — no atomicity across both

PATTERN: Saga
  1. payment PENDING + outbox event (local tx commit)
  2. consumer debits ledger (local tx)
  3. on failure → compensating credit event

┌─────────────┐                    ┌─────────────┐
│ payment-svc │                    │ ledger-svc  │
│  TX local   │      HTTP/Kafka    │  TX local   │
│ payments_db │ ─────────────────► │ ledger_db   │
└─────────────┘                    └─────────────┘
     NO 2PC/XA across services (avoid in microservices)

XA / JTA (Legacy — Avoid for New MS)

Atomikos, Narayana JTA — two-phase commit across DB + messaging
Slow, operational complexity, fragile in cloud
Architect decision 2025: **Saga + outbox**, not XA

Kafka + Transaction (Preview Lesson 28)

kafka transactional producer + DB in same service:
  possible with careful "exactly-once" setup — advanced

Simpler: outbox table in same DB tx → separate relay publishes to Kafka

Part 9: Architect Perspective

Transaction Design Decisions

Propagation Decision Tree

Should work commit independently of outer failure?
  YES → REQUIRES_NEW (audit, idempotency marker sometimes)
  NO ↓

Should participate in outer unit of work?
  YES → REQUIRED (default)
  NO ↓

Must NOT run in transaction?
  NOT_SUPPORTED (rare — bulk read uncommitted external tool)

Nested partial rollback needed?
  NESTED (savepoint) — use sparingly

Optimistic vs Pessimistic Concurrency

Optimistic (@Version) Pessimistic (FOR UPDATE)
Mechanism Version column check at flush DB row lock at read
Conflict OptimisticLockException Blocks/waits
Use Low contention updates Hot account, inventory
Banking General payment metadata Ledger balance debit

ADR — No Distributed XA

## ADR-162: Saga + outbox instead of XA across payment and ledger

### Decision
Local @Transactional per service; cross-service consistency via outbox events and compensations

### Rationale
XA doesn't span HTTP; operational pain; cloud-native pattern is event-driven saga

Part 10: Decision Matrix

Propagation Selection

Scenario Propagation
Normal business method REQUIRED
Audit must persist on failure REQUIRES_NEW
Idempotency key record (always store attempt) REQUIRES_NEW or separate design
Read-only helper joining caller tx SUPPORTS or REQUIRED + readOnly
Must be called inside tx MANDATORY
Must never run in tx NEVER / NOT_SUPPORTED

Isolation Selection

Scenario Isolation
Default OLTP banking DB default (READ_COMMITTED)
Report same tx re-read REPEATABLE_READ (careful)
Financial ledger hot row Pessimistic lock > SERIALIZABLE
Avoid SERIALIZABLE globally

Rollback Configuration

Exception type Configuration
RuntimeException Default rollback
Checked business failure rollbackFor
Checked you want to commit Default (document clearly)
Swallowed exception Never swallow in tx

Part 11: Comparison Tables

Propagation Full Comparison

Propagation New tx? Suspends outer? Outer rollback affects inner?
REQUIRED If needed No Yes (same tx)
REQUIRES_NEW Always Yes No (independent)
NESTED Savepoint No Yes (outer rollback rolls nested)
SUPPORTS No No N/A
NOT_SUPPORTED No Yes (outer) N/A
MANDATORY No No Must exist
NEVER No — Throws if tx exists

@Transactional vs Programmatic

Declarative Programmatic (TransactionTemplate)
Readability High Lower
AOP proxy required Yes No
Dynamic tx per chunk Awkward Good
Self-invocation issue Yes No
Use Default Batch chunks, libraries

Local TX vs Saga vs 2PC

Local @Transactional Saga 2PC/XA
Scope One DB Multi service Multi resource
Consistency Strong local Eventual Strong global
Complexity Low Medium High
Microservices Per service Preferred cross Avoid

Junior Level

Senior Level

  1. Explain REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW with example.
  2. Why @Transactional on private method fails?
  3. Why checked exception commits by default?
  4. What is readOnly=true?
  5. Connection held during @Transactional — pool implications?
  6. Self-invocation and @Transactional?
  7. What is optimistic locking vs pessimistic?

Staff / Architect Level

  1. Design transaction boundaries for payment + outbox + Kafka.
  2. Why not XA across payment-db and ledger-db?
  3. NESTED vs REQUIRES_NEW — when each?
  4. Phantom read example in reconciliation report.
  5. HTTP call inside @Transactional — diagnose pool exhaustion.
  6. How does JpaTransactionManager bind EntityManager to connection?
  7. @Async + @Transactional pitfalls?
  8. Idempotency storage transaction design for retries.
  9. Oracle READ_COMMITTED vs SERIALIZABLE for hot account?

Model Answer — Q6 (REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW)

A: REQUIRED joins existing transaction or creates new if none — all participants share one commit/rollback. REQUIRES_NEW suspends outer transaction, opens new independent transaction on (typically) new connection, commits inner immediately. Inner work persists even if outer rolls back afterward. Use REQUIRES_NEW for audit trails that must survive business failure, or independent side effects that must not roll back with main work. Use REQUIRED for single business operation atomicity across repositories in same database.

Model Answer — Q14 (No XA)

A: Payment and ledger are separate microservices with separate databases and separate connection pools. @Transactional is local to one PlatformTransactionManager and one DataSource. HTTP between services is not enrolled in JDBC transaction. XA 2PC adds availability and latency costs, brittle in cloud, and most orgs ban it for new MS. Use saga: local tx commits payment + outbox; async message triggers ledger local tx; compensation on failure. Achieves eventual consistency with clear failure modes.

Part 13: Common Mistakes

# Mistake Consequence Fix
1 @Transactional on controller Long tx, wrong layer Service only
2 Checked exception commits Data inconsistency rollbackFor
3 Self-invocation Tx not applied Separate bean
4 HTTP inside tx with lock Pool/deadlock Move external call out
5 Assume cross-service atomicity Split brain Saga/outbox
6 SERIALIZABLE everywhere Deadlocks READ_COMMITTED + locks
7 Swallow exception in tx Partial commit intent unclear Rethrow or rollback
8 No @Version on concurrent fields Lost update Optimistic/pessimistic
9 @Transactional on private method Ignored Public proxy method
10 REQUIRES_NEW everywhere Connection churn, confusion Minimal use

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Service-layer @Transactional — one use case per method
  2. Constructor injection + public methods for AOP
  3. rollbackFor all business failure exceptions that must not commit
  4. Short transactions — no remote calls inside
  5. readOnly=true on queries
  6. timeout on lock-prone operations
  7. Pessimistic lock or @Version for financial rows
  8. Outbox in same local tx for events
  9. Saga for cross-service — not XA
  10. Integration tests assert rollback with @Rollback or @Commit carefully

Part 16: Revision Notes

Quick Revision — Transactions

@Transactional = AOP TransactionInterceptor + PlatformTransactionManager

ACID: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability

PROPAGATION:
  REQUIRED (default) — join or new
  REQUIRES_NEW — suspend outer, independent commit
  NESTED — savepoint
  SUPPORTS, NOT_SUPPORTED, MANDATORY, NEVER

ISOLATION: READ_UNCOMMITTED < READ_COMMITTED < REPEATABLE_READ < SERIALIZABLE
  Default DB READ_COMMITTED usually OK

ROLLBACK: RuntimeException + Error default YES
  Checked Exception default NO — use rollbackFor

readOnly=true: queries, skip dirty check
timeout: seconds, rollback if exceed

Connection bound ThreadLocal per thread during tx
Short tx = less lock + pool hold

NO cross-microservice @Transactional — Saga/outbox
Self-invocation breaks tx — separate @Service bean

Pessimistic FOR UPDATE vs @Version optimistic

Memory Mnemonic

"One service method, one local commit — HTTP doesn't roll back with your SQL"

Part 1: Concept

What Is Spring Security?

Spring Security is a framework for authentication (who you are) and authorization (what you may do). It implements security as a Servlet Filter chain (for MVC) or WebFlux Security chain (reactive), plus optional method-level security via AOP — structurally similar to @Transactional (Lesson 15).

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    REQUEST FLOW — BANKING PAYMENT API                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  Client (JWT / OAuth2 token)                                           │
│       │                                                                  │
│       ▼                                                                  │
│  API Gateway (optional — Lesson 42)                                      │
│       │                                                                  │
│       ▼                                                                  │
│  Spring Security Filter Chain                                            │
│       │ authenticate → SecurityContext                                   │
│       │ authorize URL / role                                             │
│       ▼                                                                  │
│  @RestController                                                         │
│       │                                                                  │
│       ▼                                                                  │
│  @PreAuthorize (optional method security)                                │
│       │                                                                  │
│       ▼                                                                  │
│  @Service @Transactional  ← Lesson 18 (business + DB tx)                 │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Authentication vs Authorization

Authentication Authorization
Question Who are you? What can you do?
Mechanism Login, JWT validation, OAuth2 Roles, scopes, @PreAuthorize
Failure 401 Unauthorized 403 Forbidden
Banking example Corporate user JWT from IdP Role PAYMENT_INITIATOR to POST /payments
Stored in SecurityContext → Authentication GrantedAuthority list

Core Components Master Table

Component Purpose Banking Example
SecurityFilterChain Ordered HTTP security rules Permit /actuator/health, auth /api/**
AuthenticationManager Validates credentials/token Validates JWT signature
UserDetailsService Loads user by username Load from LDAP/DB (legacy)
PasswordEncoder Hash passwords BCrypt — never plain text
JwtDecoder Parse/validate JWT Validate bank IdP RS256 token
OAuth2 Resource Server Bearer token APIs Microservice validates access token
OAuth2 Client Call external IdP Client credentials to fraud API
SecurityContextHolder Thread-local auth state Current user in service layer
@PreAuthorize Method authorization hasRole('TELLER')

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why Spring Security Exists

Without framework security With Spring Security
Custom filters everywhere Standard filter chain
Inconsistent auth checks Centralized configuration
CSRF, session fixation overlooked Built-in protections
Role checks copy-pasted @PreAuthorize declarative
OAuth2/JWT complex to wire Resource server starter

Why Architects Own Security Architecture

REGULATORY (PCI-DSS, SOX, RBI guidelines):
  - Strong authentication for payment initiation
  - Audit who performed transaction (principal in logs)
  - Least privilege — role per operation
  - Secrets never in code — vault/K8s secrets

ARCHITECT DECISIONS:
  - Gateway auth vs service auth vs both (defense in depth)
  - JWT validation at each microservice (zero trust)
  - Service-to-service: mTLS, client credentials, or internal mesh
  - Actuator endpoints never public

Security Runs Before Transactions

Order matters:

1. Security filters — reject unauthorized before business logic
2. Controller validation — input
3. @PreAuthorize — method auth
4. @Transactional — DB work

Never start @Transactional work for unauthenticated caller
(waste connection + audit noise)

Part 3: Internal Working

Security Filter Chain

HTTP Request
     │
     ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐
│ SecurityContextPersistenceFilter │  restore/create SecurityContext
├─────────────────────────┤
│ LogoutFilter            │
├─────────────────────────┤
│ BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter │  OAuth2 JWT (Resource Server)
│   OR UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter (form login)
├─────────────────────────┤
│ ExceptionTranslationFilter │  → 401/403 entry point
├─────────────────────────┤
│ FilterSecurityInterceptor │  URL authorization (final filter)
└─────────────────────────┘
     │
     ▼
DispatcherServlet → Controller

JWT Resource Server Flow (Microservices — Primary Pattern)

Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs...

BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter:
  1. Extract Bearer token
  2. JwtDecoder.decode(token) — verify signature, exp, iss, aud
  3. JwtAuthenticationConverter → Authentication object
       principal: Jwt
       authorities: from scope/roles claim
  4. SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(auth)
  5. Continue filter chain

Invalid/expired token → 401 before controller

JWT STRUCTURE:

HEADER.PAYLOAD.SIGNATURE

Payload claims (example):
{
  "sub": "user-12345",
  "iss": "https://idp.bank.com",
  "aud": "payment-api",
  "exp": 1719398400,
  "scope": "payments:write accounts:read",
  "roles": ["PAYMENT_INITIATOR"]
}

SecurityContextHolder — ThreadLocal

Thread-1 (HTTP request):
  SecurityContextHolder
    → Authentication
         principal: Jwt / UserDetails
         authorities: [ROLE_PAYMENT_INITIATOR, ...]
         authenticated: true

Same model as TransactionSynchronizationManager (Lesson 18) — per thread

@Async / CompletableFuture / Kafka listener:
  SecurityContext NOT propagated by default
  → pass userId in message or configure DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor

Method Security — AOP (Lesson 15 Parallel)

@PreAuthorize("hasRole('PAYMENT_INITIATOR') and #request.debtorAccountId != null")
public PaymentResult createPayment(@AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt, PaymentRequest request) {
    ...
}

MethodSecurityInterceptor (AOP around service/controller method):
  1. Evaluate SpEL expression
  2. Access SecurityContextHolder
  3. Deny → AccessDeniedException → 403
  4. Allow → proceed()

Like @Transactional — must call through SPRING PROXY
Self-invocation bypasses @PreAuthorize too

OAuth2 Roles in Enterprise

Role Direction Banking use
Resource Server Validates incoming tokens payment-svc API
Authorization Server Issues tokens Bank IdP (often Keycloak, Okta, Azure AD)
Client Obtains token to call others payment-svc → fraud-svc (client credentials) 
USER FLOW (Authorization Code + PKCE — mobile/web):
  User → IdP login → authorization code → token → calls payment API with Bearer JWT

SERVICE FLOW (Client Credentials):
  payment-svc → IdP token endpoint (client_id + secret) → access token → fraud-svc

Password Encoding (Legacy / Internal Users)

@Bean
public PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
    return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(12);  // strength factor
}

NEVER: MD5, SHA1, plain text
BCrypt: adaptive hash, salt embedded, slow by design (brute-force resistance)

Part 4: Memory View

Security Runtime Footprint

PER REQUEST (heap):

JWT validation:
  Parse JWT string → Jwt object (claims map)
  JWK set cache (public keys from IdP) — Metaspace + heap cache
  Signature verification — CPU, minimal allocation

SecurityContext + Authentication objects — short-lived (Young Gen)

Session-based auth (legacy):
  HttpSession in memory/redis — NOT preferred for stateless MS APIs

ThreadLocal SecurityContext — no cross-thread sharing (Lesson 8)

JWK Set Caching

spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.jwk-set-uri=https://idp.bank.com/.well-known/jwks.json

Spring caches JWK keys — periodic refresh
Startup: first request may fetch JWK if not eager-loaded
Outage of IdP JWK endpoint → all auth fails — architect: cache TTL + monitoring

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Security Performance

Operation Cost Note
JWT local validation (RS256) ~1–5 ms CPU crypto
JWT remote introspection ~10–50 ms Network — avoid if possible
@PreAuthorize SpEL Microseconds After auth
BCrypt verify ~100 ms intentional Login only, not per API call with JWT
Session lookup (Redis) ~1–5 ms Legacy

Stateless JWT Benefits for Microservices

No server-side session store lookup per request (after JWT validated)
Horizontally scale payment pods without sticky sessions
Trade-off: token revocation harder — short TTL + refresh token pattern

Filter Chain Order and Short-Circuit

Invalid token rejected at BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter
  → controller never invoked
  → @Transactional never started
  → efficient rejection

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: OAuth2 Resource Server — JWT

package com.bank.payments.config;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.configuration.EnableWebSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.http.SessionCreationPolicy;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())  // stateless JWT API — disable CSRF for pure APIs
            .sessionManagement(sm -> sm.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/health", "/actuator/health/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/**").hasRole("OPS")
                .requestMatchers("/api/v1/payments/**").hasAnyRole("PAYMENT_INITIATOR", "ADMIN")
                .anyRequest().denyAll()
            )
            .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth2 -> oauth2.jwt(jwt -> {}))
            .build();
    }
}

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://idp.bank.com/realms/corporate-banking
          # or jwk-set-uri for explicit JWK location

Example 2: Method Security

package com.bank.payments.config;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.method.configuration.EnableMethodSecurity;

@Configuration
@EnableMethodSecurity(prePostEnabled = true)
public class MethodSecurityConfig {}

package com.bank.payments.service;

import org.springframework.security.access.prepost.PreAuthorize;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Service
public class TransferService {

    @Transactional
    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('TRANSFER_MAKER') and @paymentAuthz.canTransfer(authentication, #cmd)")
    public TransferResult transfer(TransferCommand cmd) {
        // business logic
        return TransferResult.success(cmd.transferId());
    }
}

@Component("paymentAuthz")
public class PaymentAuthorizationService {

    public boolean canTransfer(Authentication auth, TransferCommand cmd) {
        // custom: user branch must match account branch, limits, etc.
        Jwt jwt = (Jwt) auth.getPrincipal();
        String userBranch = jwt.getClaimAsString("branch_code");
        return branchPolicy.allows(userBranch, cmd.debtorAccountId());
    }
}

Example 3: Controller — Principal for Audit

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/payments")
public class PaymentController {

    private final PaymentService paymentService;

    @PostMapping
    public PaymentResponse create(
            @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt,
            @Valid @RequestBody PaymentRequest request) {

        String initiatedBy = jwt.getSubject();
        return paymentService.process(request, initiatedBy);
    }
}

Example 5: Security Context in Audit Entity

@Service
public class PaymentAuditService {

    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void record(String paymentId, String action) {
        Authentication auth = SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();
        String userId = auth != null ? auth.getName() : "SYSTEM";
        auditRepository.save(new AuditEntity(paymentId, action, userId, Instant.now()));
    }
}

    .requestMatchers("/actuator/**").hasRole("OPS")
)

Part 7: Production Usage

Spring Security in Production Banking

Defense in Depth Layers

Layer 1: API Gateway — WAF, rate limit, coarse JWT validation
Layer 2: Service SecurityFilterChain — fine-grained URL rules
Layer 3: @PreAuthorize — business authorization
Layer 4: Database — row-level if needed (Oracle VPD — rare)

Don't rely on gateway alone — zero trust between services

JWT Best Practices

Practice Why
Short access token TTL (5–15 min) Limit stolen token window
Validate iss, aud, exp Prevent wrong token reuse
RS256 asymmetric keys Services validate with public JWK
No sensitive data in JWT payload Base64 readable — only claims needed
Rotate signing keys IdP key rotation + JWK cache refresh
mTLS internal + JWT Service mesh double protection

Secrets Management

# NEVER in Git
spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.fraud-service.client-secret: ${FRAUD_CLIENT_SECRET}

K8s secrets, AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault — injected as env vars.

CSRF

Browser cookie session apps: CSRF protection ON
Pure mobile/API JWT Bearer: CSRF disabled (no cookie auth)
Banking web portal with cookies: CSRF ON + SameSite cookies

Production Checklist

Check Why
Stateless session for APIs Scale pods
Actuator not public Attack surface
denyAll default Whitelist endpoints
Method security for sensitive ops Defense in depth
Principal in audit logs Compliance
OAuth2 client secret rotated Credential hygiene
Security tests in CI Regression
401 vs 403 correct Client behavior

Part 8: Microservice Usage

Security Across Microservices

Token Propagation vs Token Exchange

OPTION A: Forward same user JWT
  payment-svc → ledger-svc with same Bearer token
  ledger-svc validates JWT, same user context
  Risk: broad scope — ledger needs only ledger:write scope

OPTION B: Token exchange / client credentials + user context header (signed)
  payment-svc gets service token, passes X-User-Id signed internal header
  Requires trust boundary — mTLS + internal network

OPTION C: Service mesh (Istio) mTLS
  Identity at transport layer; app-level JWT optional

Gateway vs Service Validation

                    ┌─────────────┐
 Client JWT ────────►│  API GW     │ validate JWT (optional)
                    └──────┬──────┘
                           │ forward Authorization header
                    ┌──────▼──────┐
                    │ payment-svc │ validate JWT AGAIN (recommended)
                    └─────────────┘

Architect: Each service validates JWT — compromised gateway doesn't bypass auth.

Kafka Security (Preview Lesson 31)

Kafka: SASL/SSL for broker auth
Message payload: don't trust — include correlationId, not JWT in every message
Consumer: service account auth, not end-user JWT (unless event carries signed userId)

Multi-Tenant Banking

@PreAuthorize("@tenantAuthz.tenantMatches(#request.tenantId)")
public PaymentResult create(PaymentRequest request) { ... }

// JWT claim: tenant_id must match resource tenant

Pattern Use Avoid

  2. Gateway validates JWT — should microservice re-validate?

  8. Secure Actuator in K8s without exposing to internet?

Model Answer — Q14 (Re-validate JWT)

A: Yes — zero trust. Gateway compromise or misconfiguration could forward unauthenticated requests. Each microservice as OAuth2 Resource Server validates signature, issuer, audience, expiry independently using IdP JWK. Adds ~1–5ms CPU but consistent policy enforcement and audit. Gateway handles rate limiting and WAF; service handles authorization truth.

Model Answer — Q13 (Maker-Checker)

A: Separate roles TRANSFER_MAKER and TRANSFER_APPROVER in IdP. Maker POST creates transfer in PENDING status — @PreAuthorize("hasRole('TRANSFER_MAKER')"). Approver PUT /transfers/{id}/approve — @PreAuthorize("hasRole('TRANSFER_APPROVER')") plus rule approver ≠ maker (different user id from JWT sub). Separate @Transactional methods; approval triggers execution. Audit logs both principals. Four-eyes principle for high-value transfers.

Quick Revision — Spring Security

AUTHENTICATION = who | AUTHORIZATION = what
401 = not authenticated | 403 = denied

Filter chain BEFORE DispatcherServlet
JWT Resource Server: BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter → JwtDecoder → SecurityContext

SecurityContextHolder = ThreadLocal (like tx binding)

@EnableMethodSecurity + @PreAuthorize SpEL

OAuth2:
  Resource Server = validate incoming JWT
  Client = client_credentials for S2S
  Authorization Server = IdP (external)

STATELESS API: SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS, CSRF off (Bearer)
Roles: hasRole('X') expects ROLE_ prefix or granted authority converter

@PreAuthorize needs public method + proxy (same as @Transactional)

Never log Bearer token | Actuator restricted | denyAll default
Maker-checker: separate roles/endpoints
Each microservice validates JWT (zero trust)

Prerequisites: Lesson 4 (Streams) · Lesson 7–11 (Threads, CompletableFuture) · Lesson 17 (JPA — blocking) · Lesson 18 (Transactions — ThreadLocal) · Lesson 19 (Security filter chain)

Part 1: Concept

What Is Reactive Programming?

Reactive programming models computation as asynchronous data streams with non-blocking I/O. In Spring, the reactive stack is Spring WebFlux (HTTP) + Project Reactor (Mono, Flux) + optionally R2DBC (reactive DB driver).

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              BLOCKING (Spring MVC) vs REACTIVE (WebFlux)                 │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  BLOCKING MVC                         REACTIVE WEBFLUX                   │
│  ─────────────                        ────────────────                   │
│  Tomcat thread pool                   Netty event loop (few threads)     │
│  1 request ≈ 1 thread blocked         1 thread handles many requests   │
│  JPA / JDBC blocks thread             R2DBC / external calls async       │
│  Simple mental model                  Backpressure, composition          │
│  Default for CRUD banking APIs        Streaming, gateways, fan-out       │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Core Types — Project Reactor

Type Emits Banking Example
Mono\<T> 0 or 1 item Single payment lookup by ID
Flux\<T> 0..N items Stream of settlement events
Publisher Reactive Streams spec Interface both implement
Subscriber Consumes events WebClient response handler

Reactive Streams Contract

Publisher  ──onSubscribe──►  Subscriber
           ◄──request(n)───   (backpressure)
           ──onNext(data)──►
           ──onComplete───►  (or onError)

Backpressure: Subscriber controls how fast it consumes — prevents overwhelming slow consumers (e.g., fraud scoring pipeline).

Spring Reactive Stack Map

Layer Blocking (MVC) Reactive (WebFlux)
HTTP server Tomcat Netty
Controller @RestController Same annotation, returns Mono/Flux
Client RestTemplate (deprecated) WebClient
Security Servlet Filter chain WebFilter chain
DB JPA / JDBC R2DBC (not JPA)
Messaging Kafka sync consumer Reactor Kafka

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why Reactive Exists

Problem (blocking) Reactive approach
10K concurrent long-poll connections exhaust thread pool Few event-loop threads handle I/O wait
Gateway fan-out to 5 services blocks 5 threads per request Compose 5 Mono calls without blocking
SSE / WebSocket streaming awkward on servlet threads Native Flux streaming
Thread pool tuning fragile under spike Elastic concurrency via event loop

Why Architects Must Be Skeptical

REACTIVE IS NOT FREE:

✓ Good fit:
  - API Gateway / BFF aggregating multiple services
  - Real-time payment status SSE stream to mobile app
  - High-concurrency I/O-bound endpoints (no DB or external async only)
  - Streaming Kafka → WebSocket dashboard (logistics tracking)

✗ Poor default fit:
  - Standard payment CRUD with JPA + Oracle
  - @Transactional business logic (blocking by nature)
  - Team unfamiliar → harder debug, ThreadLocal traps
  - "Make it reactive" without bottleneck = complexity tax

RULE: Use reactive where I/O concurrency is the bottleneck AND stack is end-to-end reactive.
      Blocking MVC + good thread pools often wins for banking CRUD.

Link to Prior Lessons

Lesson 11 CompletableFuture: imperative async composition
Reactor Mono/Flux: declarative stream composition + backpressure

Lesson 18 @Transactional: ThreadLocal-bound — breaks on reactive thread hop
Lesson 17 JPA: blocking — cannot run on Netty event loop without blocking it

Lesson 19 Security: SecurityContextHolder ThreadLocal — same propagation issue

Part 3: Internal Working

Netty Event Loop vs Tomcat Thread-Per-Request

TOMCAT (blocking):
  Request-1 ──► Thread-1 ──► [wait DB 50ms] ──► [wait HTTP 30ms] ──► response
  Request-2 ──► Thread-2 ──► ...
  200 threads max → 200 concurrent blocked requests

NETTY (non-blocking):
  EventLoop-1 ──► Req-1 register I/O ──► Req-2 register I/O ──► Req-3 ...
       │                │                      │
       │         (DB callback when ready)      │
       └──────────────────────────────────────► compose response

  Few threads (e.g., CPU cores × 2) — never block on I/O wait
  BLOCKING CALL ON EVENT LOOP = DISASTER (stalls all requests on that loop)

Mono Execution Flow

return paymentRepository.findById(id)           // Mono<Payment>
    .flatMap(p -> fraudClient.score(p))         // Mono<FraudScore>
    .map(score -> toResponse(payment, score))
    .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic());   // if blocking inside

EXECUTION TIMELINE:

1. subscribe() called (by WebFlux framework)
2. findById schedules R2DBC query (async)
3. event loop free — handles other requests
4. DB response arrives → flatMap runs fraudClient (WebClient async)
5. map transforms result
6. signal onNext → serialized to HTTP response

flatMap = async bind (like CompletableFuture.thenCompose)
map     = sync transform (like thenApply)

Schedulers

Scheduler Use
Schedulers.immediate() Current thread
Schedulers.boundedElastic() Blocking calls (legacy JDBC) — offload from event loop
Schedulers.parallel() CPU-bound work
Schedulers.single() Sequential single thread 
ARCHITECT RULE:
  Never call jdbcTemplate.query() on event loop thread
  → subscribeOn(boundedElastic) or run blocking stack on separate pool
  Better: don't mix blocking in reactive chain at all

WebFlux Request Handling

Client HTTP request
       │
       ▼
Netty Channel (event loop)
       │
       ▼
DispatcherHandler
       │
       ▼
HandlerMapping → @RestController method returning Mono<ResponseEntity>
       │
       ▼
Return Mono (lazy — not executed until subscribe)
       │
       ▼
ReactiveAdapter subscribes, writes response as signals arrive

WebClient Internals

WebClient (reactive HTTP client — replaces RestTemplate)

GET /accounts/{id}
  → ExchangeFunction (Netty HTTP client)
  → Mono<ClientResponse>
  → bodyToMono(Account.class)

Non-blocking socket read; thread not blocked waiting for bytes

Hot vs Cold Publishers

Cold (default) Hot
Behavior New subscription = new execution Shared stream, late subscribers miss earlier
Example Mono.fromCallable(() -> db.find()) Sinks.many().multicast() Kafka bridge
Banking Each API call fresh query Live FX rate ticker SSE

Part 4: Memory View

Reactive Runtime Memory

PER SUBSCRIPTION:

Mono/Flux operator chain = linked operators (lightweight objects)
Subscriber demand = backpressure buffer (bounded if configured)

Netty:
  ByteBuf pooled (direct memory off-heap) — less GC pressure for I/O
  Channel per connection

DANGER — unbounded buffers:
  flux.buffer() without limit on fast producer → OOM
  Always apply backpressure or limitRate()

ThreadLocal (SecurityContext, MDC, Transaction):
  NOT on same thread throughout reactive chain
  Context propagation via Reactor Context API (Lesson 20 key topic)

Reactor Context

return Mono.deferContextual(ctx -> {
    String correlationId = ctx.get("correlationId");
    return paymentService.find(id, correlationId);
})
.contextWrite(Context.of("correlationId", id));

Replaces ThreadLocal for reactive pipelines
Security: spring-security-webflux uses reactive SecurityContext in Context

Part 5: Performance Analysis

When Reactive Wins and Loses

Scenario Blocking MVC WebFlux Winner
Simple CRUD + JPA Good with 200 threads Blocking JPA kills event loop MVC
Gateway aggregating 5 HTTP calls 5 × thread blocked 5 Monos zip WebFlux
50K SSE connections Thread exhaustion Event loop WebFlux
CPU-heavy pricing calc Thread pool Still needs parallel scheduler Tie — optimize algo
Kafka consume → DB insert (JPA) Straightforward Awkward mixing MVC

Latency Composition

// Parallel fan-out (like CompletableFuture.allOf)
Mono.zip(
    accountClient.getAccount(debtorId),
    accountClient.getAccount(creditorId),
    limitClient.checkLimit(debtorId)
).map(tuple -> buildPaymentPreview(tuple));

Wall-clock ≈ max(individual latencies), not sum
vs sequential blocking: sum of latencies

5 services × 40ms each:
  Sequential blocking: 200ms
  Parallel zip: ~40ms (+ overhead)

Overhead

Reactor operator chain: small allocation per operator
For low-concurrency CRUD: overhead may exceed benefit
Measure with load test (Lesson 12 JMH mindset) before choosing WebFlux

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: WebFlux Controller

package com.bank.gateway.api;

import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import reactor.core.publisher.Mono;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/payments")
public class PaymentStatusController {

    private final PaymentQueryService queryService;

    public PaymentStatusController(PaymentQueryService queryService) {
        this.queryService = queryService;
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}/status")
    public Mono<PaymentStatusResponse> getStatus(@PathVariable String id) {
        return queryService.getStatus(id);
    }

    @GetMapping(value = "/stream", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
    public Flux<PaymentEvent> streamEvents(@RequestParam String accountId) {
        return queryService.streamPaymentEvents(accountId);
    }
}

Example 2: Service with WebClient Fan-Out

@Service
public class PaymentPreviewService {

    private final WebClient accountClient;
    private final WebClient limitClient;

    public Mono<PaymentPreview> preview(String debtorId, String creditorId, BigDecimal amount) {
        Mono<Account> debtor = accountClient.get()
            .uri("/accounts/{id}", debtorId)
            .retrieve()
            .bodyToMono(Account.class);

        Mono<Account> creditor = accountClient.get()
            .uri("/accounts/{id}", creditorId)
            .retrieve()
            .bodyToMono(Account.class);

        Mono<LimitCheck> limit = limitClient.get()
            .uri("/limits/{id}?amount={amount}", debtorId, amount)
            .retrieve()
            .bodyToMono(LimitCheck.class);

        return Mono.zip(debtor, creditor, limit)
            .map(t -> PaymentPreview.of(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3(), amount));
    }
}

Example 3: R2DBC Repository (Reactive DB)

public interface PaymentRepository extends ReactiveCrudRepository<PaymentEntity, String> {
    Flux<PaymentEntity> findByAccountIdAndStatus(String accountId, PaymentStatus status);
}

@Service
public class PaymentQueryService {

    private final PaymentRepository repository;

    public Mono<PaymentStatusResponse> getStatus(String paymentId) {
        return repository.findById(paymentId)
            .map(PaymentStatusResponse::from)
            .switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(new PaymentNotFoundException(paymentId)));
    }
}

spring:
  r2dbc:
    url: r2dbc:postgresql://db.internal:5432/payments
    username: ${DB_USER}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}

NOTE: JPA/Hibernate does NOT work on reactive stack
R2DBC = different API, no lazy loading, no persistence context like Lesson 17

Example 4: Error Handling

return repository.findById(id)
    .switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(new PaymentNotFoundException(id)))
    .onErrorMap(DataAccessException.class, ex -> new ServiceUnavailableException("DB error", ex))
    .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
    .onErrorResume(TimeoutException.class, ex -> Mono.just(PaymentStatusResponse.degraded(id)));

Example 5: Reactor Context for Correlation ID

public Mono<Payment> process(PaymentRequest req) {
    return Mono.deferContextual(ctx -> {
        String corrId = ctx.getOrDefault("correlationId", "unknown");
        log.info("Processing payment corrId={}", corrId);
        return paymentRepository.save(toEntity(req, corrId));
    });
}

// WebFilter sets context
@Component
public class CorrelationIdWebFilter implements WebFilter {
    @Override
    public Mono<Void> filter(ServerWebExchange exchange, WebFilterChain chain) {
        String id = exchange.getRequest().getHeaders().getFirst("X-Correlation-Id");
        if (id == null) id = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        return chain.filter(exchange)
            .contextWrite(Context.of("correlationId", id));
    }
}

Example 6: Blocking Bridge (Anti-Pattern — Know It)

// NEVER in production reactive endpoint:
Payment payment = paymentRepository.findById(id).block();  // blocks event loop

// If you MUST call blocking code:
return Mono.fromCallable(() -> jdbcPaymentDao.find(id))
    .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic());
// Architect: this is a smell — isolate blocking service behind MVC or use R2DBC

SSE — Real-Time Payment Status

@GetMapping(value = "/{id}/events", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
public Flux<ServerSentEvent<PaymentStatus>> paymentEvents(@PathVariable String id) {
    return paymentEventSource.subscribe(id)
        .map(status -> ServerSentEvent.builder(status).id(status.version()).build())
        .delayElements(Duration.ofMillis(100));  // optional pacing
}

Use case: corporate treasury portal watching bulk payment batch completion.

WebClient Production Config

@Bean
WebClient accountWebClient(WebClient.Builder builder) {
    return builder
        .baseUrl("https://account-svc.internal")
        .defaultHeader(HttpHeaders.ACCEPT, MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
        .filter(oauth2ClientFilter)  // Lesson 19 client credentials
        .clientConnector(new ReactorClientHttpConnector(
            HttpClient.create()
                .responseTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
                .option(ChannelOption.CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MILLIS, 3000)
        ))
        .build();
}

Production Checklist

Check Why
No .block() on event loop Prevents stall
Timeouts on all Monos Avoid hung requests
Circuit breaker (Resilience4j reactor) Cascade failure control
Metrics (reactor.netty, Micrometer) Observe queue depth
R2DBC connection pool sized Not same as Hikari defaults
Context for MDC/correlationId Replace ThreadLocal
Load test at target concurrency Validate reactive choice
Document hybrid blocking/reactive boundaries Ops clarity

Part 8: Microservice Usage

Reactive in Microservice Landscape

BFF Pattern (Backend for Frontend)

Mobile needs one screen: account balance + pending payments + FX rate

BFF (WebFlux):
  Mono.zip(balances, pendingPayments, fxRate) → aggregated JSON

Without BFF: mobile makes 3 calls (ok but chatty)
With blocking BFF: 3 threads blocked per mobile user
With reactive BFF: 1 event-loop friendly composition

API Gateway Responsibilities

Spring Cloud Gateway (WebFlux-based):
  - Route /auth JWT validation (Lesson 19)
  - Rate limiting (Redis reactive)
  - Request aggregation
  - Retry / circuit break

Domain microservices remain MVC + JPA — valid and common

Kafka + Reactive (Preview Lesson 31)

// Reactor Kafka — non-blocking consumer
Flux<ReceiverRecord<String, PaymentEvent>> inbound = KafkaReceiver.create(options).receive();

inbound.flatMap(record ->
    processEvent(record.value())
        .then(record.receiverOffset().commit())
)
.subscribe();

Logistics: stream shipment GPS events → WebSocket to tracking UI.

Anti-Pattern: Reactive All Layers

payment-svc WebFlux + JPA (blocking) + @Transactional
  → every DB call needs boundedElastic
  → loses event loop benefit
  → harder than MVC

ADR should say NO unless full R2DBC migration planned

## ADR-172: API Gateway on Spring Cloud Gateway (WebFlux)

### Context
Mobile clients need aggregated views; 15K concurrent SSE connections for payment tracking.

### Decision
Gateway/BFF reactive; core payment processing remains Spring MVC + JPA on Oracle.

### Consequences

Model Answer — Q13 (When WebFlux for Payment)

A: Not for core payment CRUD with JPA and @Transactional — MVC + tuned Tomcat/Hikari pool is simpler and proven. WebFlux for: API gateway/BFF with high concurrent fan-out to account/fraud/limit services; SSE stream of batch payment status to corporate dashboard; logistics-style real-time tracking. If requirement is 20 TPS CRUD with Oracle ACID, MVC wins. Reactive payment processing only if committed to R2DBC end-to-end and team skill — rare in traditional banks.

Model Answer — Q18 (@Transactional + Reactive)

A: Spring @Transactional binds connection to thread via ThreadLocal (Lesson 18). Reactor may execute operators on different threads — transaction context lost. JPA session is not thread-safe. Options: keep transactions in blocking MVC service layer; use TransactionalOperator with R2DBC (reactive transactions); or bridge with boundedElastic for isolated blocking transaction (hybrid smell). Architect default: don't mix JPA @Transactional inside WebFlux controller chain.

Part 13: Common Mistakes

# Mistake Consequence Fix
1 .block() on event loop Latency spike all users Never block loop
2 JPA in WebFlux service Blocked Netty threads MVC service or R2DBC
3 Reactive entire bank stack Complexity, bugs Gateway/BFF only
4 Ignore backpressure OOM on fast producer limitRate, bounded buffer
5 ThreadLocal MDC in reactive Wrong/missing logs Reactor Context
6 No timeouts on WebClient Hung Monos timeout(), connector config
7 flatMap with high concurrency Downstream overload flatMap(fn, concurrency)
8 Subscribe without error handler Silent failures onError* operators
9 Assume reactive = faster Overhead for low load Load test
10 Mix security ThreadLocal Missing auth in chain WebFlux security context

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Default to MVC + JPA for domain payment services
  2. WebFlux for gateway, BFF, streaming where I/O concurrency matters
  3. WebClient with timeouts and circuit breakers
  4. Never block event loop — code review .block()
  5. Reactor Context for correlationId, not MDC ThreadLocal
  6. R2DBC only with clear migration plan — not drop-in JPA replacement
  7. Mono.zip for parallel independent I/O
  8. Explicit error handling — switchIfEmpty, onErrorResume
  9. Load test before reactive rewrite
  10. Document hybrid boundaries in ADR for team clarity

Part 16: Revision Notes

Quick Revision — Reactive Programming

WebFlux = Netty + Project Reactor (Mono, Flux)
Non-blocking: thread not waiting on I/O — event loop handles many connections

Mono = 0..1 | Flux = 0..N
map = sync | flatMap = async bind
Mono.zip = parallel wait (like allOf)
backpressure = subscriber requests n items

WebClient replaces RestTemplate for reactive HTTP
NEVER .block() on event loop — use boundedElastic only for isolated blocking

JPA + @Transactional = ThreadLocal — DOES NOT fit reactive chain
R2DBC for reactive DB — no lazy loading

Reactor Context replaces ThreadLocal for MDC/correlationId
Security: WebFilter chain, reactive method security

USE REACTIVE: gateway, BFF fan-out, SSE/WebSocket, high concurrent I/O
STAY MVC: payment CRUD, JPA, complex transactions

Hybrid: WebFlux gateway → MVC microservices (common bank pattern)

Memory Mnemonic

"Event loop never waits — Mono composes I/O; JPA stays on Tomcat"
