Part 1: Concept

What Is SQL?

SQL (Structured Query Language) is the declarative language for querying and mutating relational data. As a Solution Architect, you don't write every query — but you review critical paths, design schemas, and decide what runs in the database vs the application.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    SQL IN THE PAYMENT STACK                              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  PaymentService (@Transactional)                                         │
│       │                                                                  │
│       ▼                                                                  │
│  JPA / JDBC / MyBatis                                                    │
│       │                                                                  │
│       ▼                                                                  │
│  SQL ──► Oracle / PostgreSQL / DB2                                       │
│       │                                                                  │
│       ├── SELECT  (read — joins, aggregates, windows)                    │
│       ├── INSERT  (create payment, ledger entry)                         │
│       ├── UPDATE  (status PENDING → COMPLETED)                           │
│       └── DELETE  (rare — soft delete preferred)                         │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

SQL Sub-Languages

Category Commands Banking Use
DDL CREATE, ALTER, DROP Schema migrations (Flyway/Liquibase)
DML SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE Payment CRUD, reconciliation
DCL GRANT, REVOKE Least-privilege DB users
TCL COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT Transaction boundaries (Lesson 18)

Relational Model Essentials

TABLE: payments
┌────────────┬──────────────┬────────────┬──────────┬─────────────┐
│ payment_id │ debtor_acct  │ amount     │ status   │ created_at  │
├────────────┼──────────────┼────────────┼──────────┼─────────────┤
│ PMT-001    │ ACC-1001     │ 50000.00   │ COMPLETED│ 2026-06-01  │
│ PMT-002    │ ACC-1002     │ 1200.50    │ PENDING  │ 2026-06-02  │
└────────────┴──────────────┴────────────┴──────────┴─────────────┘

PRIMARY KEY: payment_id
FOREIGN KEY: debtor_acct → accounts(account_id)
INDEX: (status, created_at) — pending payment queue queries

Join Types Master Table

Join Returns Banking Example
INNER JOIN Matching rows only Payments with valid account
LEFT JOIN All left + matching right All accounts, even with zero payments
RIGHT JOIN All right + matching left Rare — rewrite as LEFT
FULL OUTER All from both Reconciliation mismatches
CROSS JOIN Cartesian product Avoid — usually bug
SELF JOIN Table to itself Employee → manager hierarchy

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why SQL Mastery Matters for Architects

Without SQL depth With SQL depth
N+1 fixed in Java loops Fixed with one JOIN query
Full table scan at scale Index strategy in design
Business logic in app for aggregates Push-down to DB (Lesson 6)
Can't review DBA escalation Read execution plans
Schema drift across services Consistent ledger design

The Cost of Bad SQL at Bank Scale

PAYMENT SEARCH API — 10 million rows in payments table

Bad:  SELECT * FROM payments WHERE UPPER(status) = 'PENDING'
     → function on column → index unusable → full scan → 8 seconds

Good: SELECT payment_id, amount, status, created_at
      FROM payments
      WHERE status = 'PENDING'
        AND created_at >= :since
      ORDER BY created_at
      LIMIT 50
     → index (status, created_at) → 5 ms

SQL vs Application Logic (Architect Decision)

PUSH TO SQL when:
  - Filtering large datasets (millions of rows)
  - Aggregations (SUM, COUNT, GROUP BY)
  - Joins across normalized tables
  - Pagination with ORDER BY + LIMIT
  - Window functions (ranking, running totals)

KEEP IN APP when:
  - Complex business rules changing weekly
  - External API calls needed mid-flow
  - Small in-memory datasets already loaded
  - Multi-step orchestration (saga — Lesson 18/29)

Part 3: Internal Working

How the Database Executes a Query

SQL Query
    │
    ▼
┌───────────────┐
│    Parser     │  syntax check
└───────┬───────┘
        ▼
┌───────────────┐
│   Optimizer   │  choose plan: index scan vs seq scan, join order
└───────┬───────┘
        ▼
┌───────────────┐
│  Executor     │  read pages from buffer pool / disk
└───────┬───────┘
        ▼
    Result set

EXPLAIN / Execution Plan

-- PostgreSQL
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT TEXT)
SELECT p.payment_id, p.amount, a.account_name
FROM payments p
INNER JOIN accounts a ON p.debtor_acct = a.account_id
WHERE p.status = 'PENDING'
  AND p.created_at >= TIMESTAMP '2026-06-01';

Typical good plan:
  Index Scan on payments using idx_payments_status_created
    → Nested Loop
      → Index Scan on accounts using pk_accounts

Red flags:
  Seq Scan on payments (full table scan on large table)
  Hash Join with huge build table
  Sort with high cost (missing index for ORDER BY)
  Rows estimate wildly wrong → stale statistics

Index Internals — B-Tree (Default)

B-TREE INDEX on (status, created_at):

                    [COMPLETED|2026-05]
                   /         |         \
          [PENDING|...]  [PENDING|...]  [...]
               │              │
          leaf pages → row pointers (payment_id locations)

Range query: status = 'PENDING' AND created_at >= X
  → tree seek to first matching leaf → sequential leaf scan

LEFTMOST PREFIX RULE (composite index):
  Index (status, created_at, debtor_acct)
  ✓ WHERE status = 'PENDING'
  ✓ WHERE status = 'PENDING' AND created_at >= X
  ✗ WHERE created_at >= X  (status not in predicate — index partial use or skip)

Join Algorithms (Optimizer Chooses)

Algorithm When Used Note
Nested Loop Small outer, indexed inner OLTP point lookups
Hash Join Large equi-joins, no useful index Memory for hash table
Merge Join Both sides sorted on join key Large sorted scans 
payments INNER JOIN accounts ON debtor_acct = account_id

Nested Loop (10 pending payments, accounts PK indexed):
  For each payment → index lookup account → fast

Hash Join (1M payments × 500K accounts report):
  Build hash on smaller table → probe — may spill to disk if huge

Window Functions — Internal Concept

SELECT payment_id, amount, status,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY debtor_acct ORDER BY created_at DESC) AS rn
FROM payments
WHERE status = 'COMPLETED';

Per partition (debtor_acct):
  Sort by created_at DESC
  Assign row numbers
  → "Latest N payments per account" without self-join hack

Architect: one SQL vs N queries in Java (N+1 at SQL level)

Part 4: Memory View

Database Memory vs Application Memory

DATABASE SERVER (Oracle/PostgreSQL):

Shared Buffer Pool (RAM)
  └── Data pages (8KB typical) cached from disk
  └── Hot payment rows / index pages stay in buffer

Sort/Hash work areas
  └── Large GROUP BY / Hash Join → temp disk if exceeds work_mem

Connection (per app pod):
  HikariCP connection → server session memory
  Prepared statement cache

APPLICATION (JVM):
  Result set fetched row-by-row or batch
  fetchSize=500 → 500 rows in JVM heap per round-trip
  Lesson 17: loading 1M Payment entities → heap pressure

Pagination Memory Trap

// BAD: load all, paginate in Java (Lesson 6)
List<Payment> all = repo.findAll(); // 2GB heap

// GOOD: SQL pagination
SELECT ... FROM payments WHERE ... ORDER BY created_at DESC
OFFSET 10000 LIMIT 50;  -- still costly at high OFFSET

// BETTER: keyset pagination
SELECT ... FROM payments
WHERE created_at < :cursor
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 50;

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Query Performance Factors

Factor Impact Mitigation
Missing index Full scan Composite indexes on filter + sort columns
SELECT * Extra I/O, network Project only needed columns (covering index)
Function on indexed column Index skip status = 'X' not UPPER(status)
High OFFSET pagination Scans skipped rows Keyset pagination
Implicit conversion Index skip Match parameter types to column types
Stale statistics Bad plan ANALYZE / auto stats
Lock contention Slow updates Short transactions, index order (Lesson 18)

Complexity at Scale

Rows (payments)     | Seq Scan      | Index Scan
--------------------|---------------|-------------
10K                 | ~10 ms        | ~1 ms
1M                  | ~500 ms       | ~2 ms
100M                | seconds–min   | ~5 ms (with selective predicate)

Architect sign-off: any query touching 100M+ rows must have EXPLAIN proof

Covering Index

-- Query only needs payment_id, amount, status, created_at
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_pending_covering
ON payments (status, created_at)
INCLUDE (payment_id, amount);  -- PostgreSQL INCLUDE; Oracle index-only possible

→ Index-only scan — heap access avoided for covered columns

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Banking Schema — Core Tables

CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id      VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    account_type    VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,  -- SAVINGS, CURRENT, NOSTRO
    currency        CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
    balance         NUMERIC(19,4) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    status          VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE',
    branch_code     VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,
    created_at      TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    CONSTRAINT chk_balance_nonneg CHECK (balance >= 0)
);

CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id      VARCHAR(36) PRIMARY KEY,
    debtor_acct     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(account_id),
    creditor_acct   VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(account_id),
    amount          NUMERIC(19,4) NOT NULL,
    currency        CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
    status          VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,  -- PENDING, APPROVED, COMPLETED, FAILED
    payment_type    VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,  -- NEFT, RTGS, IMPS, INTERNAL
    idempotency_key VARCHAR(64) UNIQUE,
    initiated_by    VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    created_at      TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    updated_at      TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    version         BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0  -- optimistic lock (Lesson 17)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_payments_status_created ON payments (status, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_debtor_created ON payments (debtor_acct, created_at DESC);

Example 2: Joins — Payment with Account Details

-- Inner join: payments with debtor account name
SELECT p.payment_id,
       p.amount,
       p.status,
       p.created_at,
       da.account_id   AS debtor_id,
       da.branch_code  AS debtor_branch,
       c.customer_name AS debtor_name
FROM payments p
INNER JOIN accounts da ON p.debtor_acct = da.account_id
INNER JOIN customers c ON da.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE p.status IN ('PENDING', 'APPROVED')
  AND p.created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7' DAY
ORDER BY p.created_at DESC
FETCH FIRST 100 ROWS ONLY;

-- Left join: accounts with no payments in last 30 days (inactivity report)
SELECT a.account_id, a.balance, a.last_activity_at
FROM accounts a
LEFT JOIN payments p
  ON p.debtor_acct = a.account_id
 AND p.created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30' DAY
WHERE a.status = 'ACTIVE'
  AND p.payment_id IS NULL;

Example 3: Aggregations — Daily Payment Volume

SELECT DATE(created_at) AS payment_date,
       payment_type,
       COUNT(*) AS payment_count,
       SUM(amount) AS total_amount,
       AVG(amount) AS avg_amount
FROM payments
WHERE status = 'COMPLETED'
  AND created_at >= DATE '2026-06-01'
  AND created_at <  DATE '2026-07-01'
GROUP BY DATE(created_at), payment_type
HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000000
ORDER BY payment_date, payment_type;

Example 4: Window Functions — Top 3 Payments per Account

WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT p.payment_id,
           p.debtor_acct,
           p.amount,
           p.created_at,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY p.debtor_acct
               ORDER BY p.amount DESC, p.created_at DESC
           ) AS rn
    FROM payments p
    WHERE p.status = 'COMPLETED'
      AND p.created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '90' DAY
)
SELECT payment_id, debtor_acct, amount, created_at
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 3;

Example 5: Double-Entry Ledger (Preview Lesson 22)

CREATE TABLE ledger_entries (
    entry_id        BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    transaction_id  VARCHAR(36) NOT NULL,
    account_id      VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(account_id),
    debit_amount    NUMERIC(19,4) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    credit_amount   NUMERIC(19,4) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    entry_type      VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    posted_at       TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    CONSTRAINT chk_debit_xor_credit CHECK (
        (debit_amount > 0 AND credit_amount = 0) OR
        (credit_amount > 0 AND debit_amount = 0)
    )
);

-- Transfer PMT-001: debit debtor, credit creditor
INSERT INTO ledger_entries (transaction_id, account_id, debit_amount, credit_amount, entry_type)
VALUES ('PMT-001', 'ACC-1001', 50000.00, 0, 'PAYMENT_DEBIT');

INSERT INTO ledger_entries (transaction_id, account_id, debit_amount, credit_amount, entry_type)
VALUES ('PMT-001', 'ACC-2002', 0, 50000.00, 'PAYMENT_CREDIT');

Example 6: Idempotent Insert (Payment API)

INSERT INTO payments (
    payment_id, debtor_acct, creditor_acct, amount, currency,
    status, payment_type, idempotency_key, initiated_by, updated_at
)
VALUES (
    :paymentId, :debtor, :creditor, :amount, :currency,
    'PENDING', :type, :idempotencyKey, :userId, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
)
ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO NOTHING
RETURNING payment_id;
-- PostgreSQL; Oracle: MERGE; DB2: MERGE

Example 7: Fixing N+1 at SQL Level (Lesson 17 Companion)

-- JPA N+1: 1 query payments + N queries accounts

-- Single query with JOIN FETCH equivalent in native SQL:
SELECT p.*, a.account_id, a.branch_code, a.balance
FROM payments p
INNER JOIN accounts a ON p.debtor_acct = a.account_id
WHERE p.payment_id IN (:ids);

Exercise 1

Write SQL to find duplicate idempotency attempts: same idempotency_key prefix, different payment_id, last 24 hours.

Exercise 2

Given index (status, created_at), which queries use it fully, partially, or not at all?

A) WHERE status = 'PENDING' ORDER BY created_at DESC
B) WHERE created_at > '2026-06-01'
C) WHERE status = 'PENDING' AND created_at > '2026-06-01'
D) WHERE UPPER(status) = 'PENDING'

Part 7: Production Usage

SQL in Production Banking

Migration Management

Flyway / Liquibase in CI/CD:
  V001__create_payments.sql
  V002__add_idempotency_key.sql
  V003__idx_payments_status_created.sql

Never manual DDL in prod without ticket + rollback script
Index CREATE CONCURRENTLY (PostgreSQL) — avoid long locks

Read vs Write Routing

Primary (Oracle RAC node 1): INSERT, UPDATE payment status
Read replica: payment search, reports, reconciliation dashboards

Architect: replica lag (seconds) — don't read-your-writes on replica for UX-critical path

Audit Table Pattern

CREATE TABLE payments_audit (
    audit_id        BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    payment_id      VARCHAR(36) NOT NULL,
    old_status      VARCHAR(20),
    new_status      VARCHAR(20),
    changed_by      VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    changed_at      TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    change_reason   VARCHAR(255)
);

-- Trigger or application-level audit (prefer app + REQUIRES_NEW — Lesson 18)

Production Query Review Checklist

Check Pass Criteria
EXPLAIN on prod-like volume No seq scan on large tables
Projections No SELECT * in hot paths
Parameterization Prepared statements — no SQL injection
Timeout Statement timeout configured
Lock impact UPDATE/DELETE scoped by PK or indexed column
Idempotency UNIQUE constraint on business key
Soft delete deleted_at IS NULL in all queries

SQL Injection — Never Concatenate

// FORBIDDEN
jdbcTemplate.query("SELECT * FROM payments WHERE id = '" + userInput + "'");

// CORRECT
jdbcTemplate.query("SELECT * FROM payments WHERE payment_id = ?", paymentId);

Part 8: Microservice Usage

SQL Across Microservices

Database per Service

payment-svc  → payments_db (PostgreSQL)
account-svc  → accounts_db (Oracle)
ledger-svc   → ledger_db (PostgreSQL)

NO cross-database JOIN at runtime
Join in application (BFF — Lesson 20) or materialized view / CDC sync for read models

Shared Database Anti-Pattern

Two microservices writing same payments table
  → coupling, migration conflict, unclear ownership
Architect: one writer per aggregate table

Reporting / CQRS Read Model

OLTP: normalized payments + accounts (3NF)
OLAP read model: denormalized payment_search_view fed by Kafka CDC

SQL on read model:
  SELECT payment_id, debtor_name, amount, status, created_at
  FROM payment_search_mv
  WHERE status = :status AND created_at BETWEEN :from AND :to;

No 5-table join at query time — pre-joined in pipeline

Cross-Service Consistency

Payment row in payment-svc DB
Account balance in account-svc DB
→ No single SQL transaction (Lesson 18 saga)
→ eventual consistency + reconciliation SQL on batch job

Part 9: Architect Perspective

Schema and Query Design Ownership

Normalization Level

Form Rule Banking
1NF Atomic columns No comma-separated beneficiary list
2NF No partial key dependency Composite keys rare — use surrogate PK
3NF No transitive dependency customer_name in accounts? → separate customers table
Denormalize Controlled redundancy Read models, reporting only

Index Strategy ADR

## ADR-201: Composite index (status, created_at DESC) on payments

### Context
Pending payment queue API: filter by status, sort by created_at, 80M rows.

### Decision
Composite B-tree; INCLUDE payment_id, amount for covering scan.

### Consequences
Extra write overhead on INSERT/UPDATE status (~5%).
Monitor index bloat; REINDEX scheduled quarterly.

When to Escalate to DBA

- Query > 500ms sustained in prod
- Lock wait timeouts on payment status updates
- Partition strategy for payments > 500M rows (by created_at monthly)
- Oracle execution plan regression after stats job

Part 10: Decision Matrix

SQL Feature Selection

Need SQL Feature
Combine related tables JOIN
Filter groups HAVING (after GROUP BY)
Rank / running total Window functions
Prevent duplicate payment UNIQUE + ON CONFLICT / MERGE
Paginate large result Keyset pagination
Explain slowness EXPLAIN ANALYZE
Historical snapshot Audit table / temporal tables
Bulk load reconciliation COPY / SQL*Loader + staging table

Index Decision Matrix

Query Pattern Index
PK lookup Primary key (automatic)
FK join column Index on FK column
Filter + sort Composite (filter cols first, then sort col)
Low cardinality alone Often useless (status only on 50/50 split)
Text search Full-text / Elasticsearch (Lesson 24)

OFFSET vs Keyset Pagination

OFFSET/LIMIT Keyset (seek)
Page 1 Fast Fast
Page 10000 Slow (scans 10000 rows) Fast
Stable under inserts Duplicates/skips possible Needs tie-breaker column
Banking search UI OK for page 1–10 Required for deep scroll

Part 11: Comparison Tables

INNER vs LEFT JOIN

INNER JOIN LEFT JOIN
Unmatched rows Excluded Left preserved, NULL right
Use Must exist on both sides Optional relationship
Banking Payment + valid account All accounts, payments optional

WHERE vs HAVING

WHERE HAVING
Filters Rows before grouping Groups after GROUP BY
Aggregates Cannot use (usually) Can use SUM, COUNT
Example status = 'COMPLETED' SUM(amount) > 1000000

DELETE vs Soft Delete

Hard DELETE Soft DELETE (deleted_at)
Compliance Loses history Audit friendly
Queries Simpler Must filter deleted_at IS NULL
Banking Rare for payments Preferred

Oracle vs PostgreSQL vs DB2 (Architect View)

Oracle PostgreSQL DB2
Typical bank use Core banking legacy Modern MS, cloud Enterprise legacy
EXPLAIN EXPLAIN PLAN EXPLAIN ANALYZE EXPLAIN
Upsert MERGE ON CONFLICT MERGE
Pagination FETCH FIRST LIMIT/OFFSET FETCH FIRST
Sequences SEQUENCE SERIAL/BIGSERIAL IDENTITY

  4. What is GROUP BY?

Senior Level

  2. What is an execution plan? How read Seq Scan vs Index Scan?
  3. N+1 problem — fix at SQL level?
  4. OFFSET vs keyset pagination?
  5. What is a covering index?
  6. Explain window function ROW_NUMBER vs RANK.
  7. How implement idempotent payment insert in SQL?

Staff / Architect Level

  1. Design payments + ledger schema for double-entry transfers.
  2. 80M row payments table — pending queue query slow — diagnosis steps?
  3. Database per service — how handle report needing payment + account data?
  4. When denormalize vs keep 3NF?
  5. Index on (status) alone — when useless?
  6. SQL push-down vs Java aggregation for daily totals?
  7. Partitioning strategy for payments by date?
  8. How prevent SQL injection in microservices using JPA native queries?

Model Answer — Q14 (Slow Pending Queue)

A: (1) Capture slow query text and bind variables from APM. (2) EXPLAIN ANALYZE on prod-like data volume. (3) Check for seq scan — missing or wrong index; function on column; implicit cast. (4) Verify composite index (status, created_at) matches filter + ORDER BY. (5) Check stale statistics — run ANALYZE. (6) Review SELECT * — reduce columns for covering index. (7) Check lock contention if mixed with bulk updates. (8) Consider partial index WHERE status IN ('PENDING','APPROVED') if selective. (9) ADR if schema change needed.

Model Answer — Q13 (Double-Entry Schema)

A: payments table holds business state (PENDING→COMPLETED). ledger_entries append-only: each transfer creates two rows (debit debtor, credit creditor) linked by transaction_id. CHECK constraint ensures debit XOR credit per row. Separate from payment status — ledger posts on COMPLETED inside same service transaction or saga step. accounts.balance updated via controlled procedure or derived from ledger — architect chooses: balance column with optimistic lock vs computed balance (trade-off: read speed vs consistency). Audit table on payment status changes. Idempotency on idempotency_key.

Part 13: Common Mistakes

# Mistake Consequence Fix
1 SELECT * in hot path I/O, network bloat Project columns
2 No index on FK Slow joins Index FK columns
3 Function on indexed column Full scan Store normalized, index plain column
4 OFFSET deep pagination Slow pages Keyset pagination
5 Cross-DB joins in MS Coupling BFF aggregation / read model
6 String concat SQL Injection Prepared statements
7 Missing idempotency UNIQUE Duplicate payments Business key constraint
8 Long transaction + report query Locks Read replica, short tx
9 Index every column Write slowdown Index for proven queries
10 Ignore EXPLAIN in review Prod surprises Mandatory for new hot queries

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Every hot query has EXPLAIN proof on realistic volume
  2. Composite indexes match filter + sort column order
  3. Prepared statements always — JPA/JDBC parameterized
  4. Idempotency keys with UNIQUE constraint
  5. Soft delete for compliance entities
  6. Audit tables for status changes on payments
  7. Keyset pagination for large search UIs
  8. Push aggregations to SQL when scanning millions of rows (Lesson 6)
  9. One writer per table in microservices
  10. Flyway/Liquibase — versioned DDL in pipeline

Part 16: Revision Notes

Quick Revision — SQL Fundamentals

DDL/DML/DCL/TCL
JOIN: INNER (match), LEFT (all left + optional right)
WHERE = row filter | HAVING = group filter after GROUP BY

EXPLAIN: Seq Scan bad on big table | Index Scan good
B-tree composite: leftmost prefix rule
Covering index: includes SELECT columns → index-only scan

Window: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY x ORDER BY y)
Aggregates: push to SQL for large datasets (Lesson 6)

Pagination: keyset (created_at < cursor) beats OFFSET at depth
Idempotency: UNIQUE(idempotency_key) + ON CONFLICT

MS: no cross-database JOIN — read model or app aggregation
Audit + soft delete for banking compliance

N+1 fix: JOIN or IN batch — not loop in Java (Lesson 17)

Memory Mnemonic

"Filter in SQL, explain before ship, index matches WHERE and ORDER BY"

Part 1: Concept

What Is Database Design?

Database design is the process of defining entities, relationships, constraints, and evolution strategy so data is correct, queryable, scalable, and compliant. Architects own the logical model; DBAs own physical tuning (Lesson 21 indexes, partitions).

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              DATA MODEL LAYERS — CORPORATE PAYMENTS PLATFORM             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  CONCEPTUAL MODEL          LOGICAL MODEL           PHYSICAL MODEL        │
│  (business language)       (tables, FKs, 3NF)      (indexes, partitions)   │
│                                                                          │
│  Customer ──has──► Account ──initiates──► Payment                       │
│       │                    │                      │                      │
│       │                    └── posts to ──► Ledger Entry               │
│       │                                                                  │
│  LOGIC: ER diagram         LOGIC: DDL scripts    LOGIC: EXPLAIN plans    │
│  Owner: Architect + BA     Owner: Architect + Dev Owner: DBA + Architect│
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

ER Modeling Building Blocks

Element Symbol / Meaning Banking Example
Entity Thing with identity Customer, Account, Payment
Attribute Property of entity amount, status, currency
Relationship Association Customer owns Account
Cardinality How many on each side One Customer → Many Accounts
Primary Key Unique row identifier payment_id, surrogate BIGSERIAL
Foreign Key Referential integrity debtor_acct → accounts.account_id

Cardinality Patterns

ONE-TO-MANY (1:N) — most common in banking:

    Customer ────────< Account
    (1)              (N)

    Account ────────< Payment
    (1)              (N)

MANY-TO-MANY (M:N) — resolve with junction table:

    Payment >──────< Beneficiary   →  payment_beneficiaries(payment_id, beneficiary_id)

ONE-TO-ONE (1:1) — rare, split for security or optional data:

    Payment ──────── PaymentApproval
    (1)              (1)   maker-checker record

Naming Conventions (Production Standard)

Rule Good Bad
Tables plural snake_case payments, ledger_entries Payment, tblPay
PK explicit payment_id id alone (ambiguous in joins)
FK matches referenced PK debtor_acct → accounts.account_id debtor (unclear)
Timestamps consistent created_at, updated_at UTC mixed local time
Status as VARCHAR enum status VARCHAR(20) + CHECK/app enum magic numbers
Money as NUMERIC NUMERIC(19,4) FLOAT, DOUBLE

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why Rigorous Design Matters

Poor design Consequence Good design prevents
No FK constraints Orphan payments, bad joins Referential integrity
Duplicate customer rows Wrong KYC, compliance failure Normalized customers
Balance only in one column, no ledger Cannot reconcile Double-entry audit trail
Nullable everything Unknown vs empty confusion NOT NULL + defaults
Schema change without migration tool Prod drift, outages Flyway versioned DDL
Shared DB across microservices Coupling, conflicting migrations DB per service

Banking Regulatory Drivers

SOX / RBI / PCI implications on DATA MODEL:

- WHO changed WHAT WHEN → audit tables, immutable ledger
- Payment traceability → payment_id links ledger, events, logs
- Data retention → archive strategy designed upfront
- PII separation → customers table access-controlled
- Idempotency → UNIQUE business keys at schema level
- Four-eyes → separate approval entity/table

Design Before Code (Architect Workflow)

1. Event storming / domain workshop → nouns become entities
2. ER diagram → agree with business + compliance
3. Logical DDL (3NF) → peer review
4. Map to JPA entities (Lesson 17) — impedance check
5. Flyway V001..Vn → CI applies to ephemeral DB
6. Load test + EXPLAIN (Lesson 21) → physical indexes
7. ADR for denormalization / read models if needed

Part 3: Internal Working

Normalization — How Tables Decompose

First Three Normal Forms (Architect Must Know)

UNNORMALIZED (bad):
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ payment_id │ debtor_acct │ debtor_name │ debtor_address │ ... │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  debtor_name repeats on every payment → update anomaly

1NF — atomic values, unique rows:
  Each cell single value; primary key defined

2NF — no partial dependency on composite key:
  If PK is (payment_id, line_no) — line attributes depend on full key

3NF — no transitive dependency:
  payment → debtor_acct → customer_name
  customer_name belongs in customers, not payments

3NF PAYMENT DOMAIN:

customers ──< accounts ──< payments
    │              │
    │              └──< ledger_entries
    │
    └──< customer_addresses (SCD — history)

When Denormalization Is Intentional

OLTP (write path): normalized — single source of truth
OLAP / search (read path): denormalized materialized view

payment_search_mv:
  payment_id, debtor_name, creditor_name, amount, status, branch_name
  ← populated by Kafka CDC from payment-svc + account-svc

Trade-off: read speed + simple SQL vs sync lag + storage

Double-Entry Ledger — Internal Mechanics

TRANSFER ₹50,000 from ACC-1001 → ACC-2002

Rule: SUM(debits) = SUM(credits) per transaction_id

ledger_entries:
┌──────────────┬────────────┬──────────────┬───────────────┐
│ transaction  │ account_id │ debit_amount │ credit_amount │
├──────────────┼────────────┼──────────────┼───────────────┤
│ TXN-PMT-001  │ ACC-1001   │ 50000.00     │ 0             │
│ TXN-PMT-001  │ ACC-2002   │ 0            │ 50000.00      │
└──────────────┴────────────┴──────────────┴───────────────┘

accounts.balance updated atomically WITH ledger insert (same @Transactional)
OR balance derived from ledger (stricter audit, slower read)

ARCHITECT CHOICE — Balance Storage:

Option A: balance column + ledger (common)
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 50000 WHERE account_id = 'ACC-1001' AND version = :v
  INSERT ledger_entries ...
  Optimistic lock @Version on accounts (Lesson 17)

Option B: ledger-only, balance = SUM(credits) - SUM(debits)
  Always correct from audit trail
  Heavy read — materialized balance or cache

Banking production: Option A with nightly reconciliation job comparing balance vs ledger SUM

Slowly Changing Dimension (SCD) — Type 2

Customer address changes for KYC — need HISTORY, not overwrite:

customer_addresses:
┌────────────┬─────────────┬─────────────┬────────────┬────────────┐
│ address_id │ customer_id │ address_line│ valid_from │ valid_to   │
├────────────┼─────────────┼─────────────┼────────────┼────────────┤
│ 1          │ CUST-001    │ Old Street  │ 2020-01-01 │ 2024-06-01 │
│ 2          │ CUST-001    │ New Tower   │ 2024-06-01 │ NULL       │
└────────────┴─────────────┴─────────────┴────────────┴────────────┘

Query "address at time of payment":
  JOIN customer_addresses WHERE valid_from <= payment.created_at
    AND (valid_to IS NULL OR valid_to > payment.created_at)

Multi-Tenant Schema Strategies

STRATEGY 1: Shared table + tenant_id column
  payments(tenant_id, payment_id, ...)
  UNIQUE(tenant_id, idempotency_key)
  Row-level security (PostgreSQL RLS) or app filter ALWAYS

STRATEGY 2: Schema per tenant
  tenant_abc.payments, tenant_xyz.payments
  Moderate isolation, migration × N tenants

STRATEGY 3: Database per tenant
  Maximum isolation — large corporate clients
  Ops overhead highest

Architect: start Strategy 1 + RLS for SaaS banking platform;
           Strategy 3 for regulated dedicated instances

Part 4: Memory View

Schema Impact on Runtime Memory

NORMALIZED OLTP:
  JPA fetch payment → lazy account → 1 + N queries if not careful (Lesson 17)
  Small row width → more rows per buffer page → cache efficient

DENORMALIZED READ MODEL:
  Wide rows (20 columns names included) → fewer joins at read time
  More bytes per row over network → larger JVM heap if fully loaded
  Architect: pagination + projection, don't load 100K wide rows

LEDGER APPEND-ONLY:
  Table grows forever → partition by posted_at (monthly)
  Old partitions → cold storage / archive tablespace
  Hot partition fits in buffer pool

Entity-Table Mapping Memory (JPA)

@Entity Payment → payments table
  @OneToMany List<LedgerEntry> → separate table, lazy = proxy collection
  EAGER load payment + 500 ledger lines → heap spike

Design: don't map full ledger history on Payment entity for API responses
        use DTO query or separate read repository

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Design Decisions and Performance

Design choice Read perf Write perf Consistency
3NF OLTP Join cost Fast inserts Strong
Denormalized wide table Fast read Slow updates (many copies) Sync lag
Surrogate BIGINT PK Smaller indexes Fast joins Neutral
Natural business key PK Readable Larger VARCHAR indexes Domain visible
Ledger append-only History queries need partition prune Insert-only fast Audit strong
balance column O(1) read balance Update contention hot account Needs reconciliation

Hot Account Contention

Corporate settlement account ACC-SETTLEMENT-001:
  5000 credits/hour → row-level lock on balance UPDATE

Mitigations (design level):
  - Sharded sub-accounts (hash bucket) merge in batch
  - Queue writes, single-thread updater per account
  - Event sourcing + async balance projection
Architect documents in ADR when single account becomes bottleneck

Index Design from Model (Lesson 21 Link)

From access patterns derived from ER model:

payments:
  PK (payment_id)
  UNIQUE (idempotency_key)
  INDEX (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC)  -- multi-tenant queue
  INDEX (debtor_acct, created_at DESC)        -- account statement

ledger_entries:
  INDEX (transaction_id)
  INDEX (account_id, posted_at DESC)
  PARTITION BY RANGE (posted_at)             -- monthly

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Full ER — Corporate Payments (Logical DDL)

-- CUSTOMERS & KYC
CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id     VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_type   VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,  -- INDIVIDUAL, CORPORATE
    legal_name      VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    tax_id_hash     VARCHAR(64),             -- never store plain tax id
    kyc_status      VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING',
    tenant_id       VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    created_at      TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    updated_at      TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE customer_addresses (
    address_id      BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
    address_type    VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,  -- REGISTERED, CORRESPONDENCE
    line1           VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    city            VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    country_code    CHAR(2) NOT NULL,
    valid_from      TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    valid_to        TIMESTAMP,              -- NULL = current (SCD Type 2)
    CONSTRAINT uq_current_address UNIQUE (customer_id, address_type, valid_to)
);

-- ACCOUNTS
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id      VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
    tenant_id       VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    account_type    VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    currency        CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
    balance         NUMERIC(19,4) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    available_balance NUMERIC(19,4) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    status          VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE',
    branch_code     VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,
    version         BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    created_at      TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    CONSTRAINT chk_balance CHECK (balance >= 0)
);

-- PAYMENTS (aggregate root in payment-svc)
CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id      VARCHAR(36) PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id       VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    debtor_acct     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(account_id),
    creditor_acct   VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    creditor_name   VARCHAR(200),            -- external beneficiary
    creditor_ifsc   VARCHAR(11),
    amount          NUMERIC(19,4) NOT NULL,
    currency        CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
    status          VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    payment_type    VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    idempotency_key VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    initiated_by    VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    approved_by     VARCHAR(50),
    created_at      TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    updated_at      TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    version         BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    CONSTRAINT uq_tenant_idempotency UNIQUE (tenant_id, idempotency_key),
    CONSTRAINT chk_amount_positive CHECK (amount > 0)
);

-- MAKER-CHECKER (1:1 with payment when required)
CREATE TABLE payment_approvals (
    payment_id      VARCHAR(36) PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES payments(payment_id),
    maker_id        VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    checker_id      VARCHAR(50),
    maker_at        TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    checker_at      TIMESTAMP,
    approval_status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,  -- PENDING, APPROVED, REJECTED
    CONSTRAINT chk_checker_not_maker CHECK (checker_id IS NULL OR checker_id <> maker_id)
);

-- LEDGER (append-only, immutable)
CREATE TABLE ledger_entries (
    entry_id        BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    transaction_id  VARCHAR(36) NOT NULL,
    tenant_id       VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    account_id      VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(account_id),
    debit_amount    NUMERIC(19,4) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    credit_amount   NUMERIC(19,4) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    entry_type      VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    reference_id    VARCHAR(36),           -- payment_id
    posted_at       TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    CONSTRAINT chk_debit_credit CHECK (
        (debit_amount > 0 AND credit_amount = 0) OR
        (credit_amount > 0 AND debit_amount = 0)
    )
);

CREATE INDEX idx_ledger_account_posted ON ledger_entries (account_id, posted_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_ledger_transaction ON ledger_entries (transaction_id);

Example 2: JPA Entity Alignment (Lesson 17)

@Entity
@Table(name = "payments")
public class PaymentEntity {

    @Id
    private String paymentId;

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String tenantId;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    @JoinColumn(name = "debtor_acct", nullable = false)
    private AccountEntity debtorAccount;

    @Column(nullable = false, precision = 19, scale = 4)
    private BigDecimal amount;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    private PaymentStatus status;

    @Version
    private Long version;

    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true)
    private String idempotencyKey;

    // No @OneToMany to ledger — fetch via separate repo (avoid accidental N+1)
}

Example 3: Flyway Migration — Zero-Downtime Column Add

-- V004__add_payment_priority.sql
-- Phase 1: add nullable column (no lock on reads in PostgreSQL 11+)
ALTER TABLE payments ADD COLUMN priority VARCHAR(10);

-- Phase 2: backfill in batches (application job or SQL batch)
-- UPDATE payments SET priority = 'NORMAL' WHERE priority IS NULL AND payment_id > :cursor LIMIT 10000;

-- Phase 3: V005 — set NOT NULL after backfill complete
-- ALTER TABLE payments ALTER COLUMN priority SET NOT NULL;
-- ALTER TABLE payments ALTER COLUMN priority SET DEFAULT 'NORMAL';

EXPAND-C CONTRACT pattern:
  Expand: add nullable column, deploy app reading/writing both
  Migrate: backfill data
  Contract: remove old column in later release (if replacing)

Example 4: Audit Table (Immutable History)

CREATE TABLE payments_audit (
    audit_id        BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    payment_id      VARCHAR(36) NOT NULL,
    tenant_id       VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    old_status      VARCHAR(20),
    new_status      VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    changed_by      VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    changed_at      TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    correlation_id  VARCHAR(36)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_payments_audit_payment ON payments_audit (payment_id, changed_at DESC);

Example 5: Reconciliation View (Derived Consistency)

CREATE VIEW account_balance_reconciliation AS
SELECT a.account_id,
       a.balance AS stored_balance,
       COALESCE(SUM(le.credit_amount - le.debit_amount), 0) AS ledger_balance,
       a.balance - COALESCE(SUM(le.credit_amount - le.debit_amount), 0) AS drift
FROM accounts a
LEFT JOIN ledger_entries le ON le.account_id = a.account_id
GROUP BY a.account_id, a.balance
HAVING a.balance <> COALESCE(SUM(le.credit_amount - le.debit_amount), 0);
-- Nightly job alerts if drift <> 0

Example 6: Multi-Tenant Row-Level Security (PostgreSQL)

ALTER TABLE payments ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON payments
    USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.current_tenant'));

-- App sets on connection: SET app.current_tenant = 'TENANT-ABC';

Part 7: Production Usage

Database Design in Production

Microservice Table Ownership

account-svc owns:     customers, accounts, customer_addresses
payment-svc owns:     payments, payment_approvals, payments_audit
ledger-svc owns:      ledger_entries (OR co-located with account-svc in smaller banks)

FORBIDDEN: payment-svc FK to account-svc.accounts at DB level if separate databases
  → logical FK: validate account_id via account-svc API before insert
  → store debtor_acct as VARCHAR without DB-level FK

Migration Pipeline

Developer → Flyway script in repo → CI:
  1. Spin ephemeral PostgreSQL
  2. flyway migrate
  3. Integration tests
  4. PR review: architect checks backward compatibility

Production deploy:
  1. flyway migrate (DDL before app rollout for additive changes)
  2. Rolling app deploy (K8s — Lesson 34)
  3. Monitor locks: pg_locks / Oracle v$lock

Soft Delete Pattern

ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN deleted_at TIMESTAMP;

-- All queries:
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE deleted_at IS NULL AND tenant_id = :tenant;

-- Partial index excludes deleted rows:
CREATE INDEX idx_customers_active ON customers (tenant_id, customer_id)
    WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

Archive Strategy

payments > 7 years retention (regulatory):

Active: payments (last 24 months) — SSD, full indexes
Archive: payments_archive (partition or separate tablespace) — compressed
Query old: separate archive API, not mixed with hot OLTP path

Part 9: Architect Perspective

Design Review Checklist

Questions Architects Ask in DDL Review

1. Who is the single writer of this table?
2. What is the natural business key vs surrogate PK?
3. Where is idempotency enforced? (UNIQUE constraint)
4. How is multi-tenancy isolated? (tenant_id + RLS)
5. What is immutable vs mutable? (ledger immutable, payment status mutable with audit)
6. FK at DB level or logical only? (depends on MS boundary)
7. Migration backward compatible? (expand-contract)
8. Retention and archive plan?
9. PII columns identified and encrypted/masked?
10. Reconciliation job for balance vs ledger?

ADR — Ledger Separate from Payment

## ADR-202: Ledger entries in ledger-svc, not payment-svc DB

### Context
Payment completion must post accounting entries. Compliance requires immutable ledger.

### Decision
payment-svc writes payments; on COMPLETED publishes PaymentCompleted event;
ledger-svc consumes and inserts ledger_entries idempotently by payment_id.

### Consequences
Eventual consistency window (~seconds). Reconciliation job required.
Idempotent consumer: UNIQUE(reference_id, entry_type) on ledger.

Anti-Patterns to Reject

Anti-pattern Why reject
God table transactions with 80 nullable columns for every product
Polymorphic FK reference_type + reference_id — no DB integrity
Shared sequences across services Coupling, migration pain
JSON blob for core money fields Cannot constrain, index, or audit easily
Trigger-heavy logic Hidden, untestable — prefer app + audit

Modeling Decisions

Question Option A Option B When
Primary key Surrogate BIGINT Business natural key Surrogate for joins; natural key as UNIQUE
Customer address history SCD Type 2 table Overwrite + audit Regulatory history → SCD
Balance Column on account Compute from ledger Column + nightly reconcile
Cross-svc reference Logical FK (VARCHAR) DB FK Separate DBs → logical
Tenant isolation tenant_id + RLS DB per tenant Scale vs isolation
Approval data Separate 1:1 table Columns on payment Maker-checker → separate
Delete Soft delete Hard delete Banking → soft + audit

Normalization vs Denormalize

Signal Normalize Denormalize
Write-heavy OLTP Yes No
Read-heavy search dashboard No Yes (read model)
Data changes frequently Yes Stale copy risk
Cross-service report No CQRS projection
Compliance audit trail Separate immutable tables Never merge into mutable row

SCD Type Selection

Type Behavior Use
Type 1 Overwrite Non-critical corrections
Type 2 New row, valid_from/to KYC address history
Type 3 Current + previous column Simple "old vs new" only

Surrogate vs Natural Key

Stability Never changes Business rule change painful

Exposure Opaque Domain meaningful
Banking Internal ledger entry_id payment_id UUID client-facing

DB FK vs Logical FK

Database FK Logical FK
Integrity DB enforced App + API validation
Microservices Same DB only Cross-service default
Migrations Order dependency Independent deploy
Orphans Prevented Possible on bug — monitor

Single DB vs DB per Service

Monolith DB DB per Service
JOINs Easy Not at runtime
Consistency Local ACID Saga / events

Tool Use

  4. Zero-downtime migration adding FK to 80M row table?

Model Answer — Q13 (Microservice Split)

A: customers, accounts → account-svc DB. payments, payment_approvals, payments_audit → payment-svc DB. ledger_entries → ledger-svc DB. Remove cross-DB FKs; store debtor_acct as reference validated via account-svc API at initiation. Payment completion emits event; ledger-svc creates entries idempotently on payment_id. Saga table in payment-svc tracks orchestration. Reports use CQRS read model fed by CDC — no runtime JOIN across DBs. Trade-off: eventual consistency vs independent deploy and scale.

Model Answer — Q7 (Double-Entry)

A: Every monetary movement creates balanced entries: total debits = total credits per transaction_id. Transfer debits debtor account, credits creditor. CHECK constraint enforces each row is debit XOR credit. Ledger append-only — no UPDATE/DELETE in app. accounts.balance updated in same transaction as ledger insert for read performance. Nightly view compares stored balance to SUM(ledger) — alert on drift. Links to payment_id via reference_id for traceability.

# Mistake Consequence Fix
1 No tenant_id in shared DB Cross-tenant leak tenant_id + RLS every query
2 FLOAT for money Rounding errors NUMERIC(19,4)
3 Over-normalized read path 8-table join per search Read model
4 Under-normalized OLTP Update anomalies 3NF write model
5 FK across microservice DBs Deploy coupling Logical FK
6 ddl-auto=update in prod Schema drift Flyway + validate
7 Mutable ledger rows Audit failure Append-only
8 No idempotency UNIQUE Duplicate payments Business key constraint
9 EAGER JPA on collections N+1 / heap LAZY + DTO queries
10 Big-bang NOT NULL add Lock / deploy fail Expand-contract

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Workshop ER with business before coding
  2. 3NF for OLTP write models in each service
  3. Surrogate PK + UNIQUE business keys (idempotency_key)
  4. Append-only ledger with debit/credit CHECK
  5. Audit tables for status changes on regulated entities
  6. SCD Type 2 for KYC/address history
  7. Flyway versioned migrations — expand-contract for breaking changes
  8. Soft delete + partial indexes for active rows
  9. DB per service — logical FKs, events for cross-aggregate consistency
  10. Nightly reconciliation balance vs ledger — design from day one

Part 16: Revision Notes

Quick Revision — Database Design

ER: Entity, relationship, cardinality (1:N most common)
3NF: no repeating groups, no partial deps, no transitive deps

Double-entry: 2+ rows per txn, debits = credits, append-only
Balance: column (fast read) + ledger (audit) + reconcile job

SCD Type 2: valid_from, valid_to NULL = current row
Multi-tenant: tenant_id everywhere, UNIQUE(tenant_id, business_key)

MS: table ownership per service, logical FK cross-svc
Outbox + saga tables for eventual consistency

Flyway expand-contract: nullable add → backfill → NOT NULL
Soft delete: deleted_at IS NULL in all queries

JPA: LAZY associations, don't map huge collections on aggregate
NUMERIC for money, VARCHAR enums for status, @Version optimistic lock

Memory Mnemonic

"Model in 3NF, ledger never lies, migrate expand-contract, one DB per service"

Prerequisites: Lesson 21 (SQL, indexes) · Lesson 22 (ER modeling, ledger, microservices) · Lesson 18 (ACID, sagas) · Lesson 8 (memory, caching mindset)

Part 1: Concept

What Is NoSQL?

NoSQL ("Not Only SQL") describes non-relational data stores optimized for specific access patterns: document, key-value, wide-column, graph, and time-series. Architects choose NoSQL when scale, schema flexibility, latency, or data shape don't fit relational OLTP cleanly — not because SQL is "old."

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           POLYGLOT PERSISTENCE — CORPORATE PAYMENTS PLATFORM             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  Oracle / PostgreSQL     → payments, ledger, accounts (ACID, 3NF)        │
│  Redis                   → idempotency keys, rate limits, distributed lock│
│  Cassandra               → account statement history (billions of rows)  │
│  MongoDB                 → product config, payment metadata blobs      │
│  Elasticsearch           → payment search, fraud pattern queries       │
│  Kafka                   → event log (not DB — Lesson 31)                │
│                                                                          │
│  Rule: right store for right access pattern — not one database for all   │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

NoSQL Categories Master Table

Type Model Examples Banking Use Case
Key-Value O(1) get/put by key Redis, DynamoDB Idempotency cache, session, locks
Document JSON document by ID MongoDB, Couchbase Product rules, KYC document metadata
Wide-Column Partition key + clustering Cassandra, HBase Statement lines, audit at scale
Graph Nodes + edges Neo4j Fraud ring detection, relationship traversal
Time-Series Timestamp-indexed InfluxDB, TimescaleDB Metrics, FX rate history

SQL vs NoSQL — High-Level

Dimension Relational (Lesson 21–22) NoSQL
Schema Fixed, enforced Flexible (document) or write-time (wide-column)
Joins Native, optimized Denormalize or app-side join
Transactions Full ACID (local) Varies — Redis single-key; Cassandra lightweight
Scale-out Vertical + read replicas Horizontal partition native
Consistency Strong default Tunable — eventual common
Query Ad hoc SQL Must design for access pattern upfront

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why NoSQL Exists Alongside SQL

Relational pain at scale NoSQL response
5B statement rows — JOIN slow, partition awkward Cassandra partition by account_id
Payment metadata varies by product (50 optional fields) MongoDB flexible schema
Sub-ms idempotency check at 20K TPS Redis SET NX EX
Full-text search across payment references Elasticsearch
Graph traversal "who paid whom" for AML Neo4j

Why Architects Must Not Default to NoSQL

ANTI-PATTERN: "MongoDB for payments because it's faster"

Payment core (amount, status, ledger):
  → NEEDS ACID, constraints, reconciliation
  → STAYS relational (Oracle/PostgreSQL)

NoSQL around the core:
  → cache, search index, historical read scale, config blobs
  → NEVER source of truth for money without extreme justification

CAP and PACELC (Decision Framework)

CAP (during partition):
  C = Consistency (all nodes see same data)
  A = Availability (every request gets response)
  P = Partition tolerance (network splits happen — non-negotiable in distributed)

During partition: choose C or A (not both)

PACELC (Broader — use this in interviews):
  If Partition → choose A or C
  Else (normal operation) → choose Latency (L) or Consistency (C)

Examples:
  Redis (single primary): CP-ish during failover, low latency
  Cassandra: AP — eventual consistency, tunable per query (LOCAL_QUORUM)
  PostgreSQL: CP — strong consistency, sacrifice availability during failover
  DynamoDB: tunable — strong vs eventual read

Part 3: Internal Working

Redis — Key-Value Internals

REDIS ARCHITECTURE:

Client ──► Redis Server (single-threaded event loop per shard)
              │
              ├── Hash table (key → value)
              ├── Optional persistence: RDB snapshot / AOF log
              └── Cluster: 16384 hash slots across nodes

Key: idempotency:tenant-abc:key-xyz
Value: payment_id (or PROCESSING sentinel)
TTL: 86400 seconds (auto-expire)

Idempotency Pattern (Production Critical)

SET idempotency:TENANT-1:abc123 payment-uuid-456 NX EX 86400

NX = set only if Not eXists
  → first request: OK, proceed with payment
  → duplicate request: null, return existing payment_id

Why Redis + DB UNIQUE (Lesson 22):
  Redis: fast first-line dedup at API edge
  DB UNIQUE(tenant_id, idempotency_key): authoritative if Redis miss/eviction
  Both layers — architect designs redundancy

Distributed Lock (Redisson / SET NX)

Lock: SET lock:account:ACC-1001 request-id NX EX 30

Use: serialize updates to hot account (Lesson 22 contention)
Release: Lua script compare-and-del (only owner releases)

Warning: Redis lock ≠ full consensus — use for short critical sections
         money movement still needs DB transaction as source of truth

MongoDB — Document Store Internals

DOCUMENT in collection payment_metadata:

{
  "_id": "PMT-001",
  "tenantId": "TENANT-ABC",
  "paymentType": "NEFT",
  "regulatoryFields": {
    "purposeCode": "P001",
    "remittanceInfo": "Invoice 12345"
  },
  "attachments": [
    { "docType": "INVOICE", "s3Key": "..." }
  ],
  "customFields": { "costCenter": "CC-99" }  // varies by corporate client
}

Stored as BSON — binary JSON on disk
Index on { tenantId: 1, paymentType: 1 }
Shard key: tenantId (multi-tenant isolation)

WHY NOT put amount/status in Mongo for core payment:
  No cross-document ACID with account balance (until multi-doc transactions — limited)
  Constraints weaker than CHECK + FK
  Use Mongo for EXTENDED metadata linked by payment_id to Oracle row

Cassandra — Wide-Column Internals

DATA MODEL (NOT SQL thinking):

PRIMARY KEY = (partition_key, clustering_columns...)

account_statements:
  PRIMARY KEY ((account_id), statement_date DESC, line_id)

Partition key account_id → all statement lines for one account co-located on node
Clustering order → range scan within partition by date

Query: SELECT * FROM account_statements
       WHERE account_id = 'ACC-1001'
         AND statement_date >= '2026-01-01'
       LIMIT 100;

✓ Supported — designed access pattern

Query: SELECT * WHERE statement_date = '2026-06-01'  (no partition key)
✗ Full cluster scan — FORBIDDEN in production

WRITE PATH:
  Client → coordinator node → replicate to RF nodes (e.g., 3)
  Tunable consistency: QUORUM = majority ack before return

STORAGE:
  SSTable append-only on disk — compaction merges
  TTL on rows: automatic purge after 7 years (regulatory retention)

Denormalization in Cassandra (By Design)

One query = one table — duplicate data across tables if needed:

By account:  statements_by_account (account_id, date, ...)
By payment:  statements_by_payment (payment_id, date, ...)

Same event written to both tables — event-driven dual write or Kafka consumer
Trade-off: storage for query flexibility (Lesson 22 denormalization echo)

DynamoDB (AWS — Cloud Lesson 36 Preview)

Partition key: payment_id OR tenant_id#account_id
Sort key: created_at
GSI: alternate access patterns (status-index)

On-demand vs provisioned RCU/WCU
DynamoDB Transactions: up to 25 items — not full relational replacement
Banking: idempotency table, session store, config — not core ledger

Part 4: Memory View

NoSQL Memory and Storage

REDIS:
  In-memory primary — sub-ms reads
  maxmemory policy: allkeys-lru when full → idempotency keys evicted!
  Architect: monitor memory; TTL on all cache keys; DB UNIQUE fallback

MONGODB:
  WiredTiger cache (RAM) — hot documents
  Working set must fit RAM for predictable latency
  Large documents (1MB attachments metadata) → heap pressure if loaded bulk

CASSANDRA:
  JVM heap + off-heap memtable + OS page cache
  Not "all data in RAM" — sequential disk reads on SSTable
  Partition size matters: >100MB partition = slow compaction/repair
  Design: avoid unbounded partition growth (bucket by month in clustering key)

APPLICATION (JVM):
  Redis client connection pool — small
  MongoDB driver — document deserialized to BSON/POJO — larger than slim SQL row
  Cassandra driver — paging required for large result sets (fetch in pages)

Partition Size Rule (Cassandra)

BAD partition key: status = 'COMPLETED'  → all rows one partition → hotspot

GOOD: account_id → millions of partitions spread across cluster
      optional: account_id + year in clustering to bound partition size

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Performance Characteristics

Store Read Latency Write Throughput Best When
Redis <1 ms Very high (single shard) Cache, locks, rate limit
PostgreSQL 1–10 ms indexed Moderate ACID OLTP
MongoDB 1–5 ms indexed High Flexible docs, moderate scale
Cassandra 5–20 ms Write-optimized Append-heavy, time-range by PK
Elasticsearch 10–100 ms search Index-heavy Full-text, aggregations

Redis vs DB for Idempotency

20K TPS payment API:

PostgreSQL UNIQUE check only: ~2–5 ms per insert attempt — OK with connection pool
Redis SET NX first: ~0.5 ms — rejects duplicates before DB work
Combined: Redis filter → DB authoritative insert → optimal

Cost of Redis failure:
  Fail-open: duplicates hit DB — UNIQUE catches (safe)
  Fail-closed: reject all — bad UX — prefer fail-open with DB constraint

Cassandra Read Repair / Consistency

LOCAL_ONE:  fast, stale possible — OK for statement UI "approximate recent"
LOCAL_QUORUM: majority — **default for financial reads** after write QUORUM
SERIAL: lightweight transactions — compare-and-set — limited use, latency cost

Architect SLA: statement history eventual few seconds OK; balance NOT on Cassandra

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Redis Idempotency (Spring Boot)

@Service
public class IdempotencyService {

    private final StringRedisTemplate redis;

    public Optional<String> claimKey(String tenantId, String idempotencyKey, String paymentId) {
        String key = "idempotency:" + tenantId + ":" + idempotencyKey;
        Boolean claimed = redis.opsForValue()
            .setIfAbsent(key, paymentId, Duration.ofHours(24));
        if (Boolean.TRUE.equals(claimed)) {
            return Optional.empty(); // new — proceed
        }
        String existing = redis.opsForValue().get(key);
        return Optional.of(existing); // duplicate — return existing payment_id
    }
}

// Controller flow
Optional<String> existing = idempotencyService.claimKey(tenant, key, newPaymentId);
if (existing.isPresent()) {
    return paymentService.getById(existing.get()); // 200 idempotent replay
}
return paymentService.create(...); // DB UNIQUE as second line of defense

Example 2: Redis Rate Limiting (Gateway)

public boolean allowRequest(String tenantId, String clientId) {
    String key = "ratelimit:" + tenantId + ":" + clientId + ":" + Instant.now().getEpochSecond() / 60;
    Long count = redis.opsForValue().increment(key);
    if (count != null && count == 1) {
        redis.expire(key, Duration.ofMinutes(2));
    }
    return count != null && count <= 100; // 100 req/min
}

Example 3: MongoDB — Payment Metadata (Spring Data)

@Document(collection = "payment_metadata")
public class PaymentMetadataDoc {

    @Id
    private String paymentId;
    private String tenantId;
    private String paymentType;
    private Map<String, Object> regulatoryFields;
    private List<AttachmentRef> attachments;
    private Map<String, Object> customFields;
    private Instant createdAt;
}

public interface PaymentMetadataRepository extends MongoRepository<PaymentMetadataDoc, String> {
    List<PaymentMetadataDoc> findByTenantIdAndPaymentType(String tenantId, String type);
}

Write flow:
  1. INSERT payment core row in PostgreSQL (amount, status) — @Transactional
  2. INSERT metadata doc in Mongo (same payment_id) — best-effort or outbox sync
  Read API: join in app — PG for amount, Mongo for extended fields

Example 4: Cassandra — Statement Lines (Java Driver)

@Table(keyspace = "banking", name = "statements_by_account")
public class StatementLine {

    @PartitionKey
    private String accountId;

    @ClusteringColumn
    private LocalDate statementDate;

    @ClusteringColumn(1)
    private UUID lineId;

    private String paymentId;
    private BigDecimal amount;
    private String description;
}

// Repository query — MUST include partition key
public Flux<StatementLine> findRecent(String accountId, LocalDate from, int limit) {
    return template.select(
        QueryBuilder.selectFrom("banking", "statements_by_account")
            .all()
            .whereColumn("account_id").isEqualTo(literal(accountId))
            .whereColumn("statement_date").isGreaterThanOrEqualTo(literal(from))
            .limit(limit)
            .build(),
        StatementLine.class
    );
}

CREATE TABLE banking.statements_by_account (
    account_id      text,
    statement_date  date,
    line_id         uuid,
    payment_id      text,
    amount          decimal,
    description     text,
    PRIMARY KEY ((account_id), statement_date, line_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (statement_date DESC);

Example 5: Dual-Write via Kafka (Cassandra Tables)

PaymentCompleted event:
  Consumer 1 → insert statements_by_account
  Consumer 2 → insert statements_by_payment

Idempotent consumer: PRIMARY KEY prevents duplicate lines
Eventual consistency: statement lags payment completion by seconds

PUT /payments/_doc/PMT-001
{

Check Detail

Check Detail

Check Detail

Part 8: Microservice Usage

NoSQL per Microservice

payment-svc:
  PostgreSQL — payments (SoT)
  Redis — idempotency, rate limit
  MongoDB — extended metadata (optional)

account-svc:
  Oracle — accounts, balance
  Redis — cache account snapshot (short TTL, invalidate on update)

statement-svc:
  Cassandra — historical lines (read-only scale)
  Kafka consumer — PaymentCompleted → write Cassandra

search-svc:
  Elasticsearch — denormalized index
  No writes from user — ingest only

Architect: each store owned by one service — no shared Redis DB index across teams without namespace prefix

Cache Invalidation (Account Balance)

account-svc updates balance in Oracle
  → publish AccountBalanceUpdated
  → payment-svc invalidates Redis cache key account:TENANT:ACC-1001

Stale cache risk: TTL 60s max for balance cache if used
Better: don't cache balance for debit decisions — read Oracle with short tx

Saga and NoSQL

Saga state (Lesson 29): PostgreSQL in orchestrator — needs ACID updates
Cassandra for saga? No — low volume, needs conditional updates — relational fits

Outbox in PostgreSQL → Kafka → Cassandra/ES/Mongo consumers
Pattern: relational write path, NoSQL read projections

ADR — Cassandra for Statements

## ADR-203: Statement history in Cassandra, not Oracle

### Context
500M+ statement lines; account statement API p95 2s on Oracle range scan.

### Decision
Cassandra table statements_by_account; feed from PaymentCompleted Kafka;
7-year TTL; LOCAL_QUORUM.

### Consequences
Eventual lag ~2s acceptable for UI. Balance remains Oracle only.
Dual maintenance of statement model. Team Cassandra training required.

When NOT to Use NoSQL (Architect Veto List)

✗ Core payment amount/status without relational constraints
✗ Cross-aggregate ACID transfer (debit + credit) in Mongo/Cassandra alone
✗ Ad hoc reporting without designed access pattern on Cassandra
✗ Redis as only idempotency store without DB UNIQUE
✗ Elasticsearch as system of record

Model Answer — Q13 (Polyglot Persistence)

A: PostgreSQL is SoT for payments, approvals, outbox — ACID, UNIQUE idempotency, joins to accounts in account-svc via API not DB. Oracle in account-svc for balance and ledger entries. Redis for idempotency fast path, rate limits, short-lived locks — always with DB constraint fallback. Cassandra for statement line history partitioned by account_id — fed by Kafka from PaymentCompleted, TTL 7 years, LOCAL_QUORUM. MongoDB for optional corporate custom fields and attachment metadata keyed by payment_id. Elasticsearch for ops search UI — eventually consistent index. Money never finalized in NoSQL alone; reconciliation jobs compare PG/Oracle totals to projections.

Model Answer — Q16 (Dual-Write vs Kafka)

A: Avoid dual-write (app writes PG + Cassandra in same request) — partial failure leaves inconsistency. Preferred: transactional outbox in PostgreSQL → Kafka → idempotent consumer writes Cassandra. Payment completion is atomic in PG; statement appears eventually. Consumer tracks offset; retry on failure; PRIMARY KEY idempotency in Cassandra. Architect accepts seconds lag; compensates with UI "processing" state or read-your-writes from PG for recent items, Cassandra for historical pages.

# Mistake Consequence Fix
1 MongoDB as payment SoT No strong money guarantees PostgreSQL core

4 No TTL on Redis keys OOM eviction EX on every SET
5 Cache balance for debit Overdraft Read SoT for decisions
6 ALLOW FILTERING Cluster meltdown Ban in review

10 Ignore Redis failover Lock/idempotency race Redlock limits + DB fallback

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Relational SoT for money, ledger, payment status
  2. Redis for speed layers — always with authoritative DB constraint
  3. Design Cassandra schema from queries — partition key first workshop
  4. Outbox → Kafka → NoSQL projections — not dual-write
  5. TTL on Redis and Cassandra for retention compliance
  6. LOCAL_QUORUM default for Cassandra financial reads
  7. MongoDB for optional metadata — link by payment_id
  8. Elasticsearch for search only — rebuild from event stream
  9. Monitor hot keys — Redis and Cassandra partitions
  10. Document in ADR which store is SoT for each aggregate

Part 16: Revision Notes

Quick Revision — NoSQL

NoSQL types: KV (Redis), Document (Mongo), Wide-column (Cassandra), Graph (Neo4j)

Money SoT = PostgreSQL/Oracle ALWAYS
Redis: SET NX EX idempotency, INCR rate limit, short locks — TTL mandatory
Fallback: DB UNIQUE when Redis miss

Cassandra: PRIMARY KEY (partition, clustering)
  Query MUST include partition key
  One table per query pattern — denormalize
  LOCAL_QUORUM | TTL retention | no ALLOW FILTERING

MongoDB: flexible metadata linked by payment_id — not core amount

CAP: partition → C or A; PACELC: else latency vs consistency
Outbox → Kafka → Cassandra/ES/Mongo (not dual-write)

Cache-aside + event invalidation; don't cache balance for debit decisions
Elasticsearch = search projection only

Memory Mnemonic

"SQL owns money; Redis guards the door; Cassandra remembers history; Mongo holds the extras"
