Prerequisites: Lesson 18 (ACID, propagation, saga vs XA) · Lesson 27 (outbox, async, idempotency) · Lesson 22 (saga tables, ledger) · Lesson 25 (DB per service) · Lesson 26 (Resilience4j, timeouts)

Part 1: Concept

What Is a Distributed Transaction Problem?

In microservices, a business transaction spans multiple services and databases. You cannot use one local @Transactional across payment-svc PostgreSQL and account-svc Oracle (Lesson 18). Distributed transactions require patterns that trade immediate ACID for eventual consistency with defined recovery.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         MONOLITH ACID vs MICROSERVICE SAGA — BANK TRANSFER               │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  MONOLITH (single DB):                                                   │
│    BEGIN → debit account → credit account → insert payment → COMMIT     │
│    All or nothing — one transaction boundary                             │
│                                                                          │
│  MICROSERVICES (saga):                                                   │
│    Step 1: payment-svc create PENDING                                    │
│    Step 2: account-svc debit (hold)                                      │
│    Step 3: ledger-svc post entries                                       │
│    Step 4: payment-svc mark COMPLETED                                    │
│    Failure at Step 3 → compensate: release hold, mark FAILED             │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Pattern Catalog

Pattern Idea Banking Fit
2PC / XA Coordinator commits all RM Avoid — fragile, slow, cloud-hostile
Saga (orchestration) Central coordinator + steps Complex payments, transfers
Saga (choreography) Services react to events Notifications, simple flows
TCC Try → Confirm / Cancel High-value, reserve funds explicitly
Outbox + events Reliable step triggering Every saga step handoff
Idempotency Same request → same outcome Mandatory every step

Saga Step Types

Type Action on failure Example
Forward Run compensate Debit account
Compensate Best-effort undo Release hold / reverse debit
Retryable Retry with backoff Call fraud-svc
Pivot Cannot compensate — manual SWIFT sent — ops intervention

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why XA/2PC Fails in Cloud Microservices (Lesson 18 Echo)

XA / 2PC problem Impact on banking cloud
Blocking locks Hold account row across network — minutes under failure
Coordinator SPOF Transaction manager crash → in-doubt transactions
Latency Prepare/commit phases add RTT × services
Vendor lock-in Oracle XA + PostgreSQL + Kafka — impractical
Elastic scaling Connections held through 2PC — pool exhaustion (Lesson 24)
Partial cloud support Managed services don't support XA 
ARCHITECT DECISION (industry standard):
  NO XA across microservices
  YES local ACID per service + saga + outbox + reconciliation
  Exception: single vendor stack monolith DB — still local ACID only

Why Sagas Exist

Business still requires:
  - Money not lost on partial failure
  - Auditable state transitions
  - Recovery after pod crash mid-saga
  - Idempotent retries from client and broker

Saga = explicit state machine + compensations + idempotent steps
Not magic — operations accepts eventual consistency window

Part 3: Internal Working

Saga Orchestration Internals

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    payment-svc (ORCHESTRATOR)                 │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ SagaInstance: saga_id, payment_id, state, current_step │  │
│  │ SagaStepLog:  step, status, timestamp, error           │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                          │                                    │
│    Step 1: CREATE_PAYMENT (local TX) ──► payments DB          │
│    Step 2: HTTP debit/hold ────────────► account-svc          │
│    Step 3: publish PaymentDebited ─────► outbox → Kafka       │
│    Step 4: (async) ledger consumes ────► ledger-svc           │
│    Step 5: COMPLETE (local TX) ────────► payments DB          │
│                          │                                    │
│    On failure: COMPENSATE release hold, mark FAILED           │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Orchestration vs Choreography

ORCHESTRATION:
  payment-svc knows full flow — calls account, publishes events, updates saga state
  Pros: visibility, debug, centralized failure handling
  Cons: orchestrator coupling, can become god service if not bounded

CHOREOGRAPHY:
  payment-svc emits PaymentInitiated
  account-svc listens → debits → emits AccountDebited
  ledger-svc listens → posts
  Pros: loose coupling
  Cons: hard to trace, implicit flow, compensate chains unclear

BANKING: orchestration for money movement; choreography for notify/search

State Machine — Transfer Saga

                    ┌─────────────┐
                    │  STARTED    │
                    └──────┬──────┘
                           │ create payment PENDING
                           ▼
                    ┌─────────────┐
         fail ◄────│  VALIDATING │────► fail → FAILED
                    └──────┬──────┘
                           │ account validated + fraud OK
                           ▼
                    ┌─────────────┐
                    │  DEBITING   │──── HTTP hold/debit account-svc
                    └──────┬──────┘
              fail │        │ success
                   ▼        ▼
            ┌──────────┐  ┌─────────────┐
            │ FAILED   │  │  DEBITED    │
            └──────────┘  └──────┬──────┘
                   ▲             │ ledger post (async)
                   │      fail   ▼
                   │      ┌─────────────┐
                   └──────│ COMPENSATING│ release hold
                          └──────┬──────┘
                                 │ success
                                 ▼
                          ┌─────────────┐
                          │  COMPLETED  │
                          └─────────────┘

TCC (Try-Confirm-Cancel)

TRY:     account-svc reserve 50000 (available → reserved) — no final debit
CONFIRM: account-svc confirm reservation → actual debit + ledger
CANCEL:  account-svc release reservation

Each phase idempotent with business key payment_id + phase name

Compare to simple debit:
  TCC: two-phase business semantics — clearer compensate (Cancel)
  Use: high-value corporate, FX trades, limited liquidity accounts

Compensation Semantics

COMPENSATING TRANSACTION ≠ ROLLBACK

Database ROLLBACK: erase history (within one DB)
Compensation: new forward business action — "release hold", "reverse payment"

Properties:
  - Semantic undo — not always exact time travel
  - Must be idempotent — compensate twice safe
  - May fail — retry + alert + manual ops (pivot steps)

Example:
  Forward:  POST /accounts/{id}/holds  { amount, paymentId }
  Compensate: DELETE /accounts/{id}/holds/{paymentId}
              OR POST /accounts/{id}/holds/{paymentId}/release

Exactly-Once Illusion

True exactly-once across distributed system: impossible

PRACTICAL:
  At-least-once delivery (Kafka) + idempotent handlers (UNIQUE business key)
  = effectively-once semantics

Every saga step records:
  saga_id + step_name + idempotency_key UNIQUE
  Second attempt → return previous result, don't re-debit

Part 4: Memory View

Saga Runtime State

ORCHESTRATOR DB (payment-svc):
  saga_instances — one row per transfer (~500 bytes)
  saga_step_log — append steps (~200 bytes × steps)
  payments — business aggregate

CRASH RECOVERY:
  Pod dies after Step 2 success, before Step 3
  On restart: saga poller finds IN_PROGRESS sagas older than timeout
  → resume from last COMPLETED step (idempotent Step 3)
  OR → trigger compensate if unrecoverable

MEMORY:
  In-flight sagas in heap during request — minimal
  Saga poller batch — limit 100 per tick — avoid loading 50K sagas
  account-svc hold rows — DB state, not orchestrator heap

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Saga Performance and Trade-offs

Approach Latency Throughput Consistency window
Local ACID monolith Lowest Limited vertical Zero
Sync saga (3 HTTP steps) +80–200ms Coupled to slowest Seconds
Async ledger step Lower user latency Higher Ledger lag 1–5s
XA 2PC High + locks Poor Strong — not worth it

Sync vs Async Saga Steps

USER-FACING PATH (minimize steps):
  Sync: validate + hold/debit + mark COMPLETED (payment record)
  Async: ledger post, notification

Why:
  User needs confirmation payment accepted — local payment row COMPLETED
  Ledger eventual — reconciliation catches drift (Lesson 22 view)

Compensation Cost

Failure rate 2% at debit step:
  2% × compensate HTTP call — acceptable
  Must not compensate already-SWIFT-sent payment — state guard prevents

Pivot rate target: < 0.01% — manual ops queue

Saga Table Growth

saga_instances retain 90 days for ops — archive older
Index (status, updated_at) for poller: WHERE status IN ('IN_PROGRESS') AND updated_at < now()-interval '5 min'

Example 1: Saga Instance Schema (Lesson 22 Extended)

    saga_id         VARCHAR(36) PRIMARY KEY,
    payment_id      VARCHAR(36) NOT NULL UNIQUE,

CREATE TABLE saga_step_log (
    log_id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    saga_id         VARCHAR(36) NOT NULL REFERENCES saga_instances(saga_id),
    step_name       VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    status          VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,  -- STARTED, SUCCESS, FAILED, COMPENSATED
    request_payload JSONB,
    response_payload JSONB,

);

Example 2: Orchestrator Service

@Service
public class TransferSagaOrchestrator {

    private final SagaRepository sagaRepository;
    private final PaymentRepository paymentRepository;
    private final AccountClient accountClient;
    private final OutboxPublisher outbox;

    @Transactional
    public PaymentResponse startTransfer(TransferCommand cmd, String idempotencyKey) {

        Optional<SagaInstance> existing = sagaRepository.findByPaymentIdempotency(idempotencyKey);
        if (existing.isPresent()) {
            return resumeOrReturn(existing.get());
        }

        PaymentEntity payment = paymentRepository.save(PaymentEntity.pending(cmd, idempotencyKey));
        SagaInstance saga = sagaRepository.save(SagaInstance.started(payment.getPaymentId()));

        return executeNext(saga, payment, cmd);
    }

    private PaymentResponse executeNext(SagaInstance saga, PaymentEntity payment, TransferCommand cmd) {
        return switch (saga.getState()) {
            case STARTED -> stepValidateAndDebit(saga, payment, cmd);
            case DEBITED -> stepComplete(saga, payment);
            default -> PaymentResponse.from(payment);
        };
    }

    private PaymentResponse stepValidateAndDebit(SagaInstance saga, PaymentEntity payment, TransferCommand cmd) {
        saga.logStep("DEBIT_ACCOUNT", STARTED);
        try {
            HoldResponse hold = accountClient.placeHold(
                cmd.debtorAccountId(), cmd.amount(), payment.getPaymentId());

            saga.transitionTo(DEBITED, "DEBIT_ACCOUNT");
            saga.logStep("DEBIT_ACCOUNT", SUCCESS);

            outbox.publish(new PaymentDebitedEvent(payment.getPaymentId(), hold.holdId()));

            return stepComplete(saga, payment);

        } catch (DownstreamException ex) {
            saga.transitionTo(FAILED, "DEBIT_ACCOUNT");
            payment.markFailed(ex.getMessage());
            saga.logStep("DEBIT_ACCOUNT", FAILED);
            return PaymentResponse.failed(payment);
        }
    }

    @Transactional
    protected PaymentResponse stepComplete(SagaInstance saga, PaymentEntity payment) {
        payment.markCompleted();
        saga.transitionTo(COMPLETED, "COMPLETE");
        outbox.publish(new PaymentCompletedEvent(payment));
        return PaymentResponse.from(payment);
    }
}

Example 3: Compensation Handler

@Service
public class SagaCompensationService {

    private final AccountClient accountClient;
    private final SagaRepository sagaRepository;

    @Transactional
    public void compensate(SagaInstance saga) {
        if (saga.getState() == SagaState.COMPLETED || saga.getState() == SagaState.PIVOT) {
            return; // cannot auto-compensate
        }
        if (saga.getState() == SagaState.DEBITED) {
            accountClient.releaseHold(saga.getPaymentId()); // idempotent
            saga.transitionTo(COMPENSATED, "RELEASE_HOLD");
        }
        saga.transitionTo(FAILED, "COMPENSATE");
    }
}

Example 4: Idempotent Account Hold (account-svc)

@PostMapping("/api/v1/accounts/{accountId}/holds")
@Transactional
public HoldResponse placeHold(
        @PathVariable String accountId,
        @RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String idempotencyKey,
        @RequestBody PlaceHoldRequest request) {

    return holdRepository.findByIdempotencyKey(idempotencyKey)
        .map(h -> new HoldResponse(h.getHoldId(), h.getStatus()))
        .orElseGet(() -> createHold(accountId, request, idempotencyKey));
}

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_holds_payment ON account_holds (payment_id);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_holds_idempotency ON account_holds (idempotency_key);

Example 5: Saga Recovery Poller

@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 30_000)
public void recoverStuckSagas() {
    List<SagaInstance> stuck = sagaRepository.findInProgressOlderThan(Duration.ofMinutes(5));
    for (SagaInstance saga : stuck) {
        try {
            orchestrator.resume(saga);
        } catch (UnrecoverableException ex) {
            compensationService.compensate(saga);
            alertOps(saga, ex);
        }
    }
}

Part 7: Production Usage

Sagas in Production Banking

Maker-Checker as Extended Saga

Step 1: MAKER creates payment PENDING (local)
Step 2: wait human APPROVER (hours/days — long-running saga)
Step 3: on approve → debit saga continues
Step 4: COMPLETED

Saga state persisted — survives restarts
Timeout: PENDING > 7 days → auto-cancel compensate none needed

Reconciliation (Mandatory)

-- Nightly job
SELECT p.payment_id, p.status, l.ledger_count
FROM payments p
LEFT JOIN ledger_projection l ON p.payment_id = l.reference_id
WHERE p.status = 'COMPLETED' AND l.ledger_count IS NULL;
-- Alert → ops replay event or manual pivot

Production Checklist

Check Why
Idempotency every step Safe retry
Saga state persisted Crash recovery
Compensate idempotent Double release safe
Outbox for events No lost PaymentDebited
DLT on ledger consumer Alert
Pivot playbook SWIFT sent — no auto compensate
Metrics: saga duration, fail rate SLO
No XA Architect gate review

Observability

Metrics:
  saga.started, saga.completed, saga.failed, saga.compensated
  saga.step.duration{step=DEBIT_ACCOUNT}
  saga.in_progress.gauge

Trace:
  span saga.transfer linked to account-svc hold span

Part 8: Microservice Usage

Saga Across Payment Platform

Service Responsibilities

Service Saga role Local TX
payment-svc Orchestrator, payment state Yes
account-svc Hold/debit/release Yes
ledger-svc Async participant Yes
fraud-svc Sync gate (pre-saga or step 0) Yes
notification-svc Post-completion — no compensate Best effort

Event Handoff (Lesson 27)

payment-svc COMPLETED + outbox PaymentCompleted
  ledger-svc: idempotent post — failure → retry → DLT → reconciliation
  notification-svc: failure OK — email retry — no compensation of payment

Long-Running Saga Storage

For approval waits — don't hold HTTP connection
Saga state PENDING_APPROVAL in DB
Approver action POST /payments/{id}/approve → resumes saga thread/async job
Pattern: process manager (orchestrated saga)

Anti-Pattern: Distributed Monolith Saga

Orchestrator calls 8 sync services sequentially in one HTTP request
  → same as Lesson 25 anti-pattern with extra saga table

Fix: collapse boundaries or async steps with clear SLAs

Part 9: Architect Perspective

Saga Design Decisions

When Orchestration vs Choreography

Flow Pattern
Transfer with compensate Orchestration
Payment completed → 5 notifications Choreography
NEFT batch file processing Orchestration (batch job)
Audit event fan-out Choreography

ADR — No XA, Orchestrated Transfer Saga

## ADR-601: Transfer saga orchestrated in payment-svc; no XA

### Decision
Local ACID per service. payment-svc saga state machine.
account hold via sync REST idempotent API.
Ledger async via outbox PaymentCompleted.

### Consequences
Ledger visible up to 5s later — UI messaging + reconciliation.
Saga poller required. Ops runbook for PIVOT cases.

Pivot vs Compensate Decision

COMPENSATE: hold placed, payment not sent to external network
PIVOT: funds already sent via SWIFT — forward-only correction (refund saga)

Architect marks steps IRREVERSIBLE in saga definition — blocks auto-compensate

TCC vs Hold/Release

Simple Hold/Release TCC
Complexity Lower Higher
Semantics Reserve then capture Explicit Try/Confirm/Cancel
Use Retail internal transfer FX, treasury

Step Sync in user request?

Model Answer — Q13 (Transfer Saga Design)

A: payment-svc orchestrates. Step 0 sync fraud (fail fast). Step 1 local TX: create payment PENDING, saga STARTED. Step 2 sync idempotent hold on account-svc (Idempotency-Key: paymentId). Step 3 local TX: mark DEBITED, outbox PaymentDebited. Step 4 local TX: mark COMPLETED, outbox PaymentCompleted. Async: ledger-svc consumes idempotent post; notification best-effort. Failure: before hold → FAILED no compensate. Hold OK but complete fail → release hold compensate. Recovery: poller resumes IN_PROGRESS. Reconciliation: nightly COMPLETED without ledger → replay/DLT ops. No XA. Pivot if external network sent.

Model Answer — Q16 (Exactly-Once)

A: True exactly-once end-to-end is not achievable with at-least-once networks. Effective once: client Idempotency-Key on POST; each saga step keyed by paymentId + step; DB UNIQUE constraints; Kafka consumer checks reference_id before insert; compensate idempotent. Duplicates become no-ops returning same response. Audit saga_step_log for duplicate attempts.

Quick Revision — Distributed Transactions & Saga

NO XA / 2PC across microservices — local @Transactional per service only

Saga = sequence of local TXs + compensations on failure

States: STARTED → DEBITING → DEBITED → COMPLETED | FAILED | COMPENSATING

Sync in user path: fraud + hold | Async: ledger, email
Exactly-once illusion = at-least-once + idempotent handlers

Part 1: Concept

What Is Event-Driven Architecture (EDA)?

Event-driven architecture models system behavior as production, routing, and consumption of events — immutable records that something happened in the past tense: PaymentCompleted, AccountDebited, TransferApproved. Services react asynchronously instead of calling each other in long synchronous chains.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              REQUEST-DRIVEN vs EVENT-DRIVEN — PAYMENTS PLATFORM          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  REQUEST-DRIVEN (sync)                 EVENT-DRIVEN (async)              │
│  ─────────────────────                 ────────────────────                │
│  "Do this now"                         "This happened"                   │
│  payment-svc → HTTP → ledger-svc       payment-svc → Kafka → ledger-svc │
│  Caller waits                          Producer doesn't wait consumers   │
│  Tight coupling                        Loose coupling via broker           │
│  Good for: validate, hold              Good for: index, notify, analytics│
│                                                                          │
│  Production: HYBRID — sync for decisions, events for ripples (Lesson 27)│
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Event Types Master Table

Type Definition Banking Example
Domain event Something meaningful in business domain PaymentCompleted
Integration event Cross-bounded-context message Same payload, published via outbox
Command Request to do something (imperative) ProcessPaymentCommand — not an event
Event notification Minimal — ID only { "paymentId": "PMT-001" }
Event-carried state transfer Full snapshot in payload Payment + debtor summary in event
CDC event DB row change capture Debezium payments row UPDATE

EDA Building Blocks

Component Role Technology
Event producer Publishes after business fact payment-svc + outbox
Event broker Durable log, fan-out Kafka
Event consumer Reacts idempotently ledger-svc, search-svc
Schema registry Contract enforcement Confluent / Apicurio
Event catalog Discoverability Backstage / internal portal

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why Event-Driven Architecture Exists

Without EDA With EDA
payment-svc knows all downstream endpoints payment-svc publishes one fact
New consumer requires producer code change New consumer subscribes to topic
Peak load couples all services Absorb spikes in consumer lag
Retry storms on HTTP chains Consumer retries independent
Analytics taps OLTP DB Read models fed by events

Why Architects Adopt EDA in Banking

VALID DRIVERS:
  - Decouple ledger, notification, search, warehouse from payment commit path
  - Audit trail of business facts (compliance narrative)
  - Scale consumers independently (10 search indexers vs 3 payment writers)
  - Real-time fraud feature pipelines
  - Multi-channel reactions (SMS, email, push) without payment bloat

INVALID DRIVERS:
  - "Events are modern" — replace sync validate with hope
  - Event sourcing entire core ledger on day one — ops complexity
  - Avoid designing read models — event chaos without CQRS discipline

EDA vs Saga (Lesson 28 Link)

SAGA: coordinates multi-step process with compensate — often uses events between steps
EDA:  broader paradigm — any service publishes facts, many subscribers react

Payment saga COMPLETED → emits PaymentCompleted (EDA begins where saga handoff ends)

Part 3: Internal Working

Event Flow — Outbox to Consumer

payment-svc                         Kafka                         ledger-svc
    │                                 │                                │
    │ BEGIN TX                        │                                │
    │ INSERT payment COMPLETED        │                                │
    │ INSERT outbox_events            │                                │
    │ COMMIT                          │                                │
    │                                 │                                │
    │ Outbox poller / Debezium        │                                │
    ├────────────────────────────────►│ topic: payment.completed         │
    │                                 │ key: paymentId (partition)       │
    │                                 ├───────────────────────────────►│
    │                                 │                                │ idempotent insert
    │                                 │                                │ commit offset

Domain Event vs Integration Event

DOMAIN EVENT (inside payment-svc):
  Java: PaymentCompletedEvent record — domain language
  May not leave service boundary directly

INTEGRATION EVENT (cross service):
  Avro/JSON on Kafka — stable public contract
  Mapped from domain event — anti-corruption at publish boundary

Mapping layer prevents leaking internal entity fields to enterprise bus

Event Notification vs Event-Carried State Transfer

NOTIFICATION (thin):
  { "eventId": "...", "paymentId": "PMT-001", "type": "PaymentCompleted" }
  Consumer: ledger-svc calls payment-svc GET /payments/PMT-001
  Pros: small payload, single SoT read
  Cons: sync chattiness, payment-svc load at consumer spike

STATE TRANSFER (fat):
  { "paymentId", "amount", "debtorAccountId", "creditorAccountId", "completedAt", ... }
  Consumer: ledger-svc posts without callback
  Pros: **autonomous consumer**, no runtime coupling
  Cons: schema evolution, duplicate data, stale if wrong

BANKING DEFAULT: event-carried state for PaymentCompleted (ledger must not depend on payment API uptime)
Optional fields added with backward-compatible schema (Lesson 27)

Kafka Internals — Topics, Partitions, Ordering

TOPIC: payment.completed
PARTITIONS: 12
REPLICATION FACTOR: 3

Message KEY: paymentId (or tenantId for tenant ordering)
  Same key → same partition → **ordering guaranteed per payment**

Consumer Group: ledger-svc
  Each partition assigned to one consumer instance in group
  Scale consumers ≤ partitions for parallelism

ORDERING RULE:
  Events for PMT-001 always ordered in partition
  Events across different payments — no global order (OK for ledger)

┌─────────── payment.completed topic ───────────┐
│ Part 0 │ PMT-001, PMT-013, ...                │
│ Part 1 │ PMT-002, PMT-014, ...                │
│ ...    │                                       │
│ Part 11│ PMT-012, ...                         │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
       ▲                    ▲
   ledger consumer 1   ledger consumer 2
   (same group — different partitions)

CQRS — Command Query Responsibility Segregation

WRITE SIDE (Command):
  POST /payments → payment-svc → PostgreSQL payments (normalized OLTP)
  Optimized for ACID, constraints, idempotency

READ SIDE (Query):
  payment-search-svc → Elasticsearch / materialized PostgreSQL
  Fed by PaymentCompleted, PaymentFailed events
  Optimized for search filters, aggregations, dashboards

Same logical "payment" — two models, synced eventually (seconds)

┌─────────────┐     commands      ┌──────────────┐
│   Client    │──────────────────►│ payment-svc  │──► OLTP DB
└─────────────┘                   └──────┬───────┘
       ▲                                 │ events
       │ queries                          ▼
       │                          ┌──────────────┐
       └──────────────────────────│ search-svc   │──► Read DB / ES
                                  └──────────────┘

Event Sourcing (Conceptual)

TRADITIONAL STATE:
  payments.status = COMPLETED  (current row overwrites history)

EVENT SOURCING:
  Store all events: PaymentInitiated, PaymentApproved, PaymentCompleted
  Current state = fold(replay events)
  Snapshot optional every N events for fast rebuild

BANKING:
  Rare as SoT for entire core — append-only ledger (Lesson 22) is event-like
  Common for audit log, fraud case timeline, saga step log
  Full payment ES as SoT — high complexity — most banks use relational SoT + events

Part 4: Memory View

EDA Runtime Memory

PRODUCER (payment-svc):
  Outbox batch 100 rows — small heap
  Kafka producer buffer — batch.size, linger.ms — tune for throughput vs latency

BROKER (Kafka):
  Log segments on disk — page cache — not all in RAM
  Retention: payment.completed 7 days hot, archive to S3 tiered storage

CONSUMER (ledger-svc):
  max.poll.records=500 — records in memory per poll
  Deserialized Avro objects — larger than slim SQL row
  Process + commit offset — at-least-once

READ MODEL REBUILD:
  Replay topic from beginning — consumer heap + DB write pressure
  Do off-peak with scaled consumers — architect plans replay runbooks

Fat Event Memory Trap

PaymentCompleted with 50 fields + nested beneficiary graph
  × 5000 events/sec peak = GC pressure on consumers

Architect: carry fields needed for consumer's write — not entire aggregate graph

Part 5: Performance Analysis

EDA Performance Characteristics

Aspect Sync chain Event-driven
User latency Sum/max of hops Commit path only
Peak absorption Backpressure to user Consumer lag
Failure isolation Cascading 503 Queue + retry
Consistency Immediate Eventual (lag)
Ops complexity Lower Lag, DLT, replay

Consumer Lag as SLO

ledger-svc consumer lag p95 < 5 seconds — SLO
Alert lag > 30 seconds — treasury UI stale

Scale: add consumer instances up to partition count
Beyond: increase partitions (plan ahead — key strategy)

Throughput Tuning

Knob Effect
linger.ms producer Batch more — higher throughput
Partition count Parallelism ceiling
Consumer concurrency ≤ partitions per group
Compression (snappy/lz4) Less network, more CPU
Idempotent producer Exactly-once broker write (not consumer)

Notification vs Ledger Latency Requirements

Ledger post lag 2s — acceptable with reconciliation (Lesson 28)
Email receipt lag 30s — acceptable
Fraud feature update lag 5min — batch consumer OK
Real-time AML alert — **sync or low-lag stream** — separate path

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Domain Event and Integration Event Mapping

// Domain event — internal
public record PaymentCompletedDomain(PaymentId id, Money amount, Instant at) {}

// Integration event — Kafka contract
public record PaymentCompletedIntegration(
    String eventId,
    String paymentId,
    String tenantId,
    String amount,
    String currency,
    String debtorAccountId,
    String creditorAccountId,
    long completedAtEpochMillis
) {
    public static PaymentCompletedIntegration from(PaymentEntity p) {
        return new PaymentCompletedIntegration(
            UUID.randomUUID().toString(),
            p.getPaymentId(),
            p.getTenantId(),
            p.getAmount().toPlainString(),
            p.getCurrency(),
            p.getDebtorAcct(),
            p.getCreditorAcct(),
            p.getUpdatedAt().toEpochMilli()
        );
    }
}

@Service
public class PaymentEventPublisher {

    public void enqueue(PaymentEntity payment, OutboxRepository outbox) {
        PaymentCompletedIntegration integration =
            PaymentCompletedIntegration.from(payment);
        outbox.save(OutboxEvent.of(
            payment.getPaymentId(),
            "PaymentCompleted",
            toJson(integration)
        ));
    }
}

Example 2: Kafka Producer (Outbox Poller)

@Service
public class OutboxRelay {

    private final KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka;
    private final OutboxRepository outbox;

    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 200)
    @Transactional
    public void relay() {
        List<OutboxEvent> batch = outbox.findUnpublished(100);
        for (OutboxEvent e : batch) {
            kafka.send("payment.completed", e.getAggregateId(), e.getPayload())
                .whenComplete((result, ex) -> {
                    if (ex == null) e.markPublished();
                });
        }
    }
}

Example 3: Idempotent Consumer — Ledger

@Component
public class PaymentCompletedLedgerHandler {

    private final LedgerService ledgerService;
    private final ProcessedEventRepository processed;

    @KafkaListener(topics = "payment.completed", groupId = "ledger-svc")
    public void handle(@Payload PaymentCompletedIntegration event,
                       @Header(KafkaHeaders.RECEIVED_KEY) String key) {

        if (processed.exists(event.eventId())) {
            return; // duplicate delivery
        }

        ledgerService.postEntriesIdempotent(event);
        processed.save(new ProcessedEvent(event.eventId(), Instant.now()));
    }
}

CREATE TABLE processed_events (
    event_id    VARCHAR(36) PRIMARY KEY,
    processed_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);
-- Alternative: UNIQUE(reference_id) on ledger_entries only

Example 4: CQRS Projection — Search Index

@Component
public class PaymentSearchProjector {

    private final PaymentSearchRepository searchRepo;

    @KafkaListener(topics = "payment.completed", groupId = "search-svc")
    public void project(PaymentCompletedIntegration event) {
        searchRepo.upsert(PaymentSearchDocument.builder()
            .paymentId(event.paymentId())
            .tenantId(event.tenantId())
            .amount(new BigDecimal(event.amount()))
            .status("COMPLETED")
            .debtorAccountId(event.debtorAccountId())
            .completedAt(Instant.ofEpochMilli(event.completedAtEpochMillis()))
            .build());
    }

    @KafkaListener(topics = "payment.failed", groupId = "search-svc")
    public void projectFailed(PaymentFailedIntegration event) {
        searchRepo.updateStatus(event.paymentId(), "FAILED");
    }
}

Part 7: Production Usage

EDA in Production Banking

Topic Design Conventions

DOMAIN.TOPIC naming:
  payment.completed
  payment.failed
  account.balance.updated
  fraud.alert.raised

AVOID:
  generic "events" topic — no independent scale/retention
  one topic for all bank events — schema chaos

Per-event-type topic:
  Independent consumer groups, retention, ACLs

Consumer Failure — DLT Pattern

@RetryableTopic(
    attempts = "3",
    backoff = @Backoff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 2),
    dltStrategy = DltStrategy.FAIL_ON_ERROR,
    include = { LedgerPostingException.class }
)
@KafkaListener(topics = "payment.completed", groupId = "ledger-svc")
public void handle(PaymentCompletedIntegration event) { ... }

payment.completed-dlt — ops replay after bug fix
Financial DLT depth > 0 — page on-call immediately
Never auto-discard DLT messages

Event Replay Runbook

SCENARIO: ledger-svc bug — 6 hours wrong entries

1. Stop ledger consumer group
2. Fix code, deploy
3. Identify offset range or time window
4. Reset consumer offset OR publish corrective events
5. Replay with idempotent UNIQUE keys
6. Reconciliation job validates SUM(ledger) vs payments
7. Post-mortem — add contract test

Production Checklist

Check Why
Outbox only publish No dual-write
Idempotent consumers At-least-once
Schema registry CI Breaking change blocked
Topic ACLs payment-svc write, ledger read
Consumer lag alerts SLO breach
DLT monitoring No silent loss
Event catalog updated Discoverability
PII in events minimized Compliance
Partition key = business id Ordering
Retention + archive policy Audit 7 years

Part 8: Microservice Usage

EDA Across Payment Platform

Enterprise Event Flow Map

payment-svc ──► payment.completed ──┬──► ledger-svc
                  payment.failed    ├──► search-svc
                                    ├──► notification-svc
                                    ├──► fraud-analytics (Flink)
                                    └──► warehouse (Kafka Connect → Snowflake)

Choreography Example — Notifications

PaymentCompleted → notification-svc sends email
PaymentCompleted → notification-svc sends push (same group, different handlers OR separate consumer classes)

No orchestrator — notification failure doesn't affect ledger
Each consumer group commits offset independently

CDC as Event Source (Debezium)

PostgreSQL WAL → Debezium → Kafka topic db.payments.public.payments

Pros: no outbox poller code — events from DB truth
Cons: change events not domain events — need stream processing to map
      exposes internal schema — prefer outbox for public contract control

Hybrid: outbox for public integration events; CDC for internal analytics pipeline

Stream Processing (Fraud)

Kafka Streams / Flink:
  payment.completed JOIN account.profile updates → feature vector → model score
  Windowed aggregations: 10 payments in 1 min same beneficiary → alert

Architect: stream job is separate deployable — not inside payment-svc request thread

Part 9: Architect Perspective

EDA Design Decisions

When Event-Driven vs Sync (Consolidated)

Scenario Pattern
Validate account before debit Sync HTTP (Lesson 27)
Post ledger after complete Event
Send receipt email Event
Fraud block before release Sync
Update search index Event
Maker approval wait Saga state — not Kafka poll for human

ADR — Event-Carried State for PaymentCompleted

## ADR-701: PaymentCompleted carries full posting payload

### Decision
Integration event includes amount, accounts, currency, tenantId.
ledger-svc does not call payment-svc on consume.

### Consequences
Schema versioning required. Larger payload (~1KB).
ledger-svc autonomous during payment-svc outage for backlog processing.

ADR — CQRS for Payment Search

## ADR-702: Payment search on Elasticsearch fed by Kafka; OLTP PostgreSQL SoT

### Decision
search-svc consumer group projects payment.completed/failed.
Corporate search UI reads ES only.

### Consequences
2–10s lag acceptable — UI copy "recent payments may take a moment."
Replay tool for reindex. GET /payments/{id} hits OLTP for authoritative detail.

Event Sourcing — Architect Veto / Allow

ALLOW event sourcing for:
  - Audit timeline UI
  - Saga step history
  - Dispute case evidence chain

VETO as payment SoT replacement unless:
  - Team has proven ops maturity
  - Reconciliation with regulatory reporting solved
  - Most banks: relational SoT + domain events on bus

Model Answer — Q13 (Event Catalog)

A: Catalog entry per integration event: name, version, Avro schema, topic, key, producer, consumer list, retention, SLA lag, PII classification, example payload, deprecation date. PaymentCompleted v2 on payment.completed, key paymentId, producers payment-svc only, consumers ledger/search/notify/ETL, retention 7d + S3 7yr archive, lag SLO 5s. Governance: schema registry BACKWARD compat in CI; new consumer registers in catalog PR; breaking change requires new topic or versioned subject payment.completed-value-v2.

Model Answer — Q15 (Event Sourcing for Core)

A: No for typical retail/corporate payment SoT — relational OLTP with ACID, idempotency, regulatory reporting maturity wins. Append-only ledger (Lesson 22) gives audit without full ES. ES adds replay complexity, snapshot ops, and team skill burden. Allow ES for dispute timeline, saga audit, or isolated subdomains. Hybrid: relational SoT + Kafka domain events for integration — industry standard.

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Hybrid: sync for decisions, events for side effects
  2. Outbox for all integration events from OLTP
  3. Event-carried state for autonomous financial consumers
  4. Topic per event type with clear schema registry subject
  5. Partition key = business id (paymentId, tenantId)
  6. Idempotent consumers — processed_events or business UNIQUE
  7. CQRS for search/analytics — not for authoritative balance
  8. Event catalog — discoverable enterprise contract
  9. DLT + replay runbook — financial topics never silent drop
  10. Backward-compatible schema evolution — additive fields with defaults

Part 1: Concept

What Are Resilience Patterns?

Resilience patterns are design techniques that let a distributed system degrade gracefully, isolate failures, and recover automatically when dependencies fail, slow down, or spike in load. In banking, resilience is not optional — a hung thread pool can block thousands of legitimate payments.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              WITHOUT vs WITH RESILIENCE — PAYMENT INITIATION             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  WITHOUT:                          WITH:                                 │
│  fraud-svc slow 8s                 TimeLimiter 3s → fail fast              │
│  → 200 Tomcat threads blocked      Circuit OPEN → skip wait, 503         │
│  → payment-svc OOM / timeout       Bulkhead: max 25 fraud calls           │
│  → ALL users affected              Idempotency: client retry safe        │
│  Client retries duplicate?         Rate limit: tenant quota enforced     │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Resilience Pattern Catalog

Pattern Purpose Banking Example
Timeout Cap wait time 3s account-svc Feign read
Retry Transient failure recovery Kafka consumer retry (idempotent)
Circuit breaker Stop calling sick dependency OPEN when fraud-svc 50% fail
Bulkhead Isolate resource pools Separate pool for fraud vs account
Rate limiter Protect capacity 100 req/min per tenant at gateway
Load shedding Drop low-priority work Reject bulk export during peak
Fallback Degraded response Fail closed on validate — not fake OK
Graceful degradation Reduced feature set Search stale, payment still works
Idempotency Safe retries Idempotency-Key (Lesson 25)

Failure Modes in Microservices

Failure Symptom Primary pattern
Slow dependency Thread starvation Timeout + bulkhead + CB
Hard dependency down 503 cascade Circuit breaker fail-fast
Retry storm Amplified load Retry budget + jitter + CB
Hot tenant Noisy neighbor Rate limit + bulkhead
Broker lag Stale read model Scale consumer + SLO alert
Pool exhaustion Connection timeout Bulkhead + shed load

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why Resilience Patterns Exist

Fragile integration Resilient integration
Infinite wait on downstream Bounded timeout
Retry all POST blindly Idempotent retry only
One bad svc kills platform Bulkhead isolation
Keep hammering dead svc Circuit opens — fail fast
No priority under stress Load shedding

Why Architects Own Resilience Standards

INCIDENT PATTERN (real banks):
  External fraud API latency spike
  → payment threads blocked
  → HikariCP connections held
  → DB connection pool exhausted
  → ENTIRE payment platform down

ROOT CAUSE: missing timeout + bulkhead + circuit breaker on ONE dependency

Platform ADR: resilience mandatory on every outbound call — not optional per team

Resilience vs Correctness (Banking)

RESILIENCE MUST NOT COMPROMISE MONEY CORRECTNESS:

✓ Fail payment 503 if account validate unavailable
✓ Circuit open on fraud → block or queue hold (product decision)
✗ Fallback "assume account OK" — NEVER
✗ Retry POST payment without Idempotency-Key — NEVER
✗ Skip ledger post silently — DLT + alert (Lesson 29)

Part 3: Internal Working

Circuit Breaker State Machine (Resilience4j)

                    failures exceed threshold
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                                      │
         ▼                                      │
    ┌─────────┐   success    ┌───────────┐     │
    │ CLOSED  │─────────────►│  (normal) │     │
    └────┬────┘              └───────────┘     │
         │ failures                            │
         ▼                                      │
    ┌─────────┐   wait expires   ┌───────────┐│
    │  OPEN   │─────────────────►│ HALF_OPEN ││
    └─────────┘                  └─────┬─────┘│
         ▲                             │      │
         │         trial fails         │      │
         └─────────────────────────────┘      │
                    trial succeeds → CLOSED ──┘

resilience4j.circuitbreaker.instances.fraud-svc:
  slidingWindowSize: 50              # last 50 calls
  failureRateThreshold: 50           # % failures to OPEN
  waitDurationInOpenState: 30s
  permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState: 5
  recordExceptions:
    - java.io.IOException
    - org.springframework.web.client.HttpServerErrorException
  ignoreExceptions:
    - com.bank.FraudBlockedException   # business reject ≠ infra fail

CLOSED: all calls pass — metrics recorded
OPEN: CallNotPermittedException immediately — protects fraud-svc AND payment threads
HALF_OPEN: probe calls — recover or re-open

Timeout + TimeLimiter

Feign readTimeout: 3000ms — socket level
Resilience4j TimeLimiter: 3s — wraps entire call including queue wait

If fraud-svc responds at 3500ms:
  → TimeoutException
  → counts as failure toward circuit breaker
  → thread released — not blocked forever

Bulkhead — Semaphore vs Thread Pool

SEMAPHORE BULKHEAD (default Resilience4j):
  Limits concurrent calls to fraud-svc to 25
  Caller thread waits max 100ms for permit — then reject

THREAD POOL BULKHEAD:
  Fraud calls run on dedicated pool (10 threads)
  Main Tomcat threads never block on fraud — only submit and wait on Future with timeout

payment-svc Tomcat (200 threads)
  ├── bulkhead account pool (50 concurrent)
  └── bulkhead fraud pool (25 concurrent)
         fraud slow → only fraud pool stalls — not all 200

Retry with Jitter

WRONG: 3 retries immediate — retry storm amplifies outage

RIGHT:
  maxAttempts: 3
  waitDuration: 500ms
  exponentialBackoffMultiplier: 2
  randomizedWait: true  (jitter)

Only for:
  GET account summary (idempotent)
  Kafka consumer (idempotent handler)
NOT for:
  POST payment without idempotency
  compensate release called twice without idempotent API

Rate Limiter

TOKEN BUCKET (Resilience4j / Gateway Redis):

Tenant TENANT-ABC: 100 tokens/min replenish
Each payment POST consumes 1 token
Empty bucket → 429 Too Many Requests

Gateway (global) + service (business rules) — defense in depth

Load Shedding

UNDER STRESS (CPU > 90%, pool pending > 0):

Priority queue concept:
  P0: payment POST, account debit     — always accept (until hard limit)
  P1: payment search                  — shed first
  P2: bulk export, analytics          — reject 503 Retry-After

Implementation:
  Servlet filter checks system load + priority header
  OR admission control at gateway during incident

Part 4: Memory View

Resilience and Resource Exhaustion

THREAD POOL (Tomcat payment-svc):
  maxThreads=200
  Without bulkhead: 200 blocked on fraud → 0 threads for health checks

HIKARICP (Lesson 24):
  Blocked service thread holds @Transactional connection
  200 blocked threads ≈ 200 DB connections — pool max 50 → deadlock

RESILIENCE FIX CHAIN:
  Timeout releases thread quickly
  Bulkhead caps concurrent blocked
  Circuit breaker stops calling entirely
  → connections returned to pool

BULKHEAD THREAD POOL:
  Dedicated pool queue max 100 — reject when full — fail fast
  Prevents unbounded queue memory

Gateway (Netty) Specific

Lesson 20: blocking call in Gateway filter stalls event loop
Resilience on gateway routes: response-timeout on WebClient to upstream
RequestRateLimiter Redis — non-blocking reactive filter

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Resilience Impact on Latency and Availability

Pattern Latency when healthy Latency when dependency sick System availability
No resilience Lowest Worst — cascade Low
Timeout only +0 Capped per call Medium
+ Circuit breaker +0 Fail fast μs High
+ Bulkhead +0 Queued/rejected fast Isolated
+ Rate limit +1ms Redis 429 immediate Fair

Circuit Breaker Tuning Trade-offs

Aggressive (failureRate 30%, window 20):
  Opens quickly — protects platform
  False positives on brief blips — more 503s

Conservative (failureRate 70%, window 100):
  Stays closed longer — users wait on timeouts
  Thread pool damage before OPEN

BANKING payment path: moderate — 50% over 50 calls, 30s open, half-open probe 5

Retry Budget

Google SRE retry budget concept:
  If 1% error rate target, unlimited retries can 10× effective load

Limit:
  max 2 retries on idempotent GET
  exponential backoff with jitter
  circuit breaker stops retries when OPEN anyway

Graceful Degradation Performance

Search CQRS lag 30s (Lesson 29):
  Degrade: show "search temporarily delayed" — payment POST unaffected

Fraud async path for low-value (< ₹1000):
  Sync path p95 80ms → async hold pattern p95 150ms user response
  Trade fraud immediacy for availability — product + compliance sign-off

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Resilience4j — Full Stack on Feign

resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      account-svc:
        slidingWindowSize: 50
        failureRateThreshold: 50
        waitDurationInOpenState: 30s
      fraud-svc:
        slidingWindowSize: 30
        failureRateThreshold: 40
        waitDurationInOpenState: 60s
  timelimiter:
    instances:
      account-svc:
        timeoutDuration: 3s
      fraud-svc:
        timeoutDuration: 2s
  bulkhead:
    instances:
      fraud-svc:
        maxConcurrentCalls: 25
        maxWaitDuration: 100ms
  retry:
    instances:
      account-svc-get:
        maxAttempts: 2
        waitDuration: 200ms
        enableExponentialBackoff: true
        exponentialBackoffMultiplier: 2
        retryExceptions:
          - java.io.IOException

@FeignClient(name = "account-svc", path = "/api/v1")
public interface AccountFeignClient {

    @GetMapping("/accounts/{id}/summary")
    @CircuitBreaker(name = "account-svc", fallbackMethod = "summaryFallback")
    @TimeLimiter(name = "account-svc")
    @Bulkhead(name = "account-svc", type = Bulkhead.Type.SEMAPHORE)
    CompletableFuture<AccountSummary> getSummaryAsync(@PathVariable("id") String id);

    default CompletableFuture<AccountSummary> summaryFallback(String id, Throwable t) {
        return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(
            new DownstreamUnavailableException("account-svc unavailable", t));
    }
}

Example 2: Fail-Closed Payment Service

@Service
public class PaymentInitiationService {

    public PaymentResponse initiate(PaymentRequest req, String idempotencyKey) {
        AccountSummary account;
        try {
            account = accountClient.getSummary(req.debtorAccountId()).join();
        } catch (DownstreamUnavailableException ex) {
            throw new ServiceUnavailableException("Unable to validate account — try later");
            // NEVER proceed without validation
        }

        FraudScore score;
        try {
            score = fraudClient.score(req).join();
        } catch (CallNotPermittedException ex) {
            // Circuit OPEN — product policy: reject, not bypass
            throw new ServiceUnavailableException("Fraud check temporarily unavailable");
        }

        if (score.isBlocked()) {
            throw new FraudBlockedException(score.reason());
        }

        return paymentRepository.savePending(req, idempotencyKey);
    }
}

Example 3: Bulkhead Thread Pool Isolation

@Bean
public ThreadPoolBulkheadRegistry bulkheadRegistry() {
    ThreadPoolBulkheadConfig config = ThreadPoolBulkheadConfig.custom()
        .maxThreadPoolSize(10)
        .coreThreadPoolSize(5)
        .queueCapacity(50)
        .build();
    return ThreadPoolBulkheadRegistry.of(
        Map.of("fraud-svc", config));
}

// Wrap fraud call
ThreadPoolBulkhead bulkhead = bulkheadRegistry.bulkhead("fraud-svc");
return bulkhead.executeSupplier(() -> fraudClient.score(request));

Example 4: Gateway Rate Limiter + Response Timeout

spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      httpclient:
        response-timeout: 30s
        connect-timeout: 3000
      routes:
        - id: payments
          uri: lb://payment-svc
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/v1/payments/**
          filters:
            - name: RequestRateLimiter
              args:
                redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 100
                redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 200
                key-resolver: "#{@tenantKeyResolver}"
            - name: CircuitBreaker
              args:
                name: paymentSvcCB
                fallbackUri: forward:/fallback/payments-unavailable

@RestController
public class GatewayFallbackController {

    @RequestMapping("/fallback/payments-unavailable")
    public ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> paymentsDown() {
        ProblemDetail p = ProblemDetail.forStatus(HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE);
        p.setTitle("Payment service temporarily unavailable");
        p.setProperty("errorCode", "PLATFORM_DEGRADED");
        return ResponseEntity.status(503).header("Retry-After", "30").body(p);
    }
}

Example 5: Load Shedding Filter

@Component
@Order(1)
public class LoadSheddingFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {

    private final MeterRegistry metrics;

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res,
                                    FilterChain chain) throws ServletException, IOException {

        double cpu = systemCpuLoad();
        boolean critical = req.getRequestURI().contains("/payments") && "POST".equals(req.getMethod());

        if (cpu > 0.90 && !critical) {
            res.setStatus(503);
            res.setHeader("Retry-After", "60");
            res.getWriter().write("{\"errorCode\":\"LOAD_SHED\"}");
            metrics.counter("load_shed", "path", req.getRequestURI()).increment();
            return;
        }
        chain.doFilter(req, res);
    }
}

Example 6: Kafka Consumer Resilience

@RetryableTopic(
    attempts = "4",
    backoff = @Backoff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 2.0, maxDelay = 30000),
    dltStrategy = DltStrategy.FAIL_ON_ERROR,
    autoCreateTopics = "false"
)
@KafkaListener(topics = "payment.completed", groupId = "ledger-svc")
public void consume(PaymentCompletedIntegration event) {
    ledgerService.postIdempotent(event);
}

Example 7: Health Indicator Reflecting Circuit State

@Component
public class DownstreamHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {

    private final CircuitBreakerRegistry registry;

    @Override
    public Health health() {
        CircuitBreaker cb = registry.circuitBreaker("account-svc");
        return switch (cb.getState()) {
            case CLOSED -> Health.up().withDetail("account-svc", "CLOSED").build();
            case HALF_OPEN -> Health.status("DEGRADED").withDetail("account-svc", "HALF_OPEN").build();
            case OPEN -> Health.status("DEGRADED").withDetail("account-svc", "OPEN").build();
            default -> Health.unknown().build();
        };
    }
}

Part 7: Production Usage

Resilience in Production Banking

Platform Resilience Baseline (Architect Standard)

Layer Required controls
Gateway Rate limit, timeout, JWT, optional CB to origin
Every Feign/WebClient connect + read timeout, circuit breaker
Financial validate Fail closed — no unsafe fallback
Kafka consumer Retry + DLT + idempotency
DB Hikari pool sized (Lesson 24), short transactions
Shedding Non-critical endpoints deprioritized under stress

SLO / SLI / Error Budget

SLI (indicator): payment initiation success rate (non-client-error)
SLO (objective): 99.95% success over 30 days
Error budget: 0.05% ≈ 21.6 min downtime/month at constant load

Burn rate alert:
  If 5xx rate 10× normal for 5 min → page on-call

Dependency SLO:
  account-svc p95 < 50ms — payment-svc SLO depends on it — cascade budget

Incident Playbook — Circuit OPEN on fraud-svc

1. Alert: fraud-svc circuit OPEN > 2 min
2. Verify fraud-svc health / scale pods
3. If fraud hard down:
   - Payment returns 503 PLATFORM_DEGRADED (NOT bypass)
   - Comms to corporate clients Retry-After header
4. If false positive — tune CB threshold via config refresh
5. Post-incident: verify bulkhead prevented Tomcat exhaustion

Chaos Engineering (Controlled)

NOT random prod destruction — gameday in staging/pre-prod:

Experiments:
  - Latency injection fraud-svc +500ms — verify timeout
  - Kill account-svc pod — verify CB + 503
  - Redis down — idempotency falls back to DB UNIQUE
  - Kafka broker pause — consumer lag alert fires

Steady state hypothesis:
  "Payment p95 < 500ms when one fraud pod killed"

Tools: LitmusChaos, Toxiproxy, Gremlin (with change approval)

Production Checklist

Check Pass
All outbound timeouts set No default infinite
Circuit breaker on each dependency Named per svc
Bulkhead on slowest dependency fraud-svc
No retry on non-idempotent POST Code review gate
Fallback never fakes validate Security review
429/503 with Retry-After Client-friendly
CB metrics in Grafana state, failure rate
Chaos test quarterly Last gameday < 90 days

Part 8: Microservice Usage

Resilience Across Payment Platform

Dependency Matrix

Caller Callee Timeout CB Bulkhead Retry On failure
payment-svc account-svc 3s Yes 50 GET 2× 503 fail
payment-svc fraud-svc 2s Yes 25 No 503 fail
gateway payment-svc 30s Yes — No 503 fallback
ledger-svc — (Kafka) — — consumer 3× DLT
BFF 3 services 3s each Yes parallel zip No partial degrade

Cascading Failure Prevention

BEFORE:
  payment → fraud (slow) → threads exhausted → health check fails
  → K8s kills payment pods → MORE load on survivors → death spiral

AFTER:
  fraud bulkhead 25 + timeout 2s + CB OPEN
  → payment rejects fast 503 for new fraud-dependent requests
  → threads free → health OK → pods stable
  → client retry with Idempotency-Key after recovery

Saga + Resilience (Lesson 28)

Saga debit step fails with 503:
  → saga FAILED — no compensate needed if hold never placed
  → client retries same Idempotency-Key → resume or return existing

Saga compensate release fails:
  → retry with backoff — idempotent release API
  → alert ops — manual pivot if still failing

Multi-Tenant Fairness

Tenant MEGA sends 10K req/min — crowds others

Gateway tenant rate limit: 500/min
payment-svc bulkhead per tenant (advanced) or queue priority
Architect: dedicated shard + dedicated rate quota for mega (Lesson 24)

Part 9: Architect Perspective

Resilience Architecture Decisions

Fail-Closed vs Fail-Open

Path Policy Rationale
Account validate Fail closed No unvalidated debit
Fraud score Fail closed (default) Regulatory
Fraud low-value Fail open — rare, ADR + legal Business risk
Email receipt Fail open (async retry) Non-financial
Search index Fail open (stale OK) CQRS lag acceptable

ADR — Mandatory Resilience4j on Outbound Calls

## ADR-801: Platform resilience baseline on all inter-service HTTP

### Decision
Archetype includes TimeLimiter + CircuitBreaker + Bulkhead per dependency.
Fallbacks for validate paths must throw 503, not synthetic success.

### Consequences
More 503 during dependency outages — acceptable vs platform collapse.
Platform team provides tuned YAML defaults; teams override with ADR.

ADR — Low-Value Fraud Bypass (Example Rejection)

## ADR-802-REJECTED: Allow payment without fraud when circuit OPEN

### Rejection reason
AML/regulatory exposure; fraud bypass creates audit gap.
Alternative: queue payment PENDING_FRAUD_HOLD async retry — user notified delay.

Error Budget Policy

If payment SLO error budget exhausted mid-month:
  Freeze non-critical releases
  Focus on reliability improvements
  No new feature work until budget reset or recovery plan approved

Model Answer — Q13 (fraud-svc Down)

A: fraud-svc failures/timeouts count toward circuit breaker. When OPEN, payment-svc fails fast CallNotPermittedException → 503 FRAUD_CHECK_UNAVAILABLE with Retry-After. No payment creation without fraud (fail closed default). Client retries with same Idempotency-Key after recovery. Bulkhead ensured fraud slowness never exhausted all Tomcat threads before OPEN. Gateway may also CB to payment-svc if needed. Alert on-call fraud team. Async option: queue PENDING_FRAUD_REVIEW status — separate ADR if compliance allows delayed settlement. Notification/search unaffected — event-driven decoupled.

Model Answer — Q14 (Cascade Prevention)

A: Layers: (1) TimeLimiter 2–3s on fraud/account calls. (2) Bulkhead caps concurrent fraud calls. (3) Circuit breaker stops calls when failure rate high. (4) Short @Transactional — don't hold DB connection during HTTP wait; validate HTTP before opening tx where possible. (5) Hikari pool sized per Lesson 24 formula. (6) Rate limit hot tenants. (7) Load shed non-critical endpoints under CPU stress. (8) Monitor hikaricp.connections.pending and Tomcat busy threads.

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Timeout on every outbound call — no exceptions
  2. Circuit breaker per dependency — tuned failure threshold
  3. Bulkhead on slowest/highest-risk dependency (fraud)
  4. Fail closed on validate and fraud — 503 not bypass
  5. Retry idempotent only — jitter + max 2–3 attempts
  6. Rate limit per tenant at gateway
  7. Load shed non-critical under CPU/pool stress
  8. Idempotency-Key enables safe client retry after 503
  9. SLO/error budget — drive reliability culture
  10. Chaos gameday quarterly — verify hypotheses

Part 1: Concept

What Is Apache Kafka?

Apache Kafka is a distributed commit log — a durable, partitioned, replicated stream of records. Producers append events; consumers read at their own pace with offset tracking. It is the default event backbone for microservices in banking platforms.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    KAFKA vs TRADITIONAL MESSAGE QUEUE                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  TRADITIONAL QUEUE (RabbitMQ)          KAFKA (log)                       │
│  ───────────────────────────          ────────────                       │
│  Message deleted after ack            **Retained** by policy (days/forever)│
│  One consumer per message typical     **Many consumer groups** same topic │
│  Hard to replay                       **Replay from offset**             │
│  Task/work queue focus                **Event stream / audit trail**     │
│                                                                          │
│  Banking: Kafka for payment events, audit, analytics, CDC                │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Core Terminology Master Table

Term Definition Banking Example
Broker Kafka server storing data kafka-1.bank.internal:9092
Cluster Multiple brokers 3 brokers, RF=3
Topic Named log category payment.completed
Partition Ordered sub-log of topic 12 partitions for parallelism
Offset Position in partition log Consumer at offset 4,892,011
Replica Copy of partition Leader + 2 followers
Producer Writes records payment-svc outbox relay
Consumer Reads records ledger-svc consumer group
Consumer group Cooperative consumers ledger-svc group — 1 consumer per partition max
Record key Routing + ordering paymentId
Record value Payload (JSON/Avro) PaymentCompleted event

                    │         Kafka Cluster           │
                    │  ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐       │
                    │  │ Broker 1│ │ Broker 2│ ...   │
                    │  └────┬────┘ └────┬────┘       │
                    │       │  topic: payment.completed│
                    │       │  Part0 Part1 Part2 ...  │
                    └───────┼──────────────────────────┘
                            │
         ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
         ▼                  ▼                  ▼
    payment-svc         ledger-svc         search-svc
    (producer)       (group: ledger-svc) (group: search-svc)

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why Kafka Exists in Banking Platforms

Without Kafka With Kafka
Point-to-point HTTP fan-out to 5 services One publish, many subscribe
Lost events if consumer down Retention + replay
Analytics taps OLTP DB Stream to warehouse
No central audit of facts Immutable log (retention policy)
Tight coupling on delivery Async decoupling (Lesson 29)

Why Architects Choose Kafka

REQUIREMENTS KAFKA SOLVES:
  - PaymentCompleted fan-out: ledger, search, notify, ETL, fraud analytics
  - High throughput: peak NEFT window 8K+ events/sec
  - Ordering per payment (same paymentId → same partition)
  - Replay after bug fix in ledger consumer (Lesson 29 runbook)
  - 7-year audit: tiered storage / archive to S3 (ops policy)

NOT FOR:
  - Request/response "does account exist" — use HTTP (Lesson 27)
  - Distributed transaction coordinator — use saga (Lesson 28)
  - Small task queue with complex routing — RabbitMQ may suffice

Kafka in Your Curriculum Arc

Lesson 27: outbox → Kafka (why publish)
Lesson 29: EDA, CQRS, consumer idempotency
Lesson 31: broker internals (how it works)
Lesson 32–33: advanced patterns, production ops

Part 3: Internal Working

Topic, Partition, and Replication

TOPIC: payment.completed
PARTITIONS: 12
REPLICATION FACTOR (RF): 3

Each partition is an ordered append-only log:

Partition 0: [offset 0][offset 1][offset 2]...
Partition 1: [offset 0][offset 1]...

RECORD:
  key:   PMT-001
  value: { "eventId": "...", "amount": "50000.00", ... }
  timestamp, headers (correlationId)

PARTITION ASSIGNMENT:
  hash(key) % numPartitions → partition index
  Same key → same partition → **strict order for that key**
  Null key → round-robin (no key ordering guarantee)

Leader, Follower, ISR

For Partition 0:
  Leader: Broker 2 (handles all reads/writes)
  Followers: Broker 1, Broker 3 (replicate from leader)
  ISR (In-Sync Replicas): followers caught up within threshold

Producer acks=all:
  Write committed when all ISR ack — survives broker loss

Leader dies → controller elects new leader from ISR
  Brief unavailability — clients retry

Producer Internals

ProducerRecord → Serializer (Avro/JSON) → Partitioner → Record batch
  → compress (snappy/lz4) → send to leader broker
  → wait for ack per acks setting

ACKS:
  acks=0  : fire-and-forget — **never for payments**
  acks=1  : leader ack only — risk if leader dies before replicate
  acks=all: **ISR majority ack — banking default**

Idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true):
  PID + sequence number — dedup at broker within session
  Prevents duplicate writes on producer retry — NOT consumer dedup

Consumer Internals

Consumer subscribes to topic(s) in group `ledger-svc`

Group coordinator assigns partitions:
  12 partitions, 4 consumer instances → 3 partitions each
  12 partitions, 12 consumers → 1 each (max parallelism)
  12 partitions, 15 consumers → 3 idle

Poll loop:
  1. consumer.poll(Duration)
  2. Process batch of records
  3. commit offset (auto or manual)

OFFSET COMMIT:
  Auto commit: every 5s — risk process record twice on crash
  Manual sync commit: after DB insert — **at-least-once with idempotent handler**
  Manual async commit: faster — ordering care on failure

Delivery Semantics

Semantics Producer Consumer Banking
At-most-once acks=0, commit before process Rare Lose message — bad
At-least-once acks=all + retry Commit after process Default + idempotency
Exactly-once (broker) Idempotent + transactions read_committed + tx consumer Advanced (Lesson 32) 
PRACTICAL BANKING:
  At-least-once + UNIQUE(eventId) or UNIQUE(paymentId) on ledger
  = effective-once processing (Lesson 28/29)

Consumer Rebalance

Trigger: consumer join/leave, partition count change, session timeout

During rebalance:
  Consumption pauses — **increase lag briefly**

Architect:
  cooperative-sticky assignor reduces stop-the-world
  session.timeout.ms + heartbeat tuned — avoid false rebalance storm
  max.poll.interval.ms > max processing time per batch

Part 4: Memory View

Kafka Memory and Storage

BROKER:
  Log segments on disk — sequential write — fast
  OS page cache — hot segments served from RAM
  Not "all Kafka data in heap" — broker heap for metadata/replication

  log.retention.hours=168 (7 days hot) — topic policy
  log.retention.bytes — cap per partition

PRODUCER (payment-svc):
  buffer.memory — batch before send
  batch.size, linger.ms — trade latency vs throughput

CONSUMER (ledger-svc):
  fetch.min.bytes, max.partition.fetch.bytes
  Deserialized records in heap per poll — tune max.poll.records (500 default)

  max.poll.records=500 × 1KB event = ~500KB per poll — manageable
  max.poll.records=500 × 1MB event = **OOM risk**

Partition Size and Retention

High volume payment.completed:
  12 partitions × 50GB/partition — plan retention + tiered storage
  Compacted topic (changelog) vs delete retention (event stream)

payment.completed → **delete retention** (time-based) + archive Connect
account.snapshot → compacted topic possible (key=accountId, latest value)

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Kafka Performance Factors

Factor Throughput impact Latency impact
Partition count Higher parallelism More files to manage
Replication factor Write cost × RF Minor
acks=all Safest, slower than 1 +1–5ms typical
Compression Less network Small CPU cost
Batch size / linger Higher throughput +linger ms
Consumer count Up to partition count —
Record size Linear I/O Keep events slim

Partition Count Planning

RULE OF THUMB:
  Partitions ≥ max desired consumer parallelism
  Partitions ≤ cluster throughput / single partition throughput (~10MB/s order of magnitude — measure)

Payment platform:
  payment.completed: 12–24 partitions at 5K TPS start
  Scale: add partitions — **key hash changes** — plan before production or use dual-write migration

Too few partitions: consumer cannot scale
Too many partitions: broker metadata overhead, longer rebalance

Latency vs Throughput Tuning

Low latency path (near-real-time ledger):
  linger.ms=0 or 5
  acks=all
  small batches

High throughput ETL:
  linger.ms=20
  compression=lz4
  larger batch.size

Consumer Lag as Metric

Lag = latest offset - consumer committed offset (per partition)

ledger-svc lag 5000 messages ≈ 2 seconds at 2500 msg/s
Alert: lag > 10000 or age > 30s

Fix: scale consumers (≤ partitions), optimize handler, fix slow DB

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Spring Kafka Producer (Outbox Relay)

@Configuration
public class KafkaProducerConfig {

    @Bean
    ProducerFactory<String, String> producerFactory() {
        Map<String, Object> props = Map.of(
            ProducerConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, "kafka.bank.internal:9092",
            ProducerConfig.KEY_SERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringSerializer.class,
            ProducerConfig.VALUE_SERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringSerializer.class,
            ProducerConfig.ACKS_CONFIG, "all",
            ProducerConfig.ENABLE_IDEMPOTENCE_CONFIG, true,
            ProducerConfig.RETRIES_CONFIG, 3,
            ProducerConfig.COMPRESSION_TYPE_CONFIG, "lz4"
        );
        return new DefaultKafkaProducerFactory<>(props);
    }

    @Bean
    KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafkaTemplate(ProducerFactory<String, String> pf) {
        return new KafkaTemplate<>(pf);
    }
}

kafkaTemplate.send("payment.completed", payment.getPaymentId(), jsonPayload);
// key = paymentId → ordering per payment

Example 2: Consumer with Manual Commit

@Configuration
public class KafkaConsumerConfig {

    @Bean
    ConsumerFactory<String, String> consumerFactory() {
        Map<String, Object> props = Map.of(
            ConsumerConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, "kafka.bank.internal:9092",
            ConsumerConfig.GROUP_ID_CONFIG, "ledger-svc",
            ConsumerConfig.KEY_DESERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringDeserializer.class,
            ConsumerConfig.VALUE_DESERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringDeserializer.class,
            ConsumerConfig.ENABLE_AUTO_COMMIT_CONFIG, false,
            ConsumerConfig.MAX_POLL_RECORDS_CONFIG, 200,
            ConsumerConfig.MAX_POLL_INTERVAL_MS_CONFIG, 300_000
        );
        return new DefaultKafkaConsumerFactory<>(props);
    }
}

@KafkaListener(topics = "payment.completed", groupId = "ledger-svc")
public void listen(ConsumerRecord<String, String> record, Acknowledgment ack) {
    PaymentCompletedIntegration event = parse(record.value());
    ledgerService.postIdempotent(event);
    ack.acknowledge(); // commit offset after successful processing
}

Example 3: Idempotent Consumer (Database)

@Transactional
public void postIdempotent(PaymentCompletedIntegration event) {
    if (processedEventRepository.existsById(event.eventId())) {
        return;
    }
    ledgerRepository.insertEntries(buildEntries(event));
    processedEventRepository.save(new ProcessedEvent(event.eventId()));
}

Example 4: Topic Creation (Ops / Terraform Concept)

kafka-topics.sh --create \
  --topic payment.completed \
  --partitions 12 \
  --replication-factor 3 \
  --config retention.ms=604800000 \
  --config min.insync.replicas=2

min.insync.replicas=2 + acks=all:
  Survives single broker loss without write unavailability (if ISR healthy)

Example 5: Headers for Correlation ID

ProducerRecord<String, String> record = new ProducerRecord<>(
    "payment.completed",
    null,
    paymentId,
    jsonPayload,
    List.of(new RecordHeader("X-Correlation-Id", correlationId.getBytes()))
);
kafkaTemplate.send(record);

@KafkaListener(topics = "payment.completed")
public void listen(ConsumerRecord<String, String> record) {
    Header h = record.headers().lastHeader("X-Correlation-Id");
    if (h != null) MDC.put("correlationId", new String(h.value()));
    try {
        process(record.value());
    } finally {
        MDC.remove("correlationId");
    }
}

Example 6: Multiple Consumer Groups (Fan-Out)

Same topic payment.completed:

Group ledger-svc    → posts ledger entries
Group search-svc    → updates Elasticsearch
Group notification-svc → sends email

Each group receives ALL messages independently
Each maintains own offsets

NOT the same as two consumers in SAME group (load share one copy)

Part 9: Architect Perspective

Kafka Design Decisions

Partition Key Selection

Key Ordering Hot partition risk
paymentId Per payment lifecycle Low — spread
tenantId Per tenant Mega tenant hotspot
null None Even spread — no order
status Bad All COMPLETED one partition 
DEFAULT: paymentId for payment events
Mega tenant: composite key hash(tenantId + paymentId) or dedicated topic per tenant

ADR — Kafka as Integration Bus

## ADR-901: Apache Kafka for domain integration events

### Decision
All cross-service domain events via Kafka topics with Schema Registry.
Outbox from OLTP only. RF=3, acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2.

### Consequences
Ops team owns cluster SLO. Consumer lag monitoring mandatory.
Event catalog (Lesson 29) maintained. No synchronous Kafka request-reply for payments.

When NOT to Add Kafka

✗ Team of 3, one monolith — outbox to Kafka adds ops without benefit
✗ Replacing every HTTP call — sync validation still needed
✗ "Exactly-once" expectation without idempotent consumers — false confidence
✗ Storing large PDFs in messages — use S3 + event with reference

  2. Outbox marked published but message lost — prevention?

  6. MSK cluster sizing inputs?

Model Answer — Q14 (Lost Message Prevention)

A: Use acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 so leader crash after ack doesn't lose replicated data. Enable idempotent producer for retry safety. Outbox relay: mark published only after Kafka send callback success (or use transactional outbox with two-phase mark). Never acks=0/1 for payments. Monitor under-replicated partitions. If outbox published but consumer fails — OK (at-least-once); consumer idempotency handles duplicates. Lost before consumer is broker durability issue — fixed by acks=all + ISR.

Model Answer — Q13 (Topic Design)

A: Separate topics: payment.completed, payment.failed, payment.initiated — independent retention and subscribers. Key=paymentId for ordering per payment. Partitions 12–24 based on 5K TPS target and consumer parallelism. RF=3, retention 7d + S3 sink for archive. Schema Registry Avro BACKWARD. ACLs: payment-svc write, consumers read specific topics. DLT topics per consumer group or RetryableTopic suffix. Event catalog documents each.

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2, RF=3
  2. Idempotent producer enabled
  3. Outbox — publish only after broker ack; no dual-write
  4. Key = business id (paymentId) for ordering
  5. Manual offset commit after successful idempotent process
  6. Schema Registry with BACKWARD compatibility
  7. Separate topics per event type — not one mega-topic
  8. Monitor lag, under-replicated partitions, disk
  9. DLT + replay runbook (Lessons 29–30)
  10. Slim payloads — correlation in headers, not megabyte JSON

Part 16: Revision Notes

Quick Revision — Kafka Fundamentals

Kafka = distributed commit log (not delete-on-read queue)
Topic → partitions (ordered logs) → replicas (RF=3)
Leader serves read/write; ISR = in-sync followers

Producer: key → partition hash → ordering per key
acks=all + min.insync.replicas=2 — banking durability
enable.idempotence=true — producer retry dedup at broker

Consumer group: each partition → one consumer in group max
Multiple groups on same topic = fan-out (ledger, search, notify)

Offset = position; manual commit AFTER idempotent process
At-least-once + UNIQUE(eventId) = effective-once

Rebalance: consumer join/leave — tune session/max.poll.interval
Lag = consumer behind — metric + alert

Retention delete for events; compaction for latest-by-key
Outbox → Kafka — never dual-write without outbox ack callback

Memory Mnemonic

"Log it with all acks, key for order, commit after idempotent work, lag tells the truth"

Part 1: Concept

What Are Kafka Advanced Patterns?

Kafka advanced patterns go beyond basic produce/consume: exactly-once semantics (EOS), stream processing, reliable failure handling, cross-cluster replication, long-retention economics, and integration connectors. Architects use these when basic at-least-once + idempotency is not enough—or when operational requirements (DR, analytics, CDC) demand more machinery.

│  ─────────────────────────         ──────────────────────                │
│  at-least-once + idempotency         transactions (EOS where justified)  │
│  single consumer handler             Kafka Streams joins/windows         │
│  manual retry in code                RetryableTopic + DLT patterns       │
│  7-day retention on broker           tiered storage + S3 archive         │
│  one cluster                         MirrorMaker / cluster linking (DR)  │
│  app publishes outbox                Connect: Debezium, S3 sink          │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
