Part 1: Concept

What Is CI/CD?

Continuous Integration (CI) automatically builds and validates every code change. Continuous Delivery/Deployment (CD) automatically promotes proven artifacts to environments. For architects, CI/CD is the controlled path from developer commit to production payment API — with gates, not ad hoc deploys.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    CI/CD PIPELINE — payment-svc                          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  COMMIT → CI → ARTIFACT → CD → RUNTIME                                   │
│                                                                          │
│  git push     mvn test      Docker image    ArgoCD sync    EKS pods      │
│               Pact verify   Trivy scan      staging→prod   payment-svc   │
│               Sonar         push ECR        Flyway Job     v2.4.1        │
│                                                                          │
│  Principle: build once, promote same image SHA — never rebuild per env   │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

CI vs CD vs Continuous Deployment

Term Meaning Banking typical
CI Integrate + test on every change Mandatory
Continuous Delivery Always deploy-ready; manual prod approve Common prod
Continuous Deployment Auto to prod on green main Rare for core payments
GitOps Git repo = desired state; controller syncs cluster Prod standard

Pipeline Stages Master Table

Stage Actions Gate
Source Git push, PR Branch protection
Build Maven package Compile success
Unit test JUnit, Mockito Coverage threshold
Integration Testcontainers PG/Kafka Pass
Contract Pact consumer/provider Broker verify
Quality SonarQube No new blocker bugs
Security Trivy/Snyk image scan No CRITICAL CVE
Package Docker build + push ECR Immutable tag
Deploy staging ArgoCD / Helm Smoke tests
Migrate DB Flyway Job Success
Deploy prod Manual approval + ArgoCD Change ticket
Verify Synthetic payment test Rollback if fail

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why CI/CD Exists

Manual deploy CI/CD
"Works on my machine" Same artifact all envs
Forgot to run tests Automated gates
Unknown prod JAR version Image SHA traceability
Friday hotfix panic Rollback = retag previous SHA
SOX audit "who deployed?" Git + pipeline logs

Why Architects Mandate Pipelines

REGULATORY / SOX:
  Segregation of duties — developer cannot push directly to prod cluster
  Audit trail: commit → build ID → approver → deploy timestamp
  Immutable artifacts — no tampering on server

PLATFORM CONSISTENCY:
  Every microservice uses same archetype pipeline
  Connection budget, probes, scan — not optional per team

Build Once, Deploy Many

WRONG:
  Rebuild JAR on prod deploy with prod profile baked in — different binary

RIGHT:
  CI produces payment-svc:git-abc123 once
  Staging deploys abc123 → prod deploys **same abc123**
  Config differs via ConfigMap/Secrets per env — not rebuild

Part 3: Internal Working

CI Pipeline Internals (GitHub Actions / Jenkins / GitLab CI)

TRIGGER: PR opened or merge to main

Stage 1 — Checkout + Cache
  git clone, cache ~/.m2

Stage 2 — Maven verify
  ./mvnw clean verify
  Unit tests parallel

Stage 3 — Integration tests
  Testcontainers:
    PostgreSQL container — @DataJpaTest, @SpringBootTest
    Kafka container — consumer/producer test
  docker-compose optional in CI agent

Stage 4 — Pact
  Consumer tests publish pacts to Pact Broker
  Provider verification job (account-svc verifies payment-svc pacts)

Stage 5 — SonarQube
  mvn sonar:sonar — quality gate

Stage 6 — Docker build
  docker build -t $ECR/payment-svc:$GIT_SHA .
  Uses Dockerfile multi-stage (Lesson 34)

Stage 7 — Scan
  trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --exit-code 1

Stage 8 — Push ECR
  docker push $ECR/payment-svc:$GIT_SHA
  docker push $ECR/payment-svc:$VERSION (semver from tag)

Artifacts stored:
  ECR image digest, SBOM, test reports, Pact version

CD Pipeline Internals (GitOps — ArgoCD)

REPO STRUCTURE (GitOps):

app-repo:          payment-svc Java source, Dockerfile, CI workflow
platform-repo:     k8s manifests or Helm charts — env overlays

platform-repo/
  payment-svc/
    base/
      deployment.yaml
      service.yaml
    overlays/
      staging/
        kustomization.yaml  → image: .../payment-svc:abc123
      prod/
        kustomization.yaml  → image: .../payment-svc:abc123 (after promote)

ArgoCD watches platform-repo:
  staging branch auto-sync on SHA update
  prod branch: manual PR merge after approval ticket

Sync:
  ArgoCD compares Git desired state vs EKS live
  kubectl apply diff — rolling update (Lesson 35)

Database Migration in Pipeline

ORDER MATTERS:

1. CI passes — image abc123 in ECR
2. Update staging overlay image tag abc123
3. Run Flyway Job (K8s Job) against staging Aurora
   OR pipeline step: flyway migrate with staging credentials
4. Job success → ArgoCD sync Deployment staging
5. Smoke tests: POST /payments synthetic
6. Prod: change approval → Flyway Job prod → update prod overlay → sync

NEVER:
  15 pods each running Flyway on startup — race (Lesson 35)
  Deploy app before backward-compatible migration (expand-contract Lesson 22)

Environment Promotion Flow

dev:    every PR merge to develop — auto deploy dev EKS
staging: merge release/* or main — auto after CI
prod:   manual approval + CAB ticket — same image SHA as staging

Config only differences:
  SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE
  Aurora endpoint, MSK bootstrap, Redis host — ConfigMap/Secrets per overlay

Rollback Internals

FAST ROLLBACK (preferred):
  Git revert platform-repo prod overlay to previous image SHA
  ArgoCD sync → rolling back Deployment
  DB: if migration was expand-only (nullable column) — app rollback OK
  DB: if breaking migration — forward-fix only — architect plans expand-contract

K8s: kubectl rollout undo — emergency only; GitOps drift if not committed to Git

Part 4: Memory View

CI/CD Resource Footprint

CI RUNNER:
  Maven + tests: 4–8 GiB RAM agent
  Testcontainers: Docker-in-Docker — heavy — use dedicated large runners
  Parallel modules — matrix build payment-svc + contract tests

ECR:
  Image layers cached — storage cost per tag
  Lifecycle policy: keep last 30 SHA tags, semver permanent

ArgoCD:
  Lightweight controller — watches Git — minimal
  Sync wave ordering: Job migration before Deployment

PIPELINE DURATION TARGETS:
  CI PR feedback: < 12 min (unit + key integration)
  Full staging deploy: < 30 min including migration
  Architect tracks pipeline as developer productivity metric

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Pipeline Speed vs Quality Trade-offs

Optimization Save time Risk
Maven dependency cache 2–5 min Low
Parallel test modules 3–10 min Low
Skip integration on draft PR Fast feedback Miss bugs
Testcontainers vs shared staging DB Isolation Slower CI
Full Pact on every commit +2 min Worth it
Trivy on main only Faster PR CVE in merge

Deployment Strategies Performance

Strategy Downtime Rollback Banking
RollingUpdate Zero (Lesson 35) Git revert SHA Default
Blue/Green Zero Switch service selector High-risk releases
Canary Minimal Flagger/Istio weights Gradual payment traffic 
Canary payment-svc:
  5% traffic to v2.4.2 — monitor error rate 30 min — 50% — 100%
  Requires service mesh or ALB weighted target groups

Quality Gate Failure Impact

Block CRITICAL CVE in image:
  Delay release until base image patch — correct for banking

False positive Sonar:
  Waiver process with architect approval — not silent skip

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: GitHub Actions CI (Excerpt)

name: payment-svc-ci

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main, develop]
  push:
    branches: [main]

env:
  ECR_REGISTRY: 123456789.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com
  IMAGE_NAME: payment-svc

jobs:
  build-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up JDK 21
        uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          java-version: '21'
          distribution: 'temurin'
          cache: maven

      - name: Unit and integration tests
        run: ./mvnw -B verify

      - name: Pact publish (consumer)
        if: github.event_name == 'push'
        run: ./mvnw -B pact:publish -Dpactbroker.url=${{ secrets.PACT_BROKER_URL }}

      - name: SonarQube
        run: ./mvnw -B sonar:sonar -Dsonar.qualitygate.wait=true

  docker:
    needs: build-test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Configure AWS credentials
        uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/github-actions-ecr-push
          aws-region: ap-south-1

      - name: Login to ECR
        uses: aws-actions/amazon-ecr-login@v2

      - name: Build and push
        run: |
          IMAGE_TAG=${{ github.sha }}
          docker build -t $ECR_REGISTRY/$IMAGE_NAME:$IMAGE_TAG .
          docker push $ECR_REGISTRY/$IMAGE_NAME:$IMAGE_TAG

      - name: Trivy scan
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
        with:
          image-ref: ${{ env.ECR_REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }}
          severity: 'CRITICAL,HIGH'
          exit-code: '1'

Example 2: GitOps — Kustomize Overlay

# platform-repo/payment-svc/overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - ../../base
images:
  - name: payment-svc
    newName: 123456789.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/payment-svc
    newTag: abc123def456   # updated by CI bot or manual promote PR
patches:
  - path: replicas-patch.yaml
  - path: resources-patch.yaml
configMapGenerator:
  - name: payment-config
    files:
      - application-prod.yaml

Example 3: ArgoCD Application

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: payment-svc-prod
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: payments
  source:
    repoURL: https://git.bank.com/platform/k8s-manifests.git
    targetRevision: prod
    path: payment-svc/overlays/prod
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: payments-prod
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: false
      selfHeal: true
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=false
  ignoreDifferences:
    - group: apps
      kind: Deployment
      jsonPointers:
        - /spec/replicas   # HPA owns replicas

Example 4: Flyway Job in Pipeline (Helm Hook Concept)

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: payment-svc-flyway-{{ .Values.image.tag }}
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PreSync
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: BeforeHookCreation
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: flyway
          image: flyway/flyway:10
          args: ["migrate", "-url=jdbc:postgresql://$(RDS_HOST)/payments", ...]

ArgoCD PreSync: migration Job completes before Deployment sync

Example 5: Pact Provider Verification in CI

# account-svc pipeline step
- name: Verify pacts from payment-svc
  run: |
    ./mvnw -B pact:verify \
      -Dpactbroker.url=$PACT_BROKER_URL \
      -Dpactbroker.providerTags=prod \
      -Dpactbroker.consumerVersionSelectors='[{"tag":"main"}]'

Example 6: Smoke Test Post-Deploy

#!/bin/bash
set -e
CORR_ID=$(uuidgen)
HTTP_CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" \
  -X POST "https://staging-api.bank.com/api/v1/payments/health-check-transfer" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SMOKE_TEST_TOKEN" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: smoke-$CORR_ID" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"debtorAccountId":"ACC-SMOKE","creditorAccountId":"ACC-SMOKE2","amount":"1.00","currency":"INR","paymentType":"INTERNAL"}')

[[ "$HTTP_CODE" == "201" || "$HTTP_CODE" == "503" ]] || exit 1
# 503 acceptable if downstream smoke accounts unavailable — configure per env

Part 7: Production Usage

CI/CD in Production Banking

Segregation of Duties (SOX)

Roles:
  Developer — merge to main after PR approval (peer review)
  CI system — build and push image (service account)
  Release manager — approve prod GitOps PR (not code author alone)
  Platform SRE — ArgoCD admin, emergency break-glass logged

No kubectl apply prod by developers — GitOps PR only
Break-glass: documented incident ticket + post-hoc Git reconcile

Change Advisory Board (CAB) Integration

Prod deploy requires:
  Jira change ticket CHG-12345
  Pipeline links: CI run URL, image SHA, Pact results
  Flyway scripts listed
  Rollback SHA documented
  Maintenance window for risky migrations (expand-contract still preferred)

Production Pipeline Checklist

Gate Required
Unit + integration pass Yes
Pact verify (consumers) Yes for API change
Sonar quality gate Yes
Image scan CRITICAL=0 Yes (or waiver)
Same SHA staging→prod Yes
Flyway Job success before prod sync Yes
Smoke test post staging Yes
Manual prod approval Yes
Synthetic prod monitor post deploy Yes

Secrets in CI

GitHub OIDC → AWS IAM role (no long-lived AWS keys in GitHub Secrets)
DB migrate credentials: short-lived from Secrets Manager in Job pod
Never: prod DB password in GitHub repo variables unencrypted

Part 8: Microservice Usage

CI/CD Across Payment Platform

Monorepo vs Polyrepo

Monorepo Polyrepo per MS
CI Path filters — only payment-svc builds Independent pipelines
Coupling Shared library version bump Loose
Banking Platform team libs monorepo payment-svc own repo common 
Platform repo (GitOps):
  payment-svc/, account-svc/, ledger-svc/ overlays — one ArgoCD per app
CI triggers:
  payment-svc repo merge → update platform-repo staging tag via bot PR

Contract Testing in Multi-Service Pipeline

PR payment-svc changes AccountClient:
  1. payment-svc CI publishes new pact to broker (can-i-deploy check)
  2. account-svc provider verification must pass before payment deploy prod
  OR
  Consumer-driven: account-svc verifies on their CI against latest payment pact

Architect: Pact Broker as deployment gate — prevents breaking account API

Library vs Service Release

shared-payment-lib JAR:
  Separate versioning — consumers pin version
  Library change → release lib → update each MS PR — not bundled silent

Part 9: Architect Perspective

CI/CD Architecture Decisions

GitOps vs Pipeline-Only CD

GitOps (ArgoCD) Jenkins kubectl
Drift detection Yes No
Audit Git history Pipeline logs
Rollback Git revert Redeploy script
Banking prod Preferred Legacy

ADR — GitOps + Immutable ECR Tags

## ADR-1301: Production deploy via ArgoCD and ECR image SHA

### Decision
No kubectl manual prod. platform-repo prod branch is SoT.
CI pushes ECR payment-svc:$GIT_SHA only on main green build.
Promote = PR updating kustomize newTag.

### Consequences
Rollback = revert Git tag. Flyway PreSync Job mandatory.
Developers need platform-repo PR access via release bot.

ADR — Expand-Contract Migrations Only

## ADR-1302: Flyway migrations must be backward compatible one release

### Decision
NOT NULL new columns require expand-contract (Lesson 22).
Pipeline blocks deploy if Flyway script lacks rollback notes in ticket.

### Consequences
Two-release features for breaking schema — planned in roadmap.

Canary vs Rolling for Payments

Default: RollingUpdate maxUnavailable 0 — sufficient with good probes
Canary: high-risk payment logic change — 5% corporate traffic — requires mesh/ALB weights
Never: big-bang deploy Friday 16:00 without rollback SHA ready

  1. Design full CI/CD for payment-svc to EKS prod.
  2. SOX segregation of duties in pipeline?
  3. Breaking DB migration + app rollback — prevention?
  4. Canary deployment for payment API — design?
  5. Monorepo vs polyrepo CI for 15 microservices?
  6. Trivy blocks release on CVE — process?
  7. Staging-prod parity gaps — acceptable?
  8. Emergency hotfix pipeline bypass — governance?

Model Answer — Q13 (Full Pipeline Design)

A: Developer PR → GitHub Actions: Maven verify, Testcontainers PG/Kafka, Pact consumer publish, Sonar gate, on merge to main Docker build multi-stage, Trivy scan, push ECR payment-svc:$SHA. Bot opens platform-repo PR updating staging newTag: $SHA. ArgoCD sync staging: PreSync Flyway Job on Aurora staging, then Deployment rolling update. Smoke synthetic payment. Manual CAB approval → promote same $SHA to prod overlay PR → ArgoCD prod sync, Flyway prod Job, smoke, synthetic monitor 15 min. Rollback: revert prod overlay to previous SHA. OIDC to AWS no static keys. IRSA in cluster. Contract verify with account-svc via Pact Broker can-i-deploy gate.

Model Answer — Q15 (Breaking Migration)

A: Prevent with expand-contract (Lesson 22): V1 add nullable column, deploy app v2 reading/writing, backfill, V2 add NOT NULL, deploy app v3. Rollback app to v1 always works while column nullable. Pipeline rule: Flyway SQL reviewed in PR for backward compatibility. Breaking migrations require two-release plan in ADR — no same-release rollback expectation. Forward-only repair if mistake shipped.

Part 13: Common Mistakes

# Mistake Consequence Fix
1 Rebuild per environment Different binaries Same ECR SHA
2 Flyway on pod start Race PreSync Job
3 No image scan CVE prod Trivy gate
4 kubectl prod manual Drift, no audit GitOps
5 Skip Pact Break account-svc Broker gate
6 Secrets in Git Breach OIDC + SM
7 Deploy before migration App crash Job first
8 :latest tag prod Unknown rollback SHA tag
9 No smoke test Bad deploy live Post-deploy curl
10 Breaking migration Rollback impossible Expand-contract

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Build once — promote immutable ECR SHA staging→prod
  2. GitOps ArgoCD — Git is prod desired state
  3. Flyway PreSync Job — never per-pod migrate
  4. Expand-contract migrations — backward compatible one release
  5. Pact + Sonar + Trivy gates in CI
  6. OIDC to AWS — no long-lived CI keys
  7. Manual prod approval + CAB ticket — SOX
  8. Smoke/synthetic tests post deploy
  9. Document rollback SHA in every change ticket
  10. Platform pipeline template — all MS inherit

Part 1: Concept

What Is Infrastructure as Code?

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) defines cloud resources — networks, clusters, databases, Kafka — in declarative files (Terraform HCL, CloudFormation YAML) stored in Git. The platform is reproducible, reviewable, and environment-consistent instead of click-ops in the AWS Console.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              CLICK-OPS vs INFRASTRUCTURE AS CODE                         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  CLICK-OPS (console)              IaC (Terraform)                        │
│  ───────────────────              ────────────────                       │
│  "Who changed the SG?"            Git blame on sg.tf                     │
│  Staging ≠ prod mystery           Same module, different tfvars          │
│  Disaster rebuild = panic         terraform apply from Git               │
│  No PR review on RDS size         Architect reviews scale in PR          │
│                                                                          │
│  Banking: IaC mandatory for prod — SOX change control                    │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

IaC Tooling Master Table

Tool Type Banking use
Terraform (OpenTofu) Multi-cloud HCL Primary — VPC, EKS, RDS, MSK
AWS CloudFormation AWS-native YAML/JSON AWS-only shops, org guardrails
AWS CDK Code generates CFN TypeScript/Java infra
Pulumi General-purpose languages Teams prefer Java/Python IaC
Crossplane K8s CRDs for cloud GitOps-native platform teams
Helm/Kustomize App config on K8s Lesson 37 — complements IaC

What IaC Owns vs What GitOps Owns

Layer Tool Examples
Foundation Terraform VPC, subnets, EKS, RDS, MSK, IAM
Platform add-ons Terraform or Helm AWS LB Controller, External Secrets
Application ArgoCD/Kustomize payment-svc Deployment, HPA
Data schema Flyway payments table migrations 
Architect rule:
  Terraform creates the Aurora cluster
  Flyway creates tables inside it
  ArgoCD deploys pods that connect to it
  Never mix these responsibilities in one tool

Part 3: Internal Working

Terraform Core Concepts

WORKFLOW:

1. Write .tf files (resources, modules, variables)
2. terraform init     — download providers (aws ~> 5.0)
3. terraform plan     — diff desired vs state
4. terraform apply    — create/update/delete AWS resources
5. State file tracks real resource IDs

STATE:
  S3 backend s3://bank-terraform-state/prod/payments/terraform.tfstate
  DynamoDB lock table — prevent concurrent apply corruption
  State = mapping terraform address → aws_instance.id

Module Composition (Payment Platform)

infra/
  modules/
    vpc/
    eks/
    aurora-postgres/
    msk/
    elasticache-redis/
    s3-archive/
  environments/
    dev/
      main.tf          → calls modules with dev tfvars
      terraform.tfvars → instance sizes small
    staging/
    prod/
      main.tf
      terraform.tfvars → db.r6g.xlarge, msk kafka.m5.large

# environments/prod/main.tf (conceptual)
module "vpc" {
  source = "../../modules/vpc"
  cidr   = var.vpc_cidr
  azs    = ["ap-south-1a", "ap-south-1b", "ap-south-1c"]
}

module "eks" {
  source         = "../../modules/eks"
  vpc_id         = module.vpc.vpc_id
  private_subnets = module.vpc.private_app_subnet_ids
  cluster_version = "1.29"
}

module "aurora" {
  source            = "../../modules/aurora-postgres"
  vpc_id            = module.vpc.vpc_id
  database_subnets  = module.vpc.private_data_subnet_ids
  allowed_sg_ids    = [module.eks.node_security_group_id]
  instance_class    = var.aurora_instance_class
}

Plan Output (What Architects Review)

# module.aurora.aws_rds_cluster_instance.primary will be updated in-place
~ instance_class = "db.r6g.large" -> "db.r6g.xlarge"

# module.msk.aws_msk_cluster.main will be created
+ broker_node_group_info { ... }

Architect PR review:
  ✓ Expected change?
  ✓ Downtime? (Aurora class change may brief failover)
  ✓ Cost impact?
  ✗ Unexpected destroy — STOP

State and Drift

DRIFT: Engineer changed SG in console — terraform plan shows:
  ~ ingress rule will be reverted to Git definition

selfHeal in ArgoCD for apps; terraform apply for infra drift correction
Or: deny console edits via IAM SCP — force IaC only

CloudFormation Alternative (Brief)

# AWS-native — Stack sets for org-wide guardrails
Resources:
  PaymentVPC:
    Type: AWS::EC2::VPC
    Properties:
      CidrBlock: 10.0.0.0/16

Terraform preferred multi-cloud/hybrid narrative
CloudFormation fine AWS-pure — CDK generates it
Many banks: Terraform for platform, CFN for AWS Control Tower baselines

IAM in IaC (Lesson 36 Link)

resource "aws_iam_role" "payment_svc" {
  name = "payment-svc-irsa"
  assume_role_policy = data.aws_iam_policy_document.oidc.json
}

resource "aws_iam_role_policy" "payment_svc_s3" {
  role = aws_iam_role.payment_svc.id
  policy = jsonencode({
    Statement = [{
      Effect   = "Allow"
      Action   = ["s3:PutObject"]
      Resource = "${aws_s3_bucket.archive.arn}/payment/*"
    }]
  })
}

IRSA trust policy tied to EKS OIDC provider — all in Terraform
No manual IAM console for prod roles

Part 4: Memory View

IaC and Operational Footprint

TERRAFORM STATE FILE:
  JSON mapping — not huge if structured modules
  Sensitive outputs marked sensitive = true — not logged in CI

PLAN MEMORY:
  Large monolithic state (10k resources) — slow plan
  Split state by domain:
    state/prod/network.tfstate
    state/prod/data.tfstate
    state/prod/eks.tfstate
  Reduces blast radius of apply errors

MODULE OUTPUTS feed next module:
  eks.cluster_endpoint → kubeconfig for Helm provider
  aurora.writer_endpoint → K8s ExternalSecret / ConfigMap via separate GitOps

Terraform does NOT store application data — only infrastructure metadata

Part 5: Performance Analysis

IaC Impact on Platform Performance

IaC choice Runtime performance Ops performance
Aurora class in tfvars DB TPS/latency Scale via PR
MSK broker size Kafka throughput Module variable
EKS node instance type Pod CPU/memory Node group tfvars
RDS Proxy module flag Connection pooling Enable for HPA
NAT vs VPC endpoints Latency + cost Module design

Environment Parity vs Cost

Same modules, different tfvars:

dev:     t3.medium nodes, db.t4g.medium Aurora, MSK kafka.t3.small
staging: prod-like topology, half size
prod:    r6g.xlarge Aurora, m5.large MSK brokers

Architect: staging topology mirrors prod (multi-AZ yes) — size differs
  Catch SG and subnet bugs — not single-AZ dev lie

Apply Time and Blast Radius

terraform apply prod:
  VPC change — rare, high risk — change window
  EKS node group rolling — new nodes join, drain old — coordinate with app PDB
  Aurora instance class — failover ~30s — notify on-call

-target flag for emergency narrow apply — use sparingly — causes drift if habit

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: VPC Module Variables

# modules/vpc/variables.tf
variable "name" { type = string }
variable "cidr" { type = string }
variable "azs" {
  type = list(string)
}

# modules/vpc/main.tf — simplified
resource "aws_vpc" "main" {
  cidr_block           = var.cidr
  enable_dns_hostnames = true
  tags = { Name = var.name }
}

resource "aws_subnet" "private_app" {
  count             = length(var.azs)
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id
  cidr_block        = cidrsubnet(var.cidr, 4, count.index + 1)
  availability_zone = var.azs[count.index]
  tags = { Tier = "private-app" }
}

resource "aws_subnet" "private_data" {
  count             = length(var.azs)
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id
  cidr_block        = cidrsubnet(var.cidr, 4, count.index + 10)
  availability_zone = var.azs[count.index]
  tags = { Tier = "private-data" }
}

Example 2: Aurora Module with SG

resource "aws_security_group" "aurora" {
  name   = "${var.name}-aurora"
  vpc_id = var.vpc_id

  ingress {
    from_port       = 5432
    to_port         = 5432
    protocol        = "tcp"
    security_groups = var.allowed_sg_ids
  }
}

resource "aws_rds_cluster" "main" {
  cluster_identifier = var.name
  engine             = "aurora-postgresql"
  engine_version     = var.engine_version
  database_name      = "payments"
  master_username    = var.master_username
  master_password    = var.master_password # or manage via Secrets Manager resource
  db_subnet_group_name   = aws_db_subnet_group.main.name
  vpc_security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.aurora.id]
  storage_encrypted      = true
  kms_key_id             = var.kms_key_arn
  backup_retention_period = 35
  skip_final_snapshot    = false
  deletion_protection    = true
}

Example 3: Prod tfvars

# environments/prod/terraform.tfvars
vpc_cidr              = "10.0.0.0/16"
aurora_instance_class = "db.r6g.xlarge"
aurora_instance_count = 2
msk_broker_instance   = "kafka.m5.large"
msk_broker_count      = 3
eks_node_instance_types = ["m6i.xlarge"]
eks_node_desired_size   = 6
eks_node_min_size       = 3
eks_node_max_size       = 15
redis_node_type         = "cache.r6g.large"

Example 4: Remote Backend

# environments/prod/backend.tf
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "bank-terraform-state"
    key            = "prod/payments-platform/terraform.tfstate"
    region         = "ap-south-1"
    encrypt        = true
    dynamodb_table = "terraform-locks"
  }

  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 5.0"
    }
  }
}

Example 5: CI Pipeline for Terraform

name: terraform-prod

on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ['infra/**']

jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      id-token: write
      contents: read
      pull-requests: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3

      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/terraform-plan-ci
          aws-region: ap-south-1

      - name: Terraform Plan
        working-directory: infra/environments/prod
        run: |
          terraform init -input=false
          terraform plan -input=false -out=tfplan -no-color | tee plan.txt

      - name: Comment PR with plan
        uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            // post plan.txt as PR comment for architect review

  apply:
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && github.event_name == 'push'
    needs: plan
    environment: production-infra  # manual approval gate
    steps:
      - name: Terraform Apply
        run: terraform apply -input=false tfplan

Example 6: Output to GitOps (Pattern)

output "aurora_writer_endpoint" {
  value     = aws_rds_cluster.main.endpoint
  sensitive = true
}

output "msk_bootstrap_brokers" {
  value = aws_msk_cluster.main.bootstrap_brokers_tls
}

External Secrets or SSM Parameter Store:
  Terraform writes endpoints to SSM
  EKS External Secrets syncs to payment-svc ConfigMap
  Avoid hardcoding endpoints in app repo

Part 9: Architect Perspective

IaC Architecture Decisions

Monolithic State vs Split State

Monolithic Split by domain
Plan speed Slow at scale Faster
Blast radius Large Isolated
Banking prod Avoid network / data / compute

ADR — Terraform as Infra SoT

## ADR-1401: All AWS infra via Terraform modules in bank-platform-infra

### Decision
No prod console changes except break-glass logged.
Modules for vpc, eks, aurora, msk, redis, s3.
Remote state S3 + DynamoDB lock. Plan in PR, apply on main with approval.

### Consequences
Platform team bottleneck — module requests SLA 2 days.
Drift detected weekly terraform plan cron — alert on diff.

ADR — Staging Topology Parity

## ADR-1402: Staging uses same modules as prod, scaled-down tfvars

### Decision
Multi-AZ staging mandatory. Single-AZ dev only for individual sandboxes.

### Consequences
Higher staging cost — justified by fewer prod surprises.

When CloudFormation Instead

Org already on AWS Control Tower + StackSets for account vending
Terraform for workload infra inside accounts — hybrid acceptable
Architect documents which tool owns which layer — no overlap confusion

Model Answer — Q13 (Repo Structure)

A: bank-platform-infra: Terraform modules (vpc, eks, aurora, msk, redis, s3, iam), environments/dev|staging|prod with tfvars, S3 remote state + lock, CI plan on PR apply on main with approval. bank-k8s-manifests: ArgoCD Kustomize per MS per env. payment-svc: Java + Dockerfile + GitHub Actions CI (Lesson 37). Flow: Terraform creates EKS+Aurora+MSK, outputs to SSM, External Secrets in cluster, Flyway Job uses Aurora, ArgoCD deploys image SHA. Segregation: platform owns infra repo, product owns app + k8s manifest PRs. Pact/Sonar/Trivy on app; tfsec on infra.

Model Answer — Q14 (Aurora Scale-Up)

A: PR module tfvars instance class large→xlarge. CI plan shows in-place update, estimate brief failover. Schedule CAB window if needed. Pre-check: connection pool via RDS Proxy, Hikari retry. Apply during low traffic. Post: CloudWatch DatabaseConnections, payment synthetic, lag metrics. Rollback PR revert tfvars re-apply if performance regression — second failover. Document in change ticket.

Part 13: Common Mistakes

# Mistake Consequence Fix
1 State on laptop Loss/corrupt S3 remote
2 No lock Parallel apply corrupt DynamoDB
3 Console prod edit Drift SCP deny + import
4 Secrets in tfstate plain Leak sensitive + SM
5 Monolithic 8k resources Slow/risky Split state
6 Copy-paste VPC Inconsistent Modules
7 Terraform runs Flyway Wrong tool Separate pipeline
8 0.0.0.0/0 in SG tf Open DB tfsec gate
9 dev single-AZ only Prod surprise Staging multi-AZ
10 apply without plan Destroy prod Plan mandatory

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Modules for vpc, eks, aurora, msk — environments use tfvars
  2. Remote state S3 encrypted + DynamoDB lock
  3. Plan on every PR — architect reviews diff
  4. Manual prod apply with approval — SOX
  5. Policy scan tfsec/Checkov in CI
  6. Outputs → SSM for GitOps consumption — no hardcoded endpoints
  7. Split state by domain at scale
  8. Staging topology = prod topology — size differs
  9. deletion_protection on Aurora, MSK prod
  10. Document IaC vs GitOps vs Flyway boundaries in onboarding

Part 1: Concept

What Are Architectural Patterns?

Architectural patterns are reusable solutions to recurring system-structure problems at the application and enterprise level. They describe how components relate — not individual classes. A Solution Architect selects patterns to meet scalability, consistency, team boundaries, and compliance — then records the choice in an ADR.

│                                                                          │
│  ENTERPRISE          INTEGRATION         APPLICATION        DATA         │
│  ─────────           ───────────         ────────────       ────         │
│  API Gateway         Saga                Layered service    CQRS         │
│  BFF                 Outbox              Hexagonal ports    Event Sourcing │
│  Strangler Fig       ACL                 DDD aggregates   Database/MS    │
│  Microservices       Circuit Breaker     Repository                        │
│                                                                          │
│  Architect composes patterns — does not apply all at once                │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why Patterns Matter for Architects

Ad hoc architecture Pattern-driven architecture
"We'll use Kafka everywhere" Outbox for facts, sync for validate
Shared database "microservices" Database per service + saga
One REST chain of 8 calls BFF compose + async side effects
Big bang legacy replacement Strangler Fig
Meeting debates from scratch Shared vocabulary + ADR

The Architect's Job

NOT: Draw boxes and pick trendy tech
YES:
  1. Identify quality attributes (latency, consistency, audit, scale)
  2. Map domain to bounded contexts (DDD)
  3. Select minimal pattern set that satisfies attributes
  4. Document trade-offs in ADR
  5. Ensure teams implement consistently (gateway standards, outbox mandatory)

Part 3: Internal Working

Domain-Driven Design (DDD) — Structural Foundation

Bounded Context

PAYMENT CONTEXT:
  Aggregate: Payment (paymentId, status, amount, idempotencyKey)
  Invariant: cannot COMPLETE without saga steps satisfied

ACCOUNT CONTEXT:
  Aggregate: Account (balance, holds, status)
  Invariant: balance never negative without overdraft product

LEDGER CONTEXT:
  Aggregate: LedgerTransaction (balanced entries)
  Invariant: debits = credits

Same word "Account" — different models — separate services and schemas

Aggregate Rules

AGGREGATE = consistency boundary for transactions

Payment aggregate:
  Root: PaymentEntity
  Includes: PaymentApproval (1:1) — same transaction boundary
  Excludes: LedgerEntry — different context, eventual via event

Rule: one transaction modifies one aggregate instance
Cross-aggregate: saga + events — not single @Transactional join

Ubiquitous Language

Business says: "initiate NEFT transfer"
Model says: Payment.initiate(NEFT) → status PENDING
Not: processTransactionRecordType7

Architect ensures API names, Kafka topics, DB tables align with business language
  payment.completed not generic EVENT_42

API Gateway Pattern

                    ┌─────────────┐
  Clients ─────────►│ API Gateway │  WAF, TLS, JWT, rate limit
                    └──────┬──────┘
                           │
              ┌────────────┼────────────┐
              ▼            ▼            ▼
         payment-svc  account-svc   fraud-svc

Gateway responsibilities (Lesson 26):
  Cross-cutting edge — NOT business rules
  Token validation first pass; services re-validate (zero trust)

Implementation: Spring Cloud Gateway on EKS, ALB Ingress (Lessons 35–36)

BFF (Backend for Frontend)

Corporate portal BFF (WebFlux — Lesson 20):
  GET /dashboard → zip(account, pending payments, limits)

Mobile BFF:
  Smaller DTOs, fewer fields

BFF does NOT:
  Own @Transactional payment creation — POST still to payment-svc
  Become god orchestrator for all sagas

When to use:
  Different client shapes, reduce chatty mobile calls
When to skip:
  Single API client, OpenAPI sufficient

CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)

WRITE MODEL (Command side):
  POST /payments → payment-svc → Aurora OLTP normalized schema
  Strong consistency, constraints, idempotency

READ MODEL (Query side):
  GET /payments/search → search-svc → Elasticsearch projection
  Fed by payment.completed / payment.failed events
  Eventual lag 2–10s — acceptable for search UI

Architect decision (Lesson 29 ADR):
  Authoritative detail: GET /payments/{id} → OLTP
  Search at scale: CQRS read model
  NOT: CQRS for account balance — SoT stays relational

Saga Pattern (Orchestration)

Orchestrator: payment-svc (Lesson 28)

Steps:
  1. Create Payment PENDING (local TX)
  2. Sync validate account + fraud
  3. Hold/debit account-svc (idempotent HTTP)
  4. Mark COMPLETED + outbox PaymentCompleted
  5. Async: ledger, notify, search

Compensate: release hold on failure
State: saga_instances table

vs Choreography:
  Use for notifications fan-out — not money coordination

Outbox + Event-Driven

Same DB transaction:
  INSERT payment + INSERT outbox_events

Relay → MSK payment.completed

Consumers: ledger, search, warehouse (Lesson 31)

Pattern pairs with:
  Idempotent consumers — at-least-once
  NOT dual-write to Kafka

Strangler Fig (Legacy Migration)

Phase 1: Gateway routes /api/v1/payments → new payment-svc
         account still monolith internal API
Phase 2: Extract account-svc
Phase 3: Extract ledger-svc
Phase 4: Decommission monolith module

Metrics: % traffic on strangler, error rate parity, rollback plan
Architect owns migration roadmap — not big bang

Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL)

account-svc internal:
  Domain: clean AccountSummary DTO

ACL adapter:
  Translates mainframe COBOL copybook / ugly XML ↔ domain model

payment-svc never imports mainframe JAR or sees legacy field names
All legacy quirks contained in account-svc boundary

Event Sourcing — When and When Not

EVENT SOURCING = store state changes as immutable event log; current state = replay

USE (banking):
  Audit timeline UI, dispute evidence
  Saga step log (Lesson 28)

AVOID as payment SoT (Lesson 32):
  Relational OLTP + outbox simpler for ACID money
  Team ops maturity required for ES snapshot/replay

Hybrid (common):
  PostgreSQL payment row SoT + Kafka domain events for integration

CAP / PACELC at System Level (Lesson 23 Echo)

Payment POST (sync validate):
  Choose CP — fail if account-svc unavailable (consistency over availability)

Search index:
  Choose AP — eventual lag OK (availability + partition tolerance)

Architect documents per component — not one choice for whole bank

Part 4: Memory View

Pattern Impact on Runtime Footprint

GATEWAY + BFF:
  Extra hop ~1–3ms — acceptable for edge policy
  BFF aggregation — parallel calls — memory for merged DTO (Lesson 20)

CQRS:
  Duplicate data: OLTP row + ES document — storage cost
  JVM: search-svc separate from payment-svc — isolate heap

SAGA:
  saga_instances + step_log rows — small vs payment volume
  Orchestrator state in payment DB — not in-memory only

EVENT SOURCING (if used):
  Event store growth — snapshot strategy required — architect plans retention

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Pattern Trade-offs

Pattern Latency Consistency Complexity Scale
Monolith Lowest Strong local Low Vertical
Sync microservices +network Per-service Medium Horizontal
Saga + async ledger Lower user path Eventual ledger High High
CQRS search Fast read Eventual search Medium Read scale
BFF aggregate max(parallel) Depends Medium Client UX
Gateway +1–3ms — Low Edge scale
Event sourcing Replay cost Auditable Very high Write append

Anti-Pattern Performance Tax

DISTRIBUTED MONOLITH (Lesson 25):
  8 sync calls per payment — p95 400ms+ — fragile
  Fix: saga boundaries, async side effects, BFF for reads only

REACTIVE EVERYWHERE (Lesson 20):
  WebFlux + JPA blocking — event loop stall
  Fix: gateway/BFF reactive; domain MVC + JPA

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Payment Aggregate (DDD)

@Entity
@Table(name = "payments")
public class Payment { // aggregate root

    @Id
    private String paymentId;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    private PaymentStatus status;

    private String idempotencyKey;

    @Version
    private Long version;

    public void initiate(TransferCommand cmd) {
        if (status != null) throw new IllegalStateException("Already initialized");
        this.status = PaymentStatus.PENDING;
        // invariants enforced here
    }

    public void complete() {
        if (status != PaymentStatus.DEBITED && status != PaymentStatus.PENDING)
            throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot complete from " + status);
        this.status = PaymentStatus.COMPLETED;
    }
}

Example 2: ACL in account-svc

@Component
public class MainframeAccountAdapter implements AccountPort {

    private final MainframeClient legacyClient;

    @Override
    public AccountSummary getSummary(String accountId) {
        MainframeResponse raw = legacyClient.fetchAccount(copybookRequest(accountId));
        return AccountSummary.builder()
            .accountId(accountId)
            .availableBalance(raw.getAvailBalDecimal())
            .status(mapStatus(raw.getAcctStatusCode()))
            .build();
    }
}

// payment-svc depends on AccountPort interface via Feign — never MainframeResponse

Example 3: CQRS — Command vs Query Controllers

// payment-svc — command
@PostMapping("/api/v1/payments")
public ResponseEntity<PaymentResponse> create(@RequestBody CreatePaymentRequest req) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(CREATED).body(commandService.create(req));
}

// search-svc — query (different service, ES backing)
@GetMapping("/api/v1/payments/search")
public SearchPage<PaymentSearchHit> search(@RequestParam String q, @RequestParam String status) {
    return searchService.search(q, status);
}

Example 4: Outbox in Same Transaction

@Transactional
public PaymentResponse completePayment(String paymentId) {
    Payment payment = paymentRepo.findById(paymentId).orElseThrow();
    payment.complete();
    outboxRepo.save(OutboxEvent.paymentCompleted(payment));
    return PaymentResponse.from(payment);
}

Example 5: BFF Aggregation

@GetMapping("/mobile/v1/dashboard")
public Mono<DashboardDto> dashboard(@AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) {
    String accountId = jwt.getClaim("primary_account");
    return Mono.zip(
        accountClient.getSummary(accountId),
        paymentClient.getPending(accountId),
        limitClient.getRemaining(accountId)
    ).map(t -> DashboardDto.of(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3()));
}

Example 6: ADR Template

# ADR-015: Orchestrated saga for transfer; async ledger post

## Status
Accepted

## Context
Transfer spans payment, account, ledger DBs. No XA (Lesson 18).

## Decision
payment-svc orchestrates sync hold + local COMPLETE.
Ledger via PaymentCompleted Kafka consumer idempotent.

## Consequences
Ledger lag ~2–5s. Reconciliation nightly. Saga tables in payment-svc.

Model Answer — Q13 (HLD with Patterns)

A: North-south: Route53→WAF→ALB→API Gateway (JWT, rate limit). Optional BFF for corporate dashboard aggregation. payment-svc (DDD aggregate, saga orchestrator): sync REST to account-svc (ACL to core banking) and fraud-svc; local Aurora TX; outbox→MSK PaymentCompleted. ledger-svc idempotent async consumer; search-svc CQRS ES projection; notification-svc choreography. Database per service. Strangler for remaining monolith modules. EKS/Terraform/GitOps platform. Reconciliation for eventual ledger. ADRs document each choice.

Model Answer — Q14 (Async Ledger)

A: Async ledger decouples user latency from ledger insert and survives ledger brief outage (Kafka buffers). User gets COMPLETED on payment row; ledger catches up in seconds. Sync ledger adds RTT and failure point to user path — payment fails if ledger down though money hold placed — harder compensate. Banking accepts eventual ledger with idempotent consumer + nightly reconciliation (Lessons 28–29). Sync only if regulation explicitly requires same-second ledger visibility — rare; then tighten SLO and couple availability.

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Start from bounded contexts — patterns follow domain
  2. Minimal pattern set — justify each in ADR
  3. Gateway + outbox + saga — banking microservices baseline
  4. CQRS for search — not for money SoT
  5. ACL for all legacy integration
  6. Strangler for monolith exit — measure traffic shift
  7. Orchestrate money, choreograph notifications
  8. Reject XA across services
  9. Maintain ADR catalog — link infra and app ADRs
  10. Reference HLD updated when patterns change

Part 16: Revision Notes

Quick Revision — Architectural Patterns

DDD: bounded context, aggregate, ubiquitous language
Gateway: north-south TLS JWT rate limit — not business logic
BFF: per-client aggregate read — not payment write
Microservices: DB per service, independent deploy (Lesson 25)

Saga orchestration: money cross-DB | choreography: notify/search
Outbox: same TX as OLTP → Kafka | idempotent consumers
CQRS: write OLTP, read ES projection — search not balance
ACL: legacy inside account-svc — clean ports outward
Strangler Fig: incremental extract from monolith

ES: audit/saga log OK — payment SoT usually relational
CAP: sync validate CP | search AP eventual
ADR documents every pattern choice — trade-offs explicit

Anti: distributed monolith, shared DB, Kafka sync query, ES all

Memory Mnemonic

"Bound the domain, gate the edge, saga the money, outbox the news, CQRS the search"

Lesson 39 named patterns and how to combine them. Lesson 40 teaches how to document and present architecture:

[REDACTED]

Prerequisites: Lesson 39 (patterns, ADR, reference platform) · Lessons 25–29 (microservices, communication, saga) · Lessons 36–38 (AWS, EKS, Terraform) · Lesson 30 (SLO/resilience) · Lesson 24 (capacity, connections)

Part 1: Concept

What Is High-Level Design (HLD)?

High-Level Design (HLD) is the architecture document that describes what the system is, major components, how they interact, non-functional requirements (NFRs), and key decisions — without class-level code detail (that is LLD — Lesson 41).

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    HLD vs LLD vs ADR                                     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  HLD                         LLD                      ADR                │
│  ───                         ───                      ───                │
│  System structure            Class/API detail           Single decision    │
│  C4 Context/Container        Sequence at method level   Why X not Y      │
│  NFRs, capacity              DB indexes, algorithms     Trade-offs       │
│  Stakeholder review          Developer implementation   Immutable log    │
│                                                                          │
│  Architect owns HLD sign-off before major build                          │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

HLD Document Structure (Standard Template)

Section Content Audience
1. Executive summary Problem, solution one-pager Sponsors, CAB
2. Goals & scope In/out of scope All
3. NFRs Latency, availability, RPO/RTO, TPS Architects, SRE
4. Context diagram (C4 L1) Users, external systems Everyone
5. Container diagram (C4 L2) Services, DB, Kafka, AWS Engineering
6. Key flows Sequence: happy path + failure Engineering, QA
7. Data architecture DB per service, events, retention DBA, dev
8. Security & compliance JWT, PCI scope, audit Security
9. Deployment view EKS, regions, DR Platform
10. Capacity model TPS, storage, cost estimate FinOps, architect
11. Risks & mitigations Top 10 risks Review board
12. ADR index Linked decisions All
13. Open questions TBD with owners PM

C4 Model Levels

Level Shows Payment example
L1 Context System vs world Corporate Banking Platform ↔ Users, Core Banking, SWIFT
L2 Container Apps, DB, Kafka payment-svc, Aurora, MSK, Gateway
L3 Component Inside one service Controller, SagaOrchestrator, OutboxPublisher
L4 Code Classes LLD — not HLD main body

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why HLD Exists

Without HLD With HLD
Teams build incompatible assumptions Shared blueprint
NFRs discovered in prod Latency/TPS agreed upfront
Security review late PCI scope in design phase
Capacity surprise at NEFT peak Back-of-envelope validated
"Architect said microservices" verbal only Signed document + diagrams

When Architects Produce HLD

TRIGGERS:
  New product: corporate instant payments channel
  Major migration: strangler off monolith (Lesson 39)
  Scale event: 2K → 10K TPS requirement
  Regulatory change: audit trail enhancement
  M&A integration: two payment stacks merge

GATE:
  Architecture Review Board (ARB) approval before funding / sprint 1
  HLD versioned in Confluence/Git — linked to Jira epic

HLD vs Agile

Agile does not mean "no architecture"
  HLD is living document — increment per release
  ADRs append for each significant change (Lesson 39)
  HLD scope section marks MVP vs Phase 2

NFR Specification (Concrete)

NFR Target Measurement
Availability 99.95% payment API Monthly uptime excl. maintenance
Latency p95 Initiate < 500ms APM payment-svc
Throughput 8,000 TPS peak Load test + prod metrics
RPO (payment data) < 1 min Aurora backup/replication
RTO (platform) < 30 min DR drill
Ledger lag SLO p95 < 5s Kafka consumer lag
Audit retention 7 years S3 archive policy
RTO RPO DR region RPO 30s, RTO 4h MM2 + runbook

Part 4: Memory View

Capacity Estimation — Back of Envelope

PEAK TPS: 8,000 payment initiations/sec (NEFT window)

REQUEST SIZE:
  JSON ~2 KB in, ~1 KB out
  Ingress: 8K × 3 KB ≈ 24 MB/s API payload (order of magnitude)

PAYMENT-SVC PODS:
  Assume 1 pod handles ~400 TPS (measure in load test — illustrative)
  Need ~20 pods peak → HPA max 24 (headroom)
  Per pod: 1 Gi limit, JVM 768Mi heap

DATABASE (Aurora):
  Writes: 8K INSERT/s payment row + outbox — high
  Architect: batch outbox relay, connection pool via RDS Proxy
  Instance: db.r6g.2xlarge class — validate with load test
  IOPS: provisioned or Aurora I/O-Optimized — model 8K writes + indexes

KAFKA MSK:
  8K msg/s × 1 KB ≈ 8 MB/s ingress
  Partitions: 24 for headroom (Lesson 31)
  Brokers: kafka.m5.large × 3 minimum

REDIS:
  Idempotency keys TTL 24h
  8K × 86400 × ~100 bytes key ≈ large — mostly churn with TTL
  ElastiCache: cache.r6g.large cluster — monitor memory

STORAGE (5 year payments):
  8K TPS × 86400 × 0.3 (duty cycle) × 500 bytes row ≈ 100 GB/day order of magnitude
  Partition monthly + archive S3 (Lessons 22, 32)

Part 5: Performance Analysis

HLD Performance Section — What to Include

Topic HLD must answer
Critical path Sync: gateway + payment + account + fraud + DB
Budget 500ms p95 — allocate per hop (Lesson 25)
Bottleneck Likely Aurora write or fraud-svc — mitigation
Async path Ledger not in user latency
Degradation 503 fail closed — not partial pay
Load test plan 2× peak before go-live

Sensitivity Analysis

If fraud-svc p95 200ms instead of 80ms:
  Critical path +120ms — still under 500ms if parallel account+fraud zip

If sequential not parallel:
  +120ms may breach SLO — HLD must specify parallel composition (BFF/gateway or payment-svc)

Cost Rough Order (FinOps Slide)

Component Monthly order (illustrative)
EKS nodes (6× m6i.xlarge) $$$
Aurora r6g.2xlarge $$$$
MSK 3× m5.large $$$
ElastiCache $$
NAT (if no endpoints) $$ — optimize
Total platform FinOps model from HLD inputs

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: HLD Executive Summary (Excerpt)

## Executive Summary

The Corporate Instant Payments initiative delivers API-driven NEFT/RTGS initiation
for treasury users with maker-checker, idempotency, and real-time status.

The platform extends the existing cloud microservices stack (EKS, Aurora, MSK)
with a new payment orchestration service. Core account validation remains on
hybrid-linked core banking via account-svc ACL.

Target: 8,000 TPS peak, 99.95% availability, p95 latency 500ms.
Ledger posting is asynchronous (eventual ≤ 5s) with nightly reconciliation.

Investment: Phase 1 MVP Q3 — single region; Phase 2 DR Q4.

Example 2: NFR Table in HLD

| ID | Category | Requirement | Target | Verification |
|----|----------|-------------|--------|--------------|
| NFR-01 | Performance | Payment initiate p95 | ≤ 500ms | Gatling + APM |
| NFR-02 | Throughput | Peak TPS | 8,000 | Load test 2× |
| NFR-03 | Availability | API uptime | 99.95% | Error budget |
| NFR-04 | Consistency | Ledger vs payment | Zero drift EOD | Reconcile job |
| NFR-05 | Security | OAuth2 corporate IdP | Mandatory | Pen test |
| NFR-06 | Audit | 7-year retention | S3 archive | Compliance sign-off |

Example 3: Scope Section

## In Scope (Phase 1)
- REST API payment initiate, status, maker-checker approve
- Idempotency-Key, JWT auth, API Gateway
- Saga: account hold + async ledger
- Search last 90 days (CQRS)

## Out of Scope (Phase 1)
- SWIFT cross-border (Phase 2)
- Real-time mobile push (use polling)
- Event sourcing payment SoT (rejected ADR-006)
- Multi-region active-active

Example 4: Capacity Calculation Appendix

### Appendix A — Capacity

Given:
  Peak TPS = 8,000
  Avg payment row + outbox = 800 bytes
  Duty cycle peak = 2 hours/day at max

Daily payment rows (peak day):
  8,000 × 7200 + off-peak ≈ 57.6M + baseline — model per business

Aurora write capacity: require load test sign-off at 10K TPS synthetic
HPA max pods: 24 (connection budget ADR-204: 24 × 8 = 192 via RDS Proxy)

MSK partitions: 24 (consumer parallelism ledger 12, search 12)

Example 5: Risk Register

| Risk | Impact | Likelihood | Mitigation |
|------|--------|------------|------------|
| Core banking latency | High | Med | Circuit breaker, timeout, cache read-only display |
| Connection pool exhaust | High | Med | RDS Proxy, HPA cap, ADR-204 |
| Ledger consumer lag | Med | Med | Lag SLO, scale consumers, DLT runbook |
| Fraud svc outage | High | Low | Fail closed 503 (ADR-802) |
| Schema migration break | High | Low | Expand-contract, Flyway gate |

Model Answer — Q13 (ARB Presentation Outline)

A: (1) Problem & scope Phase 1 in/out. (2) NFR table measurable. (3) C4 context — users, core banking external. (4) C4 container — gateway, payment, account, fraud, MSK, ledger async, search CQRS. (5) Happy sequence initiate payment. (6) Failure sequences account down, ledger lag. (7) Data: DB per service, event catalog. (8) Security JWT, IRSA, no PCI in payment-svc if scoped. (9) Deployment EKS Terraform GitOps. (10) Capacity 8K TPS pod/DB/Kafka sizing. (11) Risks top 5 + mitigations. (12) ADR index. (13) Timeline Phase 1/2. (14) Open questions. Q&A.

Model Answer — Q14 (8K TPS Capacity)

A: Peak 8K TPS × ~800 bytes write ≈ 6.4 MB/s DB payload plus indexes — Aurora class from load test not guess; start r6g.2xlarge, RDS Proxy, 24 payment pods max with 8 pool via proxy budget. MSK 24 partitions, 3× m5.large, acks=all. Redis idempotency with DB UNIQUE fallback. API 24 MB/s ingress — ALB scale. Load test 16K synthetic sign-off. Async ledger off critical path. Monthly partition + S3 archive for retention. FinOps monthly estimate attached.

Continuity Bridge → Lesson 41: Low-Level Design (LLD)

Lesson 40 documented system structure and NFRs. Lesson 41 zooms into implementation design within each container:

  • Class diagrams — aggregates, services, repositories
  • API contracts — OpenAPI detail, error codes
  • Database schema — tables, indexes per service
  • Sequence at component level — saga step methods
  • Concurrency — locks, idempotency implementation
  • LLD review — what tech leads sign off before sprint coding

Prerequisites: Lesson 40 (HLD, C4, NFRs) · Lesson 39 (DDD, patterns) · Lessons 17–18 (JPA, transactions) · Lesson 28 (saga) · Lesson 27 (API contracts, Pact)

Part 1: Concept

What Is Low-Level Design (LLD)?

Low-Level Design (LLD) specifies how a container (service) is built internally: classes, APIs, database schema, algorithms, concurrency rules, and error handling — enough for developers to implement without guessing. Tech leads and architects sign off LLD before sprint coding for complex domains like payments.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    HLD → LLD → CODE                                      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  HLD (Lesson 40)              LLD (Lesson 41)           Implementation   │
│  ───────────────              ───────────────           ───────────────  │
│  payment-svc exists           Package structure          Java packages   │
│  Saga orchestration           TransferSagaOrchestrator   @Service code   │
│  Aurora PostgreSQL            DDL + indexes              Flyway V001     │
│  p95 500ms                    Method-level sequence      Unit tests      │
│  Idempotency required         Redis key + UNIQUE constraint              │
│                                                                          │
│  One LLD per bounded context / microservice (not one doc for whole bank) │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

LLD Document Structure (payment-svc Template)

Section Content
1. Overview Link to HLD container, scope of this service
2. Domain model Aggregates, entities, value objects, enums
3. Class diagram Layers: api → application → domain → infrastructure
4. API specification OpenAPI paths, request/response, errors
5. Database design DDL, indexes, constraints, Flyway order
6. Component sequences Initiate, approve, saga steps, outbox publish
7. Concurrency & idempotency Locks, @Version, Redis keys
8. Integration clients Feign interfaces, timeouts, fallbacks
9. Event schema PaymentCompleted Avro/JSON fields
10. Configuration Profiles, env vars, feature flags
11. Error catalog errorCode → HTTP status
12. Testing strategy Unit, integration, Pact, scenarios
13. Non-functional mapping How p95 budget met per method
14. Open issues TBD

Layered Architecture (Spring Boot MS)

┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  api (controllers, DTOs, validation)    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  application (services, saga, use cases)│
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  domain (entities, domain services)     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  infrastructure (JPA repos, Feign, Redis)│
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

Dependency rule: inward — domain does not depend on Spring Web
Pragmatic Spring: @Entity in domain package acceptable in many banks

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why LLD Exists

HLD only HLD + LLD
"payment-svc handles idempotency" Exact header, DB UNIQUE, Redis SET NX
"Saga orchestration" State machine states + method names
Two devs invent different APIs Single OpenAPI source
Missing index discovered in prod DDL reviewed in LLD
QA unclear test cases Sequence → test scenarios

Who Owns LLD

Solution Architect: reviews LLD aligns with HLD + ADRs
Tech Lead / Senior Dev: **authors** LLD for their service
DBA: reviews indexes, partition strategy
Security: reviews authz rules on endpoints
QA: derives test cases from sequences

When LLD Is Mandatory

Mandatory:
  New microservice (payment-svc greenfield)
  Money movement state machine changes
  New external API version
  Maker-checker workflow addition

Lightweight LLD (2–3 pages):
  CRUD endpoint with no new integration
  Config-only change

Part 3: Internal Working

Domain Model (payment-svc)

Aggregates and Entities

AGGREGATE ROOT: Payment
  Entities/value embedded:
    - Payment (root)
    - PaymentApproval (1:1 entity, same aggregate)
  External references by ID only:
    - debtorAccountId (string — not Account entity)

VALUE OBJECTS:
  Money (amount + currency) — immutable
  PaymentId, TenantId — typed wrappers optional

ENUMS:
  PaymentStatus: PENDING, APPROVED, DEBITED, COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED
  PaymentType: NEFT, RTGS, IMPS, INTERNAL

API Specification (OpenAPI Detail)

paths:
  /api/v1/payments:
    post:
      operationId: createPayment
      parameters:
        - name: Idempotency-Key
          in: header
          required: true
          schema: { type: string, maxLength: 64 }
      requestBody:
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/CreatePaymentRequest'
      responses:
        '201': { description: Created, content: ... }
        '409': { description: Duplicate idempotency replay }
        '422': { description: Business rule violation }
        '503': { description: Downstream unavailable }

components:
  schemas:
    CreatePaymentRequest:
      type: object
      required: [debtorAccountId, creditorAccountId, amount, currency, paymentType]
      properties:
        amount:
          type: string
          pattern: '^\d+\.\d{2,4}$'
        tenantId:
          type: string
    ProblemDetail:
      properties:
        errorCode:
          enum:
            - PAYMENT_INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS
            - PAYMENT_FRAUD_BLOCKED
            - PAYMENT_DUPLICATE
            - PAYMENT_DOWNSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE

Database Design (LLD DDL)

-- V001__payments_core.sql
CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id       VARCHAR(36) PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id        VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    debtor_acct      VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    creditor_acct    VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    amount           NUMERIC(19,4) NOT NULL,
    currency         CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
    status           VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    payment_type     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    idempotency_key  VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    initiated_by     VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    created_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    updated_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    version          BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    CONSTRAINT uq_tenant_idempotency UNIQUE (tenant_id, idempotency_key),
    CONSTRAINT chk_amount_positive CHECK (amount > 0)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_payments_tenant_status_created
    ON payments (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC);

CREATE INDEX idx_payments_debtor_created
    ON payments (tenant_id, debtor_acct, created_at DESC);

-- V002__saga.sql (Lesson 28)
CREATE TABLE saga_instances ( ... );
CREATE TABLE saga_step_log ( ... );

-- V003__outbox.sql
CREATE TABLE outbox_events (
    event_id     BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    aggregate_id VARCHAR(36) NOT NULL,
    event_type   VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    payload      JSONB NOT NULL,
    created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    published_at TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE INDEX idx_outbox_unpublished ON outbox_events (created_at)
    WHERE published_at IS NULL;

Index Rationale (LLD Must Document)

Index Query
uq_tenant_idempotency Idempotency lookup
idx_payments_tenant_status_created Pending queue API
idx_payments_debtor_created Account statement in payment-svc

Component Sequence — Initiate Payment (LLD)

PaymentController.create()
  → IdempotencyService.claimRedis(tenant, key)  // optional fast path
  → PaymentInitiationService.initiate()
      → TransferSagaOrchestrator.start()
          → PaymentRepository.save(PENDING)
          → SagaRepository.save(STARTED)
          → AccountClient.validateAndHold()  // Feign 3s timeout
          → FraudClient.score()
          → Payment.markCompleted(); Saga.transition(COMPLETED)
          → OutboxPublisher.enqueue(PaymentCompleted)
          → @Transactional commit
  → map to PaymentResponse 201

State Machine (LLD Explicit)

PENDING ──(maker-checker)──► APPROVED ──(saga debit)──► DEBITED ──► COMPLETED
   │                              │
   └──────────► FAILED ◄──────────┘
                  ▲
                  └── compensate release hold

Guard: APPROVED requires PaymentApproval.checkerId != makerId

Concurrency and Idempotency (LLD)

LAYER 1 — Redis:
  Key: idempotency:{tenantId}:{idempotencyKey}
  Value: paymentId
  TTL: 86400s
  Command: SET NX EX

LAYER 2 — DB:
  UNIQUE (tenant_id, idempotency_key)
  On conflict: SELECT existing payment_id → return 200/409 per API policy

LAYER 3 — Optimistic lock:
  @Version on Payment.version — concurrent update → OptimisticLockException → 409

SAGA recovery:
  Scheduler every 30s: SagaRecoveryService.recoverStuck(IN_PROGRESS, >5min)

NO distributed lock on payment row for normal flow — idempotency key sufficient

Part 4: Memory View

LLD Performance Mapping

CRITICAL PATH METHOD BUDGET (payment-svc LLD appendix):

PaymentController.create()                    target 450ms p95 total
  IdempotencyService.claimRedis                 2ms
  AccountClient.validateAndHold                 80ms (parallel target)
  FraudClient.score                             100ms (parallel → max 100ms)
  PaymentRepository.save + outbox insert        15ms
  Commit                                        5ms
  Serialization                                 3ms

Parallelization LLD decision:
  CompletableFuture.allOf(account, fraud) before DB tx — Lesson 11
  DB tx only after both succeed — shorten hold duration

JPA Fetch Plan (LLD)

PaymentRepository.findById:
  No EAGER associations — Lesson 17
PaymentRepository.findPendingQueue:
  Projection DTO interface — not full entity list 10K rows

Part 5: Performance Analysis

LLD NFR Traceability

NFR (HLD) LLD mechanism
p95 500ms Parallel account+fraud; tx after validate
8K TPS Stateless pods; pool 8; avoid SELECT *
Idempotency Redis + UNIQUE; duplicate O(1)
Audit saga_step_log append; outbox payload
Ledger eventual Outbox in same tx — not sync call

LLD Anti-Patterns to Reject

✗ @Transactional on controller
✗ EAGER fetch Account on Payment entity cross-DB
✗ SELECT * pagination 50K rows in memory
✗ block() WebClient on Tomcat without timeout
✗ Single giant PaymentService 2000 lines — split orchestrator

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Application Service Signature

public interface PaymentInitiationUseCase {
    PaymentResponse initiate(CreatePaymentCommand command, IdempotencyContext idempotency);
}

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PaymentInitiationService implements PaymentInitiationUseCase {

    private final TransferSagaOrchestrator sagaOrchestrator;
    private final IdempotencyService idempotencyService;

    @Override
    public PaymentResponse initiate(CreatePaymentCommand command, IdempotencyContext ctx) {
        return idempotencyService.executeOnce(ctx, () -> sagaOrchestrator.start(command));
    }
}

Example 2: Domain Method on Aggregate

public void approve(String checkerId, String makerId) {
    if (!status.equals(PaymentStatus.PENDING))
        throw new InvalidPaymentStateException(status, PaymentStatus.APPROVED);
    if (checkerId.equals(makerId))
        throw new MakerCheckerViolationException();
    this.status = PaymentStatus.APPROVED;
    this.updatedAt = Instant.now();
}

errorCode HTTP When

PAYMENT_FRAUD_BLOCKED 422 Fraud score block

PAYMENT_INVALID_STATE 422 Approve non-PENDING

Example 4: Feign Client LLD Spec

@FeignClient(name = "account-svc", path = "/api/v1")
public interface AccountClient {

    @PostMapping("/accounts/{accountId}/holds")
    HoldResponse placeHold(
        @PathVariable String accountId,
        @RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String idempotencyKey,
        @RequestBody PlaceHoldRequest request);
}

LLD documents:
  connectTimeout: 2000ms
  readTimeout: 3000ms
  CircuitBreaker: account-svc
  Fallback: throw DownstreamUnavailableException (fail closed)
  Idempotency-Key: paymentId for hold

Part 9: Architect Perspective

LLD Review Checklist (Architect)

□ Aligns with HLD container and NFR budgets
□ Aggregate boundaries respected — no cross-aggregate @Transactional
□ Idempotency at API + DB documented
□ Saga states match ADR-601
□ No downstream in readiness probe (Lesson 35)
□ Indexes for every hot query in LLD
□ Fail-closed on validate/fraud — no unsafe fallback
□ Outbox — no dual-write
□ Error codes stable — mobile mapping
□ Security @PreAuthorize on write endpoints
□ Connection pool aligns connection budget ADR
□ Expand-contract for new migrations

ADR → LLD Traceability

When LLD Is Overkill

Skip heavy LLD:
  Config toggle, log message change
  Internal refactor no API change — update LLD minor version optional

Never skip:
  New money path, schema change, auth change

Model Answer — Q14 (Maker-Checker LLD)

A: New endpoints: POST /payments (maker, PENDING), PATCH /payments/{id}/approve (checker). State machine: PENDING→APPROVED→saga continues→COMPLETED. PaymentApproval table 1:1 with checkerId, makerId, CHECK constraint ≠. @PreAuthorize roles TRANSFER_MAKER / TRANSFER_APPROVER. Saga paused at PENDING until approve webhook/API resumes orchestrator from APPROVED state — saga_instances.current_step = AWAITING_APPROVAL. Idempotency on create only. Sequences for approve path. Tests T-06 maker≠checker. ADR reference four-eyes.

Model Answer — Q15 (Outbox in LLD)

A: LLD specifies OutboxPublisher.enqueue() in same @Transactional as PaymentRepository.save after COMPLETED. Table outbox_events with partial index unpublished. Poller 200ms or Debezium — infra LLD reference. Forbidden: kafkaTemplate.send in service method without outbox row. Consumer idempotency on eventId. Matches ADR-502 and Lesson 27.

Part 1: Concept

What Is a System Design Case Study?

A system design case study is a structured problem — design a payment platform, ride dispatch system, or reconciliation pipeline — answered in 45–60 minutes (interviews) or days (real projects). You demonstrate requirements → architecture → deep dives → trade-offs → failure handling.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              SYSTEM DESIGN SESSION STRUCTURE (45 MIN)                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  0–5 min   Clarify requirements (functional + non-functional)            │
│  5–10 min  Back-of-envelope capacity                                     │
│  10–20 min High-level diagram (C4 L2) + data flow                       │
│  20–35 min Deep dives (2–3): idempotency, scale, consistency             │
│  35–42 min Failure scenarios + monitoring                                │
│  42–45 min Summary + trade-offs                                          │
│                                                                          │
│  Interviewer scores: communication, depth, trade-offs — not perfection   │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why System Design Interviews / Case Studies Matter

Coding interview System design
Single machine algorithm Distributed trade-offs
Correctness on leetcode NFRs under failure
Junior–mid signal Staff/Architect signal

What Architects Prove in Case Studies

NOT: Memorized "Netflix architecture"
YES:
  - Ask clarifying questions
  - State assumptions explicitly
  - Numbers for scale (even rough)
  - Name patterns with why (saga, CQRS, outbox)
  - Fail closed on money
  - Know what to defer to Phase 2

Part 3: Internal Working

Universal Framework: RESHADE (Mnemonic)

Step Letter Action
R Requirements Functional + NFR; users; scale
E Estimation QPS, storage, bandwidth
S Storage DB, cache, object store
H High-level API, services, diagram
A API Key endpoints, events
D Deep dive 2–3 hard parts
E Evolution Phase 2, migration, DR

Case Study A — Corporate Payment API (10K TPS)

Step 1: Clarifying Questions

Functional:
  - Initiate transfer, status, maker-checker approve?
  - Single region or multi-tenant SaaS?
  - Read search vs only by ID?

Non-functional:
  - Peak TPS? (assume 10K if not given)
  - p95 latency initiate?
  - Exactly-once money or eventual ledger OK?
  - Regulatory audit 7 years?

Out of scope (state explicitly):
  - Cross-border SWIFT Phase 2
  - Mobile push — polling OK

Step 2: Estimation

Peak 10K TPS write (payment initiate)

Ingress: 10K × 3 KB ≈ 30 MB/s API
Aurora writes: 10K × ~800 bytes row + outbox ≈ 8 MB/s + indexes → need load-tested Aurora tier
Pods: 10K / 400 TPS per pod ≈ 25 pods → HPA max 30
MSK: 10K msg/s, 24 partitions, 3 brokers kafka.m5.xlarge
Redis idempotency: 10K SET/s — cluster node
Storage 5yr (duty cycle 20% avg 2K TPS): model ~100–200 TB cumulative → partition + S3 archive

Step 3: High-Level Design

Client → WAF → ALB → API Gateway (JWT, rate limit)
       → payment-svc (saga orchestrator)
            sync → account-svc, fraud-svc
            local → Aurora (payment + outbox)
            async → MSK PaymentCompleted → ledger, search, notify

Patterns (Lesson 39): Gateway, saga, outbox, CQRS search, DB per service
No XA (Lesson 28)

Step 4: Deep Dives

Idempotency:

Idempotency-Key header → Redis SET NX → INSERT UNIQUE(tenant, key) → same response on replay

Saga:

PENDING → validate → hold → COMPLETED + outbox; compensate release on failure
Ledger async — user sees COMPLETED on payment row; reconciliation EOD

10K TPS bottleneck:

Aurora write + connection pool → RDS Proxy, HPA cap tied to pool ADR, monthly partition

Step 5: Failure Scenarios

Failure Behavior
account-svc down 503 fail closed
fraud down 503 (default)
Kafka lag Payment OK; ledger catches up; alert lag
Duplicate client retry Idempotent
AZ loss EKS multi-AZ; Aurora failover

Case Study B — Real-Time Shipment Tracking (Logistics)

Requirements Clarification

Functional:
  - Shippers publish GPS every 5–30 sec per truck
  - Customers see map + ETA
  - 100K active shipments, 500K GPS points/min peak

NFR:
  - Read latency map < 2s
  - GPS ingest durable
  - 90 day hot history, 2 year archive

Estimation

500K points/min ≈ 8.3K writes/s
Each point: shipmentId, lat, lng, ts ≈ 100 bytes → ~830 KB/s ingest
Read: 50K concurrent viewers — CDN for static; API for live position

Storage 90 days hot:
  500K/min × 60 × 24 × 90 × 100 bytes ≈ 6.5 TB order of magnitude (adjust duty cycle)

High-Level Design

Mobile/GPS device → API Gateway → ingestion-svc
  → Kafka topic shipment.gps (key=shipmentId, partition order)
  → stream processor (Kafka Streams / Flink) → latest position cache Redis
  → Cassandra/TSDB historical (Lesson 23 — wide column, TTL)
  → WebSocket/SSE to tracking UI (WebFlux — Lesson 20)

CQRS: write path append GPS; read path latest from Redis + trail from Cassandra

Deep Dives

Why Kafka not direct DB write:

Spike absorb, replay, multiple consumers (analytics, ETA engine)

Partition key = shipmentId:

Ordering per shipment; parallel across shipments

ETA calculation:

Separate eta-svc consumes stream — not in ingest hot path

Failure

Device offline → buffer upload batch with timestamps
Redis miss → fallback Cassandra latest point — higher latency

Case Study C — Payment Reconciliation (Batch + Real-Time)

Requirements

Compare: payment-svc COMPLETED vs ledger-svc entries vs core banking statement file
Detect drift within 24h; zero tolerance EOD for settled amounts
Volume: 5M payments/day

Design

REAL-TIME (soft):
  Kafka PaymentCompleted → reconciliation-svc increments expected ledger count
  Ledger posts → increment actual; mismatch counter alert

BATCH (authoritative EOD):
  CronJob 02:00 IST:
    Extract payments COMPLETED from Aurora (partition yesterday)
    Extract ledger by reference_id
    JOIN in Spark/Athena on S3 parquet export OR SQL in warehouse
    Output exception report → ops queue

  File-based: Core banking SFTP statement → S3 → parse → three-way match

Patterns: CQRS analytics store, idempotent batch job, not OLTP join cross-DB

Deep Dive — Three-Way Match

Payment platform amount = Ledger sum = Core statement line
Exception types: MISSING_LEDGER, AMOUNT_MISMATCH, DUPLICATE
Workflow: case management svc, not auto-reverse without human

Case Study D — Ride Dispatch (Transportation / Uber-like)

Requirements

Riders request ride; match nearby driver; track trip; surge pricing optional
Peak: 50K requests/min metro; 20K active drivers
p95 match < 15s

High-Level Design

Rider app → Gateway → trip-svc (create request)
  → matching-svc:
      Geo index Redis/Grid — drivers by geohash cell
      Kafka trip.requested → matching workers
  → assignment → trip.assigned event
  → location-svc (Case B pattern) for live track
  → payment-svc at trip end (link to Case A)

Storage:
  Trip state machine: PostgreSQL
  Driver locations: Redis geospatial + Kafka stream

Deep Dive — Geospatial Matching

Geohash prefix precision 5 (~5km cell):
  Query drivers in cell + neighbors
  Filter available, rating, vehicle type
  Atomic accept: Redis SETNX tripId driverId — first wins

Trade-off Narration

Strong consistency driver location vs fresh enough for match — accept 2–5s stale
Surge: precomputed zones in Redis — not per-request global lock

Part 4: Memory View

Estimation Cheat Sheet (Memorize Orders of Magnitude)

1 day = 86400 sec ≈ 100K sec (easy math)
1M requests/day ≈ 12 QPS average
1M requests/day peak 10× ≈ 120 QPS (not 10K — clarify peak factor)

Storage:
  1 char ≈ 1 byte; JSON payment ~500B–2KB
  1M rows × 1KB = 1 GB

Memory cache:
  1M keys × 100 bytes = 100 MB

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Interview Trade-Off Table (Speak Aloud)

Tension Option A Option B When say A
Consistency vs availability Fail 503 Queue async Money validate
Sync vs async ledger User waits Eventual Async default banking
SQL vs Cassandra history JOIN reports Scale writes GPS / statements
Push vs pull status WebSocket Poll High fanout mobile
Monolith vs MS Speed ship Scale teams >8 engineers, clear contexts
ES vs SQL search Flexible ACID Search only

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Interview Opening Script (Payment)

"Before I draw boxes, I'd like to confirm scope.
Are we designing initiate-only or include maker-checker approval?
What's peak TPS and is eventual ledger posting acceptable?
I'll assume 10K peak, p95 500ms, async ledger with reconciliation,
multi-tenant SaaS, single primary region with DR as Phase 2.
Does that match your expectations?"

Example 2: Idempotency Deep-Dive Script

"For payment POST I'll require Idempotency-Key.
Fast path Redis SET NX with paymentId, authoritative UNIQUE on (tenant_id, key) in PostgreSQL.
On duplicate, return same paymentId with 200 or 409 per API convention.
This survives Redis eviction and client retries after 503."

Example 3: Reconciliation SQL Sketch (Batch)

-- warehouse layer — not runtime OLTP cross-join
SELECT p.payment_id, p.amount, l.ledger_total, (p.amount - l.ledger_total) AS drift
FROM payments_fact p
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT reference_id, SUM(credit_amount - debit_amount) AS ledger_total
  FROM ledger_entries_fact
  GROUP BY reference_id
) l ON p.payment_id = l.reference_id
WHERE p.status = 'COMPLETED' AND p.business_date = :yesterday
  AND (l.reference_id IS NULL OR p.amount <> l.ledger_total);

Example 4: GPS Ingest API (Logistics)

POST /api/v1/shipments/{shipmentId}/locations
Headers:
  X-Device-Id, Authorization
Body:
  latitude, longitude, recordedAt, sequenceNumber
Responses:
  202 Accepted — async Kafka ingest
  409 — duplicate sequence (idempotent device retry)

Example 5: Trip State Machine (Transportation)

REQUESTED → MATCHING → ASSIGNED → IN_PROGRESS → COMPLETED
              ↓                      ↓
          CANCELLED              CANCELLED (policy)

Service Boundaries Comparison

System Core services
Payment A gateway, payment, account, fraud, ledger, search
