Part 9: Architect Perspective

How to Narrate Trade-Offs (Interview Gold)

Template:
  "We have two options: [A] and [B].
   [A] gives [benefit] but costs [downside].
   [B] gives [benefit2] but [downside2].
   Given [requirement X], I choose [A] because [reason].
   We can evolve to [B] in Phase 2 if [trigger]."

Example Narration (Ledger Sync vs Async)

"Synchronous ledger post keeps strong consistency but adds 40ms and couples availability —
if ledger is down, payment fails after hold, requiring compensate.
Async via outbox matches our 500ms SLO and industry practice for corporate banking channels,
with nightly reconciliation as control. I choose async with idempotent ledger consumer."

Red Flags Interviewers Penalize

✗ Jump to Kafka without requirements
✗ Single database for everything
✗ No numbers at all
✗ Ignore failure
✗ "We'll use microservices" without boundaries
✗ No questions asked

Part 12: Interview Questions

Junior/Mid (Component)

  1. Design URL shortener (warm-up scale).
  2. How add idempotency to payment POST?
  3. Cache aside pattern explain.

Senior (Full system — 45 min)

  1. Design corporate payment API 10K TPS.
  2. Design shipment tracking 500K GPS/min.
  3. Design ride-hailing matching.
  4. Design payment reconciliation.

Staff/Architect (Probe depth)

  1. Payment: fraud down — fail open or closed? Defend.
  2. Tracking: partition skew one hot shipment?
  3. Reconciliation: payment COMPLETED ledger missing — automated fix?
  4. Dispatch: thundering herd at concert exit?
  5. Multi-region active-active payments — why reject?
  6. Estimate storage 5yr payments 10K peak.
  7. How migrate monolith payment to MS without big bang?
  8. CQRS search 10 min lag — acceptable for whom?

Model Answer — Q4 (45-Min Outline)

A: Clarify 10K peak, maker-checker, eventual ledger. Estimate pods, Aurora, MSK. Draw Gateway → payment-svc → account/fraud sync, Aurora+outbox, MSK → ledger/search. Deep dive idempotency + saga. Failure account down 503, lag reconcile. Mention DR Phase 2. Trade-offs narrated. Summary.

Model Answer — Q10 (Missing Ledger)

A: Do not auto-credit customer. Alert SEV-2, DLT/reconciliation job creates exception ticket. Ops replay Kafka event idempotent or manual pivot if duplicate risk. Root cause consumer bug/schema. Prevent: idempotent consumer UNIQUE, DLT monitoring zero tolerance, nightly batch authoritative match blocks EOD sign-off.

  • Architecture Review Board (ARB) — intake, approval, exceptions
  • Technical debt registers and migration roadmaps

Part 1: Concept

What Is Architecture Governance?

Architecture governance is the set of processes, roles, standards, and controls that ensure systems across an organization are aligned with business goals, compliant with regulations, technically coherent, and evolvable — not merely “whatever each squad shipped last sprint.”

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              ARCHITECTURE GOVERNANCE — CONTROL PLANE                     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│   STRATEGY          STANDARDS           REVIEW              EVOLUTION    │
│   ────────          ─────────           ──────              ─────────    │
│   Target            Reference           ARB / Design        Tech debt    │
│   architecture      architecture        review gates        register     │
│   Roadmap           Pattern catalog     HLD / LLD sign-off  ADR index    │
│   Build vs buy      NFR templates       Exception process   Post-PIR     │
│                                                                          │
│         │                  │                  │                  │         │
│         └──────────────────┴──────────────────┴──────────────────┘         │
│                                    │                                     │
│                                    ▼                                     │
│                         DELIVERY TEAMS (payment-svc, etc.)               │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Governance vs Design

Activity Who Output When
Design Squad architect / Tech Lead HLD, LLD, code Per feature
Governance Enterprise / domain architect Standards, approval, exceptions Continuous
Review ARB + peers Approved / rework / exception Gate milestones

Core Artifacts (Your Operating System)

1. Reference Architecture     — "This is how we build payments on AWS"
2. Standards Catalog          — Mandatory / recommended / prohibited
3. ADR Index                  — Decisions with context (Lesson 39–40)
4. Architecture Review Pack   — HLD + NFRs + risks + ADRs
5. Tech Debt Register         — Known gaps with business impact
6. Exception Register         — Approved deviations with expiry
7. Fitness Functions          — Automated architecture tests in CI

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why Banks and Enterprises Need Governance

Without governance, a 9-year Tech Lead’s team builds Kafka + saga + outbox — while another team builds Oracle XA + EJB monolith callbacks — and reconciliation becomes a multi-year migration nightmare.

WITHOUT GOVERNANCE                    WITH GOVERNANCE
────────────────────                  ────────────────
3 different API styles                OpenAPI 3 + standard errors
2 payment idempotency schemes         Idempotency-Key + Redis+UNIQUE ADR
Shadow IT vendor SaaS                 Build vs buy rubric + security review
"Microservices" = 200 shared DB       DB-per-service enforced in ARB
No DR proof                           RPO/RTO in HLD mandatory section
Post-incident: blame                  Post-incident: ADR + standard update

Why This Matters for Solution Architect Role

Tech Lead focus Architect + governance focus
Deliver sprint Sustain platform 5 years
Team velocity Org-wide coherence
Local trade-offs Documented enterprise trade-offs
Code review HLD/LLD + ARB review
Fix bug Update pattern catalog / fitness test

Regulatory Driver (Banking)

RBI / internal audit asks:
  "How do you ensure all payment channels follow maker-checker?"
  "Show approval for introducing new fraud vendor API"
  "Prove segregation of duties in deployment pipeline"

Governance artifacts ARE the audit answer — not Slack threads

Part 3: Internal Working

The Architecture Review Board (ARB)

Purpose

The ARB is a cross-functional forum (architecture, security, ops, compliance, product) that reviews significant changes before expensive commitment.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    ARB REVIEW LIFECYCLE                                  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  1. INTAKE          2. TRIAGE           3. REVIEW           4. OUTCOME │
│  ─────────          ─────────           ────────           ──────────── │
│  Team submits       Classify tier       Present 30–45 min   Approved   │
│  review pack        Tier 1 skip ARB     Q&A panel           Conditional│
│  (template)         Tier 2 async        Action items        Rework     │
│                     Tier 3 full ARB     Follow-up           Exception  │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Review Tier Matrix (Typical Bank)

Tier Change examples Gate
T0 Bug fix, config tweak Squad only
T1 New internal API field Tech Lead + architect async
T2 New microservice, new Kafka topic, new external integration ARB async
T3 New payment rail, multi-region, core banking replacement, PII new store Full ARB session
T4 Merger integration, cloud region exit Steering committee + ARB

Review Pack Contents (Mandatory Sections)

1. Executive summary (1 page)
2. Problem & scope / out of scope
3. C4 Context + Container diagrams (Lesson 40)
4. NFR table: latency, TPS, RPO/RTO, retention
5. Capacity estimate (back-of-envelope)
6. Sequence: happy path + 2 failure paths
7. Data classification (PII, PCI scope)
8. Security: authN/Z, secrets, network zones
9. ADRs (new or references)
10. Migration / rollout plan (strangler, feature flags)
11. Risk register (top 5)
12. Tech debt created OR retired
13. Operational: dashboards, alerts, runbooks
14. Cost estimate (FinOps)

ARB Session Flow (45 Minutes)

0–5 min   Presenter: problem + scope
5–15 min  Architecture walkthrough (diagram-first)
15–25 min Security + compliance probes
25–35 min Ops/SRE: failure, scaling, DR
35–40 min Cost + timeline
40–45 min Decision: approve / conditional / rework / exception

Conditions example:
  "Approve if LLD adds idempotency section per STD-PAY-003"
  "Approve if load test proves 8K TPS before prod"

Exception Process

Not every squad can meet every standard on day one — exceptions are governed, not informal.

Exception record:
  - Standard violated (e.g., shared database with legacy)
  - Business reason (regulatory deadline)
  - Compensating controls (read-only replica, audit log)
  - Owner + expiry date (max 12 months)
  - Remediation plan + budget
  - ARB chair approval

Without expiry → exception becomes permanent architecture (failure mode)

Standards Catalog

Structure

STANDARD ID    TITLE                          STATUS
───────────    ─────                          ──────
STD-API-001    OpenAPI 3 + versioning         MANDATORY
STD-API-002    Error envelope RFC7807-like      MANDATORY
STD-PAY-003    Idempotency-Key on POST        MANDATORY
STD-PAY-004    No XA across services          PROHIBITED
STD-EVT-001    Outbox for domain events       MANDATORY
STD-EVT-002    Schema Registry for Kafka      MANDATORY
STD-SEC-001    mTLS service mesh (prod)       MANDATORY
STD-SEC-002    Secrets in AWS SM / not env    MANDATORY
STD-DATA-001   DB per service                 MANDATORY
STD-DATA-002   PII encryption at rest         MANDATORY
STD-OBS-001    OpenTelemetry traces           MANDATORY
STD-RES-001    Timeouts on all sync calls     MANDATORY

Standard Document Template

Each standard includes:

Purpose → Scope → Requirement → Rationale → Verification → Exceptions → References
Verification = how ARB knows you complied (checklist item, fitness test, CI gate)

Architecture Fitness Functions

Fitness functions (term from evolutionary architecture) are automated checks that continuously verify architecture rules — not one-time ARB promises.

Build vs Buy vs Partner

Decision Rubric

Criterion Weight Build score Buy (SaaS) score
Core differentiator High High if core Low if core
Time to market High Low High
Regulatory control High High Needs legal review
Integration complexity Medium Known Unknown API
TCO 5 year Medium Dev+ops License + exit cost
Team skill fit Medium Java/Kafka strong → build —
Vendor lock-in Medium Low High

Capability Typical decision Rationale

Fraud ML platform Buy (FICO, SAS) + integrate Model expertise

ARB Questions for Vendor Selection

Where is data stored? Subprocessors? Exit clause?
SLA vs our NFR? SSO/SAML? Audit logs exportable?
Pen test report? SOC2? On-prem option for DR?

Post-Incident Architecture Review (PIR → Architecture)

Sequence after SEV-1 payment outage:

1. Incident timeline (ops)
2. Root cause (technical)
3. Architecture contributing factors:
     - Missing timeout on fraud call?
     - No bulkhead between channels?
     - Idempotency gap?
4. Actions:
     - Immediate: config fix
     - Structural: ADR + standard update + fitness function
5. ARB retro: was this design reviewed? Gap in checklist?

Example outcome:
  STD-RES-001 amended: "All Feign clients MUST declare connect+read timeout"
  ArchUnit rule added in platform parent POM
  HLD template updated with failure sequence mandatory

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: ArchUnit Fitness Function (Payment Service)

@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "com.bank.payment")
class PaymentArchitectureTest {

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule domain_must_not_depend_on_infrastructure =
        classes().that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")
            .should().onlyDependOnClassesThat()
            .resideInAnyPackage("..domain..", "java..", "jakarta..");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule no_direct_legacy_core_banking =
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..payment..")
            .should().accessClassesThat()
            .resideInAPackage("..legacy.oracle.core..");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule controllers_are_thin =
        classes().that().areAnnotatedWith(RestController.class)
            .should().onlyCallMethodsThat(
                new DescribedPredicate<>("are delegated to services") {
                    @Override
                    public boolean test(JavaMethod method) {
                        return method.getOwner().isAnnotatedWith(Service.class)
                            || method.getOwner().isAnnotatedWith(RestController.class);
                    }
                });
}

Example 2: ADR Template (Governance Artifact)

# ADR-042: Mandate Idempotency-Key for Payment POST

## Status
Accepted

## Context
Duplicate corporate API retries caused double holds in Q1 incident.

## Decision
All payment initiation POST endpoints require Idempotency-Key header.
Implementation: Redis SET NX + UNIQUE(tenant_id, idempotency_key).

## Consequences
+ Safe retries
- Clients must generate UUID keys
- Redis cluster required

## Compliance
Maps to STD-PAY-003. Verified by integration test suite PAY-IDEM-001.

## Review date
2025-06 — reassess if gRPC adoption changes header model

violation: Reads beneficiary table in shared Oracle schema LEGACY_BEN
business_justification: Regulatory go-live 2024-09; strangler not complete
compensating_controls:

  - no writes to LEGACY_BEN from payment-svc

How to Run a Review (You as Chair)

DO:
  - Ask clarifying questions before judging
  - Anchor on NFRs and risk — not personal taste
  - Offer patterns from catalog ("consider outbox per STD-EVT-001")
  - Document conditions clearly
  - Praise good trade-off narration (Lesson 42)

DON'T:
  - Rewrite their design in the meeting
  - Block without alternative
  - Approve without verification method
  - Let "we'll fix later" skip debt register entry

Part 12: Interview Questions

Senior / Tech Lead

  1. What is architecture governance vs design?
  2. What goes in an HLD review pack?
  3. What is a technical debt register entry?
  4. Why tier ARB reviews?

Solution Architect / Staff

  1. How do you handle a squad that wants shared database for speed?
  2. Design an exception process for legacy Oracle reads during migration.
  3. What fitness functions would you add after a duplicate payment incident?
  4. How do you prioritize tech debt vs features with product?
  5. Build vs buy for fraud engine — walk through rubric.
  6. How does post-incident review change architecture standards?

Model Answers (Architect Level)

Q5 — Shared database request

A: Acknowledge time pressure. Explain STD-DATA-001: coupling deploy, schema conflicts, PCI scope bleed, blocks independent scaling. Offer alternatives: (1) strangler ACL service with read API over legacy, (2) time-boxed exception with read-only user + expiry + debt register TD entry, (3) accelerated Aurora migration slice if funded. Approve exception only with compensating controls and remediation date — never silent approval.

Q7 — Fitness functions after duplicate payment

A: Immediate: STD-PAY-003 verification in CI integration test; ArchUnit ensuring POST handlers route through IdempotencyFilter; contract test that duplicate Idempotency-Key returns same body; monitoring alert on UNIQUE constraint violation rate; ADR mandating Redis+DB dual layer. Optional: mutation test removing idempotency — must fail build.

Q9 — Build vs buy fraud

A: Fraud is specialized but not always core IP — score vendor on model quality, explainability (regulatory), latency SLA, data residency, integration effort. If bank lacks ML ops, buy with ACL adapter; if proprietary behavioral models are competitive advantage, build scoring svc consuming events from MSK. Hybrid common: buy rules engine, build feature pipeline.

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Tier reviews — proportionate control, not one-size ARB
  2. Short templates — 10-page HLD max for T2; appendices for depth
  3. ADR every significant decision — link in review pack
  4. Automate enforceable rules — ArchUnit, Pact, tfsec
  5. Exception register public — transparency reduces shadow IT
  6. Tech debt is visible — Jira epics with business impact
  7. Reference architecture living doc — versioned quarterly
  8. Architects say yes with conditions — not default no
  9. Post-incident → standard update — close the loop
  10. Measure governance value — reduced incidents, faster T2 reviews over time

  • Zero trust for microservices (mTLS, service identity, IRSA)
  • Threat modeling (STRIDE) for payment flows

[REDACTED]

Prerequisites: Lesson 19 (Spring Security, JWT, OAuth2) · Lesson 43 (governance, standards, ARB) · Lesson 39 (gateway, ACL, patterns) · Lesson 40–41 (HLD/LLD security sections) · Lesson 36–38 (AWS IAM, VPC, IRSA, IaC) · Lesson 35 (K8s network policies)

Part 1: Concept

What Is Security Architecture?

Security architecture is the deliberate design of trust boundaries, identity, encryption, authorization, monitoring, and failure behavior across a distributed system — so that security is built in, not bolted on after ARB approval.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              SECURITY ARCHITECTURE LAYERS                                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  L7  APPLICATION     Input validation, idempotency, business authZ       │
│  L6  API / IDENTITY  OAuth2/OIDC, JWT, scopes, mTLS service identity     │
│  L5  DATA            Encryption at rest, tokenization, masking, KMS      │
│  L4  NETWORK         VPC zones, NACLs, SGs, WAF, private endpoints       │
│  L3  PLATFORM        EKS, IRSA, Pod Security, NetworkPolicy, secrets   │
│  L2  SUPPLY CHAIN    SAST, dependency scan, signed images, SBOM       │
│  L1  GOVERNANCE      Threat model, standards, pen test, audit evidence   │
│                                                                          │
│  "Defense in depth" — breach of one layer must not expose PAN/money    │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Security Architecture vs Application Security

Application security (Lesson 19) Security architecture (this lesson)
@PreAuthorize, JWT filter Zone model, PCI scope minimization
Login flow Identity federation (corporate IdP, m2m)
Password hashing KMS key hierarchy, rotation
CSRF on web form Zero trust — every hop authenticated
Single service Platform-wide fail-closed policy

Core Principles (Banking Platform)

1. LEAST PRIVILEGE     — IAM role per svc, per env, per operation
2. DEFENSE IN DEPTH    — WAF + mTLS + authZ + encryption + audit
3. FAIL CLOSED         — auth/fraud/validate down → deny, not bypass
4. ZERO TRUST          — never trust network location; verify every request
5. MINIMIZE PCI SCOPE  — tokenize PAN; keep card data out of payment-svc if possible
6. AUDIT EVERYTHING    — who accessed what PII, immutable logs
7. SECRETS NOT IN CODE — SM/KMS; rotate; no .env in Git

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why Security Architecture Is Non-Negotiable in Payments

Incident without architecture:          With security architecture:
─────────────────────────────          ───────────────────────────
Fraud svc down → payments proceed      Fail closed → 503, no money move
JWT secret in GitHub                   CI blocks; secret rotated
Flat VPC — any pod → Aurora           NetworkPolicy: only payment-svc → DB
PAN in application logs                Tokenization + log scrubbing standard
Shared DB → PCI scope = entire bank    Scope isolated to card vault svc
Vendor API key in ConfigMap            IRSA + Secrets Manager + audit

Regulatory and Business Drivers

Driver Architectural response
PCI DSS CDE segmentation, tokenization, pen test
RBI / local banking Data residency, audit trails, maker-checker
GDPR / DPDP PII classification, retention, right to erasure design
SOC 2 / ISO 27001 Control mapping in HLD
Customer trust Breach = brand + fines + exec liability

Architect Accountability

At Solution Architect interviews and in ARB (Lesson 43), you are asked:

"Walk threat model for corporate payment API"
"Where is PAN stored? Who can decrypt?"
"What happens when Okta is down?"
"How do services authenticate each other without shared passwords?"

Part 3: Internal Working

Zero Trust Architecture (Microservices on AWS/EKS)

Zero trust means: no implicit trust based on network zone. Every request is authenticated, authorized, encrypted, and logged — whether from internet or from inside the VPC.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    ZERO TRUST — PAYMENT REQUEST PATH                     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  [Corporate Client]                                                      │
│         │ TLS 1.2+ + mTLS (optional corporate)                           │
│         ▼                                                                │
│  [AWS WAF] ── rate limit, geo, OWASP rules                               │
│         ▼                                                                │
│  [ALB + ACM cert]                                                        │
│         ▼                                                                │
│  [API Gateway] ── JWT validate (OIDC JWKS), scope check, rate limit      │
│         │ service mesh mTLS (east-west)                                  │
│         ▼                                                                │
│  [payment-svc Pod] ── IRSA role (no static AWS keys)                     │
│         │ mTLS + S2S token OR mesh identity                              │
│         ├──► [account-svc]  (authorize: payment.initiate)                │
│         ├──► [fraud-svc]    (fail closed)                                │
│         └──► [Aurora]       (SG: only payment-svc SG, TLS in transit)    │
│                                                                          │
│  Every hop: identity + policy + encrypt + audit                          │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Service-to-Service Identity Options

Pattern How When
mTLS (Istio/Linkerd/App Mesh) Cert per workload identity Default prod east-west
OAuth2 client credentials Token from IdP per service Cross-cluster, vendor style
JWT propagation User context forwarded User-initiated chains
AWS SigV4 IAM on API Gateway/Lambda AWS-native internal APIs

Anti-pattern: Shared INTERNAL_API_KEY in all pods — rotation nightmare, blast radius entire platform.

Network Zones and Data Classification

Typical Banking Zone Model

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         VPC — ap-south-1                                 │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  PUBLIC SUBNET          DMZ / EDGE           APP PRIVATE               │
│  ─────────────          ──────────           ────────────               │
│  ALB, NAT               WAF (regional)       EKS worker nodes            │
│                                              payment, account, fraud     │
│                                                                          │
│  DATA PRIVATE              CDE (PCI)           MGMT / TOOLS              │
│  ────────────              ─────────           ───────────               │
│  Aurora, Redis, MSK        Card vault svc      Bastion-less SSM only     │
│  (encrypted)               HSM/KMS keys        CI runners (isolated)   │
│                                                                          │
│  NO: app subnet → direct internet                                          │

└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Data Classification → Controls

Class Examples Controls
Public Marketing rates CDN, integrity
Internal Non-PII config VPC private
Confidential Account balance, beneficiary name Encrypt, RBAC, audit
Restricted / PCI PAN, CVV, PIN block CDE, tokenization, HSM, no log

Threat Modeling (STRIDE) — Payment Initiate Flow

STRIDE Applied

Threat Payment example Mitigation
S Spoofing Fake corporate client OAuth2 + mTLS + client cert
T Tampering Alter amount in transit TLS + signed JWT claims + server-side amount from DB
R Repudiation "We didn't send payment" Immutable audit log, correlation ID
I Information disclosure PAN in logs Tokenization, log scrubbing
D Denial of service Flood initiate API WAF, rate limit, bulkhead
E Elevation of privilege Call approve without checker role RBAC + maker-checker + scope

[Client] --(1) HTTPS POST /payments--> [Gateway]
              STRIDE: S,T,D

[Gateway] --(2) JWT + mTLS--> [payment-svc]
              STRIDE: S,E
              Controls: scope payment:write, mesh policy

[payment-svc] --(3) sync--> [fraud-svc]
              STRIDE: S,I,D

[payment-svc] --(4) write--> [Aurora]

[payment-svc] --(5) outbox--> [MSK]

Identity: OAuth2/OIDC Edge vs Service-to-Service

Edge (Human + Corporate API Client)

Flow: Authorization Code + PKCE (mobile/web)
      Client Credentials (B2B machine client)

  - iss, aud, exp, nbf (Lesson 19)

  - tenant_id claim for multi-tenant SaaS

Token: short-lived access (5–15 min) + refresh with rotation
JWKS cache with kid rotation support

Service-to-Service

Option A — Mesh mTLS (preferred internal):

Option B — Client credentials:

User context propagation:
  X-Correlation-Id + original sub claim in signed internal header
  NEVER trust client-supplied userId without JWT validation

Tokenization vs Encryption (PCI)

Encryption Tokenization
Reversible Yes (with key) Only vault maps token→PAN
Scope Any confidential data PAN primary use
In payment-svc DB Encrypted PAN (still PCI) Token only (out of scope)
Example AES-256-GCM beneficiary address tok_8f3a... replaces PAN 
Client sends PAN → [Tokenization Vault / PCI CDE] → returns token
payment-svc stores token only → reconciliation uses token
PAN never in Kafka, logs, or non-CDE Aurora

Authorization Architecture

Layers

1. COARSE (Gateway)     — scope: payment:initiate
2. FINE (Service)       — @PreAuthorize + domain rules
3. DATA (Row-level)     — tenant_id filter, account ownership
4. WORKFLOW             — maker-checker state machine (Lesson 41)

Maker-Checker (Banking)

INITIATED (maker) → PENDING_APPROVAL → APPROVED (checker) → processing
                         │
                    different userId
                    different JWT sub
                    audit: who/when/IP/device

Architect: checker role MUST NOT be assignable to same principal as maker
           enforce in IdP group mapping + service rule

Fail-Closed Policy (STD-SEC-003 Example)

IF fraud-svc unreachable OR timeout OR invalid response
THEN payment-svc returns 503 — NOT proceed

IF JWT invalid/expired
THEN 401 — no anonymous fallback

IF scope missing
THEN 403

Document in LLD error catalog — Lesson 41

JWT in Memory (Lesson 19 Extended)

Access token 5–15 min → parse once at gateway → forward claims
Avoid storing full JWT in Redis session unless necessary
Refresh token: httpOnly cookie (web) or secure vault (mobile)
Revocation: short TTL + refresh denylist for logout/compromise

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Security vs Latency Trade-Offs

Control Latency cost Mitigation
JWT validate at gateway 1–5 ms (JWKS cache) Local JWKS cache, kid refresh
mTLS handshake 1–3 ms first conn Session reuse, mesh
KMS encrypt/decrypt 5–20 ms Envelope encryption, data key cache (bounded)
Fraud sync call 50–200 ms Timeout 300ms, fail closed, async scoring Phase 2
WAF inspection 2–10 ms Edge caching not for POST payments
Field-level encrypt JPA CPU + query pain Tokenize PAN instead

Capacity Note

10K TPS payment with 200ms fraud sync = 2000 concurrent fraud calls
Architect: bulkhead fraud pool; circuit breaker; don't share thread pool with read APIs
Security control that collapses throughput → ARB must acknowledge NFR impact

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Spring Security — Fail-Closed Fraud Client

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class FraudScreeningClient {

    private final FraudApi feignClient;
    private final MeterRegistry metrics;

    public FraudDecision screen(FraudScreenRequest request) {
        try {
            FraudDecision decision = feignClient.screen(request);
            if (decision == null || decision.status() == null) {
                metrics.counter("fraud.invalid_response").increment();
                throw new FraudServiceUnavailableException("Invalid fraud response");
            }
            return decision;
        } catch (FeignException | SocketTimeoutException ex) {
            metrics.counter("fraud.unavailable").increment();
            // FAIL CLOSED — do not default to APPROVE
            throw new FraudServiceUnavailableException("Fraud screening unavailable", ex);
        }
    }
}

Example 2: Gateway JWT Scope Check (Conceptual Filter)

@Component
public class PaymentScopeGatewayFilter implements GlobalFilter {

    private static final Map<String, String> ROUTE_SCOPES = Map.of(
        "POST:/api/v1/payments", "payment:initiate",
        "GET:/api/v1/payments/*", "payment:read"
    );

    @Override
    public Mono<Void> filter(ServerWebExchange exchange, GatewayFilterChain chain) {
        Jwt jwt = exchange.getAttribute("jwt");
        if (jwt == null) {
            return unauthorized(exchange);
        }
        String required = requiredScope(exchange);
        if (required != null && !jwt.getClaimAsStringList("scope").contains(required)) {
            return forbidden(exchange);
        }
        return chain.filter(exchange);
    }
}

    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:

      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 5432   # Aurora via private endpoint

Example 5: Log Scrubbing — Prevent PCI Leak

public class PaymentLogSanitizer {

    private static final Pattern PAN_LIKE = Pattern.compile("\\b\\d{13,19}\\b");

    public static String sanitize(String message) {
        if (message == null) return null;
        return PAN_LIKE.matcher(message).replaceAll("[REDACTED-PAN]");
    }
}

// Never: log.info("Payment for card {}", pan);
// Always: log.info("Payment for token {}", tokenId);

Model Answers

Q4 — Zero trust EKS payments

A: WAF+ALB TLS termination; API Gateway validates OIDC JWT scopes; EKS private subnets; App Mesh mTLS east-west with AuthorizationPolicy per service pair; IRSA per deployment for SM/KMS/RDS; NetworkPolicy default-deny then allowlist; Aurora SG only from payment-svc; MSK TLS+ACLs; no PAN outside CDE tokenization svc; CloudTrail+app audit immutable; CI secret scan+SAST+image scan; fail-closed fraud and auth.

Q12 — Multi-tenant isolation

A: tenant_id on every row + mandatory JPA filter / RLS in PostgreSQL; JWT tenant claim validated at gateway matches path/header; separate encryption keys per tenant optional for premium; rate limits per tenant; no cross-tenant cache keys; integration tests for tenant A cannot read B; ARB standard STD-TENANT-001.

Part 1: Concept

What Is Solution Architecture (Capstone View)?

Solution architecture is the end-to-end design of a business capability — people, process, applications, data, integration, infrastructure, security, and migration — aligned to measurable outcomes and stakeholder constraints. Part 2: Why It Exists

Why Organizations Hire Solution Architects

Enterprises do not fail from lack of Spring Boot developers. They fail from:

✗ Three payment channels with three idempotency models
✗ Logistics tracking bolted on without API strategy
✗ Cloud migration = lift-and-shift Oracle with no exit plan
✗ Board sees "digital transformation" with no measurable milestones
✗ Audit finds PCI scope covered entire EKS cluster

Capstone Proves You Can

Business Context

Bank operates:

  - Retail mobile (UPI + internal transfer)
  - Branch teller (legacy terminal)

Problem: 3 stacks, 3 reconciliations, 18-month feature duplication

Constraint: Core Oracle ledger remains 24 months; no big-bang

Multi-Rail Adapter Pattern

Each rail is a bounded adapter — not if/else in payment-svc.

Payment aggregate:
  railType: NEFT | RTGS | UPI | INTERNAL
  saga steps vary by rail policy

NEFT adapter:  cut-off windows, beneficiary IFSC validation
UPI adapter:   NPCI message format, VPA resolution
INTERNAL:      sync account-svc only, no external rail

New rail = new adapter svc + ARB T3 + conformance tests

p95 initiate 500 ms APM
Availability 99.95% SLO error budget
RPO / RTO 15 min / 1 hr DR drill
Audit retention 7 years S3 Glacier + index
PCI Token-only in hub QSA scope doc

Deep Dive — Corporate Maker-Checker Across Channels

State machine (same payment aggregate — Lesson 41):
  DRAFT → PENDING_APPROVAL → APPROVED → PROCESSING → COMPLETED

Corporate: explicit checker JWT role payment:approve
Retail:    auto-approve under limit + step-up OTP
Branch:    ACL maps teller + supervisor PIN to same model

Architect: ONE domain model, channel-specific policies as strategy pattern
           NOT three payment tables

Reconciliation (Case A + Lesson 42-C)

EOD batch: warehouse three-way (payment, ledger, core statement)
Exception → case management — no auto-reverse (Lesson 42)

Case C — Train / Transportation Management

Business Context

Regional rail operator: schedules, seat inventory, live train run status
Channels: passenger app, station displays, ops control room
Peak: festival weekend 2M seat lookups/day, 5K GPS pings/min per active fleet

Architecture

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              TRAIN OPERATIONS & PASSENGER PLATFORM                       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                          │
│  PASSENGER DOMAIN              OPERATIONS DOMAIN                         │
│  ────────────────              ─────────────────                         │
│  schedule-svc                  fleet-location-svc (Case B pattern)       │
│  booking-svc                   disruption-svc                            │
│  inventory-svc (seats)         crew-svc (Phase 2)                        │
│                                                                          │
│  booking-svc: optimistic lock on seat bucket (@Version — Lesson 41)     │
│  schedule-svc: read-heavy — cache + CDN static timetable               │
│  live status: Kafka train.run.updated → SSE to apps + station displays   │
│                                                                          │
│  Payment at booking: sync call to Case A payment hub (INTERNAL rail)     │
│                                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Seat Inventory — Concurrency Design

Train 12345, Coach A1, 50 seats:
  inventory row: available_count + version
  booking: UPDATE ... WHERE version = ? AND available_count >= n
  failure → 409 SOLD_OUT to user

Architect: do NOT distributed lock entire train — partition by coach
Festival surge: cache schedule reads; write path stays authoritative DB

Ops Control Room

Aggregated view:
  - All active trains map layer (fleet-location)
  - Delay propagation: disruption-svc publishes revised ETA
  - Integration: legacy SCADA via ACL adapter (Lesson 39)

Read model: CQRS projection `train_status_board` refreshed from events

Example 4: Board Milestone KPI SQL (Warehouse)

-- % payment volume on new hub vs legacy (weekly board metric)
SELECT week_start,
       SUM(CASE WHEN source = 'PAYMENT_HUB' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS hub_amount,
       SUM(amount) AS total_amount,
       100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN source = 'PAYMENT_HUB' THEN amount ELSE 0 END)
         / NULLIF(SUM(amount), 0) AS hub_pct
FROM payments_fact
GROUP BY week_start
ORDER BY week_start DESC;

Example 5: Booking Seat Optimistic Lock (Transportation)

@Transactional
public BookingResult bookSeats(BookRequest req) {
    Inventory inv = inventoryRepo.findByTrainCoachForUpdate(
        req.trainId(), req.coachId());
    if (inv.getAvailable() < req.seats()) {
        throw new SoldOutException();
    }
    inv.decrement(req.seats()); // @Version triggers OptimisticLockException on clash
    return bookingRepo.save(Booking.from(req));
}

Part 9: Architect Perspective

Capstone Narration for Solution Architect Interview

Prompt: "Design a digital banking and logistics platform for a conglomerate."

Strong opening (2 min):

"I'll separate bounded contexts: payment hub, logistics command center,
and rail passenger ops — shared platform (EKS, MSK, Gateway) but separate
data and release cycles. Payments fail-closed with saga; logistics favors
eventual GPS consistency. I'll propose 18-month strangler for core banking,
Phase 1 corporate payments, not big-bang. May I confirm which channel is
revenue priority and regulatory jurisdiction?"

Decision Highlights to Verbalize

1. DB-per-service — no shared payment/shipment schema
2. One Kafka backbone — domain topic naming convention
3. Tokenization for any card touch — PCI scope
4. Reconciliation as first-class — batch authoritative
5. Reference architecture governs squads — exceptions expire
6. Hybrid ACL honest about pain — funded integration team

Part 12: Interview Questions

Solution Architect / Principal

  1. Design unified payment hub for corporate + UPI + legacy core.
  2. How would you architect logistics command center sharing platform with bank?
  3. 18-month core modernization — phases and gates?
  4. Seat overselling at festival — architectural fix?
  5. Board asks "why not buy SaaS payment vendor?" — respond.
  6. Reconciliation drift on hybrid — who owns what?
  7. Same Kafka cluster for payments and logistics — yes or no?
  8. Present PCI scope to auditor in 5 minutes.
  9. Conglomerate prioritization: payment vs logistics first?
  10. KPIs proving migration success?

Model Answer — Q1 (Unified Hub Outline)

A: Clarify channels, 10K TPS, core stays. C4: Gateway, BFFs, payment-svc saga, account/fraud sync, rail adapters per NEFT/UPI/internal, Aurora+outbox, MSK→ledger/search. ACL to Oracle. Idempotency, maker-checker, fail-closed fraud, tokenization if cards. EOD reconciliation. Phased strangler M6 corporate M12 retail. ADRs for async ledger, no XA. Governance STD catalog. DR Phase 1 passive.

Model Answer — Q5 (Build vs Buy SaaS)

A: Corporate banking APIs are differentiated and auditable — build on reference arch. Evaluate SaaS for commodity (SMS, KYC OCR) not core orchestration. Vendor lock-in, data residency, maker-checker customization, reconciliation to internal core — integration cost often exceeds build over 5yr. Hybrid: build hub, buy fraud rules engine with ACL.

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Start with business OKRs — architecture serves measurable outcomes
  2. Bounded contexts — payment ≠ shipment ≠ booking
  3. Shared platform, separate domains — one MSK, clear topic ACLs
  4. Strangler with gates — measurable phase exit criteria
  5. One reference architecture — variants documented, not reinvented
  6. Reconciliation day one — hybrid needs it before go-live
  7. Stakeholder artifacts pre-built — board slide template ready
  8. FinOps in roadmap — not surprise at M12
  9. Retire exceptions — migration completes when EXC closed
  10. Capstone story in interviews — tie to your real CV domains authentically

Part 1: Concept

What Is a Java Technical Interview at Architect Level?

A Java interview for Senior → Staff → Solution Architect roles tests depth, not trivia. Interviewers probe whether you understand memory, threads, GC, collections complexity, and failure modes — because production payment systems fail on these, not on syntax.

│  L4 STAFF         GC tuning, deadlock analysis, CompletableFuture chains │

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why Java Fundamentals Still Matter for Architects

Microservices myth: "We use Spring — JVM details don't matter"
Reality at 10K TPS payment hub:
  - Wrong HashMap initial capacity → rehash storm under load
  - parallelStream() on ForkJoinPool.commonPool() → latency spikes
  - @Async on unbounded pool → OOM and GC pause → missed NEFT cut-off
  - equals/hashCode bug on PaymentId → duplicate detection fails audit

What Interviewers Signal-Check

Signal Strong answer shows
Depth Internal workings, not API names
Production "We saw this in prod when…"
Trade-offs When NOT to use a tool
Scale Memory/GC/thread impact at 10K TPS
Leadership "We standardized ArchUnit + pool sizing guide"

Part 3: Internal Working

How to Structure Any Java Interview Answer

Use WHTPC (same spirit as RESHADE for system design):

W — What it is (one sentence)
H — How it works internally
T — Trade-off vs alternative
P — Production example (banking/logistics)
C — Caveat / when not to use

Example — "Explain HashMap"

W: HashMap is array of buckets with linked lists or trees for collisions.
H: hashCode → bucket index; equals() resolves chain; JDK8+ treeify at 8 nodes.
T: O(1) avg vs TreeMap O(log n) — no ordering needed → HashMap.
P: Idempotency cache keyed by tenant+key — initial capacity 10K to avoid rehash.
C: Not thread-safe — ConcurrentHashMap for shared cache; fail on null key.

Topic Deep-Dives (Interview-Ready Internals)

1. equals() and hashCode() Contract

Contract:
  if a.equals(b) then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()
  Consistent for unchanged object
  Reflexive, symmetric, transitive

HashMap uses:
  hashCode → bucket (fast narrow)
  equals → exact match in bucket (correct)

Broken contract symptom:
  Put in HashMap, cannot get back — "ghost" keys in payment dedup cache

2. ArrayList vs LinkedList vs ArrayDeque

ArrayList:  dynamic array, amortized O(1) append, O(1) indexed get
LinkedList:  doubly linked, O(n) get, O(1) insert at known node — rarely wins
ArrayDeque:  ring buffer — best queue/stack in Java

Interview trap: "LinkedList for frequent insert" — only if inserting mid-list
                with iterator; otherwise ArrayList wins cache locality

3. HashMap Internals (JDK 17+)

Structure: Node[] table → Node (list) or TreeNode (RB tree if bucket ≥ 8)
Load factor 0.75 → resize 2× rehash
hash spread: (h = key.hashCode()) ^ (h >>> 16)

Treeify threshold 8, untreeify 6 — DOS protection vs balance

4. ConcurrentHashMap vs synchronizedMap

ConcurrentHashMap:
  Segment/bucket-level locking (JDK8+ synchronized first node or CAS)
  get usually lock-free
  size() approximate under concurrency

Collections.synchronizedMap:
  lock on every operation — simple but contended at 10K TPS

Payment idempotency in-memory fallback: ConcurrentHashMap per pod OK;
authoritative still Redis + DB UNIQUE

5. JMM and volatile

Problem: CPU cache + compiler reorder → thread B never sees thread A's write

happens-before edges:
  unlock → lock
  volatile write → volatile read
  thread start → actions in thread
  CompletableFuture completion → thenApply

volatile: visibility + ordering, NOT atomic i++

Fix payment status flag: volatile boolean OR AtomicReference<Status>
Counter: AtomicLong, not volatile long++

6. synchronized vs ReentrantLock

synchronized: intrinsic lock, automatic release, no tryLock
ReentrantLock: tryLock, fair queue, Condition variables, must unlock in finally

Architect: prefer higher-level java.util.concurrent before raw locks
Use ReentrantLock when: tryLock with timeout, fair ordering needed

7. Thread Pool Sizing (Lesson 10 — Always Asked)

CPU-bound:  pools ≈ N_cpu (+1 optional)
IO-bound:   pools ≈ N_cpu × (1 + wait_time/compute_time)

Payment svc example:
  8 vCPU, 200ms fraud IO, 5ms compute → 8 × (1 + 200/5) ≈ 328 theoretical
  Cap lower: bulkhead 50–100, queue bounded, reject or 503 — don't OOM

NEVER: Executors.newCachedThreadPool() for payment peak — unbounded threads

8. CompletableFuture Patterns

thenApply   — transform result (same thread pool as previous stage unless async)
thenCompose — flatten nested CF
thenCombine — merge two async results
allOf       — wait all; anyOf — first wins

Production:
  CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fraudCheck(), fraudPool)
    .orTimeout(300, MILLISECONDS)
    .exceptionally(ex -> FAIL_CLOSED)

Architect: name the Executor — never commonPool for payment path

9. Stream API — Lazy and Traps

Intermediate ops lazy until terminal
parallelStream() uses ForkJoinPool.commonPool — shared across JVM

Trap: parallelStream on small data or with synchronized side effects
Payment report 10M rows batch EOD: parallel OK on dedicated pool + pure ops
Online API hot path: sequential stream or plain loop — predictable latency

10. GC and JVM (Lesson 12 — Staff+ Favorite)

G1GC (default Java 17): region-based, pause target -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis
ZGC: sub-ms pauses, large heaps, Java 17+ production ready

Symptoms:
  Full GC loops → heap too small or leak
  Metaspace OOM → classloader leak (hot redeploy without restart)

Flags architects know:
  -Xms = -Xmx (avoid resize)
  -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
  -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 (containers — Lesson 12)

Part 4: Memory View

Interview Diagram — Object Layout on Heap

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         JVM HEAP (G1)                            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  YOUNG (Eden + Survivors)     │  OLD (Tenured regions)          │
│  ─────────────────────────    │  ─────────────────────          │
│  New Payment DTOs             │  Cached reference data          │
│  Short-lived JSON parse       │  Idempotency map (if mis-sized) │
│                               │  Leaked ThreadLocal entries     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  METASPACE: classes, static metadata                             │
│  THREAD STACKS: local vars, frame per method call                │
│  DIRECT / NATIVE: NIO buffers, JNI                               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Question: "Where is static counter?" → Metaspace/class data (JDK8+)
Question: "Where is local int amount?" → stack frame
Question: "Where is new Payment()?" → heap Eden → possibly Old if long-lived

ThreadLocal Leak (Classic Senior Question)

Thread pool worker thread lives forever
ThreadLocal<Map> set but never remove()
Old gen fills with stale tenant context maps → Full GC → payment timeout

Fix: try { ... } finally { threadLocal.remove(); }
Architect standard: ban ThreadLocal for request context without remove policy
                     prefer MDC with filter cleanup (Spring)

Collections Complexity Master Table (Interview Must-Know)

Structure get add remove contains Ordered Null key
ArrayList O(1) O(1)* O(n) O(n) insertion yes
HashMap O(1)* O(1)* O(1)* — no one null
TreeMap O(log n) O(log n) O(log n) — sorted no
LinkedHashMap O(1)* O(1)* O(1)* — insertion one null
ConcurrentHashMap O(1)* O(1)* O(1)* — no no
PriorityQueue peek O(1) O(log n) O(log n) O(n) heap order no

*Average case; worst HashMap O(n) pre-treeify; O(log n) after treeify

Concurrency Utility Selection

Need Use Avoid
Counter AtomicLong volatile long++
Lazy init Holder idiom or synchronized once broken DCL without volatile
Map cache ConcurrentHashMap HashMap + sync
Rate limit Semaphore busy-wait
Wait for 3 svc CountDownLatch / CompletableFuture.allOf Thread.join loops
Read-heavy lock ReadWriteLock sync on every read

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Broken equals/hashCode (Interview Bug-Find)

// BAD — breaks HashMap contract if only equals overridden
public class PaymentKey {
    private final String tenantId;
    private final String idempotencyKey;

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) { /* ... */ }

    // missing hashCode → all keys hash to same bucket → degrades to list
}

// GOOD — record or explicit both
public record PaymentKey(String tenantId, String idempotencyKey) {}

Example 2: Double-Checked Locking (JMM)

public class FraudRulesCache {
    private volatile static FraudRulesCache instance;

    public static FraudRulesCache getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) {
            synchronized (FraudRulesCache.class) {
                if (instance == null) {
                    instance = new FraudRulesCache();
                }
            }
        }
        return instance;
    }
}
// volatile on instance mandatory — without it, partially constructed object visible

Example 3: Proper Thread Pool (Payment Bulkhead)

@Bean
public Executor fraudExecutor() {
    int poolSize = 50;
    ThreadPoolExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
        poolSize, poolSize,
        0L, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
        new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(200),
        new ThreadFactoryBuilder().setNameFormat("fraud-%d").build(),
        new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy() // fail fast → 503 upstream
    );
    return executor;
}

Example 4: CompletableFuture Fail-Closed Chain

public CompletableFuture<FraudDecision> screenAsync(Payment p) {
    return CompletableFuture
        .supplyAsync(() -> fraudClient.screen(p), fraudExecutor)
        .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
        .exceptionally(ex -> {
            throw new FraudUnavailableException("Fail closed", ex);
        });
}

Example 5: try-with-resources (Lesson 5)

public void exportReconciliation(Path path) throws IOException {
    try (BufferedWriter writer = Files.newBufferedWriter(path);
         Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection()) {
        // streams and connections closed in reverse order — even on exception
    }
}

Example 6: Deadlock — Explain + Fix

// DEADLOCK: thread1: lock A then B; thread2: lock B then A
// Fix: global lock ordering — always acquire accountId smaller first
public void transfer(String from, String to, BigDecimal amount) {
    String first = from.compareTo(to) < 0 ? from : to;
    String second = from.compareTo(to) < 0 ? to : from;
    synchronized (lockFor(first)) {
        synchronized (lockFor(second)) {
            // debit/credit
        }
    }
}

Part 9: Architect Perspective

How Staff/Architect Answers Differ from Senior

SENIOR: "HashMap is O(1) average"
STAFF:  "HashMap O(1) with load factor 0.75; we presize 10K entries for
         idempotency warm cache to avoid rehash during peak NEFT"
ARCHITECT: "Above + if cross-pod consistency required, HashMap is optimization
         only — Redis SET NX + DB UNIQUE is source of truth; in-memory
         is per-pod best-effort — document in LLD STD-PAY-003"

Incident Walkthrough Template (OOM)

1. Symptom: pod restart loop, Exit 137, latency 503
2. Evidence: kubectl top, GC log, heap dump MAT dominator tree
3. Hypothesis: unbounded queue on fraud executor
4. Fix: bounded queue + AbortPolicy + scale pods
5. Prevent: fitness test max pool size, dashboard thread pool active count
6. Trade-off: reject vs slow — payment chooses reject (fail closed)

Model Answers — Staff / Architect Level

Q7 — HashMap internals

A: Array of buckets. hashCode spread XOR high bits, index (n-1) & hash. Collision: linked list; treeify at 8 nodes to RB tree, untreeify at 6. Load factor 0.75 doubles capacity rehash. Not thread-safe. Null key allowed once. For concurrent payment dedup map use ConcurrentHashMap or Caffeine with TTL; authoritative dedup remains DB UNIQUE constraint.

Q15 — Thread pool parameters

A: Core pool size threads always alive; tasks beyond core go to bounded queue; above core+queue, expand to max; beyond max, rejection policy runs. For IO-bound fraud calls I size pool using Little's law intuition, cap ~50–100 per pod with bounded queue 200 and AbortPolicy so we fail closed with 503 instead of unbounded memory. Never CachedThreadPool on money path. Expose pool metrics to Micrometer.

Q18 — G1 heap

A: G1 divides heap into equal regions, tracks garbage per region, collects mixed young+old to meet pause target. Eden + Survivors for short-lived payment DTOs; Old for long-lived caches. Tuning -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200, equal -Xms/-Xmx, container -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75. If pauses still breach SLO on huge heap, evaluate ZGC.

Q23 — Thread-safe rate limiter

A: Options: (1) Guava RateLimiter single JVM; (2) Redis sliding window for cluster-wide 10K TPS gateway limit; (3) token bucket with AtomicLong last refill for per-pod soft limit. Architect: edge rate limit at API Gateway (AWS WAF/API GW) authoritative; in-JVM limiter is defense in depth. Return 429 with Retry-After. Fail closed doesn't apply to rate limit — it's intentional reject.

Q26 — Idempotency Java-level

A: Filter extracts Idempotency-Key. ConcurrentHashMap optional fast path. Authoritative: DB INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING or UNIQUE on (tenant_id, key) returning existing row. Use @Transactional so insert and business row atomic. Return same paymentId and status on replay. Redis SET NX with TTL for cross-request in-flight dedup. All mutable domain fields in equals for response comparison not needed if return stored snapshot.

Q28 — JVM in K8s 2Gi

A: Container limit 2Gi includes heap + metaspace + thread stacks + native + direct buffers. Set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 not fixed 2g heap — leaves ~512MB headroom. Monitor actual RSS. If OOMKilled 137, check native/direct (Netty) or thread count. Request Kubernetes memory request ≈ limit for payment svc stability.

[ payment-svc request thread ]
        │
        ├── @Transactional (DB connection from pool)
        │
        ├── CompletableFuture → [ fraudExecutor pool ]
        │                              │
        │                              └── HTTP to fraud-svc
        │
        └── Kafka producer (serializer thread-safe)

Shared wrongly: HashMap idempotency cache → race duplicate payment
Shared correctly: CHM local + Redis cluster + DB UNIQUE

Phase 1 Java fundamentals power Phase 2 Spring interviews. Lesson 47 focuses on what architects get wrong in production Spring loops:

  • IoC / bean lifecycle traps in @Transactional self-invocation
  • JPA N+1, persistence context, and @Version optimistic lock
  • Transaction propagation and isolation in saga-style payment flows
  • Spring Security filter chain vs gateway JWT
  • @Async, @Cacheable, and AOP proxy pitfalls (JDK vs CGLIB — Lesson 15)
  • Spring Boot auto-config exclusions and actuator in interviews
  • WebFlux vs MVC — when to say which in architect round

You know how the JVM behaves. Lesson 47 covers how Spring wraps the JVM — and where that wrapper breaks at 10K TPS.

Part 2: Why It Exists

Why Spring Interviews Separate Senior from Architect

Production failure patterns (real banking):
  ✗ @Transactional on private method — no rollback, silent partial commit
  ✗ this.processPayment() internal call — bypasses proxy, no transaction
  ✗ N+1 on GET /payments?page=100 — DB melts at 10K TPS read
  ✗ @Async on default executor — thread explosion → OOM (Lesson 46)
  ✗ JWT validated in svc A but trusted userId header in svc B — IDOR
  ✗ open-in-view=true hides lazy load bomb in JSON serialization

What Interviewers Signal-Check

Signal Strong answer
Proxy awareness Self-invocation, JDK vs CGLIB
Transaction boundary Where saga step commits
JPA pitfalls N+1, flush order, optimistic lock
Security layers Gateway vs service @PreAuthorize
Pragmatism MVC+JPA domain, WebFlux at edge (Lesson 20)

Scope Bean instances Use Payment example

@Autowired Resolution

1. By type

2. AOP and Proxies (Lesson 15) — Most Asked

How @Transactional Actually Works

Client → Spring proxy → TransactionInterceptor → target method
              │
              ├── begin transaction (if REQUIRED)
              ├── invoke method
              ├── commit OR rollback on RuntimeException (default)
              └── not rollback on checked exception unless rollbackFor

Self-Invocation Trap

@Service
public class PaymentService {
    public void initiate(Payment p) {
        this.saveWithTx(p);  // DIRECT CALL — NO PROXY — NO @Transactional
    }

    @Transactional
    public void saveWithTx(Payment p) { /* ... */ }
}

Fixes: inject self interface, ApplicationContext.getBean, or merge into one @Transactional public method, or use TransactionTemplate.

JDK Dynamic Proxy vs CGLIB

JDK proxy CGLIB
Requires Interface Concrete class
Mechanism Reflect on interface Subclass bytecode
Final methods N/A Cannot proxy final
Default Boot 2.x+ Interface beans → JDK Class without interface → CGLIB
spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true Forces CGLIB for all Common in Boot apps

Interview: "Why didn't @Cacheable work?" — often self-invocation or private method (AOP can't advise private).

How It Works

@SpringBootApplication
  = @Configuration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan

META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports
  → conditional @Configuration classes (@ConditionalOnClass, OnProperty, OnMissingBean)

Common Interview Probes

Q: Disable auto-config for DataSource in test?
A: @SpringBootTest(properties) or @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(REPLACE_NONE)
   or exclude DataSourceAutoConfiguration

Q: Custom starter purpose?
A: Bundle auto-config + dependency for internal platform (metrics, tracing)

Q: Actuator endpoints expose what?
A: health, metrics, env, beans — secure in prod (Lesson 19/44)

4. JPA & Hibernate (Lesson 17) — Very High Yield

Persistence Context (Session)

@Entity transaction-scoped Persistence Context (default)
  - 1st level cache per transaction
  - dirty checking at flush time
  - lazy associations need active session OR fetch join

N+1 Problem

SELECT * FROM payments LIMIT 100;          -- 1 query
For each payment: SELECT * FROM beneficiary -- 100 queries

Fix:
  @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "beneficiary")
  JOIN FETCH in JPQL
  @BatchSize on collection
  DTO projection query — best for read APIs

Entity Lifecycle States

transient → persist() → managed → remove() → removed
managed → detach → detached (updates ignored unless merge)

Payment saga: don't pass detached entities across Kafka — use IDs + reload

@Version Optimistic Lock

@Version
private Long version;

// concurrent update → OptimisticLockException → map to 409 CONFLICT

Transport/booking parallel: seat inventory (Lesson 45) — same pattern.

Second-Level Cache

Rare in payment OLTP — stale balance risk
OK: reference data (bank codes, IFSC list) with TTL eviction
Architect: Redis app cache preferred over Hibernate 2LC for clarity

5. Transactions (Lesson 18) — Saga Context

Propagation (Must Memorize)

Propagation Behavior Payment use
REQUIRED (default) Join or create Normal service method
REQUIRES_NEW Suspend, new tx Audit log always commits
NESTED Savepoint Rare — DB support varies
NOT_SUPPORTED Suspend tx External API call outside tx
MANDATORY Must exist Enforce caller has tx
NEVER Must not exist Utility

Saga Pattern + Spring Transactions

WRONG: one @Transactional across HTTP calls to account-svc + fraud-svc
RIGHT: local transaction per service; saga state in payment DB

payment-svc:
  @Transactional
  void executeSagaStep() {
      update payment row + insert outbox;  // single local commit
  }
  // then Feign to account-svc — separate service transaction

Isolation Levels

Level Issue prevented Payment note
READ_COMMITTED dirty read Default most DBs
REPEATABLE_READ non-repeatable read MySQL InnoDB default
SERIALIZABLE phantom Too slow for 10K TPS

Interview: "Lost update on balance?" — optimistic @Version or pessimistic PESSIMISTIC_WRITE on account row — prefer hold API in account-svc not raw JPA in payment-svc.

Rollback Rules

Default: rollback on unchecked (RuntimeException)
Checked Exception: NO rollback unless @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)

Payment: use domain exceptions extending RuntimeException + explicit rollbackFor for business failures needing compensate

Filter Chain Order (Conceptual)

Request
  → SecurityContextPersistenceFilter
  → LogoutFilter
  → UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter (form) / BearerToken (resource server)
  → AuthorizationFilter
  → FilterSecurityInterceptor
  → DispatcherServlet → Controller → @PreAuthorize

Gateway JWT vs Service Security

ARCHITECT PATTERN (Lessons 39, 44):
  Gateway: validate JWT signature, exp, scope
  payment-svc: OAuth2 Resource Server OR trust mTLS + internal signed claims
  NEVER trust X-User-Id header from client without validation

@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('payment:approve')") on approve endpoint
Method security enabled: @EnableMethodSecurity

Common Interview Questions

Session vs JWT: stateless microservices → JWT + short TTL
CSRF: disable for pure JSON API with Bearer token; enable for cookie session BFF
OAuth2 flows: Auth Code + PKCE (user), Client Credentials (B2B)

7. @Async, @Cacheable, @Scheduled

@Async Internals

@EnableAsync → AsyncAnnotationBeanPostProcessor → proxy wraps method
Default executor: SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor (new thread per task!) — dangerous

ALWAYS: custom Executor bean + @Async("fraudExecutor")

@Cacheable Pitfalls

- Self-invocation bypasses cache proxy
- Cache key must include tenantId for multi-tenant
- Stale balance if caching account entity — DON'T
- OK: IFSC directory, feature flags

@Scheduled

Single instance or distributed lock (ShedLock) for reconcile job
Don't run EOD batch on all pods without leader election

@Transactional + Connection Hold Time

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Correct Transaction Boundary (Payment)

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PaymentInitiationService {

    private final PaymentRepository repo;
    private final OutboxRepository outbox;
    private final FraudScreeningClient fraud; // external — outside tx

    public PaymentResponse initiate(InitiateCommand cmd) {
        FraudDecision decision = fraud.screen(cmd); // no DB connection held
        if (decision.isReject()) {
            throw new FraudRejectedException();
        }
        return persistAccepted(cmd);
    }

    @Transactional
    protected PaymentResponse persistAccepted(InitiateCommand cmd) {
        Payment p = repo.save(Payment.pending(cmd));
        outbox.save(OutboxEvent.paymentCreated(p));
        return PaymentResponse.from(p);
    }
}

Example 2: Fix N+1 with DTO Query

@Query("""
    SELECT new com.bank.payment.api.PaymentSummary(
        p.id, p.amount, p.status, b.name)
    FROM Payment p JOIN p.beneficiary b
    WHERE p.tenantId = :tenantId
    """)
Page<PaymentSummary> findSummaries(String tenantId, Pageable pageable);

Example 3: Optimistic Lock Handling

@Transactional
public void approve(UUID paymentId, String checkerId) {
    Payment p = repo.findById(paymentId)
        .orElseThrow(PaymentNotFoundException::new);
    p.approve(checkerId); // @Version check on flush
}

@ExceptionHandler(OptimisticLockException.class)
public ResponseEntity<?> conflict() {
    return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT).body(/* ... */);
}

Example 4: Resource Server JWT (payment-svc)

@Configuration
@EnableMethodSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/health").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/api/v1/payments")
                    .hasAuthority("payment:initiate")
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth -> oauth.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
            .build();
    }
}

Example 5: Custom @Async Executor

@Configuration
@EnableAsync
public class AsyncConfig {

    @Bean(name = "notificationExecutor")
    public Executor notificationExecutor() {
        ThreadPoolTaskExecutor ex = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
        ex.setCorePoolSize(5);
        ex.setMaxPoolSize(10);
        ex.setQueueCapacity(100);
        ex.setThreadNamePrefix("notify-");
        ex.setRejectedExecutionHandler(new CallerRunsPolicy());
        ex.initialize();
        return ex;
    }
}

Example 6: WebFlux Gateway Route (Edge Only)

@Bean
public RouteLocator routes(RouteLocatorBuilder builder) {
    return builder.routes()
        .route("payment-route", r -> r.path("/api/v1/payments/**")
            .filters(f -> f.requestRateLimiter(c -> c.setRateLimiter(redisLimiter)))
            .uri("lb://payment-svc"))
        .build();
}

Model Answers — Staff / Architect

Q6 — @Transactional internals

A: Spring creates proxy (JDK or CGLIB) around bean. TransactionInterceptor opens transaction via PlatformTransactionManager before method, commits on success, rolls back on unchecked exception by default. Transaction binds to thread via TransactionSynchronizationManager. Connection obtained from pool on first DB access. Proxy only intercepts external calls through Spring bean reference.

Q8 — REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW

A: REQUIRED joins caller transaction or creates one — default for payment write. REQUIRES_NEW suspends current, opens independent transaction — use for audit log that must persist even if business tx rolls back, or isolated idempotency record. Don't use REQUIRES_NEW for saga steps that must be atomic with payment row — that stays one local REQUIRED tx including outbox insert.

Q11 — N+1 fix

A: N+1: one query for parents, N lazy loads for children. Detect: Hibernate statistics, datasource-proxy logging. Fix: JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph for controlled fetches; better for APIs: JPQL constructor DTO projection; pagination with keyset not offset for large tables. Prevention: open-in-view=false forces explicit fetch in service layer. For payment list API we return DTO never expose lazy beneficiary entity.

Q21 — Saga + Spring transactions

A: Each microservice owns one local @Transactional boundary. payment-svc: single tx updates payment state + outbox. Feign to account-svc is after or before local tx depending on step — hold funds: call account first, on success local tx to PENDING_HELD; on local failure compensate via release call. No distributed @Transactional. Orchestration logic in application service; consider state machine table. Idempotency outside or inside tx with UNIQUE constraint.

Q22 — WebFlux + JPA

A: Bad combination for request path. JPA blocks thread; WebFlux expects non-blocking. Blocking on reactor event loop thread degrades entire pod. Pattern: Gateway/BFF WebFlux; domain services MVC on Tomcat with sized thread pool; or R2DBC if truly reactive data — rare in enterprise banking JPA shops. Lesson 20 hybrid is intentional.

Q26 — Multi-tenant JPA

A: tenant_id column every table; Hibernate @Filter or Spring @Aspect sets tenant from JWT in ThreadLocal before repository calls; enforce in repository methods findByIdAndTenantId. Test cross-tenant isolation. Gateway validates tenant claim matches path. Never global @SQLRestriction without test coverage. RLS in PostgreSQL as defense in depth (Lesson 44).

Part 14: Best Practices

  1. Constructor injection only — team standard
  2. Transaction smallest scope — no external IO inside tx
  3. DTO for reads — entities never cross API boundary
  4. open-in-view=false — force explicit fetch
  5. Named thread pools for @Async and CompletableFuture
  6. Resource server on every domain svc — defense in depth
  7. Feign + Resilience4j — timeout, breaker, bulkhead
  8. Actuator locked down — network policy + auth
  9. ArchUnit — layer rules, no field injection
  10. Integration tests — assert rollback and optimistic lock 409

Why Distributed Interviews Matter for Solution Architects

Monolith interview: "Fix the bug in one repo"
Microservice interview: "Payment COMPLETED but ledger missing — who owns fix?"

Kafka interview: "At-least-once delivery" means your code WILL see duplicates
Architect who ignores that → duplicate money movement → audit failure

Symptom Tests your knowledge of

Part 3: Internal Working

Answer Framework: D-FACTS (Distributed)

D — Define the boundary / consistency model
F — Failure modes (what breaks first)
A — Architecture pattern (saga, outbox, CQRS)
C — Consistency guarantee (strong local, eventual cross-svc)
T — Trade-off vs alternative (2PC, dual-write)

1. Microservice Fundamentals (Lesson 25)

When Microservices vs Modular Monolith

MICROSERVICES when:
  - Clear bounded contexts (payment ≠ shipment)
  - Independent scale (GPS ingest vs payment OLTP)
  - Separate release cadence / teams > 8 per domain
  - Polyglot justified (ML fraud svc Python)

MONOLITH when:
  - Startup MVP, small team
  - Strong consistency everywhere required AND low scale
  - No org readiness for distributed ops

Architect interview: "We chose MS for payment hub because corporate API
10K TPS and UPI adapter release independently — not because Netflix uses it"

DB-per-Service (Non-Negotiable in Interviews)

WRONG: payment-svc and ledger-svc share Oracle schema PAYMENTS
RIGHT: each svc owns schema; integrate via API or events

Exception: time-boxed legacy read via ACL (Lesson 43 EXC register)

2. Inter-Service Communication (Lessons 26–27)

Sync vs Async Decision Matrix

Use sync HTTP/gRPC Use async Kafka
User waits for answer (hold funds?) Side effects (notify, search index)
Strong immediate validation High fanout (PaymentCompleted)
Low fanout, query Absorb traffic spikes (GPS ingest)
Saga decision step with timeout Reconciliation, analytics

API Design Interview Points

- OpenAPI source of truth in Git
- Idempotency-Key on POST (STD-PAY-003)
- Error envelope consistent (422 insufficient funds)
- Versioning: /v1/ URL or Accept header — pick one org-wide
- Pagination: keyset not offset for large payment lists (Lesson 21)
- Consumer-driven contracts: Pact in CI (Lesson 43 fitness)

3. Saga, 2PC, Outbox (Lesson 28) — Bar Raiser Favorite

Why Not 2PC/XA Across Microservices

2PC (two-phase commit):
  Coordinator locks resources across DBs
  Blocking, fragile, poor availability (CAP)
  Cloud-native DBs discourage XA

Interview answer:
  "We reject XA across payment and ledger microservices (STD-PAY-004).
   Local ACID per service + saga orchestration + reconciliation EOD.
   Industry standard for banking channels at scale."

Saga Orchestration vs Choreography

Orchestration Choreography
Control payment-svc state machine Each svc reacts to events
Visibility Central saga table Harder trace
Change Easier add step Spaghetti risk
Banking Preferred for payments OK for notifications

Outbox Pattern Internals

SAME local transaction:
  INSERT payment status = COMPLETED
  INSERT outbox (event_id, payload, status=PENDING)

Separate outbox relay process:
  poll outbox → publish Kafka → mark SENT

WHY: avoids dual-write (DB commit + Kafka publish) inconsistency
NEVER: write DB then try Kafka in separate tx without outbox

Saga State Machine (Whiteboard)

PENDING → VALIDATED → FUNDS_HELD → RAIL_SUBMITTED → COMPLETED
    │         │            │              │
    └─────────┴────────────┴──────────────┴──→ FAILED → COMPENSATING → REVERSED

Each transition: local DB update + optional outbox event
Compensate: release hold, mark REVERSED, audit

4. Event-Driven Architecture (Lesson 29)

Event vs Command

Event Command
Tense PaymentCompleted (past) HoldFunds (imperative)
Routing Pub/sub topic Queue often point-to-point
Coupling Loose Tighter
Example ledger consumes completed account-svc POST /hold

Interview: "PaymentCompleted is event; HoldFunds is sync command — both in same flow."

Schema Evolution (Avro + Schema Registry)

BACKWARD compatible (default safe):
  Add optional field with default — old consumers still read

FORWARD: new consumer reads old events — need defaults on new fields

BREAKING: rename field without alias — CI schema check fails

Payment event: never remove amount field; add railMetadata optional

5. Resilience Patterns (Lessons 29–30)

Circuit Breaker States

CLOSED → failures exceed threshold → OPEN (fail fast)
OPEN → after wait → HALF_OPEN (probe)
HALF_OPEN → success → CLOSED | failure → OPEN

Resilience4j config interview:
  slidingWindowSize 50, failureRateThreshold 50%, waitDuration 30s

Fraud svc: OPEN → payment returns 503 fail closed — NOT fallback APPROVE

Retry — When Safe

Operation Retry? Why
GET status Yes (idempotent) Safe
POST payment with Idempotency-Key Limited retry Key makes safe
POST without idempotency No Duplicate risk
Kafka consumer business logic After dedup check At-least-once
Compensating release hold Yes with idempotency Must complete

Bulkhead

Separate thread pools:
  payment-api pool (Tomcat threads)
  fraud Feign bulkhead (max 50 concurrent)
  kafka-listener container (concurrency = partitions per consumer)

One slow fraud vendor must not exhaust all Tomcat threads

Timeout Stack (Must Narrate)

Client timeout  >  Gateway  >  payment-svc  >  Feign to fraud
   3s                 2.5s         2s              300ms read

Rule: each hop shorter than caller — otherwise hang cascades

6. Kafka Fundamentals (Lesson 31)

Core Concepts

Topic:     logical stream (payment.completed)
Partition: ordered log subset — unit of parallelism
Offset:    position in partition log
Producer:  append with key → partition hash
Consumer group: partitions divided among group members
Replication: leader + ISR followers — acks=all for durability

Partition Key Strategy (Interview Gold)

Domain Key Why
Payment events paymentId or tenantId Order per payment
GPS ingest shipmentId Order per shipment
Audit all tenants tenantId Risk hot partition if one huge tenant
Dead letter original key preserved Debugging

Hot partition problem: One mega-tenant → one partition saturated → lag on that partition only → fix: sub-key sharding or dedicated topic per large tenant.

7. Kafka Internals (Lesson 32) — Staff+ Questions

ISR and acks

acks=0: fire and forget — NOT payments
acks=1: leader ack — risk data loss on leader fail before replicate
acks=all: all ISR ack — **payment outbox relay default**

min.insync.replicas=2 on 3 brokers — producer gets error if ISR < 2

Consumer Group Rebalance

Trigger: consumer join/leave, partition count change, session timeout

Problem: stop-the-world rebalance → lag spike during deploy

Mitigations:
  cooperative-sticky assignor (incremental)
  static group membership (group.instance.id)
  avoid frequent rolling restart during peak NEFT window
  scale consumers ≤ partitions (extra consumers idle)

Exactly-Once Semantics (EOS)

Kafka EOS (transactional producer + read_committed consumer):
  Useful: stream processing exactly-once within Kafka pipeline
  NOT magic across DB + Kafka — still need outbox for DB→Kafka

Interview: "EOS reduces duplicate publish within Kafka; payment idempotency
           still required at business layer for external side effects"

Log Retention vs Compaction

retention.ms=7d — events age out — audit events also copy to S3
compacted topic — last value per key — config/state snapshots
payment.completed — retention + tiered storage, NOT compacted (need history)

8. Kafka Production (Lesson 33)

Consumer Lag Debug Flow

1. Check lag per partition: kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe
2. Hot partition? → key skew
3. All partitions lag? → slow handler or insufficient consumers
4. Lag after deploy? → rebalance or bug slower path
5. Handler throws? → retry loop or DLT fill
6. DB bottleneck? → consumer commits slow because processing slow

Fix: scale consumers (≤ partitions), optimize handler, increase partitions (plan carefully — key order)

DLT (Dead Letter Topic)

After 3 retries with backoff → publish to payment.completed.DLT
Alert on DLT rate > 0 — zero tolerance money path
Manual replay tool with idempotent consumer

Consumer Offset Commit Timing

auto commit (default): commit every 5s — risk: process fail after commit → lost message processing
manual commit after DB write: at-least-once + idempotent handler → **recommended payment**

Order: process → write DB idempotency → commit offset
Wrong: commit offset → crash → message lost forever

Part 5: Performance Analysis

Microservice + Kafka at Scale

System Target Bottleneck Knob
Payment 10K TPS p95 500ms Aurora write, fraud sync HPA, pool, async ledger
Outbox relay 10K evt/s Poll batch size Dedicated relay pods
MSK 10K msg/s lag < 1s Partitions, broker CPU 24 partitions, m5.xlarge
GPS 8K/s durable ingest Producer batch linger.ms, compression lz4
Ledger consumer eventual DB upsert idempotent INSERT

Kafka Producer Tuning (Interview)

batch.size, linger.ms — throughput vs latency trade-off
compression.type=lz4 — CPU vs network
enable.idempotence=true — producer dedup within session — good, not substitute business idempotency
max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=1 with idempotence — ordering per partition

Part 6: Code Examples

Example 1: Outbox Entity + Relay (Concept)

@Entity
@Table(name = "outbox_events")
public class OutboxEvent {
    @Id
    private UUID id;
    private String aggregateType;
    private UUID aggregateId;
    private String eventType;
    @Column(columnDefinition = "jsonb")
    private String payload;
    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    private OutboxStatus status; // PENDING, SENT
    private Instant createdAt;
}

// Relay: @Scheduled or Debezium CDC → Kafka

Example 2: Idempotent Kafka Consumer

@KafkaListener(topics = "payment.completed", groupId = "ledger-svc")
public void onPaymentCompleted(PaymentCompletedEvent event) {
    if (processedEventRepo.existsByEventId(event.eventId())) {
        return; // duplicate delivery — safe exit
    }
    ledgerService.postEntry(event);
    processedEventRepo.save(new ProcessedEvent(event.eventId()));
    // offset commit after successful processing (manual ack mode)
}

Example 3: Resilience4j — Fraud with Circuit Breaker

@CircuitBreaker(name = "fraud", fallbackMethod = "fraudUnavailable")
@Bulkhead(name = "fraud")
@TimeLimiter(name = "fraud")
public CompletableFuture<FraudDecision> screen(Payment p) {
    return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fraudClient.screen(p), fraudExecutor);
}

public CompletableFuture<FraudDecision> fraudUnavailable(Payment p, Throwable t) {
    return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(new FraudUnavailableException(t));
}

Example 4: Saga Compensation

@Transactional
public void compensateFundsHeld(Payment payment) {
    payment.transitionTo(CompensatingStatus.REVERSING);
    accountClient.releaseHold(payment.getId(), payment.getHoldReference());
    payment.transitionTo(CompensatingStatus.REVERSED);
    outbox.publish(new PaymentReversedEvent(payment.getId()));
}

Example 5: Feign Timeout (Mandatory)

resilience4j.timelimiter:
  instances:
    fraud:
      timeout-duration: 300ms

spring.cloud.openfeign.client.config:
  fraud-svc:
    connectTimeout: 200
    readTimeout: 300

Example 6: Kafka Topic Design (Terraform Snippet)

resource "aws_msk_topic" "payment_completed" {
  name               = "payment.completed"
  partitions         = 24
  replication_factor = 3
  config = {
    "min.insync.replicas" = "2"
    "retention.ms"        = "604800000" # 7d — archive to S3 separately
  }
}
